lead: ResectionEXPERTISE BCLC 2026 calls liver resection, preferably minimally invasive, the recommended first step when there is no clinically significant portal hypertension.
text: Resection A EXPERTISE BCLC 2026 calls liver resection, preferably minimally invasive, the recommended first step when there is no clinically significant portal hypertension. Indications Preferred when Solitary tumour, adequate future liver remnant, preserved function, acceptable portal-hypertension risk. With mildly increased CSPH, minimally invasive surgery remains an option for a single peripheral tumour with an adequate remnant. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid CSPH raises operative risk and should trigger transplant assessment in any patient within Milan — it is not an absolute bar. Record which criterion established it (HVPG, a Baveno specific sign, or non-invasive rule-in) and its value, not just the conclusion. Evidence & sources Part of the reason is pathology: microvascular invasion and satellite nodules are validated predictors of recurrence and may support ab initio transplant. lead: Thermal ablationEXPERTISE When transplant is not feasible, ablation is the recommended option — radiofrequency or microwave. BCLC 2026 prefers microwave up to 3–4 cm on local-control evidence. Sugimoto 2025 found two-year lesion progression of 16.4% with MWA versus 30.4% with single-needle RFA, without a demonstrated survival advantage; earlier trials did not show a significant difference. Also the “ablate and wait” strategy: ablate now and consider transplant at recurrence if still within criteria.
text: Thermal ablation A EXPERTISE When transplant is not feasible, ablation is the recommended option — radiofrequency or microwave. BCLC 2026 prefers microwave up to 3–4 cm on local-control evidence. Sugimoto 2025 found two-year lesion progression of 16.4% with MWA versus 30.4% with single-needle RFA, without a demonstrated survival advantage; earlier trials did not show a significant difference. Also the “ablate and wait” strategy: ablate now and consider transplant at recurrence if still within criteria. Indications Preferred when Tumour ≤3 cm, up to three nodules, with a safe percutaneous route and a circumferential ablative margin achievable. Preferred at ≤2 cm. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Lesions abutting central bile ducts, bowel, gallbladder, diaphragm, heart, or major vessels where a heat sink is expected — use an adjunctive technique or another modality. Also: target not reliably visible, unsafe access, uncorrectable coagulopathy. At 3–5 cm, single-probe ablation alone is not curative-intent therapy. An anatomic contraindication can justify upfront SBRT or Y-90 segmentectomy. Evidence & sources Liver-directed therapy evidence Thermal ablation RFA / MWA SURF: mostly solitary HCC ≤3 cm (median largest diameter 1.8 cm); difficult locations excluded. lead: Transplant Consider when transplantation can address both the cancer and the underlying liver disease.
text: Transplant B Consider when transplantation can address both the cancer and the underlying liver disease. Indications Preferred when Clinically significant portal hypertension, decompensation, or a recurrence pattern that the liver disease itself is driving. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid A solitary lesion <2 cm is OPTN T1 and does not attract exception points — listing must be justified by the liver disease, not the tumour. BCLC 2026 adds that an AFP above 1,000 ng/mL signals an unacceptably high risk of post-transplant recurrence. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Definitive SBRT or Y-90 segmentectomyDOSIMETRY EXPERTISE May be discussed when surgery and thermal ablation are unsuitable. This does not require prior TACE.
text: Definitive SBRT or Y-90 segmentectomy B DOSIMETRY EXPERTISE May be discussed when surgery and thermal ablation are unsuitable. This does not require prior TACE. Indications Preferred when SBRT: difficult access or vessel-adjacent target with adequate uninvolved liver. Segmentectomy: solitary localized tumour with full arterial coverage and ablative dosimetry. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid SBRT — insufficient uninvolved liver, refractory ascites, unsafe dose to adjacent bowel or stomach, overlapping prior dose, decompensation. Segmentectomy — hepatic reserve inadequate for the treated volume, unsafe lung-shunt fraction or non-target flow, personalised dosimetry unavailable. Evidence & sources Liver-directed therapy evidence Radiation segmentectomy Y-90 to one or two segments RASER: solitary HCC ≤3 cm unsuitable for ablation. LEGACY: solitary HCC ≤8 cm, Child-Pugh A. lead: Transplant Consider transplantation when portal hypertension, decompensation, or recurrent disease makes treatment of both the tumor and the underlying liver disease appropriate.
text: Transplant A Consider transplantation when portal hypertension, decompensation, or recurrent disease makes treatment of both the tumor and the underlying liver disease appropriate. Indications Preferred when Clinical selection: Milan criteria (one tumor ≤5 cm or 2–3 tumors each ≤3 cm). Standardized exception: OPTN T2 (one Class 5 lesion 2–5 cm or 2–3 Class 5 lesions each 1–3 cm), with the applicable AFP rule. Refer early. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Macrovascular invasion or extrahepatic spread excludes the standardized HCC exception. NLRB guidance allows selected patients with treated primary portal-vein branch invasion or ruptured HCC and at least 12 months of stability to be considered through nonstandard review; main portal-vein or hepatic-vein invasion remains a contraindication. An AFP that has ever exceeded 1,000 ng/mL blocks the standard exception until it falls below 500 and stays there. Repeated locoregional procedures while transplant referral is pending can delay assessment and reduce liver reserve. Refer early. lead: Radiation segmentectomyDOSIMETRY EXPERTISE PAYER Y-90 to one or two segments, as a selected definitive curative-intent option.
text: Radiation segmentectomy C DOSIMETRY EXPERTISE PAYER Y-90 to one or two segments, as a selected definitive curative-intent option. Indications Preferred when Solitary localized HCC with ablation unsuitable, full arterial coverage and ablative dosimetry. Strongest prospective evidence is solitary ≤3 cm. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Hepatic reserve inadequate for the treated volume, unsafe lung-shunt fraction or non-target flow, overlapping prior radiation dose, personalised dosimetry unavailable. ≤8 cm is not a universal curative cutoff, and segmentectomy's curative claim does not transfer to lobar Y-90. Evidence & sources Liver-directed therapy evidence Radiation segmentectomy Y-90 to one or two segments RASER: solitary HCC ≤3 cm unsuitable for ablation. LEGACY: solitary HCC ≤8 cm, Child-Pugh A. lead: Superselective conventional/DEB-TACE: define delivery, response target and when to stop or switch.
text: Standard A Superselective conventional/DEB-TACE: define delivery, response target and when to stop or switch. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Superselective conventional or drug-eluting-bead TACE. Plan selective delivery, define the intended response, and specify when to stop or change treatment. Indications Preferred when Multinodular arterialised liver-confined disease, preserved reserve, patent portal flow, superselective access achievable. Also bridge or downstage. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Decompensation, ALBI grade 3, diffuse or infiltrative pattern, impaired portal flow, renal or infection risk, and inadequate benefit despite technically adequate treatment. Reassess after each session rather than against a fixed session count. lead: Systemic therapy when locoregional treatment is unsuitable.
text: Standard A Systemic therapy when locoregional treatment is unsuitable. Indications Preferred when Diffuse, high-burden or TACE-unsuitable disease. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Pivotal evidence is Child-Pugh A and ECOG 0–1. Document variceal assessment and treat high-risk varices before the first dose of atezolizumab–bevacizumab. Evidence & sources Systemic therapy evidence Atezolizumab + bevacizumab Preferred first-line option IMbrave150: 501 patients with unresectable HCC, Child-Pugh A, ECOG 0 or 1, no previous systemic therapy; varices treated before entry. Bleeding, portal hypertension, blood pressure, proteinuria and immune toxicity affect selection. Do not compare its survival median directly with a different trial. Open in the systemic therapy matrix → Systemic therapy evidence Durvalumab + tremelimumab (STRIDE) Preferred first-line option HIMALAYA: 1,171 patients with unresectable HCC, Child-Pugh A, BCLC B or C, no previous systemic therapy; main portal vein thrombosis excluded. Main portal-vein invasion was excluded from the pivotal trial. Immune toxicity remains important; avoiding bevacizumab does not remove treatment risk. Open in the systemic therapy matrix → Systemic therapy evidence Nivolumab + ipilimumab Preferred first-line option CheckMate 9DW: 668 patients with unresectable HCC, Child-Pugh 5 or 6, ECOG 0 or 1, no previous systemic therapy; Vp4 invasion excluded. Survival curves crossed: mortality was higher during the first six months (HR 1.65). Grade 3–4 treatment-related events occurred in 41% versus 42%; treatment-related deaths were 12 versus 3. lead: Systemic therapy is primary. If eligible, start an immunotherapy combination; do not delay it for a liver-directed procedure.
text: Standard A Systemic therapy is primary. If eligible, start an immunotherapy combination; do not delay it for a liver-directed procedure. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Systemic therapy is the main treatment. Start an immunotherapy combination when eligible and do not delay it for a liver-directed procedure. Indications Preferred when Child-Pugh A, ECOG 0–1 — where almost all the pivotal evidence sits. Three first-line combinations, none ranked above the others on evidence. The exploratory non-viral IMbrave150 subgroup had an imprecise OS estimate (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.68–1.63); this does not establish absence of benefit or a validated aetiology-based exclusion. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Atezolizumab–bevacizumab requires documented variceal assessment and treatment of high-risk varices first, and bleeding is not a varices-only risk: all five fatal upper-gastrointestinal bleeds on atezolizumab–bevacizumab in IMbrave150 were in patients with Vp3–Vp4 invasion (four Vp4, one Vp3). Nivolumab–ipilimumab carries excess mortality in the first six months (HR 1.65, nine fatal hepatic events), which matters for a patient with a short expected survival; tremelimumab–durvalumab shows no early excess but its curves separate only after nine months, so neither pattern should be read as a class effect. Child-Pugh B9 and above is rarely appropriate outside a trial. Pre-transplant checkpoint exposure only through transplant-specific review. Evidence & sources Systemic therapy evidence Atezolizumab + bevacizumab Preferred first-line option IMbrave150: 501 patients with unresectable HCC, Child-Pugh A, ECOG 0 or 1, no previous systemic therapy; varices treated before entry. Bleeding, portal hypertension, blood pressure, proteinuria and immune toxicity affect selection. Do not compare its survival median directly with a different trial. Main portal-vein invasion was excluded from the pivotal trial. Immune toxicity remains important; avoiding bevacizumab does not remove treatment risk. Open in the systemic therapy matrix → Systemic therapy evidence Nivolumab + ipilimumab Preferred first-line option CheckMate 9DW: 668 patients with unresectable HCC, Child-Pugh 5 or 6, ECOG 0 or 1, no previous systemic therapy; Vp4 invasion excluded. Survival curves crossed: mortality was higher during the first six months (HR 1.65). Grade 3–4 treatment-related events occurred in 41% versus 42%; treatment-related deaths were 12 versus 3. lead: Consider radiation or radioembolization with systemic therapy. Evidence used sorafenib comparators; RTOG 1112 missed its primary survival endpoint, and Asan used TACE–radiation. Neither tested an immunotherapy backbone.
text: Reasonable B Consider radiation or radioembolization with systemic therapy. Evidence used sorafenib comparators; RTOG 1112 missed its primary survival endpoint, and Asan used TACE–radiation. Neither tested an immunotherapy backbone. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Add external beam radiotherapy or radioembolisation alongside systemic therapy. Both supporting trials used a sorafenib comparator: RTOG 1112 missed its primary survival endpoint (HR 0.77, 90% CI 0.59–1.01, one-sided p=0.06) and 15% of its patients then never started sorafenib, while the Asan trial gave TACE plus radiotherapy instead of sorafenib, with 91% crossover. Neither tested adding radiation to an immunotherapy backbone. Indications Preferred when Liver-dominant control, portal-vein tumour thrombus, or symptom control, where the anatomy is liver-confined, reserve is preserved and dosimetry is feasible. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let it delay or displace the systemic start — the most common harm in this group is a delayed systemic start, not the radiation itself. Document why local therapy is being added and when systemic therapy starts or resumes. Evidence & sources Liver-directed therapy evidence Radiation with or instead of systemic therapy macrovascular invasion Locally advanced HCC with macrovascular invasion. Open the liver-directed therapy reference → Liver-directed therapy evidence Y-90 (TARE) advanced / portal-vein invasion Locally advanced HCC; no overall-survival gain over sorafenib; dosimetry is the open question. Open the liver-directed therapy reference → No randomised trial has tested this against a modern immunotherapy backbone. Both supporting trials used a sorafenib comparator. lead: Re-evaluate for transplant.
text: Reasonable B Re-evaluate for transplant. Indications Preferred when Decompensation rather than tumour is driving performance status — the liver failure, not the cancer, is the indication. lead: Stage with contrast CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis and add a liver MRI with hepatocyte-specific or diffusion-weighted sequences before any hepatectomy or ablation.
text: Standard Evidence B Stage with contrast CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis and add a liver MRI with hepatocyte-specific or diffusion-weighted sequences before any hepatectomy or ablation. Indications Preferred when Every patient in whom local therapy is contemplated: MRI detects lesions CT misses and changes the operative plan, and ESMO asks for liver contrast MRI with hepatobiliary agents in every candidate for locoregional therapy [II, A]. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not plan a hepatectomy or an ablation from CT alone; an incomplete map produces an incomplete operation. Image before the first dose of chemotherapy where possible, because lesions are easier to see untreated. Evidence & sources NCCN prefers hepatic MRI with extracellular or hepatobiliary contrast over CT to assess the exact number and distribution of foci for local treatment planning. The Chinese 2024 consensus makes liver-specific contrast MRI the preferred baseline study (Grade I) and does not use PET/CT first line. lead: If transplantation is a possibility, stage to the transplant standard: PET/CT and colonoscopy in addition, inside the OPTN time windows.
text: Standard Evidence D If transplantation is a possibility, stage to the transplant standard: PET/CT and colonoscopy in addition, inside the OPTN time windows. Indications Preferred when Any patient who might reach Phase 3. The threshold for excluding extrahepatic disease is higher for transplantation than for resection, because graft scarcity and lifelong immunosuppression change the consequence of being wrong. IHPBA 2021 recommends FDG PET/CT to rule out extrahepatic disease and high-resolution chest CT to exclude pulmonary metastases. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat resection-grade staging as evidence of transplant eligibility. Imaging adequate to plan a hepatectomy is not adequate to establish exception eligibility. Evidence & sources The OPTN guidance route requires CT/MRI of chest, abdomen and pelvis plus PET within one month before the initial request, with the PET performed at least four weeks after chemotherapy is stopped, and colonoscopy within 12 months before the request. IHPBA 2021 instead asks for colonoscopy within 3 months of transplant. Graded D rather than B: these are review-board guidance and consensus windows with no comparative evidence that any of them changes outcome, and the two documents already disagree on the colonoscopy interval. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: At metastatic diagnosis: obtain RAS, BRAF, MMR/MSI and HER2 results; broaden profiling when an actionable finding would change treatment.
text: Standard Evidence A At metastatic diagnosis: obtain RAS, BRAF, MMR/MSI and HER2 results; broaden profiling when an actionable finding would change treatment. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Resulted RAS, BRAF, mismatch-repair or microsatellite status and HER2 at diagnosis of metastatic disease, with broader profiling where a rare actionable alteration would change treatment. Indications Preferred when Before the first-line decision, every patient. ESMO asks for molecular work-up at diagnosis in all patients reported within 14 days [I, A]; the Chinese 2024 consensus tests RAS and BRAF in all patients before treatment (Grade I, Class 1A). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let a single mutation set margin width, the extent of parenchymal resection, or exclusion from otherwise feasible clearance. BRAF mutation carries an adverse prognosis after resection; it is not an operative contraindication. Evidence & sources A POLE or POLD1 variant needs variant-level and phenotype interpretation before it is used to justify checkpoint therapy. Mismatch-repair deficiency or a suggestive family history prompts hereditary cancer assessment. Genotype is prognostic; the direction and duration of response during effective therapy carry more decision weight. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Doublet plus anti-EGFR ASCO 2023 recommends anti-EGFR plus doublet chemotherapy first line for left-sided RAS wild-type disease (strong recommendation) and not for right-sided tumours: versus bevacizumab, overall survival HR 0.71 (0.58–0.85) on the left and 1.35 (1.0–1.8) on the right.
text: Doublet plus anti-EGFR Evidence B ASCO 2023 recommends anti-EGFR plus doublet chemotherapy first line for left-sided RAS wild-type disease (strong recommendation) and not for right-sided tumours: versus bevacizumab, overall survival HR 0.71 (0.58–0.85) on the left and 1.35 (1.0–1.8) on the right. Indications Preferred when Left-sided, RAS and BRAF wild-type, mismatch-repair proficient disease when maximal shrinkage is the goal. In the final RAS wild-type FIRE-3 population centrally reviewed response was 72.0% versus 56.1% and early shrinkage of 20% or more 68.2% versus 49.1% with cetuximab — both post hoc, in a trial whose investigator-assessed response and progression-free survival did not differ and which did not analyse sidedness. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Right-sided primary, or RAS or BRAF V600E mutation. Do not read a shrinkage advantage as a survival advantage: CALGB/SWOG 80405 found median overall survival 30.0 months with cetuximab versus 29.0 with bevacizumab, HR 0.88 (0.77–1.01), p=0.08, so the two biologics give similar survival in KRAS wild-type disease. Do not read it as a conversion advantage either: in the left-sided RAS and BRAF wild-type comparison of CAIRO5, panitumumab raised objective response from 53% to 80% (p<0.0001) and median depth of response from 33% to 49% (p<0.0001), yet complete local treatment was 58% in both arms (p=1.00) and those two groups were closed early for futility (progression-free survival HR 1.11, 0.84–1.48, p=0.46). Evidence & sources Graded B rather than A for this use. Sidedness was collected post hoc in CALGB 80405 and the chemotherapy backbone was chosen by physician and patient, so the mFOLFOX6 subgroup favouring cetuximab is an unplanned subgroup of a non-randomised comparison; FIRE-3's own primary endpoint, investigator-assessed response, was negative and the 72% figure comes from a central review performed after the survival difference was known. The first-line recommendation for left-sided RAS wild-type disease stands; the claim that it converts more livers does not. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: FOLFOXIRI plus bevacizumab CAIRO5 supported regimen choice by sidedness and molecular status. In right-sided or RAS/BRAF V600E-mutant initially unresectable liver-only disease, FOLFOXIRI–bevacizumab improved progression-free survival (median 10.6 versus 9.0 months, HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.60–0.98, p=0.032) and complete local treatment (51% versus 37%, p=0.013).
text: FOLFOXIRI plus bevacizumab Evidence B CAIRO5 supported regimen choice by sidedness and molecular status. In right-sided or RAS/BRAF V600E-mutant initially unresectable liver-only disease, FOLFOXIRI–bevacizumab improved progression-free survival (median 10.6 versus 9.0 months, HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.60–0.98, p=0.032) and complete local treatment (51% versus 37%, p=0.013). Indications Preferred when A fit patient with right-sided or RAS/BRAF V600E-mutant disease in whom conversion response is the limiting factor. Preferred for that defined phenotype, not a general default. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Unfit patients, and left-sided RAS/BRAF wild-type disease, where FOLFOXIRI was never tested in CAIRO5. Grade 3 or worse events were 76% versus 59% with dose reductions in 55% and seven treatment-related deaths in the triplet arm; overall survival is not yet reported. Evidence & sources Resectability in CAIRO5 was a panel judgement with unanimous agreement in only 66% of baseline and 42% of follow-up assessments, so the complete local treatment endpoint is investigator-dependent. lead: Encorafenib, cetuximab and mFOLFOX6 BREAKWATER met its primary endpoint in first-line BRAF V600E-mutant disease: median progression-free survival 12.8 versus 7.1 months, HR 0.53 (95% CI 0.41–0.68), with interim overall survival 30.3 versus 15.1 months, HR 0.49 (0.38–0.63).
text: Encorafenib, cetuximab and mFOLFOX6 Evidence A BREAKWATER met its primary endpoint in first-line BRAF V600E-mutant disease: median progression-free survival 12.8 versus 7.1 months, HR 0.53 (95% CI 0.41–0.68), with interim overall survival 30.3 versus 15.1 months, HR 0.49 (0.38–0.63). Indications Preferred when BRAF V600E mutation, first line. NCCN asks that these patients receive an encorafenib-containing regimen during one line of therapy, with a chemotherapy-containing option preferred first line. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not read it as a conversion result: no resection, conversion or local-treatment endpoint was reported, and grade 3 or 4 toxicity in 81.5% with permanent discontinuation in 26.7% is demanding for a patient being worked up for liver surgery. Evidence & sources BRAF V600E is an exclusion in current transplant protocols, so this branch and Phase 3 rarely meet. The survival analysis is interim at 242 of 297 expected events and MSI-high patients were excluded. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Nivolumab plus ipilimumab CheckMate 8HW: progression-free survival favoured nivolumab plus ipilimumab over nivolumab alone in centrally confirmed MSI-high or dMMR disease, HR 0.62 (95% CI 0.48–0.81), and against chemotherapy first line median 54.1 versus 5.9 months, HR 0.21 (0.14–0.31).
text: Nivolumab plus ipilimumab Evidence A CheckMate 8HW: progression-free survival favoured nivolumab plus ipilimumab over nivolumab alone in centrally confirmed MSI-high or dMMR disease, HR 0.62 (95% CI 0.48–0.81), and against chemotherapy first line median 54.1 versus 5.9 months, HR 0.21 (0.14–0.31). Indications Preferred when MSI-high or mismatch-repair deficient disease. Sustained molecular control may postpone, replace or change the role of liver-directed treatment, judged on serial cross-sectional imaging against a defined framework rather than on symptoms or a single scan. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not list such a patient on the described OPTN exception route, which requires microsatellite stability; IHPBA 2021 excludes MSI-high and dMMR patients from transplantation altogether. Pre-transplant checkpoint exposure and post-transplant rejection risk must be addressed before the first dose. Evidence & sources Overall survival in CheckMate 8HW remains masked under the hierarchical testing plan and adding ipilimumab roughly doubled grade 3–4 toxicity (22% versus 14%). In KEYNOTE-177 pembrolizumab improved progression-free survival over chemotherapy, 16.5 versus 8.2 months, HR 0.60, but 29.4% had progressive disease as best response and survival was immature with 59% effective crossover. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

Pembrolizumab vs chemotherapy: PFS 16.5 vs 8.2 mo, HR 0.60; but 29.4% had progressive disease as best response Survival immature with 59% effective crossover

lead: Sotorasib plus panitumumab CodeBreaK 300, after chemorefractory progression in KRAS G12C disease: median progression-free survival 5.6 versus 2.0 months with sotorasib 960 mg plus panitumumab, HR 0.48 (95% CI 0.30–0.78), objective response 26.4% versus 0%.
text: Sotorasib plus panitumumab Evidence B CodeBreaK 300, after chemorefractory progression in KRAS G12C disease: median progression-free survival 5.6 versus 2.0 months with sotorasib 960 mg plus panitumumab, HR 0.48 (95% CI 0.30–0.78), objective response 26.4% versus 0%. Indications Preferred when KRAS G12C mutation after chemorefractory progression — a reasonable consideration, not a conversion strategy. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not promise survival: the trial was not powered for it and overall survival was immature with HR 0.77 (0.40–1.45) crossing 1. No resection or ablation outcomes were reported, and the standard-care comparator was overtaken by SUNLIGHT and FRESCO-2 during the trial. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Record integrated clinical-molecular risk alongside the Fong score where the assay is available.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Record integrated clinical-molecular risk alongside the Fong score where the assay is available. Indications Preferred when A resected metastasis with tissue available for mRNA and miRNA profiling, used for prognosis and surveillance intensity. In the New EPOC validation cohort 5-year progression-free survival was 43% for the immune, 26% for the stromal and 14% for the canonical subtype (log-rank p=0.004), and integrated risk groups gave 5-year overall survival 78%, 56% and 43%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not use it to decide operability or to choose systemic therapy. It is prognostic only, the three-way overall survival comparison was not significant (p=0.08), the assay needs resected metastatic tissue so it cannot inform the preoperative decision, and the low-risk 78% rests on wide confidence intervals (44–93%). Evidence & sources Validated in a biomarker subset of a trial whose experimental arm harmed patients; subtypes predicted from the matched primary tumour were not prognostic. Adding subtype to the Fong score raised the Gonen and Heller concordance statistic only from 0.55 to 0.62 for progression-free survival and from 0.59 to 0.63 for overall survival, and the best-prognosis group rests on 28 immune metastases. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: New EPOC validation: 5-y PFS 43% immune vs 26% stromal vs 14% canonical (p=0.004); integrated risk groups 5-y OS 78%, 56%, 43% (p=0.08, NS) Prognostic only; needs resected tissue; low-risk 78% has wide CI 44–93%

lead: Assess clinical-trial eligibility at every decision point, and record it.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Assess clinical-trial eligibility at every decision point, and record it. Indications Preferred when Every discussion, in both directions: a trial may be the best available option, and enrolment constraints may set the timing of local treatment. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let a trial screening window displace a feasible clearance operation that is ready to go.

lead: Indiscriminate triplet intensification, and triplet chemotherapy combined with an anti-EGFR antibody.
text: Avoid Evidence B Indiscriminate triplet intensification, and triplet chemotherapy combined with an anti-EGFR antibody. Why Why Intensify only where conversion response is the limiting factor, in a fit patient, with a defined clearance endpoint and toxicity review recorded. Additional cautions Additional cautions Adding irinotecan to cetuximab–FOLFOX did not raise response in TRICE (84.7% versus 79.7%, odds ratio 0.70, p=0.42) and did not raise complete local treatment (54.2% versus 52.7%), while increasing grade 3 or worse neutropenia; progression-free survival numerically favoured the doublet, so harm from intensification is not excluded. Evidence & sources The roadmap's position is individualised consideration for fit patients rather than a blanket Avoid; the worksheet asks whether Avoid should be narrowed to triplet plus anti-EGFR only, with triplet plus bevacizumab relabelled a reasonable consideration. TRICE was powered on response at a two-sided alpha of 0.10 in 146 patients, judged resectability locally with no central review, and was an all-Asian cohort given irinotecan at 150 mg/m² with no UGT1A1 variants, so Western toxicity will be higher than the 5.9% grade 3 diarrhoea reported. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: n=146: adding irinotecan to cetuximab–FOLFOX did not raise response (p=0.42) or complete local treatment; more grade ≥3 neutropenia; PFS numerically favoured doublet Powered on response at two-sided alpha 0.10; resectability judged locally; all-Asian cohort

lead: Using genotype alone to exclude a patient from a feasible clearance operation, or to set margin width.
text: Avoid Evidence D Using genotype alone to exclude a patient from a feasible clearance operation, or to set margin width. Why Why Let observed response on effective therapy carry the decision weight; a single mutation stratifies prognosis rather than determining operability. Additional cautions Additional cautions A larger resection, a wider margin or a refusal to operate justified by a BRAF or RAS result alone.

lead: Parenchymal-sparing resection is the reference clearance strategy, because it is the only route that permits pathologic margin assessment.
text: Standard Evidence B Parenchymal-sparing resection is the reference clearance strategy, because it is the only route that permits pathologic margin assessment. Indications Preferred when Disease clearable with an adequate remnant and preserved inflow, outflow and biliary drainage. Use a minimally invasive or robotic approach where it does not compromise completeness. Preserve parenchyma deliberately: recurrence is common and repeat liver-directed treatment produces meaningful survival in selected patients. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Inadequate remnant, prohibitive vascular or biliary anatomy, or progression on appropriate therapy. A positive margin and extrahepatic disease were the two most influential adverse factors in the 1001-patient Fong series (5-year survival 20% and 18%) and the authors treat both as contraindications to resection. Evidence & sources Needs demonstrated team experience with the specific operation. Graded B rather than A: no randomised trial compares hepatectomy with non-operative management, and the cited series is a single tertiary centre, retrospective, pre-oxaliplatin and pre-PET, describing outcome after resection rather than comparing resection with anything. What holds the recommendation up is that resection is the only route that yields a pathologic margin, not the strength of the comparative evidence. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Single-centre retrospective series, 1001 resected: 5-y survival 20% with positive margin, 18% with extrahepatic disease Pre-oxaliplatin, pre-PET; describes outcome after resection, no comparator

lead: Small lesions: curative-intent ablation ± resection, treating every original site with a confirmed circumferential margin.
text: Standard Evidence B Small lesions: curative-intent ablation ± resection, treating every original site with a confirmed circumferential margin. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Thermal ablation alone or with resection is a curative-intent clearance option for small lesions, provided every original site is treated and a circumferential margin is confirmed. Indications Preferred when Lesions of 3 cm or less, up to ten, where all sites are treatable and a margin beyond 5 mm is achievable — an initial option in that phenotype, not a consolation after surgical failure. NCCN prioritises feasible thermal ablation in selected lesions of 3 cm or less and ESMO goes further, recommending thermal ablation over resection for metastases under 3 cm [II, B]. COLLISION randomised 300 patients, analysed 148 against 146, and stopped early when the conditional likelihood of proving non-inferiority reached 90.5%: adverse events of any grade 19% versus 46%, serious events 7% versus 20%, median stay 1 versus 4 days, no treatment-related deaths versus three, and 5-year overall survival 51.2% versus 58.0%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Within 1 cm of a major bile duct, where a heat sink is expected, where the target is not reliably visible, or where only a margin under 5 mm is achievable. In the 233-tumour Memorial Sloan Kettering series local recurrence was 90% at a 0 mm margin, 60% at 1–5 mm, 15% beyond 5–10 mm and 5% beyond 10 mm, and a margin of 5 mm or less carried HR 9.9 (4.9–20) for shorter local progression-free survival. Evidence & sources Graded B rather than A. COLLISION stopped at interim on conditional power rather than a confidence interval excluding its margin: the overall survival HR was 1.05 with a 95% CI of 0.69–1.58, whose upper bound crosses the prespecified non-inferiority limit of 1.30, and the authors say definitive non-inferiority conclusions are difficult, especially in the under-represented intermediate (n=91) and high (n=21) burden subgroups. The arms were not clean — 18% of the ablation arm also had a lesion resected and 35% of the resection arm had a non-target lesion ablated, only 57% of ablations were percutaneous — a mid-trial amendment removed solitary deep lesions needing major hepatectomy, the cases where resection carries most risk, and the trial was funded by an ablation device manufacturer. This is clearance, not debulking: treat every original site. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Ablation vs resection: OS HR 1.05 (95% CI 0.69–1.58), stopped early on conditional power; any AE 19% vs 46%, serious 7% vs 20%; 5-y OS 51.2% vs 58.0% CI upper bound crosses NI limit 1.30; few intermediate (91) and high (21) burden patients

lead: Simultaneous resection of liver and primary NCCN states that patients with resectable metastatic disease and a primary tumour in place should have both sites resected with curative intent, and that staged procedures can be liver-first or primary-first.
text: Simultaneous resection of liver and primary Evidence C NCCN states that patients with resectable metastatic disease and a primary tumour in place should have both sites resected with curative intent, and that staged procedures can be liver-first or primary-first. Indications Preferred when Both operations limited: a minor hepatectomy with an uncomplicated colonic primary. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Adam 2015 does not advocate one-stage surgery for a major hepatectomy of three or more segments, a complex colonic tumour or a low rectal primary; one-stage resection is more risky than two separate resections. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Liver-first Useful when rectal therapy would otherwise delay control of substantial hepatic disease. Sequence by the dominant oncologic threat rather than by chronology.
text: Liver-first Evidence C Useful when rectal therapy would otherwise delay control of substantial hepatic disease. Sequence by the dominant oncologic threat rather than by chronology. Indications Preferred when Hepatic burden drives the risk, particularly with a rectal primary whose pelvic treatment will take months. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid A primary that threatens obstruction, substantial bleeding or perforation — that threat is treated first. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Primary-first Appropriate where the primary is the dominant threat, or where it must be cleared before transplant consideration.
text: Primary-first Evidence C Appropriate where the primary is the dominant threat, or where it must be cleared before transplant consideration. Indications Preferred when Symptomatic or obstructing primary; and in a possible transplant candidate, where the primary is resected after a favourable response to systemic therapy. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid An asymptomatic primary with broadly unresectable liver disease: resecting it first delays the systemic therapy that is also the biological test. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Perioperative chemotherapy for clearly resectable disease is optional, not mandatory; where it is used, state the six-month total framework.
text: Standard Evidence C Perioperative chemotherapy for clearly resectable disease is optional, not mandatory; where it is used, state the six-month total framework. Indications Preferred when More or larger metastases, a clinical risk score above 2, or a need to observe biology before operating. ASCO recommends a total perioperative duration of six months on the basis of EORTC 40983. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat it as automatic for every patient. EORTC 40983 missed its primary endpoint as randomised: 3-year progression-free survival 35.4% versus 28.1%, HR 0.79 (0.62–1.02), p=0.058, significant only in eligible (HR 0.77, p=0.041) and resected (HR 0.73, p=0.025) patients, and at 8.5 years there was no overall survival difference (median 61.3 versus 54.3 months, HR 0.88, p=0.34). It did not raise the resection rate (83% versus 84%), and reversible postoperative complications were more frequent after chemotherapy, 25% versus 16%, p=0.04. Evidence & sources Graded C rather than B. Only 63% of patients started the postoperative half and 44% completed it, so what the trial really tested was six cycles of FOLFOX4 before surgery. It enrolled one to four metastases with 52% solitary — the best-prognosis population — which is not the population this page directs the regimen at; the extrapolation to more or larger metastases and a risk score above 2 is judgement, not trial evidence. ASCO's six-month duration is taken from this same trial, and the one other randomised adjuvant trial it cites, JCOG0603, improved disease-free survival (HR 0.67, 0.50–0.92) without improving overall survival (HR 1.25, 0.78–2.0). Do not assume adjuvant biologics are interchangeable. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Perioperative chemotherapy vs none: 3-y PFS 35.4% vs 28.1%, HR 0.79 (0.62–1.02), p=0.058, primary endpoint missed; complications 25% vs 16%, p=0.04 Significant only in eligible (HR 0.77) and resected (HR 0.73) subsets; 52% solitary
Perioperative chemotherapy vs none at 8.5 y: no OS difference, median 61.3 vs 54.3 mo, HR 0.88, p=0.34 Only 44% completed the postoperative half; 52% solitary metastases

lead: After clearance: imaging/CEA at 3–6 months, then by risk; review ablation margins at 4–8 weeks; colonoscopy and 2-/5-year follow-up.
text: Standard Evidence C After clearance: imaging/CEA at 3–6 months, then by risk; review ablation margins at 4–8 weeks; colonoscopy and 2-/5-year follow-up. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × After clearance, run the longitudinal loop: imaging and CEA at 3–6 months then by risk, ablation margins re-read at 4–8 weeks, colonoscopic follow-up, over a two-year and five-year framework. Indications Preferred when Every cleared patient. After resection the return question is the recurrence pattern and whether repeat clearance is feasible — recurrence is part of the treatment course, not automatic failure of the first operation. After ablation treat the site as incompletely treated unless a circumferential margin is confirmed; local progression risk is high when the margin is under 5 mm. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not equate persistent enhancement after SBRT or transarterial therapy with failure: expect delayed and partial radiographic change at 8–12 weeks. Evidence & sources Graded C: the intervals are guideline and consensus positions with no comparative evidence that any schedule changes outcome in CRLM. The Chinese 2024 consensus would fix the post-clearance schedule at 3-monthly CEA and cross-sectional imaging including liver MRI for the first two years (Grade I); the worksheet asks whether to adopt that in place of '3–6 months, then per risk'. The 4–8-week ablation re-read is the one element with a derivation behind it, from the margin series. Where a rectum is retained after organ preservation, add frequent local examination, endoscopy and pelvic imaging. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Clear the liver with ablation plus resection when resection alone cannot reach every site.
text: Reasonable Evidence B Clear the liver with ablation plus resection when resection alone cannot reach every site. Indications Preferred when Liver-only disease judged unresectable by distribution rather than by biology, where ablation plus resection can treat every deposit alongside systemic therapy. In EORTC 40004 (CLOCC) overall survival favoured combined local treatment plus systemic therapy over systemic therapy alone, HR 0.58 (0.38–0.88), with 5- and 8-year survival 43.1% and 35.9% versus 30.3% and 8.9%, and progression-free survival 16.8 versus 9.9 months, HR 0.57. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not read it as evidence for ablation on its own: nearly half the combined arm (26 of 57) also needed resection, so the gain belongs to complete liver clearance. The trial was downsized to randomised phase 2, closed early for poor accrual at 119 patients with overall survival a secondary endpoint, and its control arm had no anti-EGFR therapy and no RAS or BRAF selection. Evidence & sources The survival curves separate only after 3 years; unresectability was decided locally with no central review. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Local treatment + systemic vs systemic alone: OS HR 0.58 (0.38–0.88); 5-y OS 43.1% vs 30.3%, 8-y 35.9% vs 8.9%; PFS 16.8 vs 9.9 mo, HR 0.57 Randomised phase 2 closed early at 119; OS secondary; 26 of 57 also needed resection

lead: SBRT with definitive local intent when resection and margin-verified ablation are both unsuitable.
text: Reasonable Evidence C SBRT with definitive local intent when resection and margin-verified ablation are both unsuitable. Indications Preferred when Selected oligometastatic disease where all disease can be addressed and safe ablative dosing is feasible, or where the patient prefers a non-invasive approach. NCCN favours BED10 above 100 Gy for oligometastases when organ-at-risk limits allow; ASCO supports selected use after systemic therapy in unresectable liver oligometastases. In the multi-institution phase I/II trial in-field local control was 95% at 1 year and 92% at 2 years, and 100% at 2 years for lesions of 3 cm or less versus 77% above 3 cm. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not claim equivalence to margin-verified clearance, and do not use it without full staging, with insufficient uninvolved liver or with an unsafe normal-organ dose. Imaging response is not margin-verified clearance. Evidence & sources Graded C: the cure evidence is much weaker than the local-control evidence. Only 15 of 47 patients in the phase I/II trial had colorectal metastases, colorectal-specific outcomes were not reported, 13 patients were treated below 60 Gy, control was scored in only 49 of 63 lesions and the authors note the competing risk of death may exaggerate it. ASCO's recommendation rests on 18 non-randomised studies (1-year overall survival 67%, 2-year local control 59%) and is graded low quality, weak. SABR-COMET is a 99-patient phase 2 screening design run at a two-sided alpha of 0.20 — its primary report gave median overall survival 41 versus 28 months, HR 0.57 (0.30–1.10), p=0.090 — and in the long-term analysis 5-year overall survival was 42.3% versus 17.7%, falling to p=0.085 once prostate-cancer patients are excluded; only 18 of 99 patients had a colorectal primary and one of 12 five-year survivors, liver lesional control was the worst of any site at 50%, and treatment-related mortality was 4.5%. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Phase I/II trial, 47 patients: in-field local control 95% at 1 y, 92% at 2 y; at 2 y 100% vs 77%, lesions ≤3 cm vs >3 cm Only 15 of 47 had colorectal metastases; CRC-specific outcomes not reported
Guideline evidence base of 18 non-randomised studies: 1-y OS 67%, 2-y local control 59% Graded low quality, weak recommendation

lead: Cytoreductive surgery with systemic chemotherapy for peritoneal metastases, in a specialised centre and only where complete cytoreduction is feasible.
text: Reasonable Evidence B Cytoreductive surgery with systemic chemotherapy for peritoneal metastases, in a specialised centre and only where complete cytoreduction is feasible. Indications Preferred when Peritoneal disease assessed by a peritoneal surface malignancy team rather than routed through this liver pathway. ESMO recommends cytoreductive surgery for peritoneal-only disease [II, A]. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Incomplete cytoreduction, or managing peritoneal disease as an extension of the hepatic clearance plan. Any peritoneal disease ends transplant intent. Evidence & sources Needs demonstrated team experience. ASCO's cytoreduction recommendation requires no extraperitoneal metastases, so combined liver and peritoneal disease sits outside it and is a systemic-therapy-first, case-by-case decision. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Adding cetuximab to perioperative chemotherapy in resectable KRAS wild-type liver metastases.
text: Avoid Evidence B Adding cetuximab to perioperative chemotherapy in resectable KRAS wild-type liver metastases. Why Why Nothing. There is no perioperative phenotype in which the roadmap accepts it, and no evidence supports other anti-EGFR agents perioperatively. Additional cautions Additional cautions New EPOC found median overall survival 81.0 months with chemotherapy alone versus 55.4 months with added cetuximab, HR 1.45 (1.02–2.05), p=0.036, with worse post-progression survival (HR 1.55) and the harm falling on good-prognosis patients (no adverse feature HR 2.35, 1.37–4.03). Preoperative response and resection rates did not differ, so there was no offsetting surgical gain. Evidence & sources Both halves: the interim progression-free survival detriment (HR 1.48, p=0.030) was no longer significant on long-term follow-up (HR 1.17, p=0.304), overall survival was a secondary endpoint without multiplicity adjustment or correction for the earlier interim look, and the trial closed early for futility at 58% of planned events — which is why this is graded B and not A, even though the practice message is not in doubt. Entry tested KRAS exon 2 only, with no NRAS, BRAF, mismatch-repair or sidedness data, so the harm has never been studied in a modern biomarker-selected population and no mechanism has been identified. This is also why the roadmap separates the resectable and unresectable settings: an agent that helps in unresectable disease shortened survival given perioperatively. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Interim: PFS worse with chemotherapy + cetuximab vs chemotherapy alone, HR 1.48, p=0.030 No longer significant on long-term follow-up (HR 1.17, p=0.304); closed early for futility

Median OS 81.0 vs 55.4 mo, chemotherapy alone vs + cetuximab, HR 1.45 (1.02–2.05) against cetuximab, p=0.036; long-term PFS HR 1.17, p=0.304, NS OS secondary, no multiplicity adjustment; closed for futility at 58% of events; KRAS exon 2 only

lead: Oxaliplatin-based HIPEC added to cytoreduction.
text: Avoid Evidence B Oxaliplatin-based HIPEC added to cytoreduction. Why Why Nothing outside a trial. ESMO does not recommend HIPEC outside trials [II, D]. Additional cautions Additional cautions Adding it to complete cytoreduction as routine practice. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Partial debulking, and accumulating regional-control procedures as a route to cure.
text: Avoid Evidence D Partial debulking, and accumulating regional-control procedures as a route to cure. Why Why Nothing. NCCN states that partial debulking of less than an R0 resection is not recommended. Additional cautions Additional cautions A treatment that achieves regional control is not a substitute for clearance when clearance is achievable, and a succession of control procedures is not a route to cure. The roadmap calls this the single most common source of error in multidisciplinary discussion of this disease.

lead: De-escalating or shortening treatment and surveillance on the strength of a negative circulating tumour DNA result.
text: Avoid Evidence B De-escalating or shortening treatment and surveillance on the strength of a negative circulating tumour DNA result. Why Why Keep ctDNA inside a defined research or prospective registry role; IHPBA 2021 places circulating biomarker profiling within research. Additional cautions Additional cautions NCCN states there is currently insufficient evidence to recommend routine ctDNA use outside a clinical trial and that de-escalation decisions should not be based on ctDNA results. It is prognostic; it cannot replace imaging or justify clearance on its own. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Give conversion therapy against a defined surgical endpoint, and reassess resectability with a surgeon in the room every 8 weeks.
text: Standard Evidence D Give conversion therapy against a defined surgical endpoint, and reassess resectability with a surgeon in the room every 8 weeks. Indications Preferred when Every patient treated with conversion intent. Choose the regimen by sidedness and molecular status as in Phase 1; in CAIRO5 complete local treatment of all metastases was reached in 51% versus 37% of right-sided or RAS/BRAF-mutant patients with the triplet. ESMO asks for resectability to be redefined at baseline on imaging under four weeks old, every 2–3 months on first-line treatment and again in later lines in very good responders [IV, A]. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let conversion therapy become chemotherapy continued until progression or cumulative liver injury. When response has made safe complete clearance possible, operate now rather than continue. Evidence & sources The 8-week interval is an operating judgement with no comparative evidence; the Chinese 2024 consensus asks for surgical reassessment every 1.5–2.0 months and operation as soon as the disease is resectable, 6–8 weeks after the last bevacizumab dose. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: CAIRO5, right-sided or RAS/BRAF-mutant: complete local treatment of all metastases 51% vs 37%, triplet vs doublet Right-sided or RAS/BRAF-mutant patients only

lead: Hepatic arterial infusion plus systemic therapy to convert liver-dominant or liver-only disease to clearance, planned early rather than kept as terminal salvage.
text: Standard Evidence C EXPERTISE Hepatic arterial infusion plus systemic therapy to convert liver-dominant or liver-only disease to clearance, planned early rather than kept as terminal salvage. Indications Preferred when Selected unresectable liver-only CRLM at a credentialed pump centre. Review during first-line planning, reassess after systemic therapy, and discuss before hepatic radiation. Early referral does not waive NCCN treatment eligibility. D’Angelica phase II (PMID 24646562): n=49, 47% conversion, 76% response, median OS 38 months. Distinct from Kemeny phase I (PMID 19470932): n=49, 47% conversion and 92% response. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid No dedicated pump programme; unsuitable arterial anatomy; extrahepatic disease; portal hypertension; prior liver radiation; direct bilirubin above 1.5 mg/dL or alkaline phosphatase at or above twice the upper limit of normal. NCCN also requires at least one prior systemic line and operative fitness, and HAI cannot be delivered with concurrent bevacizumab or other VEGF inhibitors. Evidence & sources Conversion is a surrogate and the evidence is single-arm and centre-concentrated: median disease-free survival after R0 resection was only 7.6 months, 12 of 23 resected patients needed portal vein embolisation and 10 needed intraoperative ablation, and response in that series was scored by WHO-type criteria rather than RECIST, which inflates the 92% figure against modern trials. The only baseline factor that predicted conversion was female sex (81% versus 30%), from an uncorrected univariate scan in 49 patients, so nothing here lets a surgeon predict who converts. Toxicity rises with exposure — grade 3 or worse chemotherapy toxicity in 38% during the first two cycles and 66% by six months in the Dutch study, with late biliary sclerosis unresolved at six months and expected later. Biliary toxicity and pump complications are not occasional-case risks, and delivery depends on payer authorisation in a clinically useful interval. Duke expanding-program cohort (PMID 39565488): 102 patients, 97% previously treated, 20% conversion, 23% HAI-specific complications and 6% biliary sclerosis. Selected cohort outcomes are not institutional performance targets. Record conversion to complete clearance separately from pump response. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Single-arm phase I, n=49: conversion 47%, response 92% Response by WHO-type criteria rather than RECIST, which inflates the 92%
Dutch study, toxicity: grade ≥3 chemotherapy toxicity 38% in the first two cycles and 66% by 6 mo Late biliary sclerosis unresolved at six months and expected later
Single-arm phase II, n=49: conversion 47%, response 76%, median OS 38 mo Conversion is a surrogate; single-arm, centre-concentrated evidence
Duke expanding-program cohort, n=102 (97% pretreated): conversion 20%; HAI-specific complications 23%, biliary sclerosis 6% Selected cohort; outcomes are not institutional performance targets

lead: Broadly unresectable liver disease: leave an asymptomatic primary during systemic therapy. Resect for a local threat, and before transplant after favorable response.
text: Standard Evidence B Broadly unresectable liver disease: leave an asymptomatic primary during systemic therapy. Resect for a local threat, and before transplant after favorable response. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Leave an asymptomatic primary in situ during systemic therapy when liver disease is broadly unresectable; resect it for a defined local threat, and before transplantation after a favourable response. Indications Preferred when An asymptomatic primary with unresectable metastases — the whole Adam 2015 panel agreed on optimal chemotherapy first to achieve resectability, and ESMO states that primary resection cannot be recommended for an asymptomatic primary with unresectable synchronous metastases [I, D]. Where transplantation is contemplated, the primary is resected after a favourable response, with clear margins and a circumferential margin of at least 1 mm for a rectal cancer. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Imminent obstruction, substantial bleeding, perforation or another local threat: resect first. NCCN advises colon resection only in that situation. Evidence & sources A rectal primary managed by watch-and-wait after a clinical complete response does not meet the transplant requirement for a resected primary — a clinical complete response is not proof that every tumour cell is gone — and must be resolved before listing. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Portal vein embolisation or liver venous deprivationEXPERTISE Remnant augmentation enables clearance; it does not itself clear disease in the remnant.
text: Portal vein embolisation or liver venous deprivation Evidence B EXPERTISE Remnant augmentation enables clearance; it does not itself clear disease in the remnant. Indications Preferred when Anticipated remnant too small but disease otherwise clearable and biology controlled. Rescue ALPPS after failed portal vein occlusion closed most of the resection-rate gap in LIGRO (82% versus 92%, not significant), so an embolisation-first strategy with ALPPS held in reserve is not excluded by that trial. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Disease in the future remnant left unaddressed, progressing biology, or a dropout and morbidity risk exceeding the realistic chance of clearance. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Resection rate 82% vs 92%, portal vein occlusion with rescue ALPPS vs upfront ALPPS — not significant

lead: Two-stage hepatectomyEXPERTISE The conventional staged route to an adequate remnant.
text: Two-stage hepatectomy Evidence B EXPERTISE The conventional staged route to an adequate remnant. Indications Preferred when Bilobar disease where the remnant can be cleared first and hypertrophy awaited; tolerable where the interval can be covered by systemic therapy. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid High dropout risk between stages. In LIGRO the two-stage arm completed resection in only 57% (28 of 49) against a strict 30% remnant threshold, below published rates of 60–75%. lead: Selected Y90 radiation lobectomy to grow the future remnant, with the operation supplying the curative step.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Selected Y90 radiation lobectomy to grow the future remnant, with the operation supplying the curative step. Indications Preferred when A patient whose remnant will not come up by embolisation and in whom lobar radioembolisation is technically attractive, planned as a route to an operation. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not present it as the curative treatment, and do not extrapolate HCC segmentectomy cure claims to CRLM. Assess any future HAI pathway before liver irradiation, because NCCN Colon v2.2026, original PDF p. 39, excludes prior liver radiation from HAI selection. Any proposed departure requires explicit MDT review; this is not a claim of universal technical impossibility. Evidence & sources Depends on personalised dosimetry planning and radiation-safety review; the CRLM hypertrophy evidence is a small part of mixed series. lead: Adjuvant hepatic arterial infusion after resection, as a separate expert-centre indication.
text: Reasonable Evidence C EXPERTISE Adjuvant hepatic arterial infusion after resection, as a separate expert-centre indication. Indications Preferred when A completely resected patient at a credentialed pump centre. The randomised Memorial Sloan Kettering trial gave 2-year survival free of hepatic progression of 90% versus 60% (p<0.001) and 2-year overall survival 86% versus 72% (p=0.03). Selective MDT discussion; not routine for every low-risk resection. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Extrahepatic disease or a positive margin, where the propensity-matched series found no benefit (37 versus 33 months and 37 versus 28 months). Do not offer it outside a programme with credentialed surgeons, oncologists and pump management. Evidence & sources Both halves: in that trial the whole overall survival curves were not significantly different (p=0.21 by log-rank) and the positive result is the prespecified two-year landmark, against an obsolete bolus fluorouracil comparator, with only 26% of patients receiving more than half the planned floxuridine because of biliary toxicity. The 2368-patient propensity analysis (median overall survival 67 versus 44 months, adjusted HR 0.67, 0.59–0.76) is retrospective across 21 years in patients six years younger and more recently treated, a published letter argued the propensity model and covariate balance were reported in too little detail to assess, and its largest effects fell in node-negative and low-risk patients — the opposite of where a regional therapy should help most. Dutch adjuvant PUMP has reported at ASCO 2026 (LBA3506; DOI 10.1200/JCO.2026.44.17_suppl.LBA3506): CRS 0–2, 243 randomized and 218 analysed, HAIP alone versus resection alone without adjuvant systemic therapy in either arm. PFS HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.62–1.25), P=.48; median PFS 15 versus 16 months. No significant PFS benefit; overall survival is immature. This does not support routine adjuvant HAI after every low-risk resection and does not test HAI plus modern systemic therapy or unresectable conversion. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

Retrospective propensity analysis, n=2368, adjuvant HAI vs none: median OS 67 vs 44 mo, adjusted HR 0.67 (0.59–0.76) Spans 21 years; HAI patients younger, more recent; no benefit if extrahepatic disease or R1

lead: A larger operation as the answer to disease progressing on an appropriate systemic regimen.
text: Avoid Evidence D A larger operation as the answer to disease progressing on an appropriate systemic regimen. Why Why Redirect. Biologic unresectability is not reversible by surgery; restage and reconsider complete treatment rather than escalating the operation. Additional cautions Additional cautions Escalating from resection to augmentation, staged surgery or ALPPS in a patient whose disease is growing through therapy. lead: Adding Y90 radioembolisation to first-line chemotherapy expecting a survival benefit.
text: Avoid Evidence B Adding Y90 radioembolisation to first-line chemotherapy expecting a survival benefit. Why Why Nothing in the first line. If hepatic control is the goal, say so and label it control, not conversion. Additional cautions Additional cautions The prospectively planned combined analysis of FOXFIRE, SIRFLOX and FOXFIRE-Global in 1103 patients found median overall survival 22.6 versus 23.3 months, pooled HR 1.04 (0.90–1.19), p=0.61, with no benefit in the liver-only subgroup (HR 1.00) and identical hepatic resection rates (17% versus 16%), at the cost of grade 3 or worse events in 74% versus 67%. Evidence & sources Both halves: liver control did improve — first progression in the liver 31% versus 49%, subdistribution HR 0.51 — but non-liver progression rose (HR 1.76), and in SIRFLOX the primary endpoint of progression-free survival at any site was negative (10.7 versus 10.2 months, HR 0.93) while liver progression-free survival improved from 12.6 to 20.5 months. Resection rates did not move in either trial. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

text: Deceased-donor transplantation under the nonstandard review route Evidence B PROTOCOL REGISTRY TransMet randomised 94 patients with permanently unresectable liver-only disease controlled on chemotherapy: intention-to-treat 5-year overall survival 56.6% versus 12.6% with chemotherapy alone, HR 0.37 (95% CI 0.21–0.65), p=0.0003; per protocol 73.3% versus 9.3%, HR 0.16. CRLM is not a standardised OPTN exception, so listing goes through nonstandard Adult Transplant Oncology Review Board review with the CRLM diagnosis form and a written narrative requesting consideration at MMaT-20, with Policy 9.4.E setting a floor of 15. Indications Preferred when A patient inside both the OPTN guidance decision points and the local protocol: BRAF wild type, microsatellite stable, 12 months from CRLM diagnosis, six months of stability or regression, CEA below 80 µg/L, with an exact value of 80 requiring explicit review because initial and extension guidance differ, no pretreatment lesion above 10 cm, primary resected R0 with a clear colonoscopy, ECOG 0–1, age considered with physiologic reserve rather than alone. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Any uncontrolled or non-curable extrahepatic disease, progression on an appropriate regimen, new lesions, declining reserve, prohibitive comorbidity, active infection or psychosocial risk. Disease clearable by reasonable resection, margin-verified ablation, augmentation, staged surgery is not a transplant indication. Assess HAI conversion feasibility alongside transplant candidacy; do not require exhaustion of HAI before referral. Evidence & sources Both halves: 19% of the transplantation arm never received a graft, recurrence after transplant was 74% with 5-year progression-free survival 19.9%, and the survival gain rests on repeatedly treating recurrence — mostly pulmonary, 54% of isolated recurrences lung-only, with 46% of those treated with curative intent. Selection was extreme: an independent panel excluded 40% of screened patients, and the trial depended on negotiated national prioritisation that delivered grafts at a median 50.5 days after randomisation. Without exception points these low-MELD patients do not compete, and a longer wait raises the 19% dropout. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

The three-centre North American series transplanted 10 of 91 evaluated patients, with 1.5-year overall survival 100% and recurrence-free survival 62% and full donor recovery. lead: Declare permanent unresectability formally, in writing, after dedicated hepatobiliary and transplant review of every alternative.
text: Standard Evidence D Declare permanent unresectability formally, in writing, after dedicated hepatobiliary and transplant review of every alternative. Indications Preferred when Before any transplant referral. Permanent unresectability is a formal determination, not an impression: record why resection, margin-verified ablation, portal vein embolisation or liver venous deprivation, staged hepatectomy, ALPPS and hepatic arterial infusion each cannot achieve clearance at acceptable functional risk. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Referring on an impression, or treating a local complete response as an automatic transplant exception. Functional unresectability that may recover with a chemotherapy holiday and nutritional recovery is not yet permanent. lead: Keep the candidate inside protocol while waiting: review every 2–3 months and renew the exception every three months with CT/MRI of chest, abdomen and pelvis and CEA.
text: Standard Evidence D Keep the candidate inside protocol while waiting: review every 2–3 months and renew the exception every three months with CT/MRI of chest, abdomen and pelvis and CEA. Indications Preferred when Every listed or referred patient. Renewal requires no hepatic progression, no extrahepatic disease and CEA below 80 µg/L; exceptions generally need 90-day extensions, and the coordinator records source version, eligibility dates, request and extension dates, imaging, laboratory values and a named renewal owner, with transplant leadership signing the allocation assessment. Agree the surveillance and recurrence plan during selection, not after — recurrence after transplantation is common and predominantly pulmonary, often indolent and amenable to further local treatment. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let indefinite chemotherapy run while a candidate waits: it erodes nutrition, marrow, neurologic function and liver quality. Sustained control should prompt coordinated timing of definitive clearance rather than drift. Evidence & sources Two boundaries in the guidance need clarifying before filing: the initial exclusion is CEA above 80 while the renewal wording is below 80, so an exact value of 80 requires explicit review rather than an assumed pass; and footnotes 20–21 describe progression as more than a 10% increase in diameter or new lesions while labelling this RECIST 1.1, which differs from the usual target-lesion threshold. Preserve the source wording and flag it — do not silently substitute 20%. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Use the Oslo score, the largest lesion diameter and PET metabolic tumour volume as prognostic refinements inside the eligibility decision points, not as substitutes for them.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Use the Oslo score, the largest lesion diameter and PET metabolic tumour volume as prognostic refinements inside the eligibility decision points, not as substitutes for them. Indications Preferred when Counselling and protocol stratification. In the 61-patient Oslo cohort median overall survival was 60.3 months, with an Oslo score of 0 giving 5- and 10-year survival of 88.9% while a score of 3–4 gave 8.3% and 0%; a largest lesion of 5.5 cm or more gave 25.3 versus 92.0 months and CEA above 80 µg/L 26.6 versus 90.5 months. Metabolic tumour volume below 70 cm³ on PET gave 5- and 10-year survival of 76% and 50% versus 21% and 7%, and the signal held only when the scan was within 90 days of transplant. The SECA-II 10-year report gives median overall survival 128.2 months with 5-year 77.8% and 10-year 51.5% in 25 patients. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not relax the allocation decision points because the prognostic scores look good, and do not use a favourable score to justify listing outside the protocol. These are separate prognostic considerations and do not replace the pretreatment 10-cm limit or the CEA exclusion. Evidence & sources Graded D: these are one centre's thresholds tested in the patients they were derived from. The Oslo score was derived from the first 21 SECA-I patients, the 70 cm³ cut-off was defined by ROC analysis in the same 40-patient cohort in which it is then tested, the CEA 80 µg/L bar comes from SECA-I, and prognostic factors were tested one at a time by log-rank in 60 patients with no multivariable model and no correction for multiple testing. In the 19-patient score comparison every patient with a Fong score of 0–2 also had a metabolic tumour volume below 70 cm³ and an Oslo score of 0–2, so the three scores cannot be separated, and the PET signal held only when the scan was within 90 days of transplant. The SECA-II survival figures come from 25 highly selected patients at one centre — the authors' own simulation found only 2 to 3 eligible patients per year in a population of 5.5 million — with relapse in 48% at a median relapse-free survival of 24.3 months and one death from hepatic artery thrombosis (4% operative mortality). Survival calculated from transplant excludes the 11 of 72 listed patients never grafted; from listing, median overall survival for all 72 was 50.8 months with 5-year survival 42.6%. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

PET metabolic tumour volume <70 cm³ vs ≥70 cm³: 5-y OS 76% vs 21%, 10-y 50% vs 7% ROC cut-off set and tested in same 40-patient cohort; held only if PET ≤90 days pre-transplant

lead: Listing an MSI-high or mismatch-repair deficient patient on this exception route, even after a checkpoint response.
text: Avoid Evidence D Listing an MSI-high or mismatch-repair deficient patient on this exception route, even after a checkpoint response. Why Why If such a patient is to be considered at all, it requires a separate approved protocol with a written pre-transplant checkpoint-inhibitor policy, including washout and the approval route, agreed before any such patient is listed. Additional cautions Additional cautions The supplied exception route requires microsatellite stability, and IHPBA 2021 states that MSI-high and dMMR patients should not currently be considered for transplantation. Sustained checkpoint response does not create eligibility. Evidence & sources Graded D: the IHPBA exclusion rests on the risk of graft rejection if immunotherapy were needed after transplant rather than on transplant outcome data in these patients, its own reviewers call it the statement most likely to be overtaken, and ESMO 2026 sets no MSI exclusion at all. The checkpoint evidence does not settle it either: overall survival in CheckMate 8HW is still masked, treatment lines are masked, and no trial reports what happens to liver-limited dMMR disease taken to clearance. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Transplanting with any extrahepatic, nodal or peritoneal disease, or with an uncontrolled primary.
text: Avoid Evidence D Transplanting with any extrahepatic, nodal or peritoneal disease, or with an uncontrolled primary. Why Why Nothing. Treatable lung disease may still permit resection; it does not permit transplantation under current pathways. Additional cautions Additional cautions IHPBA 2021 finds no evidence to support transplantation in patients who present with extrahepatic disease, and the OPTN exclusions cover extrahepatic disease after primary resection, nodes outside the original primary nodal resection, local primary relapse and CEA above 80 µg/L. Undifferentiated or signet-ring histology excludes and N2 nodal disease is a relative exclusion. Any peritoneal disease ends transplant intent. Evidence & sources Graded D: this is a policy and consensus boundary, not a measured outcome difference. IHPBA 2021 records that it found no evidence to support transplantation in patients presenting with extrahepatic disease — an absence of evidence rather than evidence of harm — and every randomised and cohort series that reports survival excluded these patients by design, so no comparison exists. lead: Ad hoc listing without auditable criteria, a defined graft strategy or a recurrence plan.
text: Avoid Evidence D Ad hoc listing without auditable criteria, a defined graft strategy or a recurrence plan. Why Why A written protocol, a transplant-oncology MDT, a prospective registry and an agreed recurrence plan — the programme domain of the selection table. Additional cautions Additional cautions The roadmap names this the failure mode to avoid. A research or living-donor pathway outside the guidance criteria needs its own approved protocol and must not imply eligibility for this exception route.

lead: Record the intent as control, name the reassessment date, and restage before repeating any procedure.
text: Standard Evidence D Record the intent as control, name the reassessment date, and restage before repeating any procedure. Indications Preferred when Every control-intent decision: record the intended outcome, why the clearance alternatives do not fit, the systemic-treatment plan, the reassessment date and the next action. After progression or toxicity, restage and reconsider complete treatment rather than automatically repeating the same procedure. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not apply a fixed sequence of ablation, SBRT, Y90, TACE, HAI and histotripsy. An upfront alternative chosen for anatomy or organ reserve is not a post-progression second line, and there is no established priority between the transarterial options. Evidence & sources Protect what is left: remnant volume, vascular and biliary integrity, prior ablation zones, marrow and nutritional reserve, and the ability to treat recurrence. Clinical-trial eligibility is reassessed here too. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Y90 radioembolisation, second line EPOCH randomised 428 patients with disease progressing on first-line therapy: progression-free survival 8.0 versus 7.2 months, HR 0.69 (0.54–0.88), and hepatic progression-free survival 9.1 versus 7.2 months, HR 0.59 (0.46–0.77), both co-primary endpoints met.
text: Y90 radioembolisation, second line Evidence B EPOCH randomised 428 patients with disease progressing on first-line therapy: progression-free survival 8.0 versus 7.2 months, HR 0.69 (0.54–0.88), and hepatic progression-free survival 9.1 versus 7.2 months, HR 0.59 (0.46–0.77), both co-primary endpoints met. Indications Preferred when Chemotherapy-resistant or refractory liver-dominant disease, after review of the systemic and complete-treatment options, where hepatic control is the goal. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not offer it for survival: median overall survival was 14.0 versus 14.4 months, HR 1.07 (0.86–1.32). Grade 3 or worse events were 68.4% versus 49.3%, with three possibly related deaths from radiation-induced liver disease, hepatic failure and portal hypertension at 3 to 5 months — a real cost in hepatic reserve if later resection, ablation or transplantation is still conceivable. Assess any future HAI pathway before liver irradiation. Evidence & sources A positive trial on surrogate endpoints with a flat survival curve: the absolute progression-free survival gain was 0.8 months, the trial was not powered for survival, 28 of 215 patients (13%) assigned to radioembolisation never received it, and the control arm was not contemporary standard of care for RAS and BRAF wild-type disease (NRAS and BRAF were never tested and only 17% received a first-line EGFR inhibitor). It was sponsored by the device manufacturer, which supplied the device and collaborated on design, data collection and analysis, with a company employee as co-author. ASCO does not recommend SIRT routinely at all, judging harms to outweigh benefits on low-quality evidence. In the earlier 46-patient refractory trial, time to liver progression was 5.5 versus 2.1 months (HR 0.38) with no survival difference (10.0 versus 7.3 months), which the authors attribute to 10 of 23 control patients crossing over. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
