lead: TACE or DEBIRI May be considered in selected liver-dominant refractory CRLM by an experienced MDT. The only randomised data are a two-centre trial in 74 patients after two or three prior lines, which reported median overall survival 22 versus 15 months with DEBIRI against FOLFIRI (p=0.031) and progression-free survival 7 versus 4 months (p=0.006).
text: TACE or DEBIRI Evidence D May be considered in selected liver-dominant refractory CRLM by an experienced MDT. The only randomised data are a two-centre trial in 74 patients after two or three prior lines, which reported median overall survival 22 versus 15 months with DEBIRI against FOLFIRI (p=0.031) and progression-free survival 7 versus 4 months (p=0.006). Indications Preferred when Later-line selected hepatic control, or a trial, where reserve and biliary anatomy allow. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid It should not substitute for feasible resection or margin-complete ablation, and neither technical response nor debulking establishes curative benefit. Reserve and biliary infection risk matter. Evidence & sources Graded D: too weak to carry a survival claim. Seventy-four patients in a low-impact journal, with the authors framing it as sizing an effect for a larger trial; the FOLFIRI comparator had no oxaliplatin, bevacizumab or anti-EGFR agent and was capped at eight cycles while DEBIRI patients could be retreated, so the arms differ in intensity (70 procedures against 277 cycles) as well as route; response was scored by RECIST or EASL at investigator discretion in an open-label trial; and the report is internally inconsistent on two p values. Evidence and techniques across TACE are heterogeneous and there is no established universal priority over Y90, SBRT or HAI. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

text: Hepatic arterial infusion for unresectable liver-only disease Evidence C EXPERTISE CALGB 9481 randomised 135 patients with unresectable liver-only disease: median overall survival 24.4 versus 20.0 months (p=0.0034), hepatic response 47% versus 24% and time to hepatic progression 9.8 versus 7.3 months. Indications Preferred when Liver-only disease at a credentialed pump centre where hepatic control is the objective and conversion has not been achieved. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid No pump programme, extrahepatic disease, prior liver radiation or concurrent VEGF inhibition. Time to extrahepatic progression was shorter with HAI (7.7 versus 14.8 months) and overall time to progression did not differ, so the survival claim rests entirely on hepatic control. Cercek retrospective salvage series (PMID 27566258): 57 liver-only patients, response 33% and median OS 20 months; 53 with limited extrahepatic disease, response 36% and OS 11.4 months. lead: Histotripsy outside a prospective trial or institutional registry.
text: Avoid Evidence D Histotripsy outside a prospective trial or institutional registry. Why Why Only under a protocol or mandatory outcomes registry, with explicit consent about oncologic uncertainty, suitable ultrasound visibility and acoustic access, a device-compliant target size and depth, and an independent standard-treatment review. Additional cautions Additional cautions There is no tumour-specific curative evidence in CRLM. FDA device clearance for tumour destruction does not establish survival benefit or equivalence to established ablation; the HOPE4LIVER one-year update in 47 patients with 52 tumours reported local control of 63.4% on its prespecified primary core-laboratory assessment against 90% on a post hoc read made once all one-year imaging was available, with the two reads agreeing only 71–84% of the time. Median treated tumour diameter was 1.3 cm, 88% of tumours lay in segments II to IV and none in VII or VIII, 12-month overall survival among the metastatic patients was 48.6%, and treatments after day 30 were not tracked so no progression-free survival exists. A bridge-to-transplant use remains protocol-based, and a technical response does not establish transplant eligibility. Evidence & sources Do not count technical success as proven complete oncologic clearance. Single-arm with no comparator, funded by the device manufacturer, in a population that was 94% multifocal with half the metastatic patients carrying extrahepatic disease. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Single-arm, 47 pts/52 tumours: one-year local control 63.4% on prespecified primary core-lab read vs 90% post hoc (agreement 71–84%); 12-mo OS 48.6% in metastatic Manufacturer-funded; median tumour 1.3 cm, none in VII/VIII; no PFS data

lead: Extrapolating HCC segmentectomy cure claims, or any complete radiographic response, to oncologic clearance in CRLM.
text: Avoid Evidence D Extrapolating HCC segmentectomy cure claims, or any complete radiographic response, to oncologic clearance in CRLM. Why Why Nothing. Local control, complete radiographic response, complete pathologic necrosis in a treated lesion and overall survival are different outcomes, and bridge or downstaging treatment is recorded separately from definitive local treatment. Additional cautions Additional cautions Curative segmentectomy evidence is not established in CRLM, and a local complete response is not an automatic transplant exception.

lead: No imaging-only diagnosis. Histology is required before systemic therapy or tissue-defined transplant assessment. Selected clearly resectable masses may proceed directly to surgery after multidisciplinary review.
text: Standard Evidence B No imaging-only diagnosis. Histology is required before systemic therapy or tissue-defined transplant assessment. Selected clearly resectable masses may proceed directly to surgery after multidisciplinary review. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × There is no imaging-only diagnosis of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma: unlike hepatocellular carcinoma, where LR-5 imaging in an at-risk population is diagnostic, histologic confirmation is required before systemic therapy or a tissue-defined transplant assessment; selected clearly resectable masses may proceed directly to surgery after multidisciplinary review. Indications Preferred when Every patient whose next step is systemic therapy, trial entry or tissue-defined transplant assessment — in those destinations the tissue criteria are not optional, and transplant assessment additionally needs the biopsy to grade differentiation and to exclude a mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not demand a core from a high-suspicion, clearly resectable mass as a universal rule. NCCN states a suspicious mass on imaging in the proper clinical setting should be treated as malignant, and multidisciplinary HPB review may permit direct resection; the roadmap replaces universal pre-treatment biopsy with destination-specific confirmation. Evidence & sources AASLD 2023 and BSG 2023 require histological confirmation and LCSGJ 2022 regards biopsy as basically unnecessary for a typical resectable mass, so whether a core stays mandatory before resection is a local approval item (alignment worksheet, area 1). CEA and CA 19-9 are baseline and monitoring tests and never establish the diagnosis; CA 19-9 rises with biliary obstruction or cholangitis, so record it alongside the bilirubin and repeat it once the obstruction is relieved. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Complete staging and biliary imaging before non-emergency instrumentation. Measure the future liver remnant when major hepatectomy is being considered.
text: Standard Evidence B Complete staging and biliary imaging before non-emergency instrumentation. Measure the future liver remnant when major hepatectomy is being considered. Indications Preferred when Any patient with a tumour obstructing the biliary tree who might be resected — reactive change from a stent obscures ductal extent, which is exactly what decides whether biliary resection and reconstruction are needed. MRI is the study that characterises the biliary and vascular relationships that determine resectability, and EASL-ILCA prefers it over CT for intrahepatic staging. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not wait for imaging in cholangitis — that is drained without waiting for the discussion, and urgent sepsis treatment takes priority over the elective sequence. Evidence & sources Where the tumour obstructs the biliary tree, the need for drainage, its route and its side are decided with the hepatobiliary surgeon before any non-emergency procedure; resection without preoperative drainage can be considered when the future remnant is large. That drainage rule is grade D on its own — no comparative outcome data in intrahepatic disease were identified for it — while the grade B on this string covers the imaging sequence, which BSG 2023 and EASL-ILCA both recommend. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Exclude another primary before committing to this pathway, because metastatic adenocarcinoma can be histologically indistinguishable from intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.
text: Standard Evidence D Exclude another primary before committing to this pathway, because metastatic adenocarcinoma can be histologically indistinguishable from intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Indications Preferred when Any adenocarcinoma in the liver without an established primary, and particularly before a patient is started on a biliary-tract regimen or entered into a biliary trial. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let the immunohistochemical panel consume the whole core: BSG 2023 asks that tissue be reserved for molecular profiling when immunohistochemistry is planned, and whether to add that instruction is a local approval item (alignment worksheet, area 12). Evidence & sources Treating a colorectal or pancreatic metastasis as intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is a recognised and consequential error. Hepatitis B and C status and any cirrhosis are established at entry: they change operative risk and, where a mixed tumour is possible, the differential. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Describe every suspected tumor nodule by number, size, liver segment, and relationship to the main tumor. Distinguish liver-confined multifocal disease from regional nodal involvement and distant metastases.
text: Standard Evidence D Describe every suspected tumor nodule by number, size, liver segment, and relationship to the main tumor. Distinguish liver-confined multifocal disease from regional nodal involvement and distant metastases. Indications Preferred when Use the definitions in the “Multiple liver tumors” reference above. Confirm whether additional lesions are malignant when that uncertainty would change treatment. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not label all additional liver nodules as distant stage IV disease, assume satellites are harmless, or infer independent primary tumors from imaging alone. Evidence & sources The descriptions overlap biologically. Record imaging uncertainty and obtain expert radiology/pathology review rather than assigning a treatment solely from the label. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Plan molecular testing of a dedicated biliary specimen at the index ERCP where the disease presents as an indeterminate stricture rather than a mass and the alternative is a repeat procedure.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Plan molecular testing of a dedicated biliary specimen at the index ERCP where the disease presents as an indeterminate stricture rather than a mass and the alternative is a repeat procedure. Indications Preferred when The patient entering the pathway as an indeterminate stricture, where pathology alone is weakest: in a 6-year prospective study of 2,116 patients across 28 institutions, pathologic assessment of ERCP brushings and biopsies had 44% sensitivity overall and 36% for intrahepatic or hilar strictures, while a DNA/RNA sequencing panel on separately collected specimens in a dedicated nucleic-acid buffer reached 82% sensitivity at 98% specificity and the combination 88% at 97%. Specificity was 99% for pathology, so sequencing bought sensitivity and gave up almost nothing. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not read a negative molecular result as excluding malignancy — in the original single-centre cohort there were 37 false negatives (25%) and the negative predictive value was only 63%, with sampling failure the usual explanation; in 12 of those cases the same panel found an alteration in the resected tumour. Only 2% of neoplastic strictures in the 2026 study were purely dysplastic, so outside primary sclerosing cholangitis this is earlier diagnosis of established cancer, not early detection, and no resectability or survival benefit has been shown. Payer authorisation and the dedicated collection buffer have to be arranged before the procedure, not after. Evidence & sources Correct the yield figure: therapeutically relevant alterations were reported in 20 of 150 cancers (13%) in the original single-centre cohort, and in the 2026 multi-institutional study in 137 of 458 cholangiocarcinomas (30%) — but only on the 161-gene version of the panel. The 28-gene version used in the original cohort did not detect FGFR2 fusions at all, which with chromatin-remodelling genes accounts for up to 20% of intrahepatic tumours, so a biliary specimen substitutes for the clinical decision 2 profile only if the panel actually run reports fusions. Downgraded from B: specimens were submitted at the endoscopist's discretion rather than consecutively, a stricture could be classified neoplastic on 12 months of clinical or radiographic progression rather than on tissue, and all testing was done in the laboratory that developed the assay. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Original single-centre cohort: 37 false negatives (25%), NPV 63%; therapeutically relevant alterations in 20 of 150 cancers (13%) 28-gene panel did not detect FGFR2 fusions; negative result does not exclude malignancy

lead: Add FDG-PET selectively, for suspected occult spread and for transplant staging.
text: Reasonable Evidence B Add FDG-PET selectively, for suspected occult spread and for transplant staging. Indications Preferred when Where occult nodal or distant disease would change the operation, and in any patient being staged for a transplant protocol. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not substitute PET for MRI with MRCP in local planning; MRCP is preferred for biliary anatomy and ERCP or PTC are used more for therapeutic intervention. Evidence & sources BSG 2023 recommends FDG-PET-CT for nodal and distant disease as part of staging and EASL-ILCA recommends it routinely in apparently resectable patients, both more broadly than our selective wording — alignment worksheet, area 2. Read the strength of the broader recommendation honestly: the EASL-ILCA routine-PET statement passed its Delphi panel with only 78% agreement, the weakest consensus in that guideline's staging section, and AASLD 2023 states PET should not be used to assess the primary tumour. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not place a biliary stent in a potentially resectable patient before the biliary-protocol imaging is complete and the drainage plan is agreed with the hepatobiliary surgeon.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not place a biliary stent in a potentially resectable patient before the biliary-protocol imaging is complete and the drainage plan is agreed with the hepatobiliary surgeon. Why Why The only exception is cholangitis, which is drained immediately. Additional cautions Additional cautions Stent-related inflammation obscures ductal extent, and drainage of the wrong side or an unnecessary procedure adds cholangitis risk and can delay both surgery and systemic therapy. lead: Do not assign this pathway to perihilar or distal cholangiocarcinoma — the drainage problem, the operation and the transplant question all differ.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not assign this pathway to perihilar or distal cholangiocarcinoma — the drainage problem, the operation and the transplant question all differ. Why Why Use the separate perihilar roadmap; gallbladder cancer, mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma and paediatric disease are out of scope here. Additional cautions Additional cautions In particular, the standardised perihilar MELD exception and its neoadjuvant/stricture protocol do not transfer to intrahepatic disease. lead: Order broad molecular profiling at the diagnosis of unresectable or metastatic disease, not at the point of second-line progression.
text: Standard Evidence B Order broad molecular profiling at the diagnosis of unresectable or metastatic disease, not at the point of second-line progression. Indications Preferred when Everyone who will receive systemic therapy. The rationale is operational rather than biological: turnaround is typically two to four weeks, and a patient who progresses on first-line chemo-immunotherapy needs the result in hand at that moment. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Ordering it at progression means the second-line decision is made without it, and the default becomes FOLFOX by omission rather than by choice. The obstacle here is payer authorisation and ordering discipline, not the clinical argument. Evidence & sources Our grade B is lower than ESMO 2024's [I, A] and BSG 2023's strong recommendation on high-quality evidence. ILTS-ILCA 2024 recommends comprehensive sequencing in unresectable or metastatic iCCA but finds no evidence for using it to select transplant candidates. Capture NRG1 and other actionable findings on the same panel; do not label each matched agent category 1 merely because testing is recommended. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: FGFR2 fusion or rearrangement Preferred for a defined phenotype. Pemigatinib after prior systemic therapy, or futibatinib after gemcitabine–platinum. At final FIGHT-202 analysis, independently reviewed response was 37.0% with median progression-free survival 7.0 months and median overall survival 17.5 months in 108 patients; FOENIX-CCA2 gave response 42%, median progression-free survival 9.0 months and median overall survival 21.7 months in 103 patients.
text: FGFR2 fusion or rearrangement Evidence C Preferred for a defined phenotype. Pemigatinib after prior systemic therapy, or futibatinib after gemcitabine–platinum. At final FIGHT-202 analysis, independently reviewed response was 37.0% with median progression-free survival 7.0 months and median overall survival 17.5 months in 108 patients; FOENIX-CCA2 gave response 42%, median progression-free survival 9.0 months and median overall survival 21.7 months in 103 patients. Indications Preferred when Second line or later in a patient fit for an oral targeted agent, where the alteration reported is a fusion or rearrangement — 90% of FIGHT-202 and the whole of FOENIX-CCA2 was intrahepatic disease, so this is the alteration with the most directly applicable data. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not infer superiority over second-line chemotherapy: both trials are single-arm, neither has been compared with it, and The pemigatinib investigators explicitly warn against the cross-study comparison with pooled second-line chemotherapy (response 9.5%, progression-free survival 2.6 months) that makes the agent look better. Both drugs were approved on these single-arm data. Do not expect the alteration in an untested patient — 783 patients were screened to enrol 103 in FOENIX-CCA2, and 1,206 were prescreened to find 107 fusion-positive patients for FIGHT-202. Evidence & sources At the FIGHT-202 final analysis there were no objective responses in the cohorts with other FGF/FGFR alterations (0 of 20) or with none (0 of 17), so the effect is confined to the fusion and rearrangement class; with 20 and 17 patients that is a weak negative rather than proof. Hyperphosphataemia affected 58.5% on pemigatinib and 85% on futibatinib (grade 3 in 30%), and acquired kinase-domain resistance mutations emerged in those who shrank then progressed. Benefit is modest in absolute terms and FIGHT-302 has reported (PMID 42223137): 167 randomized patients, PFS 8.3 versus 6.8 months with pemigatinib versus GemCis (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.39–0.87; nominal P=.0078), without demonstrated OS benefit (24.4 versus 25.0 months). The trial closed early, permitted substantial crossover and did not compare against chemo-immunotherapy; it does not by itself establish a new first-line policy. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Single-arm, pemigatinib, FGFR2 fusion/rearrangement, n=108: independently reviewed ORR 37.0%, median PFS 7.0 mo, median OS 17.5 mo No comparison with second-line chemotherapy; 0 of 20 responses with other FGF/FGFR alterations
Single-arm, futibatinib, n=103: ORR 42%, median PFS 9.0 mo, median OS 21.7 mo No comparator; 783 screened to enrol 103

lead: IDH1 mutation Preferred for a defined phenotype, positioned on progression-free survival grounds only. ClarIDHy met its primary endpoint — median progression-free survival 2.7 versus 1.4 months, hazard ratio 0.37 — but the final intention-to-treat overall survival was 10.3 versus 7.5 months, hazard ratio 0.79 (95% CI 0.56–1.12), p=0.09, not significant, with 70% of placebo patients crossing over.
text: IDH1 mutation Evidence B Preferred for a defined phenotype, positioned on progression-free survival grounds only. ClarIDHy met its primary endpoint — median progression-free survival 2.7 versus 1.4 months, hazard ratio 0.37 — but the final intention-to-treat overall survival was 10.3 versus 7.5 months, hazard ratio 0.79 (95% CI 0.56–1.12), p=0.09, not significant, with 70% of placebo patients crossing over. Indications Preferred when A chemotherapy-refractory patient with an IDH1 mutation who understands that the benefit is disease stabilisation: objective response was 2% and the signal came from stable disease, 51% versus 28%. Physical functioning was better preserved than on placebo. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not promise surgical conversion: objective response was only 2%, and the trial did not test a conversion or transplant strategy. A response may still warrant MDT reassessment. The final crossover-adjusted OS estimate is model-dependent and, after the October 2026 correction, is HR 0.49 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.25–1.24), not a significant randomized survival result. Evidence & sources The comparator was placebo, not the active second-line standard, so the gain over mFOLFOX is unknown. Note the population when reading this into a liver pathway: only 9 of 185 patients (5%) had cirrhosis, 93% were metastatic and 90% of the ivosidenib arm had intrahepatic disease, so this is a non-cirrhotic metastatic cohort and nothing like a transplant or conversion candidate. Quality-of-life conclusions rest on change scores available for 62 of 113 ivosidenib and 20 of 52 placebo patients. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Ivosidenib vs placebo, primary endpoint met: median PFS 2.7 vs 1.4 mo, HR 0.37; objective response 2%; stable disease 51 vs 28% Placebo, not active second line; only 9 of 185 (5%) cirrhotic, 93% metastatic

Final ITT OS, ivosidenib vs placebo: 10.3 vs 7.5 mo, HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.56–1.12), p=0.09, not significant; 70% of placebo patients crossed over Crossover-adjusted HR 0.49 is model-based, not the trial result

lead: BRAF V600E Preferred for a defined phenotype. Dabrafenib plus trametinib: single-arm, 43 patients, response 51% by investigator and 47% by independent review, median progression-free survival 9 months and median overall survival 14 months — interim analysis.
text: BRAF V600E Evidence C Preferred for a defined phenotype. Dabrafenib plus trametinib: single-arm, 43 patients, response 51% by investigator and 47% by independent review, median progression-free survival 9 months and median overall survival 14 months — interim analysis. Indications Preferred when A previously treated patient with a centrally confirmable V600E mutation; 39 of the 43 patients (91%) had intrahepatic disease, so the population matches. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not expect the trial's 9% screening yield in practice — several sites entered already-known positives and the real rate is nearer 5–7%. Patients with bilirubin above three times normal or untreatable biliary obstruction were excluded, so this says nothing about the jaundiced patient. lead: HER2 amplification or overexpression Preferred for a defined phenotype. Zanidatamab: single-arm; at final analysis (median follow-up 33.4 months, 80 ERBB2-amplified patients) confirmed response was 41% (33 of 80, 95% CI 30–53) and median overall survival 15.5 months.
text: HER2 amplification or overexpression Evidence C Preferred for a defined phenotype. Zanidatamab: single-arm; at final analysis (median follow-up 33.4 months, 80 ERBB2-amplified patients) confirmed response was 41% (33 of 80, 95% CI 30–53) and median overall survival 15.5 months. Indications Preferred when An IHC 3+ tumour, where the activity is concentrated: response 52% (32 of 62) versus 6% (1 of 18) at IHC 2+, disease control 79% versus 33%, and median overall survival 18.1 versus 5.2 months — a post hoc split the authors themselves label as such. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not offer it on an IHC 2+ result as though the trial supported it, and do not read the 15.5-month survival as attributable to the drug: there was no control group and 44% of patients received further anticancer therapy afterwards. Evidence & sources Results are reported for biliary tract cancer as a whole with no breakdown by subsite, so the effect specifically in intrahepatic disease is unknown; HER2 is a minority of iCCA. ESMO 2024 also recommends considering trastuzumab deruxtecan for HER2 overexpression or amplification, which our table does not name — alignment worksheet, area 14. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Single-arm, 80 ERBB2-amplified: confirmed ORR 41% (95% CI 30–53), median OS 15.5 mo; post hoc IHC 3+ vs 2+: ORR 52% vs 6%, OS 18.1 vs 5.2 mo No control group; 44% had further therapy; no breakdown by subsite

lead: MSI-high or mismatch-repair deficient Preferred for a defined phenotype. Checkpoint blockade, consistent with tumour-agnostic practice.
text: MSI-high or mismatch-repair deficient Evidence C Preferred for a defined phenotype. Checkpoint blockade, consistent with tumour-agnostic practice. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not recycle checkpoint blockade without accounting for prior exposure to first-line durvalumab or pembrolizumab. text: NTRK fusion, RET fusion, other actionable alterations Evidence C Reasonable consideration. Capture on the same broad panel so a later line is not delayed by re-testing. lead: Use circulating tumour DNA when tissue is inadequate or the biopsy would delay treatment.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Use circulating tumour DNA when tissue is inadequate or the biopsy would delay treatment. Indications Preferred when The patient whose core is exhausted or whose repeat biopsy would push the start of treatment out by weeks. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not accept a negative plasma result as excluding a target — BSG 2023 notes DNA-based panels and most liquid biopsies are weaker at detecting fusions, so a negative plasma result should prompt tissue testing where it would change management. Evidence & sources Read the plasma figure for what it is: the FGFR2 fusion or rearrangement was detectable in plasma in 83 of 95 FOENIX-CCA2 patients tested (87%), but those patients were already known to be tissue-positive, so 87% is concordance in a positive population and not the chance of finding a target de novo in an unselected patient. No study in this disease reports the latter. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not defer profiling to the point of second-line progression.
text: Avoid Evidence B Do not defer profiling to the point of second-line progression. Why Why Order it at diagnosis of unresectable or metastatic disease; audit the proportion profiled before the second-line decision. Additional cautions Additional cautions The failure mode is not a wrong choice but no choice: the second-line decision gets made without the result, and FOLFOX becomes the default by omission. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Resection with regional lymphadenectomy The established curative standard. Hepatic resection with negative margins is the goal; major resections are often necessary but wedge and segmental resections are appropriate where a negative margin can be achieved, and a regional lymphadenectomy of the porta hepatis is carried out.
text: Resection with regional lymphadenectomy Evidence B The established curative standard. Hepatic resection with negative margins is the goal; major resections are often necessary but wedge and segmental resections are appropriate where a negative margin can be achieved, and a regional lymphadenectomy of the porta hepatis is carried out. Indications Preferred when Liver-confined disease where R0 is achievable with an adequate remnant and preserved or reconstructable biliary drainage, in a patient fit for the operation. Lymphadenectomy is part of the operation and informs the adjuvant decision in clinical decision 8 — nodal status is the main staging variable afterwards and clinical nodal staging is insensitive. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Multifocal disease across both lobes, additional malignant nodules that cannot all be safely resected, encasement precluding reconstruction, bilateral second-order biliary involvement, nodal disease beyond the regional basin, any extrahepatic disease, or reserve that makes the necessary resection unsafe. Evidence & sources Nodal status and tumour number dominate outcome: LCSGJ 2022 reports 5-year survival of 46.8%, 33.6% and 11.1% for one, two and three tumours, 63.4% for tumours under 2 cm, and 7–19% with nodal metastasis. The lymphadenectomy itself is the weak point in the evidence, not the resection: LCSGJ 2022 makes no recommendation on node dissection at all and warns that prophylactic dissection in cirrhosis increases complications, ESMO 2023 recommends routine hepatoduodenal-ligament dissection on level IV evidence, and neither BSG 2023 nor AASLD 2023 states an extent or a minimum node yield. Keeping it in every operation is a staging decision the programme has made, not a survival finding. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Guideline-reported 5-y survival 46.8%, 33.6% and 11.1% for one, two and three tumours; 63.4% for tumours <2 cm; 7–19% with nodal metastasis LCSGJ makes no recommendation on node dissection; no guideline sets an extent or node yield

lead: Definitive thermal ablation Potentially curative in a narrow nonsurgical group: solitary tumour under 3 cm with a complete safe margin. NCCN accepts thermal ablation for a small single primary or recurrent iCCA under 3 cm, particularly where surgery carries high risk; EASL-ILCA is narrower at single lesions under 2 cm, unresectable or inoperable, on low-level evidence.
text: Definitive thermal ablation Evidence C Potentially curative in a narrow nonsurgical group: solitary tumour under 3 cm with a complete safe margin. NCCN accepts thermal ablation for a small single primary or recurrent iCCA under 3 cm, particularly where surgery carries high risk; EASL-ILCA is narrower at single lesions under 2 cm, unresectable or inoperable, on low-level evidence. Indications Preferred when The small single lesion in a patient whose reserve or comorbidity makes resection unsuitable, where all disease can be treated with a margin of 5 mm or more and there is no uncontrolled nodal or distant disease. In a ten-centre propensity-matched cohort, microwave ablation gave 5-year overall survival of 44.8% versus 40.4% for resection (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.71–1.29, p=0.761), and when both ablative and surgical margins exceeded 5 mm disease-free survival was also similar (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.52–1.32, p=0.41). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid No safe margin obtainable, central bile duct injury risk, or disease left unaddressed. Do not extrapolate to large tumours or to more than one tumour: in meta-analysis, tumours over 3 cm (HR 2.12) and multiple tumours (HR 1.67) carried shorter survival, and pooled 5-year survival after ablation was 28.5%. Evidence & sources Disease-free survival in the matched cohort favoured resection overall (median 1.7 versus 3.6 years, HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.48–0.83, p=0.0010), with margin mediating 34.5% of that gap. Two cautions the cohort itself imposes. First, its entry criterion was Milan-equivalent — a single tumour up to 5 cm or up to three each 3 cm or less — so it does not validate our under-3 cm wording; within it, a 3–5 cm tumour was an independent risk factor for disease-free survival after ablation but not after resection, and resection also outperformed ablation in patients under 60, with hepatolithiasis, with left-lobe tumours and with GGT above 50 U/L. Second, the equivalence headline comes from a post hoc split at 2017 in which the later comparison was underpowered (p=0.129), and a nonsignificant difference is not equivalence. Ablation also yields no specimen and no nodal dissection, so the patient has no pathological node status to drive the clinical decision 8 decision, and node-negativity rests on imaging whose sensitivity for nodal metastasis is 20–61%. Agreeing the boundary — NCCN under 3 cm versus EASL-ILCA under 2 cm — is a local approval item. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Ablative radiotherapy for inoperable localized disease Selected definitive or consolidative treatment where the disease is localized but the patient is inoperable; cure evidence is limited. It may be selected directly on geometry and reserve — unsuccessful catheter therapy is not a prerequisite.
text: Ablative radiotherapy for inoperable localized disease Evidence C Selected definitive or consolidative treatment where the disease is localized but the patient is inoperable; cure evidence is limited. It may be selected directly on geometry and reserve — unsuccessful catheter therapy is not a prerequisite. Indications Preferred when Localized, liver-confined disease in a patient who cannot have an operation or an ablation, with adequate uninvolved liver, relieved biliary obstruction and safe gastrointestinal and biliary doses. A retrospective dose-response analysis of 79 patients found 3-year overall survival of 73% with a biologic equivalent dose above 80.5 Gy versus 38% below it (p=0.017) and 3-year local control 78% versus 45% (p=0.04); a multi-institutional phase II proton study reported 2-year local control of 94.1% in its 39 iCCA patients with grade 3 toxicity in 7.7%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Insufficient uninvolved liver, unrelieved biliary obstruction, overlapping prior dose or refractory ascites. For bulky disease, coordinate systemic therapy rather than replacing it by default. Evidence & sources Both datasets are nonrandomised and selected. Only 19 of 79 patients received the high dose, and that group also had significantly smaller planning target volumes (median 415 versus 614 cm³, p=0.02), so more favourable anatomy is confounded with dose; dose escalation is further confounded with era and image guidance, since patients treated after 2010 survived 50 versus 24 months (p=0.007). The proton cohort had no prespecified efficacy hypothesis at all — it was enrolled alongside a hepatocellular cohort for precision of estimates — its median delivered dose was 58.0 GyE against an intended 67.5 GyE, every local failure occurred below 60 GyE, local failures kept accruing past the 2-year landmark (six in 39) and 53.8% developed distant metastases. Dose-response associations do not prove cure or equivalence to resection. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Retrospective, 79 pts: BED >80.5 Gy vs below, 3-y OS 73% vs 38% (p=0.017); 3-y local control 78% vs 45% (p=0.04) Only 19 of 79 high dose, with smaller target volumes and later era — confounded
Multi-institutional phase II proton study, 39 iCCA: 2-y local control 94.1%; grade 3 toxicity 7.7% No prespecified efficacy hypothesis; median dose 58.0 vs intended 67.5 GyE; 53.8% distant mets

lead: Consider resection for limited multifocal disease only in highly selected cases, as an explicit exception rather than a rule.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Consider resection for limited multifocal disease only in highly selected cases, as an explicit exception rather than a rule. Indications Preferred when Unilobar limited multifocal disease in a fit patient where an R0 clearance with an adequate remnant is genuinely achievable — EASL-ILCA suggests resection may be considered in selected patients with multifocal unilobar iCCA (weak recommendation), and LCSGJ 2022 accepts resection for some node-positive patients. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid NCCN generally considers multifocal liver disease to represent intrahepatic metastatic spread and advises against resection except in highly selected limited disease. This does not mean distant M1: multiple intrahepatic tumors meet AJCC8 T2 unless higher T features apply. Do not turn a narrow exception into unrestricted eligibility; additional malignant nodules that cannot all be safely resected should prompt assessment for conversion treatment (clinical decision 4) or management of unresectable liver-confined disease (clinical decision 5). Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Consider neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy where the disease is technically resectable but only an R1 resection looks achievable.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Consider neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy where the disease is technically resectable but only an R1 resection looks achievable. Indications Preferred when The technically challenging but resectable tumour where the surgeon's honest assessment is that the margin will be positive — EASL-ILCA considers this (weak recommendation, 92% consensus), and BSG 2023 recommends multidisciplinary re-discussion of curative resection in locally advanced disease that responds well. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Not in clearly resectable disease, where the roadmap places neoadjuvant therapy off protocol in the Avoid column and BSG 2023 does not recommend routine neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Record the obstacle to R0 and the reassessment date, exactly as in clinical decision 4. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Systemic therapy with a scheduled surgical reassessment at 2–3 months. The obstacle to R0 and what would have to change must both be recorded.
text: Standard Evidence C Systemic therapy with a scheduled surgical reassessment at 2–3 months. The obstacle to R0 and what would have to change must both be recorded. Indications Preferred when Borderline or locally advanced liver-confined disease in a patient fit for chemo-immunotherapy, where conversion is a declared goal rather than a hope. Reassessment at the pre-declared point is a formal surgical re-review, not an imaging report alone. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not run conversion therapy open-endedly. If R0 is not achievable at the reassessment, say so and record that the goal has changed from conversion to control — that is the decision the board has to make. Evidence & sources The conversion figures are weaker than they sound. The rates of 36.4% and 53% come from retrospective Japanese series quoted by LCSGJ 2022, which in the same breath records no evidence of benefit for neoadjuvant chemotherapy and makes no recommendation; the denominators are not defined and the series report median survival of 24.1 months in converted patients against 25.7 months in those primarily resectable. AASLD 2023 states the role of neoadjuvant downstaging is not well defined, and BSG 2023 does not recommend routine neoadjuvant chemotherapy. The roadmap grades this pathway C for those reasons. Note also that neither chemo-immunotherapy trial supports it: TOPAZ-1 and KEYNOTE-966 were 86% and 89% metastatic and neither says anything about downstaging. lead: Hepatic arterial infusion plus systemic chemotherapyEXPERTISE Conversion or hepatic control in an approved expert programme, generally with systemic therapy; no established cure as monotherapy. In a single-arm, single-institution phase 2 study of 38 treated patients, HAI floxuridine with systemic gemcitabine–oxaliplatin gave partial response in 22 of 38 (58%) and 6-month progression-free survival of 84.1% against an 80% target, with median progression-free survival 11.8 months and median overall survival 25.0 months, and four patients went on to resection.
text: Hepatic arterial infusion plus systemic chemotherapy Evidence C EXPERTISE Conversion or hepatic control in an approved expert programme, generally with systemic therapy; no established cure as monotherapy. In a single-arm, single-institution phase 2 study of 38 treated patients, HAI floxuridine with systemic gemcitabine–oxaliplatin gave partial response in 22 of 38 (58%) and 6-month progression-free survival of 84.1% against an 80% target, with median progression-free survival 11.8 months and median overall survival 25.0 months, and four patients went on to resection. Indications Preferred when Liver-confined unresectable disease with favourable arterial anatomy in a centre with a functioning pump programme, where conversion or durable hepatic control is the stated goal. It can be considered early rather than only after a systemic line fails. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid No dedicated pump programme; distant extrahepatic metastases; unrelieved biliary obstruction or infection; unsuitable arterial/perfusion anatomy or inadequate hepatic reserve. Selected resectable regional nodal disease was included in HAI evidence and is distinct from distant spread. This does not change transplant eligibility. Avoid concurrent bevacizumab with FUDR. Evidence & sources Grade 4 toxicity forcing withdrawal occurred in 4 of 38 (11%) of the phase 2 cohort (portal hypertension, two gastroduodenal artery aneurysms, pump-pocket infection), grade 3 ALT in 42% and AST in 34%, and 11% needed biliary stents, two for chemotherapy-induced biliary sclerosis. Delivery decayed: 71% received the expected floxuridine dose over the first 3 months but only 47% over the next 6. The cohort was heavily selected — 38 of 84 screened, median tumour 8.3 cm — and the comparison is with historical systemic series; the linked JAMA Oncology editorial judged the case for locoregional therapy in unresectable cholangiocarcinoma still unsettled without a randomised trial. A retrospective single-centre comparison gave median overall survival of 30.8 months with HAI plus systemic therapy versus 18.4 months with systemic therapy alone in liver-confined disease, but all HAI patients were surgically staged and only 42% of the comparator was, so stage migration favours HAI; the comparator was 26 patients of whom only 30% had gemcitabine–cisplatin, and 44 of the 93 HAI patients came from two previously reported phase 2 trials. In that whole series only 8 of 236 patients (3%) converted to a curative-intent resection. PUMP-2 (PMID 41082695), a three-centre nonrandomized phase II study: 50 pumps placed, 48 patients started HAI, partial response 44%, six-month disease control 84%, resection 5/50 (10%), median OS 22.3 months and three-year OS 31.5%. The 2026 pooled analysis of four phase II trials (PMID 42331230) reports 142 treated patients, median OS 26 months, five-year OS 15% (ITT 14%), and 13/142 resections (9%). The pooled cohorts overlap the constituent trials; these are not independent replications or randomized comparisons with modern chemo-immunotherapy. lead: Y90 radioembolisation with first-line chemotherapyEXPERTISE Control or conversion with selected ablative use under expert review; curative evidence is emerging, not established. MISPHEC, a single-arm phase II study of 41 patients, combined Y90 with gemcitabine–cisplatin: response at 3 months was 39% by investigator assessment and 41% centrally, 9 patients (22%) were downstaged to surgery and 8 (20%) achieved an R0 resection, with median overall survival 22 months.
text: Y90 radioembolisation with first-line chemotherapy Evidence C EXPERTISE Control or conversion with selected ablative use under expert review; curative evidence is emerging, not established. MISPHEC, a single-arm phase II study of 41 patients, combined Y90 with gemcitabine–cisplatin: response at 3 months was 39% by investigator assessment and 41% centrally, 9 patients (22%) were downstaged to surgery and 8 (20%) achieved an R0 resection, with median overall survival 22 months. Indications Preferred when Liver-dominant unresectable disease in a non-cirrhotic patient with personalised dosimetry available, where conversion is the explicit plan — among the 27 patients with disease confined to one hemiliver, 8 (30%) were resected. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Cirrhosis above all: hepatic failure occurred in 9 of 12 cirrhotic patients (75%), irreversible in 5, versus 5 of 29 (17%) without cirrhosis, all reversible, and every irreversible case had whole-liver treatment. The trial's authors advise against radioembolisation plus chemotherapy in cirrhosis. Also avoid with inadequate future remnant or an unsafe shunt fraction. Evidence & sources Those results do not prove Y90 alone is curative, and grade 3–4 toxicity affected 29 of 41 patients (71%). The conversion figures describe a doubly selected cohort: 4 of 45 patients were excluded at the planning angiogram and 9 of 41 had major protocol deviations, leaving 32 per protocol. The trial was run only at centres experienced with glass microspheres and was part-funded by the microsphere manufacturer, with several authors as its consultants; the authors state tumour-absorbed dose rather than a generic liver dose probably drives outcome, so the regimen does not transfer as written. Two patients whose disease stayed unresectable but controlled were offered transplant and both recurred, at 16 and 17 months. The NCCN discussion of a tumour dose above 205 Gy is distinct from hepatocellular segment-dose thresholds. Payer authorisation and dosimetry capability are local dependencies, and the confirmatory randomised SIRCCA trial has not reported. lead: Systemic therapy is the backbone: gemcitabine and cisplatin with durvalumab, or with pembrolizumab.
text: Standard Evidence B Systemic therapy is the backbone: gemcitabine and cisplatin with durvalumab, or with pembrolizumab. Indications Preferred when Every patient fit for it. The regimens and the fitness question are in clinical decision 9; what this assessment settles is that systemic therapy is the backbone and any liver-directed treatment is added to it, not substituted for it. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid A patient whose performance status, renal or hepatic function, or contraindication to checkpoint inhibition rules out the full regimen still gets a systemic plan, modified with the reason recorded — not a catheter instead. Evidence & sources Downgraded from A. The two trials that carry the grade did not study this assessment's population. TOPAZ-1 was 86% metastatic and KEYNOTE-966 89%, both restricted to ECOG 0–1, and the TOPAZ-1 investigators state explicitly that the trial says nothing about neoadjuvant, downstaging or peri-transplant use in liver-confined disease, which is where this regimen is now borrowed. Grade A remains right for clinical decision 9, where the population matches. Clinical trial eligibility is checked at diagnosis and at each progression — Standard, grade D. lead: Radioembolisation or chemoembolisation Hepatic control. Liver-dominant disease with hepatic control as the goal, portal flow preserved and dosimetry planning available. Median overall survival was 22 months with Y90 plus gemcitabine–cisplatin in a 41-patient phase II, and 20 months from diagnosis in a 62-patient two-centre chemoembolisation cohort, where the 18 patients who also had systemic chemotherapy survived 28 versus 16 months (HR 1.94, p=0.02).
text: Radioembolisation or chemoembolisation Evidence C Hepatic control. Liver-dominant disease with hepatic control as the goal, portal flow preserved and dosimetry planning available. Median overall survival was 22 months with Y90 plus gemcitabine–cisplatin in a 41-patient phase II, and 20 months from diagnosis in a 62-patient two-centre chemoembolisation cohort, where the 18 patients who also had systemic chemotherapy survived 28 versus 16 months (HR 1.94, p=0.02). Indications Preferred when Hepatic-dominant disease where selective delivery and reserve are adequate and the goal is stated as control, with the systemic plan running alongside. Procedural safety was the strongest chemoembolisation finding: major complications after 5 of 165 procedures (3%), 0% 30-day disease-specific mortality. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Substitution for systemic therapy; use while extrahepatic disease progresses; inadequate future remnant or unsafe shunt fraction; biliary obstruction and infection risk. Avoid radioembolisation plus chemotherapy in cirrhosis, where hepatic failure occurred in 75% of cirrhotic patients and was irreversible in 5. Evidence & sources The chemoembolisation evidence is heterogeneous and nonrandomised — 40% of that cohort had adenocarcinoma of unknown primary rather than proven cholangiocarcinoma, 11% had a prior hepatectomy, 27% had no evaluable imaging follow-up, and the regimen (an ethiodol and polyvinyl alcohol emulsion of cisplatin, doxorubicin and mitomycin) predates drug-eluting beads, Y90 and gemcitabine–cisplatin. Do not read the 28 versus 16 months as an effect of adding chemotherapy: only 18 of 62 patients received it, at their own oncologists' discretion, so those were by definition the fitter patients. None of this has evidence equivalent to resection or small-tumour ablation for eradication, and there is no proven preferred sequence among TACE, Y90, HAI and ablative radiotherapy. For bulky disease, coordinate systemic therapy rather than replacing it by default. lead: Thermal ablation Potentially curative intent in a narrow group: solitary tumour under 3 cm with a complete safe margin. Pooled survival after ablation across 20 retrospective studies and 917 patients was 82.4% at 1 year, 42.1% at 3 years and 28.5% at 5 years, with technical efficacy 91.9% and major complications 5.7%.
text: Thermal ablation Evidence C Potentially curative intent in a narrow group: solitary tumour under 3 cm with a complete safe margin. Pooled survival after ablation across 20 retrospective studies and 917 patients was 82.4% at 1 year, 42.1% at 3 years and 28.5% at 5 years, with technical efficacy 91.9% and major complications 5.7%. Indications Preferred when The small solitary lesion in a patient unsuitable for resection, where every lesion can be covered with a margin. It is a selected definitive alternative, not automatically a second systemic line. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid No safe margin, central bile duct injury risk, or unaddressed disease; tumours over 3 cm and multiple tumours did worse (HR 2.12 and 1.67). Do not extrapolate to large or multifocal iCCA. Evidence & sources The pooled figures are fragile: all 20 studies were retrospective, heterogeneity reached I² 85% at 1 year, Egger testing showed publication bias in the 3-year pooling (p=0.039), and disease control was short-lived even when ablation worked — pooled recurrence-free survival was 40.0% at 1 year and 19.2% at 3 years. The 3 cm threshold rests on a dichotomised study-level variable with no individual patient data, unadjusted for margin, nodal status or liver function, and the authors' own comparison of their 28.5% pooled 5-year survival with a 30% figure from a separate resection meta-analysis carries no adjustment for stage, candidacy or era. lead: Gemcitabine and cisplatin plus durvalumab (TOPAZ-1) Overall survival hazard ratio 0.80 (95% CI 0.66–0.97), median 12.8 versus 11.5 months, with 24-month survival 24.9% versus 10.4% in 685 patients. In the intrahepatic subgroup (n=383) the hazard ratio was 0.76 (0.58–0.98).
text: Gemcitabine and cisplatin plus durvalumab (TOPAZ-1) Evidence A Overall survival hazard ratio 0.80 (95% CI 0.66–0.97), median 12.8 versus 11.5 months, with 24-month survival 24.9% versus 10.4% in 685 patients. In the intrahepatic subgroup (n=383) the hazard ratio was 0.76 (0.58–0.98). Indications Preferred when A patient fit for platinum and for checkpoint inhibition who wants the regimen with the longer tail: almost all of the benefit accrues after 6 months (hazard ratio 0.91 up to 6 months, 0.74 thereafter), and gemcitabine is capped at eight cycles. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Active or prior autoimmune or inflammatory disorders, or any contraindication to checkpoint inhibition. Do not promise the median — the absolute gain in median survival is 1.3 months, the proportional-hazards assumption was formally violated on kernel-smoothed and log-log plots so a single hazard ratio misrepresents a time-varying effect, and this was a prespecified interim analysis at 424 of 496 planned deaths, powered to about 75%. The 24-month figures are Kaplan-Meier estimates, not counted survivors. Evidence & sources Benefit did not track PD-L1 expression (hazard ratio 0.79 at tumour area positivity of 1% or more, 0.86 below 1%), and MSI status was missing for about half the cohort, with only 5 of 333 evaluable patients MSI-high, so the possibility that a small hypermutated subset carries the signal is answered by argument rather than data. Responses were investigator-assessed with no central review. Ampullary cancer was excluded and 86% of patients were metastatic, so the trial says nothing about neoadjuvant, downstaging or peri-transplant use. Point estimates were better in locally advanced than metastatic disease (0.49 versus 0.83) but the trial was not sized for subgroups and no multiplicity adjustment was made, so that cannot be acted on. text: Gemcitabine and cisplatin plus pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE-966) Evidence A Median overall survival 12.7 versus 10.9 months, hazard ratio 0.83 (95% CI 0.72–0.95) in 1069 patients, with 24-month survival 25% versus 18%. The intrahepatic subgroup (n=633) carried the effect: hazard ratio 0.76 (0.64–0.91), against 0.99 extrahepatic and 0.96 gallbladder. Indications Preferred when A patient fit for checkpoint inhibition where gemcitabine continued to progression without a cycle cap suits the plan, and where the largest intrahepatic dataset is the reassurance wanted. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Contraindication to checkpoint inhibition, or prior systemic therapy for advanced disease. The absolute gain is 1.8 months of median survival, and both supporting endpoints failed their prespecified boundaries — progression-free survival hazard ratio 0.86 (p=0.023 against 0.0125) and objective response 29% versus 29% (p=0.47) — so the benefit rests on overall survival with no response signal behind it. Treatment-related deaths were 8 (2%) versus 3 (1%), immune-mediated events 22% versus 13%, and quality of life did not improve (EORTC QLQ-C30 global health change −2.5 in both arms). Evidence & sources There is no usable predictive biomarker: the effect was the same below and above a PD-L1 combined positive score of 1 and only 10 MSI-high patients enrolled, so every patient is exposed to immune toxicity without a way to select. Crossover was not permitted and 89% were metastatic, so the trial says nothing about perioperative or conversion strategy. Objective response was 5% and disease control 33%, so this is not a conversion strategy. Evidence & sources 72 of 162 patients (44%) in ABC-06 had intrahepatic disease. More FOLFOX patients were platinum resistant or refractory (67% versus 58%), which cuts against the treatment arm rather than for it. The trial predates molecular selection and first-line chemo-immunotherapy, both of which change who would now be offered FOLFOX second line. lead: Assign the treatment intent before choosing a device. Curative intent means an attempt to eradicate all known cancer; it does not establish a cure rate.
text: Standard Evidence D Assign the treatment intent before choosing a device. Curative intent means an attempt to eradicate all known cancer; it does not establish a cure rate. Indications Preferred when Every liver-directed decision. Local control, complete radiographic response, complete pathologic necrosis in a treated lesion, and overall survival are different outcomes; conflating hepatic control with cure is the commonest reasoning error here. Bridge and downstaging preserve a later transplant or resection opportunity and are recorded separately from definitive local treatment. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not apply a fixed ablation > SBRT > Y90 > TACE > HAI > histotripsy sequence, and do not treat an upfront alternative chosen because of anatomy or organ reserve as a post-progression second line. Evidence & sources The categories in the selector are a clinical synthesis, not a new formal evidence-grading system. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Resection Goal: curative. Standard in the selector. Fits R0 achievable, liver-confined, adequate remnant and biliary drainage, fit patient.
text: Resection Evidence B Goal: curative. Standard in the selector. Fits R0 achievable, liver-confined, adequate remnant and biliary drainage, fit patient. Indications Preferred when The established curative standard whenever the anatomy and the reserve allow it — clinical decision 3. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Multifocal disease; nodal disease beyond the regional basin; inadequate remnant; any extrahepatic disease. lead: Hepatic arterial infusionEXPERTISE Goal: hepatic control or conversion. Preferred for a defined phenotype. Fits liver-confined unresectable disease, favourable arterial anatomy, with durable hepatic control or conversion as the stated goal. NCCN permits HAI in trials or experienced centres for carefully selected patients.
text: Hepatic arterial infusion Evidence C EXPERTISE Goal: hepatic control or conversion. Preferred for a defined phenotype. Fits liver-confined unresectable disease, favourable arterial anatomy, with durable hepatic control or conversion as the stated goal. NCCN permits HAI in trials or experienced centres for carefully selected patients. Indications Preferred when An approved expert programme with pump and arterial expertise, biliary toxicity monitoring and systemic coverage; it can be considered early rather than as a generic second line. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid No dedicated pump programme; distant extrahepatic metastases; unrelieved biliary obstruction or infection; unsuitable arterial/perfusion anatomy or inadequate hepatic reserve. Selected resectable regional nodal disease was included in HAI evidence and is distinct from distant spread. This does not change transplant eligibility. Avoid concurrent bevacizumab with FUDR. Evidence & sources PUMP-2 (PMID 41082695), a three-centre nonrandomized phase II study: 50 pumps placed, 48 patients started HAI, partial response 44%, six-month disease control 84%, resection 5/50 (10%), median OS 22.3 months and three-year OS 31.5%. The 2026 pooled analysis of four phase II trials (PMID 42331230) reports 142 treated patients, median OS 26 months, five-year OS 15% (ITT 14%), and 13/142 resections (9%). The pooled cohorts overlap the constituent trials; these are not independent replications or randomized comparisons with modern chemo-immunotherapy. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: SBRT or proton therapy Goal: selected definitive or consolidative local treatment. Reasonable consideration. Fits localized inoperable disease; cure evidence limited. Some of the evidence uses longer hypofractionated photon or proton schedules, not only 3–5-fraction SBRT.
text: SBRT or proton therapy Evidence C Goal: selected definitive or consolidative local treatment. Reasonable consideration. Fits localized inoperable disease; cure evidence limited. Some of the evidence uses longer hypofractionated photon or proton schedules, not only 3–5-fraction SBRT. Indications Preferred when May be selected directly on geometry and reserve; an unsuccessful catheter therapy is not a prerequisite. Requires adequate liver reserve, biliary drainage and safe gastrointestinal and biliary doses. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Insufficient uninvolved liver; unrelieved biliary obstruction; overlapping prior dose; refractory ascites. For bulky unresectable disease, coordinate systemic therapy rather than replacing it by default. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Radioembolisation or chemoembolisation Goal: hepatic control. Reasonable consideration. Fits liver-dominant disease with hepatic control as the goal, portal flow preserved and dosimetry planning available. Y90 may also be used in a planned conversion strategy.
text: Radioembolisation or chemoembolisation Evidence C Goal: hepatic control. Reasonable consideration. Fits liver-dominant disease with hepatic control as the goal, portal flow preserved and dosimetry planning available. Y90 may also be used in a planned conversion strategy. Indications Preferred when Selected hepatic-dominant disease where selective delivery and reserve are adequate, with personalised dosimetry and the systemic plan running alongside. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Substituted for systemic therapy; used while extrahepatic disease progresses; inadequate future remnant or unsafe shunt fraction. Cirrhosis is the hard stop for radioembolisation plus chemotherapy — hepatic failure in 75% of cirrhotic patients, irreversible in 5 of 12. Evidence & sources Evidence is heterogeneous and generally nonrandomised; no proven preferred sequence exists among TACE, Y90, HAI and ablative radiotherapy. Personalised dosimetry capability and payer authorisation are local dependencies. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Thermal ablation Goal: potentially curative intent in a narrow group. Reasonable consideration. Fits solitary tumour under 3 cm with a complete safe margin; EASL-ILCA is narrower at under 2 cm. Central ducts often limit feasibility.
text: Thermal ablation Evidence C Goal: potentially curative intent in a narrow group. Reasonable consideration. Fits solitary tumour under 3 cm with a complete safe margin; EASL-ILCA is narrower at under 2 cm. Central ducts often limit feasibility. Indications Preferred when A small lesion when resection is unsuitable, with all disease treated to a safe margin and no uncontrolled nodal or distant disease; also at a first intrahepatic recurrence, where microwave ablation gave median overall survival 29.8 versus 34.0 months against repeat resection (HR 0.89, p=0.31) with major complications in 5.5% versus 31.3%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid No safe margin, central bile duct injury risk, or unaddressed disease. Evidence is mainly retrospective and weaker than in hepatocellular carcinoma or colorectal liver metastases; do not extrapolate to large or multifocal iCCA. Document why the patient fits the narrower evidence base. Evidence & sources At recurrence, repeat resection gave better disease-free survival in four strata: large-duct subtype, no complication at the initial resection, a disease-free interval under 12 months, and a margin under 5 mm. Read the recurrence comparison as the authors do: the 4-month difference in median overall survival was not significant but they call it clinically noteworthy and state the study cannot exclude a real difference, 18.0% of the cohort was lost to follow-up and censored, treatment was chosen by tumour board and patient preference, the repeat-resection arm was only 119 patients, and liver function and quality of life — the outcomes that would most favour ablation — were not measured. All ten centres were Chinese tertiary hospitals with operators averaging a decade of independent ablation experience, so the 5.5% major complication rate may not transfer. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Liver transplantationPROTOCOL REGISTRY Goal: total clearance. Trial or registry only. The best-characterised setting is a single tumour of 2 cm or less first diagnosed on cirrhotic explant pathology, most having been seen before transplant as presumed hepatocellular carcinoma — 15 patients in the index series, and mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma was excluded from it.
text: Liver transplantation Evidence C PROTOCOL REGISTRY Goal: total clearance. Trial or registry only. The best-characterised setting is a single tumour of 2 cm or less first diagnosed on cirrhotic explant pathology, most having been seen before transplant as presumed hepatocellular carcinoma — 15 patients in the index series, and mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma was excluded from it. Indications Preferred when Only inside a formally approved protocol with review-board approval and registry entry — clinical decision 10. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Multifocal or larger disease outside a protocol; any extrahepatic disease; no registry entry. A technical response does not establish transplant eligibility. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: HistotripsyPROTOCOL REGISTRY Investigational oncologic role: no tumour-specific curative evidence in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Consider only under a prospective trial or institutional registry, with explicit consent about oncologic uncertainty, suitable ultrasound visibility and acoustic access, device-compliant target size and depth, and an independent standard-treatment review.
text: Histotripsy Evidence D PROTOCOL REGISTRY Investigational oncologic role: no tumour-specific curative evidence in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Consider only under a prospective trial or institutional registry, with explicit consent about oncologic uncertainty, suitable ultrasound visibility and acoustic access, device-compliant target size and depth, and an independent standard-treatment review. Indications Preferred when Nothing outside a protocol. In the one-year update of the pivotal experience, local control was 63.4% on the primary assessment versus 90% post hoc in 47 patients with 52 tumours. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid FDA device clearance for tumour destruction does not establish survival benefit or equivalence to established ablation. Be particularly cautious around central biliary structures and prior instrumentation; a bridge-to-transplant use remains protocol-based. text: Reasonable Evidence D Record the decision in the form the registry can audit: intended outcome, why the alternatives fit or do not fit, the systemic-treatment plan, the reassessment date and the next action. Indications Preferred when Every liver-directed case, because the unresolved questions above can only be answered from the programme's own data — modality, goal, hepatic progression-free survival and change in liver function. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid A note that records the device but not the goal makes the case useless for the registry and leaves the next team unable to tell a bridge from a definitive treatment. lead: Do not treat a complete local response as cure, or as a transplant exception.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not treat a complete local response as cure, or as a transplant exception. Why Why Reassess at 8–12 weeks allowing for the delayed response pattern after radiation-based therapy; nonprogression is not treatment failure. Additional cautions Additional cautions A local complete response is not an automatic transplant exception, and a technical response does not establish transplant eligibility. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Discuss adjuvant therapy with the BILCAP limitations: its primary intention-to-treat survival analysis was not statistically significant.
text: Standard Evidence B Discuss adjuvant therapy with the BILCAP limitations: its primary intention-to-treat survival analysis was not statistically significant. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Have the adjuvant conversation with the numbers in front of you: BILCAP's intention-to-treat primary analysis did not meet statistical significance — median overall survival 51.1 versus 36.4 months, adjusted hazard ratio 0.81 (95% CI 0.63–1.04), p=0.097. Indications Preferred when Every patient being offered capecitabine. Significance appeared in the prespecified intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis adjusted for nodal status, tumour grade and sex (hazard ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.55–0.92, p=0.010) and in the per-protocol analysis (hazard ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.58–0.97, p=0.028); the trial was unmasked. Say both halves. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not present it as settled. Only 84 of 447 patients (19%) had intrahepatic disease and the trial was not powered for site-specific effects, so the iCCA-specific benefit is unproven; LCSGJ 2022 reports no significant benefit in the intrahepatic subgroup, while EASL-ILCA cites an iCCA hazard ratio of 0.65 — the best of the subtypes — and still grades the recommendation on a trial that was negative on intention to treat. Evidence & sources Lymphadenectomy was not mandated for intrahepatic patients in BILCAP, yet nodal status is one of the covariates that turns the sensitivity analysis positive. Recurrence-free survival favoured capecitabine over the first 24 months (median 24.4 versus 17.5 months, adjusted hazard ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.58–0.98, p=0.033) with no difference from 24 to 60 months (hazard ratio 1.48, 0.80–2.77, p=0.21), which the authors read as deferred rather than prevented recurrence. Recruitment ran nearly nine years with no fully defined analysis plan at the outset and the monitoring committee had to reset the event target when survival on observation proved far better than assumed. Two guideline readings of the same subgroup conflict and should not be presented as two datasets: LCSGJ 2022 reports no significant benefit in the intrahepatic subgroup while EASL-ILCA cites an iCCA hazard ratio of 0.65 as the best of the subtypes — both are unpowered subgroup estimates from the trial that was negative on intention to treat. NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026 designates capecitabine preferred, category 1, while acknowledging the nonsignificant intention-to-treat analysis; our Reasonable consideration is deliberately more cautious and requires explicit multidisciplinary local approval (alignment worksheet, area 11). Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Capecitabine vs observation: ITT median OS 51.1 vs 36.4 mo, adjusted HR 0.81 (95% CI 0.63–1.04), p=0.097 — primary endpoint not met Only 84 of 447 (19%) intrahepatic; not powered for site-specific effects; unmasked

Guideline-quoted (EASL-ILCA): BILCAP iCCA subgroup HR 0.65, capecitabine vs observation, the best of the subtypes Unpowered subgroup of an ITT-negative trial; LCSGJ 2022 reports no significant intrahepatic benefit

lead: Offer adjuvant capecitabine for 6 months as a reasonable consideration, not an obligation.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Offer adjuvant capecitabine for 6 months as a reasonable consideration, not an obligation. Indications Preferred when The fit patient after R0 or R1 resection, particularly node-positive or R1 disease, who has heard the trial endpoints and wants treatment. AASLD 2023 says capecitabine should be considered for all patients with cholangiocarcinoma and BSG 2023 recommends considering 24 weeks (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid A patient for whom the toxicity outweighs an unproven site-specific gain: grade 3 or worse events affected 44% of the 213 treated patients, most often hand-foot syndrome (20%), 32% stopped for toxicity and only 55% completed all eight cycles. Serious adverse events were 21% versus 10% on observation. Evidence & sources Downgraded from B. The trial that supports it did not meet its primary intention-to-treat endpoint (adjusted hazard ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.63–1.04, p=0.097), only 84 of 447 patients (19%) had intrahepatic disease and it was not powered for site-specific effects, so for this pathway the benefit is an unpowered subgroup of a negative trial. ACTICCA-1 has not reported. Our label sits closest to LCSGJ 2022's weak recommendation and is more cautious than AASLD 2023, BSG 2023 and EASL-ILCA, each of which grades the recommendation strong. Whether it moves to Standard is unresolved approval item 3. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Discuss adjuvant chemoradiotherapy case by case at tumour board after an R1 or node-positive resection; it is not routine.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Discuss adjuvant chemoradiotherapy case by case at tumour board after an R1 or node-positive resection; it is not routine. Indications Preferred when A margin or nodal result that genuinely changes the local-failure risk, discussed as a one-off decision with the radiation oncologist present. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid In intrahepatic disease the support is retrospective only, and BSG 2023 confines its recommendation for chemoradiotherapy after an R1 resection to extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder cancer (alignment worksheet, area 11). Do not make it a standing rule for R1 iCCA. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not give adjuvant gemcitabine–oxaliplatin.
text: Avoid Evidence B Do not give adjuvant gemcitabine–oxaliplatin. Why Why PRODIGE-12 was negative on both co-primary endpoints: relapse-free survival 30.4 versus 18.5 months, hazard ratio 0.88 (95% CI 0.62–1.25), p=0.48, and median time to definitive quality-of-life deterioration 31.8 versus 32.1 months, hazard ratio 1.28 (0.73–2.26), p=0.39; overall survival numerically favoured surveillance (median 75.8 versus 50.8 months, hazard ratio 1.08, 0.70–1.66). Additional cautions Additional cautions Grade 3 toxicity affected 62% and grade 4 11%, with grade 3 peripheral sensory neuropathy in 18%. Intrahepatic patients were 86 of 194 (44%) and their relapse-free survival hazard ratio was 0.718 (0.431–1.196), so this is not a population mismatch excuse. Say what kind of negative it is: the trial was powered for a hazard ratio of 0.60 on 126 events, its medians fell on a plateau of the curves, and salvage differed sharply by arm (40 of 41 surveillance relapses received gemcitabine-based salvage versus 9 of 33 after GEMOX), so this is a failed superiority trial in a lower-risk population than BILCAP (13% R1 and 38% node-positive, against 38% and 47%) rather than a demonstration that adjuvant therapy does nothing. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not offer S-1 as the adjuvant option here, and do not use BCAT to argue against adjuvant therapy in intrahepatic disease.
text: Avoid Evidence B Do not offer S-1 as the adjuvant option here, and do not use BCAT to argue against adjuvant therapy in intrahepatic disease. Why Why ASCOT met its primary endpoint — 3-year overall survival 77.1% versus 67.6%, stratified hazard ratio 0.69 (95% CI 0.51–0.94) — but relapse-free survival did not reach significance (hazard ratio 0.80, 0.61–1.04, p=0.088) with the curves crossing at 6 years, the analysis was done at 179 deaths, 62.8% of the 285 prespecified events, and the observation arm did far better than the hypothesised 47%. It was conducted entirely in Japan and S-1 is not available in the United States; only 58 of 440 patients (13%) had intrahepatic disease and that subgroup's hazard ratio, 0.75 (95% CI 0.30–1.89), is uninformative. Additional cautions Additional cautions BCAT found no benefit for gemcitabine (hazard ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.70–1.45) but enrolled only resected extrahepatic bile duct cancer — intrahepatic disease was not eligible — which is why EASL-ILCA excluded it when answering the adjuvant question for iCCA. It is also underpowered on its own terms: recruitment stopped at 226 of a planned 300 because patients wanted adjuvant chemotherapy, and the authors calculate only a 2.8% probability the result would have reached significance even with the planned 189 deaths. Neither trial can be quoted as evidence that adjuvant therapy is futile. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
