No benefit for adjuvant gemcitabine in resected extrahepatic bile duct cancer; recruitment stopped at 226 of a planned 300 Intrahepatic disease ineligible; only 2.8% chance of significance even at 189 deaths

lead: First line: cisplatin–gemcitabine plus a checkpoint inhibitor (durvalumab or pembrolizumab). Trial outcomes and effect sizes are in the evidence panel.
text: Standard Evidence A First line: cisplatin–gemcitabine plus a checkpoint inhibitor (durvalumab or pembrolizumab). Trial outcomes and effect sizes are in the evidence panel. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Cisplatin–gemcitabine with a checkpoint inhibitor is the first-line standard: ABC-02 established the backbone (overall survival 11.7 versus 8.1 months, hazard ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.52–0.80), durvalumab added a hazard ratio of 0.80 and pembrolizumab 0.83. Indications Preferred when Either combination is acceptable and the roadmap does not rank them; no trial compares them, so the choice is made on toxicity profile, schedule and access. ESMO 2024 recommends both [I, A] and states no biomarker favours one checkpoint inhibitor over the other. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not read the backbone trial as an iCCA trial. The three trials differ sharply in how much of their population was actually intrahepatic: 80 of 410 patients (20%) in ABC-02, 383 of 685 (55.9%) in TOPAZ-1 and 633 of 1069 (59%) in KEYNOTE-966 — the last enriched because tumour tissue was mandatory and intrahepatic tumours are easier to sample. The modern figures are the ones that apply to this clinic; ABC-02's 11.7 months rests on a population in which gallbladder cancer was the largest single site at 36%, with a median follow-up of only 8.2 months, scans at weeks 12 and 24 by RECIST 1.0, and no molecular selection. Evidence & sources In both chemo-immunotherapy trials the intrahepatic subgroup carried the effect — hazard ratio 0.76 in each — which is the opposite of the adjuvant picture in clinical decision 8, where intrahepatic patients were a small minority. The absolute gains are small: 1.3 months of median survival with durvalumab and 1.8 with pembrolizumab, both bought with immune toxicity and, in KEYNOTE-966, more treatment-related deaths and no quality-of-life gain. The claim that the two are interchangeable is an indirect comparison across trials that differ in chemotherapy duration, geography and population; ESMO states no biomarker or efficacy difference separates them, and no randomised comparison exists. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Backbone trial: cisplatin–gemcitabine median OS 11.7 mo; only 80 of 410 (20%) intrahepatic, gallbladder the largest site (36%) Not an iCCA trial; median follow-up only 8.2 mo; RECIST 1.0, no molecular selection
Durvalumab added to cisplatin–gemcitabine: OS HR 0.80, median gain 1.3 mo; intrahepatic subgroup HR 0.76; iCCA 383 of 685 (55.9%) Small absolute gain; no randomised comparison with pembrolizumab
Pembrolizumab added to cisplatin–gemcitabine: OS HR 0.83, median gain 1.8 mo; intrahepatic subgroup HR 0.76; iCCA 633 of 1069 (59%) More treatment-related deaths and no quality-of-life gain

lead: Performance status, renal and hepatic function, contraindications to checkpoint inhibition and prior therapy determine whether the full regimen is appropriate and at what intensity; any modification is recorded with its reason.
text: Standard Evidence D Performance status, renal and hepatic function, contraindications to checkpoint inhibition and prior therapy determine whether the full regimen is appropriate and at what intensity; any modification is recorded with its reason. Indications Preferred when Every patient, before the first cycle. Both pivotal trials enrolled only ECOG 0–1 patients, so the standard assumes a patient fit for it. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Document the reason for omitting any treatment component. BSG 2023 regards oxaliplatin substitution in renal impairment and gemcitabine alone in poor performance status as reasonable; our roadmap leaves the choice to the treating oncologist, and whether to name defaults is a local approval item. Evidence & sources Clinical trial eligibility is checked at diagnosis and at each progression. Standard, grade D. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: At progression, use the matched agent where a driver is present and FOLFOX where none is; recognise that those are different kinds of evidence.
text: Reasonable Evidence B At progression, use the matched agent where a driver is present and FOLFOX where none is; recognise that those are different kinds of evidence. Indications Preferred when ABC-06 compared FOLFOX with active symptom control after cisplatin–gemcitabine: median OS 6.2 versus 5.3 months, adjusted HR 0.69 (95% CI 0.50–0.97), with 12-month survival 25.9% versus 11.4%. ClarIDHy also provides randomized evidence in IDH1-mutant disease; NIFTY and NALIRICC have conflicting phase 2 results. These populations and comparators do not permit ranking by cross-trial survival. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Single-arm outcomes do not establish comparative survival or a conversion strategy. Ivosidenib has a low objective response rate (2%), while other targeted agents have different response profiles; reassess any major response with MDT rather than applying a categorical bar to surgery. No randomized evidence establishes a sequence among these options. Evidence & sources ABC-06's benefit is an absolute median gain of 0.9 months and cost grade 3–5 toxicity in 69% versus 52% and three chemotherapy-related deaths; 44% of its patients had intrahepatic disease, and stratification errors discovered in data cleaning required a post hoc sensitivity analysis to confirm the result. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Move to symptom-focused care when the reassessment answers that question, and make that an explicit tumour-board decision rather than a default.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Move to symptom-focused care when the reassessment answers that question, and make that an explicit tumour-board decision rather than a default. Indications Preferred when The patient in whom the next line would add toxicity without extending survival. Biliary function is monitored alongside the disease throughout: liver biochemistry at every assessment, and a defined route for early detection of stent blockage. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let symptom-focused care mean no biliary care — BSG 2023 attributes the better-than-expected survival in the ABC-06 active-symptom-control arm to proactive treatment of biliary obstruction and infection. New jaundice, a rising bilirubin or cholangitis is evaluated promptly and does not wait for the next scheduled scan. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not recycle immunotherapy without considering prior exposure, and do not reach for a static second-line drug list instead of the molecular result.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not recycle immunotherapy without considering prior exposure, and do not reach for a static second-line drug list instead of the molecular result. lead: Treat transplantation for known intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma as trial or prospective registry only: protocol, review-board approval and registry entry are prerequisites, not formalities.
text: Standard Evidence D PROTOCOL REGISTRY Treat transplantation for known intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma as trial or prospective registry only: protocol, review-board approval and registry entry are prerequisites, not formalities. Indications Preferred when This is our added institutional restriction, and it is a judgement about graft stewardship rather than an evidence finding. It sits closest to AASLD 2023 (research protocols only) and BSG 2023 (prospective national protocol), and is stricter than OPTN 2025 and ILTS-ILCA 2024, which both support consideration for cirrhotic, unresectable, biopsy-proven tumours of 3 cm or less after a period of stability. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not state that iCCA has no exception route — OPTN review-board guidance now describes one — and do not apply the perihilar neoadjuvant or stricture pathway to intrahepatic disease. LCSGJ 2022 states iCCA is generally not an indication for transplantation at all. Evidence & sources ILTS-ILCA 2024 — published twice, in Liver Transplantation 2025 and Liver Cancer 2026 — grades the cirrhotic ≤3 cm recommendation moderate evidence, moderate strength, and confines non-cirrhotic disease to investigational protocols after at least 6 months of stability on systemic therapy (moderate evidence, weak strength). It also makes biopsy mandatory to confirm iCCA, assess differentiation and exclude mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma, and finds no evidence for using molecular profiling to select candidates. Every one of its iCCA recommendations rests on low or moderate evidence and is graded weak or moderate, and the consensus reports modern 5-year post-transplant outcomes spanning 25–73% overall survival and 29–82% recurrence-free survival, almost entirely from single-centre retrospective series — a range too wide to support a selection rule. It makes no recommendation on allocation priority, exception points or acceptable waitlist dropout, and reached no agreement on large, locally advanced or non-cirrhotic disease. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Consensus-reported range across series, modern 5-y post-LT outcomes: OS 25–73%, RFS 29–82% Almost entirely single-centre retrospective series; range too wide for a selection rule

lead: Where a protocol exists, the allocation route is a nonstandard MMaT-3 exception: select the CCA diagnosis form and submit a written narrative to the Adult Transplant Oncology Review Board.
text: Standard Evidence D Where a protocol exists, the allocation route is a nonstandard MMaT-3 exception: select the CCA diagnosis form and submit a written narrative to the Adult Transplant Oncology Review Board. Indications Preferred when iCCA, neuroendocrine liver metastasis and colorectal liver metastasis all go through nonstandard review; hepatocellular carcinoma and perihilar cholangiocarcinoma have standardised routes. Clinical transplant candidacy and local protocol approval remain separate from allocation eligibility. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat the guidance as policy: OPTN Policy 9.5 defines standardised exceptions, and the Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology document is review-board guidance, not OPTN Policy or a clinical standard of care. Evidence & sources MMaT is the median MELD at transplant for the donor hospital used in the match run, not one fixed national score; under Policy 9.4.E an MMaT-relative exception below 15 is assigned 15, and exceptions generally require 90-day extensions (9.4.C). The coordinator records source version, eligibility dates, request and extension dates, imaging, laboratory values and a named renewal owner; transplant leadership signs the allocation assessment. Required allocation record: diagnosis and histology; baseline burden and AFP/CEA where applicable; primary and last-treatment dates; serial response imaging; extrahepatic staging; request and extension dates; score route; named coordinator and physician sign-off. Reassess at progression, recurrence, new extrahepatic findings and each extension. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Open a defined, registry-tracked pathway on the OPTN 2025 and ILTS-ILCA 2024 criteriaREGISTRY The nonbinding NLRB guidance supports consideration of MMaT-3 for biopsy-proven, unresectable, solitary iCCA or mixed HCC-iCCA ≤3 cm in cirrhosis, after treatment and six months of documented stability. The six-month interval is specified directly in this guidance; it is not proof of an optimal biological observation period.
text: Open a defined, registry-tracked pathway on the OPTN 2025 and ILTS-ILCA 2024 criteria Evidence C REGISTRY The nonbinding NLRB guidance supports consideration of MMaT-3 for biopsy-proven, unresectable, solitary iCCA or mixed HCC-iCCA ≤3 cm in cirrhosis, after treatment and six months of documented stability. The six-month interval is specified directly in this guidance; it is not proof of an optimal biological observation period. Indications Preferred when The route both documents describe; OPTN 2025 gives the review board defined criteria and ILTS-ILCA 2024 reports broad community agreement on the cirrhotic ≤3 cm phenotype. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Every iCCA recommendation in the ILTS-ILCA consensus rests on low or moderate evidence and is graded weak or moderate, and the 3 cm threshold is carried forward from a small retrospective series of explant-discovered tumours whose own cut-off was 2 cm — the single-centre series behind it span 5-year survival of 25–73%. EASL-ILCA concedes the 3 cm figure is more permissive than the 2 cm cut-off used in the series and trials it cites, and ILTS-ILCA notes the 3 cm limit mirrors the June 2024 OPTN review-board criteria rather than any new data. The consensus also recommends nothing on allocation priority or acceptable waitlist dropout, which makes the criterion difficult to apply where exception priority has not been approved. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Locally advanced disease selected on sustained stability, under protocolPROTOCOL REGISTRY The Houston update analyzed 32 listed patients, of whom 18 underwent transplantation after at least six months of stability or response; 5-year OS was 49% for the analyzed listed cohort and 57% among eventual recipients, both measured from listing. Recipient 1- and 3-year OS were 100% and 71%. The earlier six-recipient report (83.3% at 3 and 5 years) overlaps and is not an independent cohort.
text: Locally advanced disease selected on sustained stability, under protocol Evidence C PROTOCOL REGISTRY The Houston update analyzed 32 listed patients, of whom 18 underwent transplantation after at least six months of stability or response; 5-year OS was 49% for the analyzed listed cohort and 57% among eventual recipients, both measured from listing. Recipient 1- and 3-year OS were 100% and 71%. The earlier six-recipient report (83.3% at 3 and 5 years) overlaps and is not an independent cohort. Indications Preferred when This prospective centre protocol supplies selected locally advanced iCCA experience, with substantial selection and no randomized comparator. NLRB guidance independently specifies six months for its different small-cirrhotic exception phenotype. Stable disease may satisfy protocol biology assessment; major shrinkage is not universally required. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Six patients, no control arm, no power calculation and no trial registration — it was run as a centre policy. Median cumulative tumour diameter was 14.2 cm with no patient under 5 cm, and 3 of 6 recurred at a median of 7.6 months. Two of the six had stable extrahepatic lesions before transplant that proved to be metastases and a third recurred after perihilar fat invasion found only on explant, so the authors concede more aggressive pre-transplant sampling is needed. Only 9 patients were listed in 6 years, so the strategy reaches a very small fraction of referrals. Selecting for 6 months of chemotherapy stability may itself be selecting indolent biology, and without a comparator it cannot be known whether these patients would have done as well on continued chemotherapy. Half the grafts were extended-criteria livers refused by every other centre — used because no MELD exception existed at the time — so the approach is not reproducible where such organs are not available. ILTS-ILCA confines non-cirrhotic locally advanced disease to investigational protocols with a weak recommendation. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: 32 listed, 18 transplanted: 5-year OS 49% in the listed cohort and 57% among recipients, both from listing Selected, nonrandomized cohort; overlaps the earlier six-recipient report

lead: If intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is found in an explant removed for another indication, enter the patient into structured surveillance and the registry.
text: Reasonable Evidence D If intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is found in an explant removed for another indication, enter the patient into structured surveillance and the registry. Indications Preferred when This is the population the published outcomes actually describe, and it is where the programme's own data will come from. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Immunosuppression minimisation and adjuvant therapy are individualised; there is no comparative evidence to support either, so do not present a protocol where none exists. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not transplant multifocal or larger disease outside a protocol, and never with any extrahepatic disease or without registry entry.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not transplant multifocal or larger disease outside a protocol, and never with any extrahepatic disease or without registry entry. Why Why The eligible phenotype is narrow and explicit — solitary, 3 cm or less, cirrhosis, treated, six months stable — but say where each limb comes from: the size ceiling and the stability requirement are guideline and review-board criteria, not findings of the explant series, whose own cut-off was 2 cm and which required no stability at all. Additional cautions Additional cautions In the explant series, larger or multifocal tumours recurred in 61% by 5 years with 45% survival, and the crude recurrence split was 2 of 15 versus 18 of 33. A broader resection or systemic-treatment population must not be treated as exception-eligible. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not treat mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma as eligible for the hepatocellular carcinoma exception pathway.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not treat mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma as eligible for the hepatocellular carcinoma exception pathway. Why Why Treat it as biliary disease for transplant purposes unless a protocol states otherwise, and flag it to the transplant team explicitly; OPTN 2025 routes mixed HCC-iCCA through the same nonstandard request as iCCA. Additional cautions Additional cautions ILTS-ILCA makes biopsy mandatory partly to exclude a mixed tumour, and reviews note that pooling mixed tumours with pure iCCA can make survival and recurrence look falsely favourable when the dominant phenotype is hepatocellular. The index explant series excluded mixed tumours within a nodule entirely, so there is no transplant outcome dataset for this phenotype to argue from in either direction. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Evidence: 15 patients with a single tumor ≤2 cm, cancer first diagnosed on explant pathology. Recurrence and survival figures are in the evidence panel.
text: Evidence C Evidence: 15 patients with a single tumor ≤2 cm, cancer first diagnosed on explant pathology. Recurrence and survival figures are in the evidence panel. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Read the supporting evidence for what it is: in 15 patients with a single tumour of 2 cm or less, the 5-year recurrence risk was 18% versus 61% for larger or multifocal disease, with 5-year survival 65% versus 45% — in explants where the cancer was first diagnosed on explant pathology. Indications Preferred when Quote it when the question is the prognosis of a very small intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma discovered on an explant removed for another reason, which is the population it describes: 15 patients, 7 of them (47%) entirely incidental, from 17 centres and 25,016 transplants. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Crucially these tumours were recognised as intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma only at explant, not selected for transplantation, so the result cannot be read as licensing transplantation of known disease. Fifteen patients leaves very few still at risk at 5 years and the authors call the 3- and 5-year rates encouraging rather than established. No lymphadenectomy was performed because iCCA was not suspected, central pathology review was possible in only 55 of 81 cases (68%), each of 17 centres used its own pathologist so number and size may be understaged, and recurrence was driven by microvascular invasion (HR 4.7, 1.6–13.8) and poor differentiation (HR 6.1, 1.9–20.2) — neither of which is knowable before transplant. Evidence & sources Three limits of this series bear directly on how it is cited here. It studied tumours of 2 cm or less, not 3 cm: the ceiling in our criteria comes from EASL-ILCA, OPTN and ILTS-ILCA, and inside this series it rests on a 6-patient subgroup of single 2.1–3 cm, not poorly differentiated tumours whose 5-year survival was 61%. It required no period of disease stability on therapy and could not have — the diagnosis was made on the explant, bridging chemoembolisation, ablation or ethanol injection was permitted but was not a selection test, and 7 of the 15 (47%) were incidental findings after transplant for decompensated cirrhosis. And it excluded mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma within a nodule outright, analysing the 33 explants with separate iCCA and hepatocellular nodules as a separate group outside the 48-patient study population, so it reports no outcome at all for the mixed tumours our assessment criteria admit. The wider literature is no firmer: a 2020 meta-analysis of 18 studies and 355 patients gave pooled 5-year survival of 42% and pooled recurrence 43%, with 5-year recurrence-free survival 67% for single tumours of 2 cm or less versus 34% for more advanced disease, and a propensity-matched National Cancer Database comparison found transplant and resection within a few percentage points of each other at 5 years — whose authors argued resection should remain preferred for localised iCCA. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Drain the sectors that will form the future liver remnant, not the most accessible duct, and name one owner for the drainage strategy.
text: Standard Evidence D Drain the sectors that will form the future liver remnant, not the most accessible duct, and name one owner for the drainage strategy. Indications Preferred when Every patient drained with a resection or protocol destination in mind — the objective is decompression of the sectors you intend to keep, which is why clinical decision 0 and the resectability assessment are discussed together at the first tumour board. ESGE 2026 suggests against routine preoperative drainage and lists severe jaundice, cholangitis and a predicted remnant of 30% or less as the accepted indications (conditional, low quality); the Milan consensus restricts it to a small remnant needing hypertrophy, cholangitis, renal or hepatic failure, severe malnutrition or pruritus, and says to drain the future liver remnant exclusively. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not drain an atrophic or to-be-resected lobe: it relieves jaundice without enabling the operation, and hypertrophy after portal vein embolisation is poor in a liver that remains cholestatic. Cholangitis after a poorly planned drain is the most common avoidable disaster in this disease. Equally, do not drain reflexively: the Coelen investigators' own conclusion from their trial was that drainage should follow resectability assessment at a specialist centre and may be unnecessary when the remnant exceeds 50% of liver volume. Evidence & sources Grade D. No trial compares remnant-focused drainage with draining the most accessible duct; the position follows from the physiology of hypertrophy in a cholestatic liver and from the guidelines' own wording, not from comparative outcome data. The Asia-Pacific panel reached only 56% full agreement on its preoperative-drainage statement. Antibiotics with the procedure, cultures sent, and a named owner for drain management. As few drains as achieve remnant decompression — multiple uncoordinated drains placed by different services is a recognised failure pattern. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: In unresectable disease being drained for palliation, aim to drain more than 50% of viable liver volume including the future liver remnant, and drain every segment that has been opacified.
text: Standard Evidence D In unresectable disease being drained for palliation, aim to drain more than 50% of viable liver volume including the future liver remnant, and drain every segment that has been opacified. Indications Preferred when Palliative drainage where the destination is systemic therapy or symptom control. ESGE 2026 raises the target to 70% or more where it can be achieved; above 50% drained gave better clinical success (OR 4.5) and longer survival (119 versus 59 days), and the Asia-Pacific statement reports longer survival above 80% drained (HR 2.46). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Generally do not drain atrophic segments, and do not inject contrast into a duct you do not intend to drain — an opacified undrained sector is a cholangitis waiting to happen. Evidence & sources Downgraded to D: no threshold here was derived. ESGE lists prospective volumetry against survival and access to chemotherapy as an unmet need, and no meta-analysis or comparative trial has tested any percentage cut-off; the supporting cohorts disagree among themselves (50%, 71%, 80%) and the 50% and 80% figures come from single-centre retrospective series (Vienne 2010, Caillol 2019) with no prospective validation. Both the ESGE and Asia-Pacific statements on this are graded low or very low quality. Sector volumes for planning: right anterior, right posterior and left each about 30%, segments I and IV about 10%, atrophic segments counted as non-viable. Bismuth I, II and IIIb can often be served by one stent; IIIa and IV need two or more to reach 50%. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Endoscopic drainage (ERCP)EXPERTISE ESGE 2026 recommends ERCP over percutaneous drainage for preoperative drainage in malignant hilar obstruction (strong recommendation, moderate quality), and ASGE suggests against routine percutaneous drainage as first-line therapy before possible resection or transplantation (conditional, low quality). NCCN leaves route to local expertise after multidisciplinary review.
text: Endoscopic drainage (ERCP) Evidence C EXPERTISE ESGE 2026 recommends ERCP over percutaneous drainage for preoperative drainage in malignant hilar obstruction (strong recommendation, moderate quality), and ASGE suggests against routine percutaneous drainage as first-line therapy before possible resection or transplantation (conditional, low quality). NCCN leaves route to local expertise after multidisciplinary review. Indications Preferred when The first route in a patient who still has a curative option, where the anatomy is reachable and the endoscopic service is experienced. DRAINAGE was stopped early because mortality between randomisation and 90 days after surgery was higher after percutaneous drainage, 11 of 27 (41%) versus 3 of 27 (11%), relative risk 3.67 (95% CI 1.15–11.69), p=0.03; a 1,085-patient meta-analysis found more implantation metastases after the percutaneous route (OR 0.35, 0.23–0.53). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Lower technical success (20 of 27, 74%, versus 25 of 27, 93%) and more pancreatitis (5, 19%, versus 1, 4%). In the trial 15 of 27 patients allocated to endoscopic drainage (56%) needed additional percutaneous drainage against 1 of 27 the other way, so this is a comparison of initial strategies, not of techniques. ESGE's own section cites a meta-analysis giving percutaneous drainage higher therapeutic success (OR 3.5, 95% CI 2.1–6.0) and 11.5-fold more reintervention after ERCP, with 10 of its 11 studies retrospective — the strong recommendation runs against the best comparative data printed beside it. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Stopped early: death to 90 d post-surgery, percutaneous vs endoscopic 11/27 (41%) vs 3/27 (11%), RR 3.67 (95% CI 1.15–11.69), p=0.03 15 of 27 (56%) endoscopic needed added percutaneous drainage; compares initial strategies

lead: Percutaneous transhepatic drainageEXPERTISE Reserved for failed or anatomically unsuitable endoscopic access, and accepted either way for palliative drainage of unresectable disease, by patient preference, disease characteristics and local expertise.
text: Percutaneous transhepatic drainage Evidence C EXPERTISE Reserved for failed or anatomically unsuitable endoscopic access, and accepted either way for palliative drainage of unresectable disease, by patient preference, disease characteristics and local expertise. Indications Preferred when Sectors that endoscopic drainage cannot reach, particularly in Bismuth IIIa and IV disease, and where percutaneous delineation of intrahepatic tumour spread will change the operative plan. It is also the route with the higher technical success in the one randomised comparison and in ESGE's pooled data. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Weigh the catheter-tract and peritoneal seeding concern heavily in anyone who may be a transplant protocol candidate: ASGE's recommendation rests on 7.8% seeding after endoscopic versus 17.1% after percutaneous drainage (OR 0.27, 0.13–0.56), with percutaneous drainage the only independent predictor of peritoneal recurrence in one adjusted cohort (OR 6.9, 1.9–25.7). Read that at its real strength — the ASGE panel itself calls this the weakest evidence in the document: a six-study meta-analysis with high heterogeneity (I² 66%) and very few events, plus one adjusted single-centre cohort, both graded very low quality. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Six-study meta-analysis: seeding 7.8% endoscopic vs 17.1% percutaneous drainage, OR 0.27 (0.13–0.56); one cohort: percutaneous OR 6.9 (1.9–25.7) for peritoneal recurrence Very low quality: I² 66%, very few events; single-centre adjusted cohort

lead: A removable plastic stent while resection, transplantation or a good systemic response remains possible; an uncovered metal stent once those options are closed.
text: Reasonable Evidence C A removable plastic stent while resection, transplantation or a good systemic response remains possible; an uncovered metal stent once those options are closed. Indications Preferred when Patients whose drainage strategy is not yet defined, or who may respond well to systemic therapy and outlive uncovered-stent patency. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Avoid uncovered metal stents in a potential transplant candidate — they cannot be removed and are difficult to deal with surgically. Metal stents give better patency and fewer reinterventions (OR 0.34) and 56 days more survival (95% CI 12–101) in the pooled ASGE analysis, but the comparator plastic arms were waited out to occlusion rather than exchanged on schedule, which is why the ASGE panel declined a strong recommendation. Evidence & sources The roadmap itself does not set a stent rule — it says to choose stent and access route through multidisciplinary review, and that the algorithm does not establish a universal stent material. The rule above is the alignment worksheet's proposal (area 3) and needs local approval. The page also takes no position on bilateral versus unilateral stenting, which is a live question: ASGE suggests bilateral absent lobar atrophy, but its pooled survival gain was 11 days (95% CI −12 to 35) and pooled patency showed no difference (SMD 0.38, −0.22 to 0.99, I² 78%), while one randomised trial reported in ESGE 2026 gave bilateral stenting clinical success 95.3% versus 84.9% and patency 252 versus 139 days. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Single RCT reported in ESGE 2026, bilateral vs unilateral stenting: clinical success 95.3% vs 84.9%; patency 252 vs 139 days Single trial quoted within the guideline; page takes no bilateral/unilateral position
ASGE pooled, metal vs plastic: better patency/fewer reinterventions OR 0.34; survival +56 days (95% CI 12–101) Plastic arms waited to occlusion, not exchanged on schedule; no strong recommendation

lead: Do not place the first stent before multiphase CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis and MRI with MRCP, unless cholangitis or a rapidly rising bilirubin makes drainage urgent.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not place the first stent before multiphase CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis and MRI with MRCP, unless cholangitis or a rapidly rising bilirubin makes drainage urgent. Why Why Document the reason when emergency decompression comes first, and complete staging promptly. Additional cautions Additional cautions A stent's inflammatory change degrades assessment of ductal extent and cannot be undone. MRI/MRCP outperforms contrast-enhanced CT both for the nature of the stricture (pooled accuracy 96% versus 89%, OR 2.1, 1.2–3.6) and for identifying the level (OR 3.3, 1.2–9.1). Evidence & sources Downgraded from B to C: the ESGE recommendation behind these numbers is conditional on low-quality evidence, and the ESGE panel found no randomised trial for any of its perihilar questions. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: ESGE pooled data, MRI/MRCP vs contrast-enhanced CT: stricture nature accuracy 96% vs 89%, OR 2.1 (1.2–3.6); stricture level OR 3.3 (1.2–9.1) Conditional recommendation on low-quality evidence; no randomised trial

lead: Do not accept a bilirubin threshold that has not been written down.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not accept a bilirubin threshold that has not been written down. Why Why Set the programme threshold locally, record it, and apply it consistently before major hepatectomy, embolic therapy, radiation and systemic therapy. Additional cautions Additional cautions There are no comparative data defining the cut-off; it is a safety convention, and an unwritten one is applied inconsistently. §11 item 3 audits post-hepatectomy liver failure by preoperative bilirubin.

lead: Stage with multiphase CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis plus MRI with MRCP; chest imaging is part of staging because distant spread changes every later assessment.
text: Standard Evidence C Stage with multiphase CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis plus MRI with MRCP; chest imaging is part of staging because distant spread changes every later assessment. Indications Preferred when Every patient, before elective instrumentation. CT and MRI are complementary and both are required; MRCP comes before ERC to avoid artefact. The AHPBA panel states a well-performed CT or MRI should exceed 75% accuracy for resectability. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid FDG-PET lacks the sensitivity and specificity for routine staging in this disease and should not replace the cross-sectional package — though note BSG 2023 does recommend FDG-PET/CT for nodal and distant disease, so this is a point of guideline disagreement, not settled fact. Evidence & sources Downgraded from B to C. The 75% accuracy figure is an ungraded expert-consensus statement from a six-person panel across four institutions, and the ESGE imaging recommendation that supports MRI/MRCP over CT is conditional on low-quality evidence. Nothing here was derived prospectively in perihilar disease. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Record Bismuth–Corlette (ductal pattern); it does not decide resectability. Assess vascular involvement, lobar atrophy, nodes and remnant volume.
text: Standard Evidence C Record Bismuth–Corlette (ductal pattern); it does not decide resectability. Assess vascular involvement, lobar atrophy, nodes and remnant volume. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Record the Bismuth-Corlette type as shorthand for the pattern of ductal involvement, but do not let it decide resectability — vascular involvement, lobar atrophy, nodal status and remnant volume do that. Indications Preferred when Communication at the board, and planning which sectors to drain and how many stents it will take. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat the preoperative type as the final extent. In the original series postoperative histology upstaged tumours, 4 operative type IV lesions becoming 9, so the preoperative type systematically understates extent. The Milan jury declined to endorse Bismuth-Corlette, or any other staging system — MSKCC included — as a predictor of resectability, and its own resectability criteria are stated to be expert opinion requiring validation. Evidence & sources Grade C, and read the denominators: the classification and its type-specific operations rest on 23 resections accumulated over 30 years at one centre, one to four patients per type, in 122 patients taken to surgery. See the quick reference for the operation each type implies. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Original single-centre series: postoperative histology upstaged 4 operative type IV lesions to 9; 23 resections over 30 years, 122 taken to surgery One to four patients per type; Milan jury declined it as a resectability predictor

lead: Treat CA 19-9 and CEA as supporting measurements, not proof of malignancy, and record each value with the bilirubin and drainage status at the time it was drawn.
text: Standard Evidence C Treat CA 19-9 and CEA as supporting measurements, not proof of malignancy, and record each value with the bilirubin and drainage status at the time it was drawn. Indications Preferred when Where a value is to count toward the transplant protocol's diagnostic criteria it is measured only after decompression and in the absence of cholangitis. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Tumour markers must not be used alone to separate a benign from a malignant stricture: pooled accuracy is 81% (76–87) for CA 19-9 and 70% (62–78) for CEA, with false-positive rates of 15% and 18%, and CA 19-9 rises in primary sclerosing cholangitis, cirrhosis and obstructive jaundice. NCCN is explicit that CEA and CA 19-9 are baseline tests and should not be done to confirm the diagnosis. Evidence & sources Downgraded from B to C: the ESGE recommendation is conditional on very low quality evidence. This matters more here than elsewhere, because CA 19-9 above 100 U/mL is one of the alternative diagnostic criteria for the transplant protocol — a 15% false-positive rate sits underneath a listing decision. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Measure the future liver remnant by CT volumetry and state the threshold the board is working to before committing to augmentation.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Measure the future liver remnant by CT volumetry and state the threshold the board is working to before committing to augmentation. Indications Preferred when Any patient in whom an extended hepatectomy is contemplated. AASLD recommends an adequate remnant of at least 30%; BSG uses 20% with normal parenchyma, 30% after chemotherapy and 40% with cirrhosis; the Milan consensus uses 30% if healthy and at least 40% if frail, cholangitic, cholestatic or malnourished, standardised by Vauthey's formula. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid A cholestatic liver fits none of those categories cleanly, which is the roadmap's reason for leaving the number to the board rather than copying one. Evidence & sources Downgraded from C to D. None of these thresholds was derived: three guidelines give three different numbers for the same decision, the Milan figure sits at level-4 expert opinion, and no comparative study tests one cut-off against another in perihilar disease. The roadmap states no numeric remnant threshold. Whether to adopt AASLD's single 30% or BSG's parenchyma-adjusted 20/30/40% is §11 item 4 territory and needs specialty approval. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not carry an iCCA or distal cholangiocarcinoma pathway into this disease.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not carry an iCCA or distal cholangiocarcinoma pathway into this disease. Why Why Perihilar disease has its own decision points: central biliary and vascular anatomy and longitudinal tumour spread differ from a small peripheral liver mass, and the transplant route, the biopsy constraint and the drainage problem are all specific to it. Additional cautions Additional cautions Intrahepatic and distal cholangiocarcinoma are covered separately and are not interchangeable with this pathway. Gallbladder cancer is out of scope.

lead: A transperitoneal biopsy of the primary tumour must be avoided in any patient who may be protocol-eligible — and that includes the endoscopic ultrasound route.
text: Standard Evidence A A transperitoneal biopsy of the primary tumour must be avoided in any patient who may be protocol-eligible — and that includes the endoscopic ultrasound route. Indications Preferred when Discuss the route with the transplant team before obtaining tissue. OPTN Policy 9.5.A, requirement 6 names percutaneous, operative and endoscopic ultrasound routes: an EUS needle reaching a perihilar tumour crosses the peritoneal cavity, so it counts. Avoidance is a condition of the standardized exception, not a weighing of evidence — taking the route removes the patient from the standardized route entirely. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid In the Mayo protocol cohort of 191 patients, 16 had a transperitoneal fine-needle aspiration of the primary elsewhere; of the 6 whose aspirate was positive for adenocarcinoma, 5 of 6 (83%) had peritoneal metastases at operative staging, against 8% (14 of 175) in those not biopsied (P=0.0097). The 9 patients with non-diagnostic aspirates had no metastases at all. The two groups did not differ in age, sex, PSC, presence or size of a mass, presenting CA 19-9 or interval to staging. Evidence & sources The grade records an absolute policy condition, not the strength of the evidence underneath it, and the two must not be confused. The evidence is six exposed patients and five events: that cannot support a risk estimate, it is not a measured seeding rate, and the roadmap does not present it as one. Because only diagnostic aspirates carried the excess, a positive aspirate may partly be marking a tumour bulky and cell-rich enough to hit with a needle rather than causing dissemination; reverse causation is not excluded by this retrospective single-programme design, and no histological features were available to match the groups on. Only patients already accepted onto the protocol were counted, so anyone whose outside aspirate took them out of consideration is invisible. The 12-centre series is often quoted here too, but its hazard ratio of 2.98 (95% CI 1.79–4.95) is for a composite off-criteria group — 21 patients with a mass over 3 cm, 16 with a direct tumour biopsy, 4 with metastases and 7 with a prior malignancy — and is not attributable to biopsy alone. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Mayo protocol cohort (n=191): peritoneal metastases 5 of 6 (83%) after positive transperitoneal FNA vs 8% (14 of 175) not biopsied, P=0.0097 Six exposed, five events; retrospective single programme; reverse causation not excluded

12-centre series: HR 2.98 (95% CI 1.79–4.95) for a composite off-criteria group: 21 mass >3 cm, 16 direct tumour biopsy, 4 metastases, 7 prior malignancy Composite group; effect not attributable to biopsy alone

lead: Take tissue at the index ERCP, with brush cytology completed by fluoroscopy-guided intraductal biopsies wherever that is technically feasible.
text: Standard Evidence C Take tissue at the index ERCP, with brush cytology completed by fluoroscopy-guided intraductal biopsies wherever that is technically feasible. Indications Preferred when Every patient having a first ERCP for a malignant-appearing hilar stricture. ASGE pools 21 studies and 2,726 patients: incremental yield of adding biopsy to brushing 20% (95% CI 9–31), sensitivity 0.66 combined against 0.52 for biopsy and 0.40 for brushing alone (P<.001). ESGE's figure is higher but rests on far less — a pooled incremental yield of 25% (11–38, OR 2.7, 1.5–4.9) from two retrospective cohorts totalling 101 patients. The Asia-Pacific statement quotes combined sensitivity about 70% against 21–56% for brushing alone and 43–67% for intraductal biopsy. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Deferring tissue to a later stent exchange is treated as costless in practice and probably is not. Note also that adding biopsy is not free: in the ASGE analysis there was no overall difference in adverse events (OR 0.53, 0.14–2.05) but the biopsy arm carried two severe events, prolonged bleeding and a perforation needing surgical choledochotomy. Evidence & sources Downgraded from B to C: every recommendation in both guidelines on this question is conditional on low or very low quality evidence, and neither panel found a randomised trial for any perihilar question. How much tissue is itself unsettled — ESGE says three to four intraductal biopsies appear sufficient, while the real-world cholangioscopy cohort below took a median of 3 and had 33% inconclusive specimens, and its authors recommend a minimum of four. Cytology sensitivity rises with brush passes: 38% at 10, 47% at 20 and 57% at 30 in a multicentre randomised trial of more than 400 patients. For an indeterminate stricture, add cholangioscopy-guided biopsies — pooled incremental yield 27% (10–45) from 13 studies and 1,529 patients, sensitivity 0.72 against 0.61 — but do not repeat the guidelines' claim that this costs nothing: the PSC meta-analysis records post-procedure cholangitis in 11% and procedural failure in 15% of PSC ducts against 2% of controls, and the Groningen cohort had adverse events in 10 of 80 (13%), including two episodes of cholangitis and one cardiac arrest with subsequent stroke. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: ESGE pooled: incremental yield of adding biopsy to brushing 25% (11–38), OR 2.7 (1.5–4.9) From two retrospective cohorts totalling 101 patients

ASGE pooled 21 studies, 2,726 pts: adding biopsy to brushing, incremental yield 20% (95% CI 9–31); sensitivity 0.66 combined vs 0.52 biopsy vs 0.40 brushing (P<.001) Low/very-low quality evidence; AEs not different overall but two severe events with biopsy
