lead: Send a separate specimen from the same ERCP for next-generation sequencing: it raises yield on the one sampling route that does not disqualify the patient from the transplant protocol.
text: Standard Evidence C Send a separate specimen from the same ERCP for next-generation sequencing: it raises yield on the one sampling route that does not disqualify the patient from the transplant protocol. Indications Preferred when Potential transplant-protocol candidates need an accepted diagnostic basis, not necessarily a positive primary-tumor biopsy. OPTN accepts a malignant-appearing stricture plus at least one of these diagnostic findings: biopsy or cytology showing malignancy, CA 19-9 >100 U/mL without cholangitis, aneuploidy, or a hilar mass <3 cm in radial diameter; transperitoneal biopsy of the primary must be avoided. In a 6-year prospective study of 2,908 ERCP-obtained specimens from 2,116 patients at 28 US institutions, with accuracy computed on the 1,979 patients who had follow-up (1,108 neoplastic, 871 benign), a DNA/RNA panel gave 82% sensitivity and 98% specificity for a neoplastic stricture, against 44% and 99% for pathological assessment of separate specimens; combining the two gave 88% at 97%. In intrahepatic or hilar strictures specifically it was 80% versus 36%, and 86% combined. Actionable alterations were found in 23% of positive malignancies and in 137 of 458 cholangiocarcinomas (30%), so the same specimen can serve diagnosis and target identification. Assay failure was about 1%. [PAYER] [DEVICE] Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Four cautions. Specificity is high but not perfect, and a false positive commits a patient to neoadjuvant chemoradiation and transplantation — the consequence of error is not symmetrical with the consequence in an ordinary diagnostic setting; sixteen false positives occurred, at variant allele frequencies of 1.5–30%. The endpoint was a neoplastic stricture, which is broader than malignancy, and a stricture could be called neoplastic on imaging plus clinical or radiographic progression over 12 months rather than on tissue, which tends to flatter the test that often prompted that work-up. Only 2% of neoplastic strictures were purely dysplastic, so outside PSC this is earlier diagnosis of established cancer, not early detection, and no survival or resectability benefit has been shown. And a negative result still does not exclude malignancy. Evidence & sources Downgraded from B to C. Identical specimens were never compared — sequencing and pathology were run on different specimens — specimens were submitted at the endoscopist's discretion rather than consecutively, FISH was never compared head to head, and all testing was done in the laboratory that developed the assay. The earlier single-centre prospective study (252 patients, 346 specimens) raised pathology sensitivity from 35% to 71% on 132 paired brushings and from 52% to 75% on 114 paired biopsies, and reported 83% versus 8% in primary sclerosing cholangitis on 12 malignant cases (95% CI 0.51–0.98). Two real-world cohorts reproduce the overall direction (65% versus 52% alone and 78% combined on 47 biopsies in one; 75% versus 42.9% in 77 patients in the other) but neither supports the PSC result — one found 20% sensitivity in PSC against 40% for brush cytology — and in the one cohort that reported it separately, the gain in cholangiocarcinoma itself was not significant (70% versus 60%, P=.72). The test is a laboratory-developed test from a single CLIA-certified laboratory, not FDA cleared, and coverage must be verified in writing before it is written into routine practice. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Proceed to resection without tissue NCCN: surgery may be performed when the index of suspicion is high, and biopsy is not required. BSG accepts surgery without histological certainty. The AHPBA consensus states pathologic confirmation is not required before resection or before starting the transplant protocol.
text: Proceed to resection without tissue Evidence C NCCN: surgery may be performed when the index of suspicion is high, and biopsy is not required. BSG accepts surgery without histological certainty. The AHPBA consensus states pathologic confirmation is not required before resection or before starting the transplant protocol. Indications Preferred when A malignant-appearing stricture with no alternative explanation, where the operative plan would not change whatever the result. For a resection-only candidate, select a safe biopsy route when tissue confirmation will change management. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid A benign aetiology is found in about 10% of resections done on a presumptive diagnosis by the AHPBA panel's figure, and about 15% in a 30-year tertiary series, in an operation whose 90-day mortality reaches 13% even in benchmark patients at expert centres. Do not use it to skip the transplant question in a patient who might be a protocol candidate. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: AHPBA consensus panel figure: benign aetiology in about 10% of resections done on a presumptive diagnosis

lead: EUS-guided aspiration of the primary ESGE suggests EUS-guided tissue acquisition for perihilar strictures only when ERCP-based modalities are insufficient and 'provided that curative resection is not feasible and/or when cross-sectional imaging has shown accessible extraluminal disease' (conditional, low quality). Pooled EUS sensitivity 78% (70–86), accuracy 84% (78–91), incremental yield over ERCP 33%.
text: EUS-guided aspiration of the primary Evidence C ESGE suggests EUS-guided tissue acquisition for perihilar strictures only when ERCP-based modalities are insufficient and 'provided that curative resection is not feasible and/or when cross-sectional imaging has shown accessible extraluminal disease' (conditional, low quality). Pooled EUS sensitivity 78% (70–86), accuracy 84% (78–91), incremental yield over ERCP 33%. Indications Preferred when Established unresectable disease with no transplant option, where a tissue diagnosis is needed to start systemic therapy and ERCP sampling has failed. Where the stricture proves distal rather than perihilar, EUS-guided acquisition becomes the higher-yield route and carries no protocol penalty. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Never in a potential protocol candidate. ESGE itself notes that the hilar seeding risk is supported in this disease by one retrospective series of 150 patients, with the rest extrapolated from pancreatic adenocarcinoma and percutaneous aspiration, and makes no recommendation for transplant candidates — so for protocol candidates the constraint rests on OPTN Policy 9.5.A and the Mayo data, not on ESGE. ASGE is explicit that if EUS is performed for a proximal or hilar stricture the endosonographer should not sample the biliary mass itself. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: EUS evaluation and aspiration of regional nodes AASLD requires EUS-FNA of regional nodes before neoadjuvant therapy in patients being evaluated for transplantation; BSG samples an involved locoregional node for staging while leaving the mass alone.
text: EUS evaluation and aspiration of regional nodes Evidence D AASLD requires EUS-FNA of regional nodes before neoadjuvant therapy in patients being evaluated for transplantation; BSG samples an involved locoregional node for staging while leaving the mass alone. Indications Preferred when Before a transplant workup is spent. Node-positive disease is itself a protocol exclusion, so a positive nodal result does not cost candidacy that existed — it identifies a patient who was never a candidate. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let a nodal pass become a pass at the primary; they are different sampling targets. AASLD also notes that no morphological criteria reliably identify malignant nodes, which weakens a 'suspicious node' trigger, and the AASLD document is explicitly expert consensus rather than a GRADE-rated guideline. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Where a stent is already in place, take tissue after removing it and send material for molecular testing — and do not assume cholangioscopic biopsy will outperform the brush.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Where a stent is already in place, take tissue after removing it and send material for molecular testing — and do not assume cholangioscopic biopsy will outperform the brush. Indications Preferred when The referred patient who arrives already stented — a common presentation, and the one where the published yields cannot be assumed to apply. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat a negative result as reassuring, and do not treat cholangioscopy as the answer here. In the real-world Groningen cohort of 80 patients, 70 (88%) had had a previous ERCP, 44 (55%) had a plastic stent removed at the start of the procedure and 32 (40%) had primary sclerosing cholangitis: cholangioscopy-guided biopsy sensitivity was 15% (95% CI 0–31), far below the 65% (35–87) pooled from 4 studies and 128 PSC patients that did not report stent status, and visual assessment was 64% sensitive with 62% specificity. Brush cytology taken at the same procedure beat both — sensitivity 47%, specificity 95%, accuracy 81%, diagnostic odds ratio 19.6 against 6.6 for the targeted biopsy. Management changed in only 13 of 77 (17%). Evidence & sources Downgraded to D, and the roadmap's earlier wording is withdrawn: the one cohort that tested a blind brush against cholangioscopy after stent removal found the brush better, so recommending cholangioscopic sampling instead of a brush is not supported. The low biopsy figure is also as much about technique as about the stent — a median of 3 biopsies with 33% of specimens inconclusive, 66 of 80 procedures on a first-generation device, and authors who recommend a minimum of four biopsies. No study quantifies sampling yield stratified by prior stent placement; targeted searches for it return nothing, and this pathway should not imply otherwise. Mechanistically stents do produce reactive change: in a blinded multi-reviewer study of 60 brushings — 30 malignant and 30 benign, half the benign cases previously stented — necrosis (17% versus 13%) and infiltrating inflammation (43% versus 33%) did not distinguish malignancy, 3 or more of 11 cytological characteristics gave sensitivity 70% at specificity 97%, and 7 of 30 malignant brushings showed none of them. That study was enriched 50:50 by design, so its predictive values do not transfer to clinic. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Cohort, 80 pts (55% stent removed): sensitivity 15% (95% CI 0–31) cholangioscopic biopsy vs 47% brush cytology; DOR 6.6 vs 19.6; brush specificity 95% Median 3 biopsies, 33% inconclusive; 66 of 80 on a first-generation device

lead: Do not biopsy the primary perihilar tumor through a transperitoneal route when transplantation remains an option. The diagnostic plan for a resection-only candidate requires separate multidisciplinary review.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not biopsy the primary perihilar tumor through a transperitoneal route when transplantation remains an option. The diagnostic plan for a resection-only candidate requires separate multidisciplinary review. Why Why Keep a mandatory local pre-biopsy transplant assessment: before biopsy, evaluate whether the patient is a resection or transplant candidate. Additional cautions Additional cautions Also avoid an exploratory resection attempt that violates the tumour plane in a borderline candidate — AASLD and the programme's own protocol list surgical violation of the tumour plane as a transplant exclusion, and the roadmap's route logic covers needles only. Evidence & sources The roadmap is internally inconsistent here and says so: its §4 Resection row does not specify a restriction on the biopsy route, while this callout extends the rule to anyone with a curative option, which includes resection. BSG states the stricter rule, and a resection candidate judged unresectable before any operative violation of the tumour plane may become a protocol candidate. Unresolved — see the limited-evidence section. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not keep resampling in pursuit of a negative result that will not be believed.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not keep resampling in pursuit of a negative result that will not be believed. Why Why Decide in advance what a negative result will change. If the answer is nothing, the patient needs a destination decision, not another ERCP. Additional cautions Additional cautions Negative predictive values are 34% for ERCP-based sampling and 47% for EUS aspiration in a 294-patient meta-analysis at 77% pretest probability, so with either modality a negative result does not exclude malignancy; repeated sampling is a common way to lose time. FISH trisomy or tetrasomy alone is uninformative (sensitivity 31%, 22–40; specificity 71%, 67–75; positive likelihood ratio 1.19, 0.65–2.21). Only polysomy carries information (51%, 43–59, and 93%, 91–95), and OPTN lists aneuploidy; how FISH polysomy satisfies the center protocol requires explicit agreement. Its positive predictive value in PSC was only 0.68 (0.58–0.76), and all eight studies in that meta-analysis came from a single centre with overlapping recruitment windows. Evidence & sources Downgraded from B to C. Both pooled estimates rest on analyses the spec's own standard would not call B: the ERCP-versus-EUS review scored high risk of selection bias in every included study and reported simple means, and the FISH meta-analysis is effectively one institution's experience with likely verification bias, since a FISH-positive patient is more likely to reach the surgery that classifies them. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Meta-analysis (294 pts, 77% pretest probability): NPV 34% ERCP-based sampling vs 47% EUS aspiration; a negative result does not exclude malignancy High risk of selection bias in every included study; simple means reported

Meta-analysis: polysomy sensitivity 51% (43–59), specificity 93% (91–95); trisomy/tetrasomy alone uninformative, LR+ 1.19 (0.65–2.21); PPV in PSC 0.68 (0.58–0.76) All eight studies from a single centre, overlapping recruitment; likely verification bias

lead: Extended hepatectomy with en bloc extrahepatic bile duct resection, regional nodes and biliary reconstruction; portal-vein resection/reconstruction when needed for R0.
text: Standard Evidence C Extended hepatectomy with en bloc extrahepatic bile duct resection, regional nodes and biliary reconstruction; portal-vein resection/reconstruction when needed for R0. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Extended hepatectomy with en bloc extrahepatic bile duct resection, regional lymphadenectomy and biliary reconstruction, with portal vein resection and reconstruction where it is required to achieve R0. Indications Preferred when Technically resectable disease in a fit patient. Margin status drives everything: in the original series survival with clear margins (n=9) was 100%, 71% and 50% at 1, 2 and 3 years, against 82%, 43% and 12% with microscopic residual disease (n=10) and death within 32 months in all four patients with gross residual disease. Local recurrence followed a positive microscopic margin in every case but one, and occurred in no patient whose margin was histologically free. Across series, R0 gives median survival 27–58 months and 5-year survival 27–45%, against 12–21 months and 0–23% with a positive margin. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not attempt local excision alone above Bismuth type I: all five type II and IIIa patients treated that way had involved margins and recurred locally. Caudate resection is obligatory from type II upward because the segment 1 ducts are almost always involved. The Milan consensus prefers left-sided hemihepatectomy where it will achieve the same clearance, because right-sided resection carries more morbidity, liver failure and mortality at equal oncological outcome, and does not recommend routine vascular resection, no-touch technique included; arterial resection belongs in expert centres only. Evidence & sources Downgraded from B to C. The margin data come from 23 resections accumulated over 30 years at one centre — 19 of 122 operated patients (15.6%) had a macroscopically curative resection and only 9 of 122 (7.4%) a histologically negative margin — with no comparison group, mean follow-up 26 months, and the survival credited to R0 therefore uncontrolled and heavily selected. The 27–58 month R0 figure is ungraded expert consensus. Outcomes are volume-dependent: even in benchmark patients at expert centres 5-year overall survival does not exceed 40%, severe complications reach 70%, 90-day mortality reaches 13%, one in five needs re-laparotomy and only two-thirds achieve a negative margin. Lymphadenectomy of stations 12 (positive in 25%), 8 (14%) and 13a (11%) with 5–7 nodes harvested; nodal positivity runs 16–60% overall; no benefit from extended dissection to the celiac axis, superior mesenteric artery or periaortic nodes. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Prepare in a sequence with dates rather than improvising: drain the remnant, embolise the portal vein when the remnant is inadequate, correct nutrition.
text: Standard Evidence C Prepare in a sequence with dates rather than improvising: drain the remnant, embolise the portal vein when the remnant is inadequate, correct nutrition. Indications Preferred when Every patient needing an extended hepatectomy. These steps take weeks, and the order is not interchangeable — hypertrophy is poor while the remnant remains obstructed, so drainage comes first. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Resection attempted without remnant drainage. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Portal vein embolisation Recommended where the anticipated remnant is inadequate and the disease is otherwise resectable. NCCN requires the contralateral liver to have intact arterial and portal inflow as well as biliary drainage.
text: Portal vein embolisation Evidence C Recommended where the anticipated remnant is inadequate and the disease is otherwise resectable. NCCN requires the contralateral liver to have intact arterial and portal inflow as well as biliary drainage. Indications Preferred when Most useful when the future liver remnant is below 30–40%. A meta-analysis of 1,140 patients found remnant gains of 8–27% with no mortality and under 3% morbidity. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not embolise a remnant that is still obstructed. If the post-embolisation remnant is 20% or less, or hypertrophy is 5% or less, resection may be contraindicated — reassess at 3–6 weeks and check remnant drainage and nutrition before abandoning the operation. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Liver venous deprivationEXPERTISE The Milan consensus places it after portal vein embolisation, for a remnant under 20–25% — a level-4 expert-opinion statement with no comparative data in this disease.
text: Liver venous deprivation Evidence D EXPERTISE The Milan consensus places it after portal vein embolisation, for a remnant under 20–25% — a level-4 expert-opinion statement with no comparative data in this disease. Indications Preferred when Expert centres where portal vein embolisation alone will not deliver the volume needed. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Not a first manoeuvre, and not a substitute for drainage of the remnant. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: ALPPSEXPERTISE REGISTRY Salvage only in the Milan consensus; BSG does not recommend it for perihilar cholangiocarcinoma at all.
text: ALPPS Evidence C EXPERTISE REGISTRY Salvage only in the Milan consensus; BSG does not recommend it for perihilar cholangiocarcinoma at all. Indications Preferred when No routine place in this disease. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Mortality was 48% in the international registry for perihilar cholangiocarcinoma. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Capecitabine for 6 months is a reasonable option after resection, not an obligation — offer it with the actual numbers.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Capecitabine for 6 months is a reasonable option after resection, not an obligation — offer it with the actual numbers. Indications Preferred when A resected patient fit for 8 cycles who wants adjuvant treatment, particularly with adverse features. BILCAP (n=447) gave median overall survival 51.1 versus 36.4 months with an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.81 (95% CI 0.63–1.04), p=0.097 — the intention-to-treat primary analysis did not meet significance. Significance appeared per protocol (210 versus 220 patients, HR 0.75, 0.58–0.97) and in the protocol-specified intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis adjusted for nodal status, grade and sex (HR 0.71, 0.55–0.92), and the trial was unmasked. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not present it as established benefit in this tumour. 128 of 447 patients (29%) had hilar tumours, the trial was not powered for site-specific effects, and the BILCAP perihilar subgroup estimate was imprecise (HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.68–1.71); Milan nevertheless recommends six months of capecitabine or S-1 (strong, level 2). The recurrence-free survival advantage was confined to the first 24 months (HR 0.75, 0.58–0.98) with none from 24 to 60 months (HR 1.48, 0.80–2.77), which the authors read as recurrence deferred rather than prevented. Grade 3 events occurred in 44% of treated patients, 55% completed all eight cycles, 46% needed a dose reduction and 32% stopped for toxicity. Evidence & sources Downgraded from B to C, because the trial is negative on its prespecified primary endpoint and the positive signal rests on a per-protocol analysis and an adjusted model; the linked commentary asks whether that is enough to define a standard of care. NCCN designates capecitabine preferred, category 1, while also acknowledging BILCAP's nonsignificant intention-to-treat analysis; the local label and grade remain more cautious and require explicit multidisciplinary local approval. ASCOT (n=440) was positive for S-1 — 3-year survival 77.1% versus 67.6%, HR 0.69 (0.51–0.94) — but relapse-free survival did not reach significance (HR 0.80, 0.61–1.04, p=0.088), the analysis was taken at 179 deaths against 285 planned events, the R1 subgroup showed nothing (HR 1.04, 0.57–1.92), the trial was conducted only in Japan and S-1 is unavailable in the United States. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Capecitabine vs observation: ITT median OS 51.1 vs 36.4 mo, adjusted HR 0.81 (95% CI 0.63–1.04), p=0.097 — primary endpoint not met 128 of 447 (29%) hilar; not powered for site-specific effects; unmasked

n=440: 3-y survival 77.1% vs 67.6%, S-1 vs observation, HR 0.69 (0.51–0.94); RFS HR 0.80 (0.61–1.04), p=0.088, not significant Japan only; analysed at 179 deaths vs 285 planned events; R1 subgroup null; no S-1 in US

lead: After an R1 resection, discuss adjuvant chemoradiation in addition to systemic therapy as a shared decision, weighing toxicity against local-recurrence benefit.
text: Reasonable Evidence C After an R1 resection, discuss adjuvant chemoradiation in addition to systemic therapy as a shared decision, weighing toxicity against local-recurrence benefit. Indications Preferred when A microscopically positive margin, with radiation oncology review of margins, nodal burden and toxicity. Local recurrence is the failure pattern radiation can address, and R1 resection is common in this disease — AASLD reports up to 50% of cases. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid NCCN lists an option; it does not make this mandatory for every R1 case. The supporting data are retrospective meta-analyses — BSG cites 21 retrospective studies and more than 1,400 patients — plus the single-arm SWOG S0809 phase II trial (79 patients, 68% bile duct and 32% gallbladder; 2-year overall survival 67% after R0 and 60% after R1, with no control arm). The Milan consensus states flatly that adjuvant radiotherapy remains unproven, with benefit suggested mainly in R1 and N1 disease. Evidence & sources Whether node-positive R0 disease should prompt the same discussion is open (§11 item 10): NCCN places nodal involvement alongside margin status as a trigger, BSG limits its recommendation to R1 resection, and the node-positive benefit rests on retrospective meta-analysis. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Adjuvant gemcitabine after resection of bile duct cancer.
text: Avoid Evidence B Adjuvant gemcitabine after resection of bile duct cancer. Why Why Nothing in this disease — use capecitabine if adjuvant treatment is given. This is the one adjuvant randomised trial confined to the population this page covers, which is why it carries weight here despite its size. Additional cautions Additional cautions BCAT (n=225, perihilar and distal bile duct cancer only, no intrahepatic and no gallbladder disease) was null: median overall survival 62.3 versus 63.8 months, hazard ratio 1.01 (95% CI 0.70–1.45), p=0.964, with no subgroup benefiting, including node-positive and R1 patients, and grade 3–4 neutropenia in 58.4% versus 3.8%. Evidence & sources Read the null honestly in both directions. Recruitment stopped at 226 of a planned 300 because most patients wanted adjuvant chemotherapy, and the authors calculate only a 2.8% probability the result would have reached significance even with the planned 189 deaths. Observed 5-year survival was about 50% against an assumed 30%, because R2 resections, distant metastases, severe surgical complications and in-hospital deaths were all excluded — a favourable cohort with too few events. This rules out gemcitabine, not adjuvant therapy. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Adjuvant gemcitabine after resected perihilar/distal bile duct cancer (n=225): null, p=0.964; no subgroup benefited, including node-positive and R1 Stopped at 226 of planned 300; favourable cohort with too few events

lead: Adjuvant gemcitabine–oxaliplatin after resection.
text: Avoid Evidence B Adjuvant gemcitabine–oxaliplatin after resection. Why Why Nothing in this disease. Additional cautions Additional cautions PRODIGE-12 was negative on both co-primary endpoints — relapse-free survival 30.4 versus 18.5 months, HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.62–1.25), p=0.48, and time to definitive deterioration of global quality of life 31.8 versus 32.1 months, HR 1.28 (0.73–2.26) — and overall survival numerically favoured surveillance (HR 1.08, 0.70–1.66). Worst adverse event was grade 3 in 62% and grade 4 in 11%, the 73% figure the roadmap quotes. Evidence & sources Both medians fell on a plateau of the survival curves, so the 30.4 versus 18.5 month gap overstates the separation; the authors say the hazard ratio is the honest summary. The population was lower risk than BILCAP (13% R1, 38% node-positive) and only 28% had extrahepatic disease. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Gemcitabine–oxaliplatin vs surveillance: both co-primaries negative; RFS 30.4 vs 18.5 mo, HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.62–1.25), p=0.48; QoL HR 1.28 (0.73–2.26) OS HR 1.08 favoured surveillance; medians on curve plateau, so HR is the honest summary

lead: Resection attempted without drainage of the future liver remnant.
text: Avoid Evidence D Resection attempted without drainage of the future liver remnant. Why Why Drain the remnant, confirm the bilirubin is falling within 1–2 weeks, and only then proceed. Additional cautions Additional cautions This is the roadmap's named Avoid for clinical decision 1 and it is a sequence error, not a judgement call.

lead: Refer potentially eligible patients before primary biopsy, treatment outside the transplant protocol, or attempted resection; assess in parallel without delaying indicated curative resection. Do not perform transperitoneal primary biopsy (including EUS/percutaneous) while transplant remains an option. Coordinate intraductal/ERCP and indicated regional-node sampling. Do not delay urgent drainage or infection treatment.
text: Standard Evidence D Refer potentially eligible patients before primary biopsy, treatment outside the transplant protocol, or attempted resection; assess in parallel without delaying indicated curative resection. Do not perform transperitoneal primary biopsy (including EUS/percutaneous) while transplant remains an option. Coordinate intraductal/ERCP and indicated regional-node sampling. Do not delay urgent drainage or infection treatment. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Refer potentially eligible patients to the transplant team before primary-tumor biopsy, chemotherapy or radiation outside the transplant protocol, or attempted resection. Coordinate assessment in parallel with surgical planning; do not delay an indicated curative resection. Do not perform transperitoneal biopsy of the primary perihilar tumor, including percutaneous or EUS-guided biopsy, while transplantation remains an option. Coordinate ERCP brushings or intraductal sampling and, when indicated, regional lymph-node sampling with the team; do not delay urgent drainage or infection treatment. Indications Preferred when Patients with potentially protocol-eligible unresectable pCCA, including PSC-associated disease, should receive early transplant review alongside assessment of biliary drainage and resection. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The sequencing recommendation rests on protocol eligibility criteria, not on a randomised comparison of referral timing — that trial does not exist. Evidence & sources AASLD goes further than the roadmap and states that transplantation is preferred over resection in all cases of primary sclerosing cholangitis, but that document is expert consensus rather than a GRADE-rated guideline. The 12-centre series found no difference in outcome by PSC status, so the PSC preference is not a finding of the primary data. Whether PSC-associated tumours should be routed here even when technically resectable is an open local decision (alignment area 9). Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Use the transplant center’s approved neoadjuvant treatment protocol, followed by operative staging and liver transplantation when all criteria remain met.
text: Reasonable Evidence C PROTOCOL REGISTRY Use the transplant center’s approved neoadjuvant treatment protocol, followed by operative staging and liver transplantation when all criteria remain met. Indications Preferred when A protocol candidate meeting every policy condition at a programme that holds the approval. In 287 patients across 12 US centres, intention-to-treat survival from the start of therapy was 68% at 2 years and 53% at 5 years. The recurrence-free survival figures quoted elsewhere are on a different and smaller denominator: 78% at 2 years (95% CI 72–84), 65% at 5 years (57–73) and 59% at 10 years among the 214 who reached transplantation, with graft survival 77%, 60% and 51%. Keep the two apart — 53% at 5 years is what the pathway delivers to a patient who enters it, 65% is what it delivers to a patient who gets through it. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not read these as a treatment effect. The experience is retrospective and multicentre with no arm of transplantation without neoadjuvant therapy and none of resection, so the benefit credited to chemoradiation is inferred from historical recurrence rates; 193 of 287 patients (67%) came from one centre; neoadjuvant protocols differed widely between centres (brachytherapy in 75%, maintenance chemotherapy in 65%, external beam dose 2,100–6,000 cGy), and that heterogeneity meant the independent effect of maintenance chemotherapy could not be determined. Selection is doing substantial work: patients transplanted outside criteria did significantly worse (HR 2.98, 95% CI 1.79–4.95, P<.001) and selection was the only independent predictor of recurrence-free survival. 71 of 287 (25%) dropped out at a median of 4.6 months, a rate averaging 11.5% per 3-month interval from the end of chemoradiation (range 7–17%). Staging surgery still found metastases in 17% (40 of 229), though with only 30 transplanted patients unstaged that comparison was underpowered (HR 0.73, 0.37–1.43). Evidence & sources Published chemoradiation protocols provide much of the clinical evidence. OPTN Policy 9.5.A requires neoadjuvant therapy and operative staging but does not prescribe a specific radiotherapy regimen. The approved center protocol determines chemotherapy, radiotherapy if included, and treatment milestones. Protocol modifications require center review. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Retrospective 12-centre series, n=287: ITT survival 68% at 2 y, 53% at 5 y; among 214 transplanted, 5-y RFS 65% (57–73) No control arm; 67% from one centre; 25% dropped out; selection drives outcome

lead: Radiotherapy, sometimes SBRT in a centre-specific protocol, may contribute to a curative transplant strategy — as a component of the approved regimen, not as a substitute for it.
text: Reasonable Evidence D PROTOCOL Radiotherapy, sometimes SBRT in a centre-specific protocol, may contribute to a curative transplant strategy — as a component of the approved regimen, not as a substitute for it. Indications Preferred when Discuss the transplant protocol before any radiation is planned. The evidence supports the whole neoadjuvant-plus-transplant pathway, not radiation alone. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not substitute an arbitrary SBRT schedule for approved neoadjuvant treatment, and do not assume it confers allocation eligibility. Isolated SBRT cure evidence is limited, and central bile duct, duodenal and infection risks can require a different fractionation. Evidence & sources A local complete response is not an automatic transplant exception. Record bridge or downstaging treatment separately from definitive local treatment. Graded D: no study in this depot isolates the contribution of radiotherapy within the protocol, and the ESMO guideline grades external beam radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy as definitive treatment of locally advanced disease [II, D], to be used only in trials. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not start non-protocol cancer treatment in a potentially eligible patient before the transplant team has reviewed the case.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not start non-protocol cancer treatment in a potentially eligible patient before the transplant team has reviewed the case. Why Why Discuss transplant eligibility at the first multidisciplinary review, together with the drainage and tissue-sampling plan. Additional cautions Additional cautions Prior treatment may affect eligibility under the center protocol. Review the actual regimen and timing; prior chemotherapy is not listed as a universal exclusion in OPTN Policy 9.5.A; clinical protocols may be more restrictive.

lead: Do not use Rea 2005 to tell a resectable patient that transplantation is the better operation.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not use Rea 2005 to tell a resectable patient that transplantation is the better operation. Why Why The defensible claim from that paper is what the Mayo protocol achieves in a selected, node-negative, mostly PSC population — not that transplantation beats resection in a patient who is resectable. Additional cautions Additional cautions The selection asymmetry is complete and the authors say so. By protocol no transplant patient was resectable, and every recipient was proved node-negative at staging laparotomy, while 8 of 26 resected patients (31%) were node-positive and 3 of 26 (12%) R1. The curves also start at different points: 82% 5-year survival is measured from transplantation among the 38 of 71 enrolled who got there, against 21% from resection among the 26 of 54 explored; from the start of treatment the comparison is 58% versus about 21%. Recipients were 15 years younger (48 versus 63, P<0.001) and 58% had PSC against 8%. 16 of 38 explants showed no residual tumour and 8 of those patients had no tissue proof of cancer before neoadjuvant therapy. Evidence & sources The node-negative R0 resection subgroup fared no better (87%, 53% and 18% at 1, 3 and 5 years), and the 20–21% 5-year survival after resection matches other specialist centres, so the comparator is not substandard. Three of 26 resections (12%) died within 30 days, and the discussants' point was that non-cancer deaths, not recurrence, drive much of the gap — recurrence after resection was 35% while 5-year survival was 20%. There is no intention-to-treat analysis and no accounting of organ cost: 38 grafts, 7 of them living donor, for 71 patients enrolled. The Milan jury acknowledged benefit in node-negative patients independent of resectability; that is a consensus position resting on one benchmark study and mixed retrospective comparisons, and TRANSPHIL, the randomised trial meant to settle it, failed to recruit. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Selected cohorts, no ITT: 5-y survival 82% from LT vs 21% from resection; from start of treatment 58% vs about 21% No LT patient resectable, all node-negative; recipients 15 y younger, PSC 58% vs 8%

lead: Apply OPTN allocation criteria exactly as written. A favorable clinical assessment does not override the requirements for a standardized exception.
text: Avoid Evidence D Apply OPTN allocation criteria exactly as written. A favorable clinical assessment does not override the requirements for a standardized exception. Why Why They are conditions of OPTN Policy 9.5.A, not entry criteria of the 12-centre series, which transplanted 48 patients outside them. Exactly 3 cm does not meet the policy mass-size assessment; referral and allocation are distinct, and NCCN's ≤3 cm referral wording is looser than the policy. Additional cautions Additional cautions Mass size caused the greatest disparity in the multicentre series: 5-year recurrence-free survival was 32% for a mass over 3 cm against 69% for 3 cm or smaller (P<.001). Evidence & sources Confirm the current OPTN policy text before any listing decision. The transplant coordinator records source version, eligibility dates, request and extension dates, imaging, laboratory values and a named renewal owner; transplant leadership signs the allocation assessment. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: 12-centre series: 5-y RFS 32% vs 69%, mass >3 cm vs ≤3 cm (P<.001) Series transplanted 48 patients outside the OPTN criteria

lead: Cisplatin–gemcitabine plus durvalumab NCCN and ESMO both recommend it first line; ESMO's interim update grades the two checkpoint combinations [I, A] together.
text: Cisplatin–gemcitabine plus durvalumab Evidence B NCCN and ESMO both recommend it first line; ESMO's interim update grades the two checkpoint combinations [I, A] together. Indications Preferred when A fit patient with adequate drainage and an acceptable bilirubin. TOPAZ-1 (n=685) gave overall survival hazard ratio 0.80 (95% CI 0.66–0.97), P=0.021, median 12.8 versus 11.5 months, with the separation in the tail — 24-month survival 24.9% versus 10.4%, and a hazard ratio of 0.91 (0.66–1.26) in the first 6 months against 0.74 (0.58–0.94) thereafter. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Address biliary infection and organ reserve before starting; prior immune exposure changes later choices. No trial compares durvalumab with pembrolizumab, and no clinical, biochemical or molecular biomarker favours one over the other — ESMO's statement that they are interchangeable is an indirect comparison across two trials that differ in chemotherapy duration and population. This was a prespecified interim analysis at 424 of 496 planned deaths powered to about 75%, the median gain is 1.3 months, and the proportional hazards assumption was formally violated, so a single hazard ratio misrepresents a time-varying effect. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Cisplatin–gemcitabine plus pembrolizumab Recommended first line alongside the durvalumab combination, unranked.
text: Cisplatin–gemcitabine plus pembrolizumab Evidence B Recommended first line alongside the durvalumab combination, unranked. Indications Preferred when The same population. KEYNOTE-966 (n=1,069) gave median overall survival 12.7 versus 10.9 months, hazard ratio 0.83 (95% CI 0.72–0.95); 24-month survival 25% versus 18%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Both supporting endpoints failed their prespecified boundaries — progression-free survival HR 0.86 (0.75–1.00), p=0.023 against 0.0125, and objective response identical at 29% versus 29%, p=0.47 — so the benefit rests on one endpoint with no response signal behind it. More importantly for this page: the trial was enriched for intrahepatic disease (59%) because tumour tissue was mandatory, and the extrahepatic subgroup, which is where perihilar tumours sit, gave an overall survival hazard ratio of 0.99 (95% CI 0.73–1.35). Immune-mediated events occurred in 22% versus 13% and treatment-related deaths in 8 (2%) versus 3 (1%), with no improvement in quality of life. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Order molecular profiling at diagnosis and screen for clinical-trial eligibility at the same visit.
text: Standard Evidence B Order molecular profiling at diagnosis and screen for clinical-trial eligibility at the same visit. Indications Preferred when Every patient entering systemic therapy. Actionable alterations do occur in perihilar disease, but not in the same pattern as intrahepatic disease. FGFR2 fusions and IDH1 mutations concentrate in intrahepatic tumours — ClarIDHy enrolled 187 patients of whom only 6 had extrahepatic or perihilar disease, and FIGHT-202 cohort A was 107 of 108 intrahepatic — while HER2 alterations occur in about 5–10% of biliary tract cancer and are commoner in extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder carcinoma, which makes HER2 the one target enriched in this disease rather than depleted. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not assume hilar disease shares the iCCA target distribution, and do not treat the gene as the target — different alterations in the same gene do not predict the same response, as ESMO notes for HER2 amplification versus mutation. ESMO also concedes there are no standardised criteria for assessing HER2 status in biliary tract cancer and that no specific test can be recommended, with gastric cancer immunohistochemistry criteria offered as the best available; two HER2-directed recommendations then rest on that undefined assay. Evidence & sources Downgraded from A to B. Profiling itself is graded [I, A] by ESMO, but almost every therapeutic recommendation that follows from it is level III, grade A — single-arm phase II or basket-trial evidence with no randomised comparator — and several named agents are FDA- but not EMA-approved. Use the source edition's full actionable panel, including NRG1 where appropriate. Preserve tissue for it; next-generation sequencing of the ERCP specimen can serve both diagnosis and target identification, and in the 6-year multi-institutional series it found actionable alterations in 30% of cholangiocarcinomas. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Enrolment: 187 patients, of whom only 6 had extrahepatic or perihilar disease IDH1 mutations concentrate in intrahepatic tumours

lead: Durable biliary drainage is a co-primary goal of treatment, not supportive care around it.
text: Standard Evidence C Durable biliary drainage is a co-primary goal of treatment, not supportive care around it. Indications Preferred when Recurrent cholangitis, not tumour progression, is often what ends treatment. Adequate drainage and an acceptable bilirubin come before the first cycle, and new jaundice or fever is managed as an urgent referral rather than waitinging for the next scan. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not deliver liver-directed therapy without relieving obstruction first. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Radiotherapy for local control or symptoms, including definitive chemoradiation for selected localised unresectable disease.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Radiotherapy for local control or symptoms, including definitive chemoradiation for selected localised unresectable disease. Indications Preferred when Local symptoms, or localised unresectable disease where the goal is control rather than cure. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Avoid radiotherapy that would compromise later protocol eligibility in a patient still under transplant consideration. Isolated SBRT cure evidence is limited, and central bile duct, duodenal and infection risks can require a different fractionation. Evidence & sources Graded D: no study in this depot supports definitive chemoradiation in perihilar disease, the AHPBA panel's figure for definitive chemoradiation in unresectable patients ineligible for transplant is a median survival of 10.7–14.6 months from uncontrolled series, and ESMO grades external beam radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy as definitive treatment of locally advanced cholangiocarcinoma [II, D] — not to be used outside trials. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Second line, FOLFOX after progression on a platinum doublet.
text: Reasonable Evidence B Second line, FOLFOX after progression on a platinum doublet. Indications Preferred when A patient who has kept performance status and wants further treatment. ABC-06 (n=162) gave median overall survival 6.2 versus 5.3 months against active symptom control, adjusted hazard ratio 0.69 (95% CI 0.50–0.97), p=0.031; 6-month survival 50.6% versus 35.5% and 12-month survival 25.9% versus 11.4%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The absolute gain is 0.9 months of median survival, with grade 3–5 events in 69% versus 52% and three chemotherapy-related deaths. Objective response was seen in only 4 of 81 patients (5%), so the benefit is disease stabilisation, not shrinkage. More patients in the FOLFOX arm were platinum resistant or refractory (67% versus 58%), an imbalance in a factor that was itself independently prognostic, and stratification errors found during data cleaning required a post-hoc sensitivity analysis (adjusted HR 0.68, 0.49–0.95). Say both halves out loud. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: FOLFOX vs active symptom control: median OS 6.2 vs 5.3 mo, adjusted HR 0.69 (95% CI 0.50–0.97), p=0.031; 12-mo OS 25.9% vs 11.4% Gain 0.9 mo; grade 3–5 events 69% vs 52%; response 5%; platinum-resistance imbalance

lead: Where a driver is present, use the agent matched to that specific alteration.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Where a driver is present, use the agent matched to that specific alteration. Indications Preferred when FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements, IDH1 mutation, BRAF V600E, HER2 overexpression (IHC 3+), MSI-high or mismatch-repair deficiency, and rare targetable fusions can all occur in this disease. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Except for IDH1, these are single-arm response data rather than comparative survival data, and the matched-therapy trials enrolled almost only intrahepatic tumours — FIGHT-202 cohort A 107 of 108 intrahepatic, FOENIX-CCA2 intrahepatic only, ROAR 39 of 43 (91%) intrahepatic, ClarIDHy 6 of 187 extrahepatic or perihilar — so their effect in perihilar disease is an extrapolation. Every one of these trials was industry sponsored with company employees among the authors, and all of them are second-line or later, so none says anything about conversion to resection. HER2 is the exception worth pursuing here, because it is enriched in extrahepatic disease: in HERIZON-BTC-01 zanidatamab gave a confirmed response rate of 41% overall but 52% (39–65) in immunohistochemistry 3+ tumours against 6% (1 of 18) in 2+, with median overall survival 18.1 versus 5.2 months — so the 3+ restriction is doing the work, and the trial reports no breakdown by anatomical subsite. Evidence & sources ClarIDHy improved PFS in previously treated IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma (2.7 versus 1.4 months; HR 0.37). Final ITT OS was 10.3 versus 7.5 months (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.56–1.12; P=.09), with 70% crossover. The October 2026 correction retains the crossover-adjusted HR 0.49 but changes its bootstrap 95% CI to 0.25–1.24; adjusted OS is not statistically significant. Response was 2%, so large shrinkage is uncommon; surgical conversion was not established. The final population was predominantly intrahepatic, with only six extrahepatic/perihilar cases; no pCCA-specific treatment effect is established. No randomized evidence establishes a sequence among all targeted options. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Ivosidenib: PFS HR 0.37; ITT OS 10.3 vs 7.5 mo, HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.56–1.12), P=.09 Corrected crossover-adjusted HR 0.49 (95% CI 0.25–1.24); neither OS analysis significant
Single-arm zanidatamab: confirmed ORR 41%; IHC 3+ vs 2+: ORR 52% (39–65) vs 6% (1 of 18), median OS 18.1 vs 5.2 mo Single-arm study; no randomized survival comparison or anatomical-subsite estimate

lead: Thermal ablation of the perihilar primary.
text: Avoid Evidence D Thermal ablation of the perihilar primary. Why Why Resection, or protocol neoadjuvant therapy followed by transplantation, should be considered first where the patient is eligible. Graded D: this is a position taken on the absence of evidence in central biliary tumours, not on a comparative study. Additional cautions Additional cautions Not an established curative option. Central biliary and vascular anatomy and longitudinal tumour spread differ from a small peripheral liver mass, so iCCA ablation selection rules do not transfer. Endobiliary ablation to improve drainage is a different procedure and does not establish cure.

lead: Y90 radioembolisation or TACE for the hilar primary.
text: Avoid Evidence D Y90 radioembolisation or TACE for the hilar primary. Why Why No standard first- or second-line role for the primary, and graded D because no study in this depot addresses a central perihilar primary. A peripheral intrahepatic recurrence or metastatic target may occasionally be discussed for hepatic control, but that is a different indication and is not the iCCA pathway; in exceptional liver-dominant recurrent disease, use only a specific multidisciplinary rationale or a trial. Additional cautions Additional cautions Neither is established for curative treatment of a central perihilar primary. Drainage, infection risk and arterial coverage require expert assessment, and prior drainage or instrumentation increases infectious risk.

lead: Hepatic arterial infusion for the hilar primary, outside a disease-specific trial.
text: Avoid Evidence D Hepatic arterial infusion for the hilar primary, outside a disease-specific trial. Why Why Research or exceptional use with an explicit control goal; standard systemic therapy remains the backbone outside curative pathways. Additional cautions Additional cautions The principal HAI studies are in unresectable intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma — the phase II trial of HAI floxuridine with systemic gemcitabine–oxaliplatin treated 38 of 84 screened patients with liver-confined iCCA and met its 6-month progression-free survival endpoint at 84.1%, with median overall survival 25.0 months against a historical comparator — and they cannot justify a routine hilar-primary pathway. That trial was single-arm and single-institution, 11% of patients had grade 4 pump or arterial complications and 30% did so in the 10-patient confirmatory cohort, and 11% needed biliary stents, two of them for chemotherapy-induced biliary sclerosis. In a tumour whose problem is central biliary obstruction, that last figure is the relevant one. Evidence & sources Graded D for this page: the evidence is in a different anatomical disease, and the toxicity that matters most here — biliary sclerosis — is the one the iCCA trial reports. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Single-arm phase II, unresectable iCCA (38 treated): 6-mo PFS 84.1%, primary endpoint met; median OS 25.0 mo vs historical comparator iCCA, not hilar; single-institution; grade 4 pump/arterial complications 11%; biliary stents 11%

lead: Histotripsy, outside a prospective trial or institutional registry.
text: Avoid Evidence D REGISTRY Histotripsy, outside a prospective trial or institutional registry. Why Why The roadmap's label here is trial or prospective registry only, with explicit consent about oncologic uncertainty, suitable ultrasound visibility and acoustic access, device-compliant target size and depth, and an independent standard-treatment review. Graded D: there is no perihilar evidence at all. Additional cautions Additional cautions No tumour-specific curative evidence. FDA device clearance for tumour destruction does not establish survival benefit or equivalence to established ablation; in the one-year HOPE4LIVER update of 47 patients and 52 tumours, local control was 63.4% on the primary assessment against 90% post hoc. A bridge-to-transplant use remains protocol-based, and a technical response does not establish transplant eligibility. Studies must address hilar anatomy, drainage and transplant consequences explicitly.

lead: Effective drainage, pruritus and pain control, nutritional support, and early specialist palliative involvement.
text: Standard Evidence C Effective drainage, pruritus and pain control, nutritional support, and early specialist palliative involvement. Indications Preferred when Every patient at this assessment, and alongside antitumour treatment at the earlier ones. Effective drainage is part of supportive care, not an alternative to it. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let a decision for supportive care become a decision against drainage — a blocked, infected biliary tree is the commonest reversible cause of the state that put the patient here. Evidence & sources Downgraded from A to C, because the package is not one intervention and only part of it has evidence in this depot. Drainage rests on guideline recommendations graded low to very low quality; early specialist palliative involvement rests on trial evidence in other cancers that this reference depot does not contain; pruritus control, pain control and nutritional support are uncontroversial but untested here. The grade should not be read as though a trial had tested the bundle. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: If jaundice and sepsis are driving performance status, re-evaluate after drainage before assigning this assessment.
text: Reasonable Evidence C If jaundice and sepsis are driving performance status, re-evaluate after drainage before assigning this assessment. Indications Preferred when The acutely unwell, newly presenting patient. This reverses more often than expected. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not assign the assessment on a performance status measured during cholangitis.

lead: Antitumour therapy without realistic benefit, and repeat interventions that cannot change the plan.
text: Avoid Evidence D Antitumour therapy without realistic benefit, and repeat interventions that cannot change the plan. Why Why One recommendation, one owner, one reassessment date — and a documented alternative considered. Additional cautions Additional cautions Repeating a procedure because it is the procedure that was done last time. After progression or toxicity, restage and reconsider the whole treatment rather than automatically repeating the same intervention. Evidence & sources Graded D: an operating rule the programme has chosen, not a comparative result. Audit it for adherence, not for effectiveness. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Obtain expert pathology reporting differentiation and representative Ki-67, with mitoses when evaluable. An adequate small biopsy may be graded with Ki-67 when mitoses cannot be assessed; inadequate or discordant tissue needs review and further sampling if it would change treatment.
text: Standard Evidence C Obtain expert pathology reporting differentiation and representative Ki-67, with mitoses when evaluable. An adequate small biopsy may be graded with Ki-67 when mitoses cannot be assessed; inadequate or discordant tissue needs review and further sampling if it would change treatment. Indications Preferred when Every patient before a pathway is assigned, and again on any specimen sampled metachronously — a well-differentiated G3 tumour and a poorly differentiated carcinoma can share a Ki-67 range and need different pathways. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not accept a report giving Ki-67 as a range, and do not let grade stand in for differentiation; if the report does not say which it is, ask the pathologist before the board meets. Evidence & sources Downgraded to C on the full-text read. The requirement is right but its evidence is consensus, not comparison: NANETS 2017 means a show of hands from a 15-member panel with no evidence grading and no systematic literature search, and consensus was recorded only that both differentiation and grade be reported, with a significant majority — 75% or more — that both mitotic rate and Ki-67 be measured and fine-needle aspiration accepted as adequate in most cases. ENETS 2023 explicitly states that Ki-67 alone cannot distinguish NET G3 from NEC. Use differentiation, morphology and appropriate immunohistochemistry; 55% is not a diagnostic boundary. A mixed neuroendocrine–non-neuroendocrine neoplasm is named as such, and its clinically dominant aggressive component sets the pathway. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Stage with somatostatin-receptor PET/CT, 68Ga-DOTATATE or equivalent, alongside cross-sectional CT or MRI.
text: Standard Evidence B Stage with somatostatin-receptor PET/CT, 68Ga-DOTATATE or equivalent, alongside cross-sectional CT or MRI. Indications Preferred when Use SSTR imaging for staging and when it will change management, including PRRT assessment or discordant progression. Use CT/MRI for routine response surveillance and repeat receptor imaging selectively. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not use receptor uptake as a substitute for anatomic burden assessment or as a universal response measure, and do not order octreotide SPECT/CT unless SSTR-PET is unavailable. Evidence & sources Graded B on diagnostic accuracy rather than on outcome: NANETS 2017 reports 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT sensitivity of 95% against 31% for octreotide SPECT, which is why the substitution is made. The EANM position itself is a modified three-round Delphi vote — necessary at staging of all NET in 19 of 23 panellists (82.6%), CT or MRI also necessary in 20 of 23 (87.0%) — with consensus set at 70% agreement for a single answer and only 50% preference in multiple-choice format, and consensus failed on 12 of 43 questions. The panel was drawn from high-volume centres with full access to Ga-68 tracer and PRRT, so availability is assumed rather than tested. Where SSTR-PET has not been done, the board records its absence explicitly rather than proceeding as if it had. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Delphi consensus: SSTR-PET necessary at staging of all NET in 19 of 23 panellists (82.6%); CT or MRI also necessary in 20 of 23 (87.0%) Consensus threshold 70%; failed on 12 of 43 questions; high-volume panel

lead: Record carcinoid syndrome, insulinoma, gastrinoma or any other functional syndrome explicitly, confirmed with tests directed at the suspected syndrome rather than a panel of every available marker.
text: Standard Evidence D Record carcinoid syndrome, insulinoma, gastrinoma or any other functional syndrome explicitly, confirmed with tests directed at the suspected syndrome rather than a panel of every available marker. Indications Preferred when Before any hepatic procedure — this changes procedural safety planning, not only symptom management, and high hepatic burden with a midgut primary is the dominant carcinoid-crisis risk combination. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat a normal marker panel as excluding a functional syndrome, and do not leave the syndrome undocumented because symptoms are currently controlled on an analogue. Evidence & sources Grade D: a named local requirement with no comparative outcome evidence behind the thresholds themselves. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Document liver burden/distribution/resectability, primary site and resection, extrahepatic sites, and the main clinical problem.
text: Standard Evidence D Document liver burden/distribution/resectability, primary site and resection, extrahepatic sites, and the main clinical problem. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × State the hepatic tumour burden, unilobar versus bilobar, resectable versus diffuse-miliary pattern, the primary site and whether it is resected, the extrahepatic sites, and which problem is driving the clinical picture. Indications Preferred when Every case at submission: burden and distribution decide whether cytoreduction, embolotherapy or transplantation is an option at all. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not open a treatment discussion where the dominant problem has not been named — hormonal symptoms and tumour progression need different answers and conflating them produces treatment without an endpoint.

lead: Obtain FDG PET where the grade is high, where behaviour is discordant with grade, where SSTR uptake is heterogeneous, or where a CT or MRI lesion shows no SSTR uptake.
text: Reasonable Evidence B Obtain FDG PET where the grade is high, where behaviour is discordant with grade, where SSTR uptake is heterogeneous, or where a CT or MRI lesion shows no SSTR uptake. Indications Preferred when Before committing to receptor-directed therapy in G2–G3 disease or rapid progression, to find receptor-negative, FDG-avid disease that PRRT will not treat. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Not for routine staging of well-differentiated disease, where NANETS found no value in it. Evidence & sources The roadmap keeps FDG selective on the Itanet triggers rather than requiring it for every G2–G3 PRRT candidate as EANM Focus 3 does. EANM endorsed FDG before PRRT in G2–G3 to exclude mismatched FDG-positive, SSTR-negative lesions in 19 of 23 panellists (82.6%) by modified Delphi, and Itanet grades the FDG trigger 3b-A. What neither establishes is that acting on the mismatch changes outcome: EANM's extension of PRRT into G3 rests on two small retrospective series confined to Ki-67 under 55%, and EANM reached no consensus at all on PRRT with mismatched lesions. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Modified Delphi: FDG before PRRT in G2–G3 endorsed by 19 of 23 panellists (82.6%) No consensus on PRRT with mismatched lesions; outcome benefit unproven

lead: Consider re-biopsy on unexpected behavioural change or discordant FDG avidity.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Consider re-biopsy on unexpected behavioural change or discordant FDG avidity. Indications Preferred when Where the original grading is years old or the disease has clearly changed pace: grade progression and transformation both occur and change the pathway. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Not as a scheduled ritual — no study defines the trigger or the interval, which is why this sits at C and remains an open local decision. Evidence & sources Itanet attaches 3a-A to re-evaluation before radioligand therapy when behaviour changes, which is stronger than the roadmap's 'consider'; whether it becomes a required step before PRRT is a local approval item. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not assign a pathway on grade alone.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not assign a pathway on grade alone. Why Why The differentiation fork drives every later decision, so the tissue standard is deliberately set high. Additional cautions Additional cautions If differentiation cannot be established on the available material, get more material rather than guessing from Ki-67.

lead: Do not manage a poorly differentiated carcinoma on the indolent-disease pathway.
text: Avoid Evidence B Do not manage a poorly differentiated carcinoma on the indolent-disease pathway. Why Why Carcinoma is managed as an aggressive carcinoma. In the SEER figures ENETS 2023 reproduces, median survival is 33.9 months for stage I–II, 16.3 months for stage III and 5.2 months for distant disease, with 5-year survival 42%, 25.6% and 4.7%; metastatic patients survive a median 11 to 12 months on palliative platinum–etoposide and about 1 month without it. Performance status then dominates: median survival 18 months at PS 0, 12 at PS 1 and 5 at PS 2. Additional cautions Additional cautions Somatostatin analogue for antiproliferative intent, PRRT, hepatic debulking for cytoreduction and transplantation are all inappropriate here. Managing a carcinoma on the indolent pathway costs months of ineffective therapy in a disease measured in months. Note what the recommendation is made of: ENETS grades both the advice against metastasectomy and the advice against PRRT in metastatic digestive NEC 5D, its weakest grade, resting on no comparative data, and well-differentiated G3 NET is outside that paper's scope by design — so the guidance is strongest exactly where the diagnosis is unambiguous and silent where it is not. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Guideline-reproduced SEER data: median survival 33.9 vs 16.3 vs 5.2 mo, stage I–II vs III vs distant; metastatic 11 to 12 mo on platinum–etoposide vs about 1 mo without Guidance graded 5D, no comparative data; well-differentiated G3 NET outside its scope

lead: Start a somatostatin analogue for antiproliferative effect and symptom control.
text: Standard Evidence A Start a somatostatin analogue for antiproliferative effect and symptom control. Indications Preferred when Receptor-positive or functional phenotypes, and anyone in whom progression would be hard to salvage. PROMID (n=85, treatment-naive midgut) gave time to progression 14.3 versus 6.0 months, hazard ratio 0.34 (95% CI 0.20–0.59); CLARINET (n=204, non-functioning enteropancreatic, Ki-67 under 10%) gave a progression-free survival hazard ratio of 0.47 (0.30–0.73) with 24-month progression-free survival 65.1% versus 33.0%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not make it mandatory for every patient. Grade A applies to the antiproliferative indication in unresectable disease: PROMID and CLARINET enrolled only patients with no curative option, unresectable disease or declined surgery. In resectable or ablatable disease, analogue versus resection or ablation is an MDT decision. Evidence & sources Neither trial established an overall-survival benefit — CLARINET found no significant difference in overall survival or quality of life, and PROMID is an interim analysis at 67 progressions and 16 deaths of a trial that enrolled 85 of a planned 162 patients and was then closed for slow accrual, so its confirmatory survival analysis at 121 deaths was never performed. The effect is stabilisation, not shrinkage: one partial remission per arm in PROMID, and objective remissions with an analogue are rare. For a liver pathway the decisive limitation is that PROMID's exploratory burden subgroups had imprecise estimates and did not establish a predictive liver-volume threshold — hazard ratio 0.17 (0.08–0.40) at 0 to 10% hepatic involvement, 0.40 (0.10–1.67) at 10 to 50% and 0.71 (0.11–4.45) above 50%, with 95% of patients having Ki-67 of 2% or less and 64/85 (75%) having 10% or less liver involvement, including those without liver disease. CLARINET held across hepatic volume, hazard ratio 0.45 (0.23–0.88) above 25%, but that dichotomy is a post hoc simplification of a prespecified five-category variable whose component hazard ratios ran 0.24 to 0.54. For carcinoid-syndrome control the source is ENETS 2024, not these trials. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Observation with scheduled imaging NCCN says observation with serial imaging is an option if the patient has a low tumour burden; ENETS 2024 supports watch and wait only for selected G1, asymptomatic, low-burden and/or stable small-intestine NET at B-2b, ESMO restricts it to Ki-67 under 2% with low burden and stable disease [IV, A], and ASCO puts the evidence strongest at Ki-67 under 10% with imaging every 3 to 6 months. The three thresholds do not agree with one another and none was derived.
text: Observation with scheduled imaging Evidence B NCCN says observation with serial imaging is an option if the patient has a low tumour burden; ENETS 2024 supports watch and wait only for selected G1, asymptomatic, low-burden and/or stable small-intestine NET at B-2b, ESMO restricts it to Ki-67 under 2% with low burden and stable disease [IV, A], and ASCO puts the evidence strongest at Ki-67 under 10% with imaging every 3 to 6 months. The three thresholds do not agree with one another and none was derived. Indications Preferred when Asymptomatic, low-volume, radiologically stable disease: cross-sectional imaging every 3 to 4 months at first and about every 6 months once stability is shown, with treatment started on progression or symptoms. The CLARINET placebo arm itself ran a median 18.0 months without progression. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Not where the syndrome is active, where receptor-positive bulk is accumulating, or where the patient will not reliably return for imaging. The 3–4-month interval is a local choice within the NCCN range of every 12 weeks to 12 months. Evidence & sources The NANETS midgut panel split roughly half and half between starting an analogue and observing, and concluded that either is acceptable — that is a recorded absence of consensus, not a positive endorsement. The strongest quantitative support for observing is the CLARINET placebo arm itself, which ran a median 18.0 months without progression and which ASCO notes can be read as support for watch and wait in favourable-biology patients; against that, only 22% of one watch-and-wait cohort ENETS cites ever needed surgery.
