lead: Hepatic cytoreduction — resection, ablation, or bothEXPERTISE Reasonable consideration, grade C: aim for maximal debulking with parenchymal-sparing resection and resect the primary where appropriate. The supporting series are single-arm with strong selection.
text: Hepatic cytoreduction — resection, ablation, or both Evidence C EXPERTISE Reasonable consideration, grade C: aim for maximal debulking with parenchymal-sparing resection and resect the primary where appropriate. The supporting series are single-arm with strong selection. Indications Preferred when Burden that can largely be cleared in a patient fit for a long operation, where the target and the expected residual can be named before the incision — see clinical decision 5 for the thresholds and what supports them. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Poorly differentiated carcinoma, diffuse miliary disease, uncontrolled extrahepatic progression, significant untreated carcinoid heart disease. Do not offer it as an alternative to an analogue on the strength of the debulking survival figures. Evidence & sources The expanded-criteria series reported 5-year disease-specific survival 90% and median liver progression-free survival 71.6 months in 52 selected patients; these are the outcomes of selected patients, not a measured treatment effect, and within that series the extent of debulking did not correlate with liver progression-free survival (P=.74) or disease-specific survival (P=.37). ENETS 2024 puts the same recommendation at B-4 — a surgical approach in stage IV G1/G2 liver-only disease if R0 is achievable — on 5-year overall survival of 71 to 74%, and 85% for R0 resections, while recording recurrence after R0 of about 80% at 5 years. ESMO attributes that 85% partly to preselection bias and notes liver metastases are often more extensive than appreciated even intraoperatively. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not read debulking series survival figures as a treatment effect.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not read debulking series survival figures as a treatment effect. Why Why Present them to patients as the outcomes of selected patients: single-arm, heavily selected, with no randomised comparison against systemic therapy alone. Additional cautions Additional cautions Quoting 90% 5-year disease-specific survival as what an operation delivers. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not offer Y90 radioembolisation without a phenotype-specific rationale.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not offer Y90 radioembolisation without a phenotype-specific rationale. Why Why Selected early use may be appropriate where the rationale is stated — lobar or segmental liver-dominant distribution, or prior Whipple or biliary instrumentation. Additional cautions Additional cautions Low-burden disease in a patient with years of treatment horizon ahead: radiation-induced liver injury accrues over exactly the time the patient has. Imaging signs of cirrhosis-like morphology or portal hypertension appeared in 15 of 52 patients (29%) followed beyond a year, more often after bilobar treatment, though no single imaging finding reached significance and the series was not powered for it. Read the denominator: of 93 patients treated, 41 had under a year of follow-up, so the long-term toxicity estimate is survivor-biased, and no radioembolisation-induced liver failure occurred in that series or in the 148-patient multicentre series. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Continue SSA when needed for functional symptoms. After clinically significant progression in nonfunctional disease, do not automatically continue SSA for antiproliferative benefit.
text: Standard Evidence C Continue SSA when needed for functional symptoms. After clinically significant progression in nonfunctional disease, do not automatically continue SSA for antiproliferative benefit. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Continue the somatostatin analogue for functional-syndrome control where it is needed, and after clinically significant progression in a nonfunctional tumour do not automatically continue it for antiproliferative benefit. Indications Preferred when Functional disease, where the analogue is doing hormonal work that nothing else in the plan replaces. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Carrying an analogue indefinitely in a nonfunctional tumour that has progressed on it, on the assumption that it is still holding the tumour back. Evidence & sources Downgraded to C: this is a position taken in the absence of evidence rather than from it. The NANETS midgut panel reached no consensus on continuing an analogue past progression, and no trial has tested continuation after documented progression in either direction — PROMID and CLARINET both enrolled patients who were not progressing, 96% of CLARINET patients having had no progression in the 3 to 6 months before randomisation. The roadmap's position is that the indication after progression is hormonal, not antiproliferative; that is a defensible reading of what the trials enrolled, not a demonstrated equivalence. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Escalate systemically on progression, with the agent chosen by primary site, receptor status, growth rate and burden — see clinical decision 6.
text: Standard Evidence B Escalate systemically on progression, with the agent chosen by primary site, receptor status, growth rate and burden — see clinical decision 6. Indications Preferred when Receptor-positive midgut disease progressing on an analogue: 177Lu-DOTATATE. Pancreatic primaries: sunitinib or capecitabine–temozolomide. Everolimus across non-functional GI and lung disease. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat the grade as a survival claim for any one agent: NETTER-1's final overall-survival analysis gave median 48.0 versus 36.3 months, hazard ratio 0.84 (95% CI 0.60–1.17), p=0.30, and did not meet its endpoint. Every other agent in the sequence is a progression-free survival result too, and ASCO rated overall-survival certainty very low for CLARINET, RADIANT-3, RADIANT-4 and the sunitinib trial and low for NETTER-1. Evidence & sources Downgraded from A to B. The class of systemic escalation is expected practice, but every ASCO recommendation covering it is graded weak on low or moderate evidence quality, and ASCO states outright that there is insufficient evidence to recommend any sequence after progression. §6 sets out what each trial actually showed. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Add a liver-directed procedure where the hepatic goal is stated: bland embolisation or conventional TACE for symptoms, progression or bulky liver-dominant disease, Y90 for selected lobar or segmental distribution.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Add a liver-directed procedure where the hepatic goal is stated: bland embolisation or conventional TACE for symptoms, progression or bulky liver-dominant disease, Y90 for selected lobar or segmental distribution. Indications Preferred when Liver-dominant bulk or a hormonal syndrome poorly controlled on an analogue, where the viable target, the goal, the liver-function cost, the owner and the reassessment date can all be named — see clinical decision 7 for the modality choice. The largest technique comparison is retrospective and non-randomised: in 69 carcinoid patients bland embolisation gave a radiologic response of 81.0% against 44.4% for chemoembolisation (multivariate odds ratio 6.41, 95% CI 1.97–20.84, P=0.002) with no difference in progression-free or overall survival, while in 54 islet-cell patients chemoembolisation trended better on response and survival without reaching significance and those patients had more resected primaries and less liver involvement. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not group bland embolisation, conventional TACE and radioembolisation as equivalent, and do not use drug-eluting embolics in NET. Evidence & sources NCCN NE-H accepts bland embolisation and conventional TACE and advises against drug-eluting embolics because of increased hepatobiliary toxicity in the NET population. Comparative superiority of bland versus conventional chemoembolisation remains unresolved, and the two ENETS papers on the page point in opposite directions: the 2024 small-intestine guidance generally prefers bland embolisation, while the 2023 functioning-pancreatic guidance says chemoembolisation is possibly more effective. Treatment choice in the supporting series was made by the referring physician, so the apparent technique effects are confounded with who was sent where. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not add a liver-directed procedure on systemic progression without a stated hepatic goal.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not add a liver-directed procedure on systemic progression without a stated hepatic goal. Why Why The trigger for a liver-directed procedure is a hepatic problem — bulk, symptoms, a dominant growing lesion — not the fact that a drug has failed. Additional cautions Additional cautions A repeat embolic or radiation cycle with no named target, goal, liver-function cost, owner or reassessment date. Worsening liver function after embolic or radiation therapy is a stop, not a reason to change device: cumulative hepatic injury is the limiting resource in a long-horizon disease.

lead: 177Lu-DOTATATE, well-differentiated G3, receptor-positive Preferred for a defined phenotype, and note which one: NETTER-2 (n=226) enrolled newly diagnosed, inoperable, SSTR-positive, well-differentiated GEP-NET with Ki-67 10–55% diagnosed within the previous 6 months, no patient having progressed on a prior analogue, and gave median progression-free survival 22.8 versus 8.5 months by blinded central review, stratified hazard ratio 0.276 (0.182–0.418), p<0.0001, with objective response 43.0% versus 9.3% and 8 complete responses (5%) versus none.
text: 177Lu-DOTATATE, well-differentiated G3, receptor-positive Evidence B Preferred for a defined phenotype, and note which one: NETTER-2 (n=226) enrolled newly diagnosed, inoperable, SSTR-positive, well-differentiated GEP-NET with Ki-67 10–55% diagnosed within the previous 6 months, no patient having progressed on a prior analogue, and gave median progression-free survival 22.8 versus 8.5 months by blinded central review, stratified hazard ratio 0.276 (0.182–0.418), p<0.0001, with objective response 43.0% versus 9.3% and 8 complete responses (5%) versus none. Indications Preferred when Receptor uptake greater than normal liver in the target disease, Ki-67 inside 10–55%, renal, marrow and hepatic reserve documented, and clinically significant burden — the last being a local selection criterion, not a trial entry criterion. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Ki-67 above 55% was not studied. Receptor-negative or FDG-avid, SSTR-negative disease will not be treated by it: NETTER-2 required uptake score 3 or 4 in all target lesions, so heterogeneous-uptake disease was never enrolled. It also excluded any previous hepatic artery embolisation or radiofrequency ablation, which excludes a large part of the population this page's clinical decision 7 creates. In a series of 69 receptor-expressing high-grade neoplasms, median progression-free survival was 9.6 months and overall survival 19.9 months, falling to 4 and 7 months once Ki-67 exceeded 55%. Evidence & sources Graded B, not A: NETTER-2 is open-label with a median follow-up of 23.2 months, overall survival not reached in either group with 48% of control patients crossed over, no difference in time to deterioration of global health status, diarrhoea, fatigue or pain, and a comparator of high-dose octreotide 60 mg that the authors themselves describe as giving only 4 to 8 months of progression-free survival in grade 3 NET. There is no comparison with the alkylating chemotherapy a board would weigh first line in a high-grade pancreatic NET, and 123 of 226 patients (54%) had pancreatic primaries. NETTER-1's final overall-survival analysis was negative (48.0 versus 36.3 months, hazard ratio 0.84, p=0.30). NETTER-2 enrolled 147 grade 2 patients with Ki-67 10–20% and 79 grade 3 patients at a median Ki-67 of 16%, so the same evidence covers G2 tumours in that band. Itanet grades the same NETTER-2 recommendation 1b-A and EANM supported first-line PRRT only in a minority of highly selected patients (17 of 22, 77.3%); the roadmap's downgrade to B is a local approval item. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Capecitabine–temozolomide, or platinum-based therapy Reasonable alternative where behaviour is aggressive and receptor expression is low or absent. E2211 (n=133 evaluable, low/intermediate-grade pancreatic NET, progression within 12 months; G3 use is extrapolation) met its primary endpoint at an interim analysis with an adjusted two-sided alpha of 0.119 in a phase 2 trial designed at a two-sided significance level of 0.20: median progression-free survival 22.7 versus 14.4 months with temozolomide alone, hazard ratio 0.58 (95% CI 0.36–0.93), P=.022. The final analysis at a median 59.9 months gave 23.2 versus 15.1 months, hazard ratio 0.71 (0.46–1.07).
text: Capecitabine–temozolomide, or platinum-based therapy Evidence B Reasonable alternative where behaviour is aggressive and receptor expression is low or absent. E2211 (n=133 evaluable, low/intermediate-grade pancreatic NET, progression within 12 months; G3 use is extrapolation) met its primary endpoint at an interim analysis with an adjusted two-sided alpha of 0.119 in a phase 2 trial designed at a two-sided significance level of 0.20: median progression-free survival 22.7 versus 14.4 months with temozolomide alone, hazard ratio 0.58 (95% CI 0.36–0.93), P=.022. The final analysis at a median 59.9 months gave 23.2 versus 15.1 months, hazard ratio 0.71 (0.46–1.07). Indications Preferred when High burden, tumour-related symptoms or rapid progression, especially with a pancreatic primary; and where receptor imaging will not support PRRT. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not apply a universal platinum regimen to all G3 NET — Itanet reports etoposide–platinum efficacy as limited in advanced G3 NET compared with its use in carcinoma, and ASCO records that platinum–etoposide has little supporting evidence in well-differentiated G3 disease. In E2211 overall survival was not significant (58.7 months with CAPTEM versus 53.8 months with temozolomide, hazard ratio 0.82, P=.42; a significant interim difference, hazard ratio 0.41, P=.012, did not persist), the response rate did not differ from temozolomide alone (39.7% versus 33.8%, P=0.59) and grade 3–4 treatment-related toxicity doubled, 45% versus 22%. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma: platinum–etoposide systemic therapy, managed as an aggressive carcinoma.
text: Standard Evidence B Poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma: platinum–etoposide systemic therapy, managed as an aggressive carcinoma. Indications Preferred when Small-cell or large-cell carcinoma morphology, whatever the hepatic burden. Carboplatin–etoposide first line gives response 30 to 50%, progression-free survival 4 to 6 months and overall survival 11 to 12 months. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not use SSA for antiproliferative intent in NEC. Metastatic surgery and PRRT are generally not recommended; rare selected exceptions require specialist review and do not establish a transplant indication. ENETS grades the recommendation against metastasectomy and against PRRT in metastatic digestive NEC 5D — its weakest grade, resting on no comparative data — but it is the statement that would close down a liver resection discussion at board. ENETS cites randomized first- and second-line chemotherapy evidence and grades the corresponding regimen recommendations 2bB; its generally-against metastatic surgery/PRRT recommendation is separately grade 5D. Evidence & sources Molecular profiling of advanced high-grade disease, where available, may identify additional treatment options. A prior history of G1 or G2 NET strongly favours G3 NET over carcinoma if G3 disease is confirmed. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: In carcinoma, use liver-directed therapy only for a specific symptomatic or oligoprogressive problem, with a stated goal and a stated duration.
text: Reasonable Evidence C In carcinoma, use liver-directed therapy only for a specific symptomatic or oligoprogressive problem, with a stated goal and a stated duration. Indications Preferred when A single bleeding, painful or obstructing deposit in a patient whose systemic disease is otherwise being controlled. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Cytoreduction for its own sake, or any liver-directed plan without an end date, in a disease whose median survival on treatment is about a year. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not assume an overall-survival benefit from the PRRT trials.
text: Avoid Evidence B Do not assume an overall-survival benefit from the PRRT trials. Why Why State plainly what they showed: NETTER-1 met progression-free survival decisively — hazard ratio 0.18 (0.11–0.29) on health-authority re-review of baseline scans, updated from the published 0.21 (0.13–0.33) — and did not meet overall survival (48.0 versus 36.3 months, hazard ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.60–1.17, p=0.30); NETTER-2 met progression-free survival with a large effect and its overall survival is immature, with 48% of control patients crossing over. Additional cautions Additional cautions Telling a patient that PRRT has been shown to make them live longer. In NETTER-1 the proportional-hazards assumption failed (Schoenfeld residuals p=0.03), 36% of controls crossed over and 32% received 177Lu-dotatate specifically, so the final comparison is closer to early versus delayed PRRT than to PRRT versus none; the crossover-adjusted hazard ratio was 0.73 (0.40–1.34). Overall survival was a secondary endpoint powered for 158 deaths and the 5-year calendar cutoff arrived first at 142, and the restricted-mean-survival analysis that carries the authors' positive message was added by protocol amendment and does not exclude zero at 5 years (5.1 months, 95% CI -0.5 to 10.7). Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not apply a universal platinum regimen to all G3 NET, and keep surgery and transplant criteria distinct from systemic-treatment options.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not apply a universal platinum regimen to all G3 NET, and keep surgery and transplant criteria distinct from systemic-treatment options. Why Why Phenotype-based G3 options: receptor status, growth rate and primary site choose the drug. Additional cautions Additional cautions Treating well-differentiated G3 as carcinoma, or reading eligibility for a G3 systemic option as eligibility for cytoreduction or transplantation. lead: For meaningful burden reduction: parenchymal-sparing resection, adjunct ablation for unsuitable lesions, and primary resection when appropriate.
text: Reasonable Evidence C EXPERTISE For meaningful burden reduction: parenchymal-sparing resection, adjunct ablation for unsuitable lesions, and primary resection when appropriate. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Operate for meaningful reduction of hepatic burden with parenchymal-sparing resection — often multiple small wedges — using ablation as an adjunct for lesions unsuited to resection, and resect the primary where appropriate. Indications Preferred when Well-differentiated disease where a substantial fraction of the burden can be cleared and the patient will tolerate a long operation. The expanded-criteria series of 52 patients reported 5-year disease-specific survival 90%, 5-year overall survival 88% and median liver progression-free survival 71.6 months (95% CI 56.0–87.3) with a 5-year liver progression-free rate of 64%, with 51 of 52 having wedge resections and 47 bilobar resections, median 15 tumours resected, median largest metastasis 2.5 cm and 65% having extrahepatic disease. ENETS 2024 makes the parallel recommendation for stage IV G1/G2 liver-only disease where R0 is achievable at B-4. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Poorly differentiated carcinoma, diffuse miliary disease, uncontrolled extrahepatic progression, poor performance status, hepatic dysfunction, or liver replacement above roughly 50 to 70% — where NANETS says embolisation, PRRT or medical therapy are preferable. Debulking must not be called complete eradication. Evidence & sources Read the series with its limits in front of you. It is retrospective, single-surgeon and single-institution; the debulking percentage is the operating surgeon's own intraoperative visual and ultrasonographic estimate, not a volumetric or blinded radiological measurement, and the same surgeon selected who was operated on at all. Decisively, patients in whom the surgeon judged intraoperatively that 70% was not achievable were not resected, so the series contains no sub-70% group and cannot test the threshold it is used to justify. Within it, extent of debulking did not correlate with liver progression-free survival (P=.74) or disease-specific survival (P=.37), progression rates were 27.3%, 27.3% and 31.6% across the 70–89%, 90–99% and 100% groups (P=.95), complete resection of all gross disease was achieved in only 12 of 52 (25%) and conferred no advantage, and the only variable that predicted anything was age — 5-year liver progression-free survival 25.7% under age 50 versus 85% at 50 or older (P=.001). The lowest-debulking group contains 11 patients, no morbidity or mortality rate is reported anywhere in the paper, only a median length of stay of 6 days, median follow-up was 37.4 months against a median liver progression-free survival of 71.6 months, and 88% were kept on octreotide LAR, which the authors themselves say may account for the unusually long progression-free survival rather than the debulking strategy. ENETS 2023 puts the target at 70 to 90% or more of visible disease with adequate liver function at level 2b, grade B, and gives no guidance on which end of that 20-point range applies to whom; ENETS 2024 does not address the 70 versus 90 question at all. Recurrence after an R0 resection in this disease runs about 80% at 5 years, so lifelong follow-up is part of the operation. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Thermal ablation as complete local treatmentEXPERTISE Selected oligometastatic complete local treatment, usually four lesions or fewer each under 3 cm as NCCN describes it; ENETS 2024 puts percutaneous ablation at three to five metastases each under 3 cm at B-3. Neither limit comes from the series that support ablation: those enrolled up to 15 tumours, up to 10 cm, with under 20% liver volume involved, a mean largest tumour of 3.6 cm and a mean of six lesions treated. Cure evidence is weak.
text: Thermal ablation as complete local treatment Evidence C EXPERTISE Selected oligometastatic complete local treatment, usually four lesions or fewer each under 3 cm as NCCN describes it; ENETS 2024 puts percutaneous ablation at three to five metastases each under 3 cm at B-3. Neither limit comes from the series that support ablation: those enrolled up to 15 tumours, up to 10 cm, with under 20% liver volume involved, a mean largest tumour of 3.6 cm and a mean of six lesions treated. Cure evidence is weak. Indications Preferred when Limited well-differentiated disease where all known sites can be addressed, alone or combined with resection, with safe access and margins — an upfront local option for suitable oligometastatic disease, or focal salvage, not necessarily after every systemic treatment. Quote local control per patient as well as per lesion: local recurrence at an ablated site occurred in 7 of 63 patients (11%) and in 22% of 89 patients, against per-lesion rates of 6.3% and 7.9%. Morbidity was 5% and 5.6% with one 30-day death (1%) in the larger series and a mean hospital stay of 1.1 days. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not call it cure: 80% of the 45 patients with imaging follow-up in one series developed new or progressive liver disease, mostly growth of sub-centimetre lesions deliberately left untreated, and in the larger series 63% developed new liver lesions and 59% developed extrahepatic disease. Neither series reports grade or Ki-67 at all — at the published discussion the authors confirmed the analysis had not been done — and both pool medullary thyroid carcinoma (9 and 11 patients) and bronchial carcinoids with gastroenteropancreatic disease, so long survival after ablation reflects indolent biology and multimodality salvage as much as the procedure. Record residual disease and grade. Evidence & sources More often the realistic goal is cytoreduction, symptom control or treatment of a growing dominant lesion; symptom relief was reported in 94% at one week with a median duration of 11 months in the smaller series, and in 97% with 73% significant or complete and a median 14 months in the larger. Survival in these series is not attributable to the ablation: during follow-up 30% had an analogue, 27% a repeat ablation, 18% chemotherapy and 10% chemoembolisation, and median follow-up of 30 months sits against a 6-year median survival. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Resection of the primary tumour with liver metastases present NCCN says resection of ileum or jejunum NETs with their mesenteric nodes should be performed when symptoms arise from the primary, and should be considered in asymptomatic cases to reduce future obstruction, mesenteric ischaemia, bleeding or perforation.
text: Resection of the primary tumour with liver metastases present Evidence C NCCN says resection of ileum or jejunum NETs with their mesenteric nodes should be performed when symptoms arise from the primary, and should be considered in asymptomatic cases to reduce future obstruction, mesenteric ischaemia, bleeding or perforation. Indications Preferred when Small-bowel primaries, where NANETS reached full consensus that resection should be considered when feasible on retrospective medians of 7.4 versus 4.0 years, 9.9 versus 4.7 years and 159 versus 47 months favouring resection; and before PRRT where mesenteric ischaemia or obstruction risk is real. Transplant candidacy depends on the primary being out. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid No universal resect-or-observe instruction for pancreatic primaries: NANETS 2020 reached no consensus, with the majority holding that resection may help only in selected circumstances — functional tumour, body or tail location, local complications. ENETS notes that at least three propensity-matched studies show no survival benefit in asymptomatic stage IV disease. Evidence & sources The supporting series are retrospective with unresected patients older, more comorbid or more heavily replaced; NANETS states that selection bias cannot be excluded, and ENETS adds that only 22% of a watch-and-wait cohort ever needed surgery. The roadmap keeps selected primary surgery after MDT review and distinguishes small-bowel from pancreatic decisions. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Guideline consensus (NANETS) on retrospective series, small-bowel primary resected vs unresected: medians 7.4 vs 4.0 y, 9.9 vs 4.7 y and 159 vs 47 mo Unresected pts older, more comorbid or more replaced; selection bias cannot be excluded
Guideline (ENETS): only 22% of a watch-and-wait cohort ever needed surgery; at least three propensity-matched studies: no survival benefit in asymptomatic stage IV

lead: Do not call debulking complete eradication, and do not operate without naming the target and the expected residual first.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not call debulking complete eradication, and do not operate without naming the target and the expected residual first. Why Why It is worth doing only if a substantial fraction of the burden can be cleared; say what fraction and what will be left before the patient consents. Additional cautions Additional cautions An operation whose success is defined after the fact by what turned out to be resectable.

lead: Do not debulk in poorly differentiated carcinoma, diffuse miliary disease, or uncontrolled extrahepatic progression.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not debulk in poorly differentiated carcinoma, diffuse miliary disease, or uncontrolled extrahepatic progression. Why Why Systemic therapy is the pathway in carcinoma; in diffuse disease that cannot reach a meaningful clearance, embolisation, PRRT or medical therapy are preferable. Additional cautions Additional cautions Significant carcinoid heart disease is a contraindication to hepatic cytoreduction until it is addressed — raised right-sided pressure increases the risk of liver surgery, and NCCN advises valve replacement before liver resection where carcinoid heart disease is significant. Do not extend the list beyond what the panels said: NANETS 2020 holds that extrahepatic disease by itself should not contraindicate resection of the primary or hepatic cytoreduction, because it is rarely the cause of death, and that grade 2 disease in the primary or the liver metastases is not a contraindication either. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: 177Lu-DOTATATE NCCN: lutetium Lu 177 dotatate is FDA-approved for SSTR-positive GEP NETs including foregut, midgut and hindgut tumours. NETTER-1 (n=229, midgut jejunoileal or proximal colon disease, Ki-67 20% or less, progressing on standard-dose octreotide) met progression-free survival decisively — 65.2% versus 10.8% progression-free at month 20, hazard ratio 0.21 (0.13–0.33), updated to 0.18 (0.11–0.29) on health-authority re-review, median not reached versus 8.4 months, objective response 18% versus 3%.
text: 177Lu-DOTATATE Evidence B NCCN: lutetium Lu 177 dotatate is FDA-approved for SSTR-positive GEP NETs including foregut, midgut and hindgut tumours. NETTER-1 (n=229, midgut jejunoileal or proximal colon disease, Ki-67 20% or less, progressing on standard-dose octreotide) met progression-free survival decisively — 65.2% versus 10.8% progression-free at month 20, hazard ratio 0.21 (0.13–0.33), updated to 0.18 (0.11–0.29) on health-authority re-review, median not reached versus 8.4 months, objective response 18% versus 3%. Indications Preferred when Receptor-positive disease with uptake greater than normal liver in the target disease on SSTR PET, renal, marrow and hepatic reserve documented before each course, and surgical evaluation first — especially where mesenteric ischaemia or obstruction is a risk. NANETS and Itanet both prefer it second line in SSTR-positive midgut disease. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The final overall-survival analysis did not meet its endpoint: 48.0 versus 36.3 months, hazard ratio 0.84 (95% CI 0.60–1.17), p=0.30. NETTER-1 enrolled progressive midgut NET after SSA. Later randomized studies include selected pancreatic/GI populations (NETTER-2, OCLURANDOM and COMPETE), with different grade, prior-treatment, receptor and product criteria. They do not establish a universal PRRT sequence. Avoid generally at GFR under 30 and use with caution at GFR 30 to 50. Where SSTR uptake is heterogeneous, a CT or MRI lesion shows no uptake, or progression is rapid, get FDG PET first to find receptor-negative disease PRRT will not treat. Evidence & sources EANM requires Krenning 3 or 4 uptake in all metastases; the comparator in NETTER-1 was octreotide LAR 60 mg, a dose never shown to control tumour growth, so the trial does not compare PRRT with everolimus, chemotherapy or liver-directed therapy. Eligibility was set by 111In-octreotide scintigraphy, not by the 68Ga- or 64Cu-DOTATATE PET used today. Myelodysplastic syndrome occurred in 2 of 111 treated patients, one fatal at 33 months and the only treatment-related death, with no control denominator because adverse-event reporting during long-term follow-up was required only in the PRRT arm; ASCO puts treatment-related myeloid neoplasia after PRRT at about 2.6% and ESMO reports up to 3 to 4% irreversible marrow toxicity and 30% long-term grade 1 or 2 renal toxicity. EANM reached no consensus on the right time point for PRRT in the sequence, and did not recommend it specifically second line for pancreatic NET. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

Final OS endpoint not met: 48.0 vs 36.3 mo, 177Lu-DOTATATE vs octreotide LAR 60 mg, HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.60–1.17), p=0.30 Midgut only; foregut/hindgut label rests on retrospective and registry data

lead: Everolimus RADIANT-3 (n=410, pancreatic): progression-free survival 11.0 versus 4.6 months, hazard ratio 0.35 (0.27–0.45). RADIANT-4 (n=302, non-functional GI and lung): 11.0 versus 3.9 months, hazard ratio 0.48 (0.35–0.67).
text: Everolimus Evidence B RADIANT-3 (n=410, pancreatic): progression-free survival 11.0 versus 4.6 months, hazard ratio 0.35 (0.27–0.45). RADIANT-4 (n=302, non-functional GI and lung): 11.0 versus 3.9 months, hazard ratio 0.48 (0.35–0.67). Indications Preferred when Non-functional disease across primary sites, and where receptor-negative biology or haematologic risk rules out PRRT. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid No survival benefit is established. RADIANT-3's overall survival is uninterpretable — 73% of the placebo arm crossed over — and RADIANT-4's interim overall survival was a first look at 70 deaths against a planned 191, hazard ratio 0.64 (0.40–1.05), one-sided p=0.037 against a boundary of 0.0002. RADIANT-4 excluded carcinoid syndrome and pancreatic primaries and 30% of patients had lung primaries with only 23% ileal and 8% jejunal, so it does not cover the functional small-bowel patient who most often reaches a liver surgeon. The cost is real: dose reduction or interruption in 67% versus 30%, non-infectious pneumonitis of any grade in 16%, and discontinuation for grade 3–4 drug-related events in 12% versus 3%. Evidence & sources The benefit is stabilisation, not shrinkage: confirmed objective response 5% in RADIANT-3 and 2% in RADIANT-4. The size of the effect depends on who read the scans — in RADIANT-4 central review gave 11.0 versus 3.9 months and local review 14.0 versus 5.5 — and in RADIANT-3 progression-free survival data were censored in 47% of the everolimus arm against 19% of placebo with 2.3 times the exposure. Both trials excluded patients embolised within 6 months or ablated within 2 months, so neither says anything about combining everolimus with liver-directed therapy. lead: Sunitinib, pancreatic primaries n=171, well-differentiated pancreatic NET with documented progression in the previous 12 months: progression-free survival 11.4 versus 5.5 months, hazard ratio 0.42 (0.26–0.66), P<0.001; overall survival hazard ratio 0.41 (0.19–0.89).
text: Sunitinib, pancreatic primaries Evidence B n=171, well-differentiated pancreatic NET with documented progression in the previous 12 months: progression-free survival 11.4 versus 5.5 months, hazard ratio 0.42 (0.26–0.66), P<0.001; overall survival hazard ratio 0.41 (0.19–0.89). Indications Preferred when Progressive pancreatic NET where a tyrosine kinase inhibitor suits the comorbidity profile. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Closed early by the data and safety monitoring committee at 171 of 340 planned patients and 81 of 260 planned events after more deaths and serious adverse events with placebo; the observed statistic did not cross the prespecified efficacy boundary (z 3.85 against 3.88), so the headline result never formally met the protocol threshold. Censoring was heavily imbalanced (65% versus 40%), response was investigator-assessed with no central review in a trial unblinded at closure, and 59 placebo patients crossed to open-label sunitinib, so the survival signal cannot be taken at face value. Ki-67 was evaluable in only about 42% of patients. Objective responses occurred in 8/86 (9.3%), including two complete responses. Response is uncommon and conversion benefit was not tested; do not promise conversion or infer it is impossible. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

text: Capecitabine–temozolomide, pancreatic primaries Evidence B E2211 (n=133): 22.7 versus 14.4 months against temozolomide alone, hazard ratio 0.58 (0.36–0.93), P=.022, declared at an interim analysis with an adjusted two-sided alpha of 0.119 in a phase 2 trial designed at a two-sided significance level of 0.20; final analysis 23.2 versus 15.1 months, hazard ratio 0.71 (0.46–1.07). Indications Preferred when Pancreatic primaries with high burden, tumour-related symptoms or rapid progression, which is where ASCO places it first line; MGMT deficiency was associated with response, 52% versus 15%, though both arms contained temozolomide so it cannot be called predictive. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Phase 2, open label, not powered for overall survival, which was not significant (58.7 months with CAPTEM versus 53.8 months with temozolomide, hazard ratio 0.82, P=.42) after a significant interim difference failed to persist; CAPTEM produced objective responses in 39.7% versus 33.8% with temozolomide (P=.59); response superiority was not established, but this does not exclude use when shrinkage is an important goal. Grade 3–4 toxicity doubled, 45% versus 22%, with seven second primary cancers including one myelodysplastic syndrome. The control arm was single-agent temozolomide, never a standard of care, so the trial does not compare the combination with everolimus, sunitinib or PRRT. lead: Cabozantinib, after PRRT or targeted therapy CABINET, placebo-controlled 2:1: extrapancreatic cohort (n=203) 8.4 versus 3.9 months, hazard ratio 0.38 (0.25–0.59); pancreatic cohort (n=95) 13.8 versus 4.4 months, hazard ratio 0.23 (0.12–0.42).
text: Cabozantinib, after PRRT or targeted therapy Evidence B CABINET, placebo-controlled 2:1: extrapancreatic cohort (n=203) 8.4 versus 3.9 months, hazard ratio 0.38 (0.25–0.59); pancreatic cohort (n=95) 13.8 versus 4.4 months, hazard ratio 0.23 (0.12–0.42). Indications Preferred when Late line, after PRRT, everolimus or sunitinib: patients had a median of two to three prior lines and 59% had already had 177Lu-dotatate. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Objective response was 5% and 19%, and there was no overall-survival benefit — 21.9 versus 19.7 months, hazard ratio 0.86 (0.56–1.31), and 40.0 versus 31.1 months, hazard ratio 0.95 (0.45–2.00) — with 33% and 41% of placebo patients crossing over. Grade 3 or higher adverse events ran 62 to 65% versus 23 to 27%, two-thirds needed dose reduction to a median of about 38 mg against the assigned 60 mg, and four patients in the extrapancreatic cabozantinib group had a grade 5 event judged at least possibly treatment-related. The trial stopped early at interim on local rather than central assessment — a different endpoint from the one reported as primary — with only 111 of 164 planned events in the extrapancreatic cohort, and 7 pancreatic patients were registered into the extrapancreatic cohort and 3 the other way. lead: Document somatostatin-receptor uptake greater than normal liver in the target disease, and renal, marrow and hepatic reserve, before every PRRT course.
text: Standard Evidence B Document somatostatin-receptor uptake greater than normal liver in the target disease, and renal, marrow and hepatic reserve, before every PRRT course. Indications Preferred when PRRT is receptor-dependent: uptake above normal liver is the NCCN threshold and EANM asks for Krenning 3 or 4 in all metastases. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not expose marrow, renal and hepatic reserve to toxicity in FDG-avid, receptor-negative disease that PRRT will not treat; assess discordant FDG-positive, SSTR-negative lesions first. Surgical evaluation should be performed before PRRT. Evidence & sources Prior liver-directed therapy may raise PRRT hepatotoxicity, and the safe sequence of radioembolisation and PRRT is unresolved — NANETS states plainly that cumulative hepatic radiation from radioembolisation followed by PRRT is unstudied, so cumulative hepatic exposure is reviewed before either. NETTER-2 excluded any prior hepatic artery embolisation or ablation outright, so the first-line PRRT evidence does not describe a patient who has already had liver-directed therapy. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Hepatic debulking before PRRT may improve response and progression-free survival, and reduces the mass of amine-producing cells before a radioligand course.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Hepatic debulking before PRRT may improve response and progression-free survival, and reduces the mass of amine-producing cells before a radioligand course. Indications Preferred when A fit patient with high hepatic burden and a functional syndrome facing PRRT, where cytoreduction is independently justified. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not build a debulking indication on this alone: NANETS/SNMMI attributes it to limited retrospective data, and the crisis-prevention argument comes from a narrative review whose own institutional audit of 127 administrations recorded no carcinoid crisis at all. Evidence & sources This is the one place where the surgeon sits inside the PRRT safety pathway rather than beside it. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Narrative review's own institutional audit: no carcinoid crisis in 127 administrations Audit undercuts the crisis-prevention argument; NANETS/SNMMI cites limited retrospective data

lead: Do not claim a sequence the evidence does not support.
text: Avoid Evidence A Do not claim a sequence the evidence does not support. Why Why Record the order chosen and the reason for it at tumour board for each patient, and track it in the registry. Additional cautions Additional cautions ASCO states explicitly that there is insufficient evidence to recommend any particular sequence after progression, because the trials used placebo controls with almost no head-to-head comparisons; overall-survival certainty was rated very low for CLARINET, RADIANT-3, RADIANT-4 and the sunitinib trial and low for NETTER-1, chiefly because of crossover, which ASCO puts at 85% in RADIANT-3 and 69% in the sunitinib trial. ESMO records that one of its own authors held PRRT should come earlier in SSTR-positive pancreatic NET. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Guideline rating: OS certainty very low (low for NETTER-1), chiefly from crossover: 85% in RADIANT-3, 69% in the sunitinib trial Placebo-controlled trials with almost no head-to-head comparisons

lead: Do not continue a somatostatin analogue for antiproliferative benefit in every nonfunctional NET after significant progression.
text: Avoid Evidence B Do not continue a somatostatin analogue for antiproliferative benefit in every nonfunctional NET after significant progression. Why Why Continue it for hormonal control where the tumour is functional. Additional cautions Additional cautions PROMID and CLARINET tested delay of progression in stable, indolent disease — 96% of CLARINET patients had no progression in the 3 to 6 months before randomisation — and neither establishes an antiproliferative role after documented progression. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Bland embolisation or conventional TACE NCCN: there are no completed randomised studies comparing TAE with conventional TACE and both are acceptable. An accepted liver-control and hormone-symptom strategy in well-differentiated NET, for symptoms or progression on an analogue or other systemic therapy, and for bulky disease without waiting for progression.
text: Bland embolisation or conventional TACE Evidence C NCCN: there are no completed randomised studies comparing TAE with conventional TACE and both are acceptable. An accepted liver-control and hormone-symptom strategy in well-differentiated NET, for symptoms or progression on an analogue or other systemic therapy, and for bulky disease without waiting for progression. Indications Preferred when Bulky or symptomatic liver-dominant disease — an early liver-directed choice, not universally second line to PRRT, Y90 or ablation. In a retrospective series of 123 patients treated between 1992 and 2000, radiologic response by WHO criteria was 66.7% in carcinoid versus 35.2% in islet-cell tumours (P<0.0001) with no complete response in any carcinoid patient, median progression-free survival 22.7 versus 16.1 months and median overall survival 33.8 versus 23.2 months. Within the carcinoid group bland embolisation outperformed chemoembolisation on response, 81.0% versus 44.4% (odds ratio 6.41, 1.97–20.84, P=0.002), with no difference in progression-free or overall survival. Plan staged treatment, liver reserve, biliary infection precautions and a carcinoid-crisis response. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Serious adverse events followed 25 embolisation sessions (8.5%) in 19 patients in that series — hepatorenal syndrome in 7, sepsis in 6, hepatic abscess in 2 and one death — and major complications ran 27.3% where liver involvement exceeded 75% against 12.9% below it, a difference that did not reach significance (P=0.11). ENETS 2024 generally prefers bland embolisation in small-intestine NET; ENETS 2023 says the opposite for functioning pancreatic NET, calling chemoembolisation possibly more effective. Evidence & sources Comparative superiority of bland versus conventional chemoembolisation remains unresolved; choose by burden, symptoms, reserve and biliary infection risk, and do not group the approaches as equivalent. Technique in the supporting series was chosen by the referring physician, not randomised, and in the islet-cell group the chemoembolisation patients had more resected primaries, less liver involvement and more sessions, so the apparent advantage may be selection. The series predates RECIST, analogue maintenance, PRRT and 68Ga-DOTATATE staging, and reports no grade or Ki-67 anywhere. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Radioembolisation — Y-90 or holmium-166EXPERTISE Revised local position, Reasonable consideration: selected lobar or segmental liver-dominant control, not restricted to last resort. A phenotype-selected alternative to bland or conventional chemoembolisation, which may be used earlier when justified; NCCN permits it especially for lobar or segmental distribution or prior Whipple or biliary instrumentation, where embolic infection risk may be lower.
text: Radioembolisation — Y-90 or holmium-166 Evidence C EXPERTISE Revised local position, Reasonable consideration: selected lobar or segmental liver-dominant control, not restricted to last resort. A phenotype-selected alternative to bland or conventional chemoembolisation, which may be used earlier when justified; NCCN permits it especially for lobar or segmental distribution or prior Whipple or biliary instrumentation, where embolic infection risk may be lower. Indications Preferred when Lobar or segmental liver-dominant disease with a positive rationale stated. In a 10-centre series of 148 patients and 185 treatments, imaging response at 3 months was partial in 112 treatments (60.5%) and complete in 5 (2.7%), with median survival 70 months from first treatment. Adding 166Ho-SIRT to PRRT in 24 matched pairs gave 2-year hepatic progression-free survival 82% (57–96) versus 50% (28–72) and best objective response 71% versus 25%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Weigh late hepatic injury, bilobar treatment, prior radiation and future PRRT. Imaging signs of cirrhosis-like morphology or portal hypertension appeared in 15 of 52 patients (29%) followed beyond a year, more often after bilobar treatment though no single finding reached significance, and ALP and AST elevations were still present in the 11 followed beyond four years. In that same single-centre cohort of 93 patients median survival was 28.0 months, not 70, and baseline findings changed the conversation entirely: 7.3 months with ascites versus 53.8 without, and 21.1 months with extrahepatic disease versus 58.0 without. A long expected survival raises the threshold for radioembolisation rather than lowering it. Evidence & sources The 70-month median cannot be read as a treatment effect — 78% of patients were alive at a median follow-up of 42 months, response assessment was not standardised and used CT, MRI or scintigraphy with each investigator giving a best estimate where WHO or RECIST could not be applied, participation was voluntary and half the patients came from self-described centres of excellence. Neither Y90 series reports grade or Ki-67. The HEPAR PLuS comparison was a prospective single-arm cohort against a retrospective control with only 24 of a planned 120 pairs matched, median liver tumour burden 8% versus 20% so the population was not uniformly bulky, no overall-survival benefit and medians unseparated, a higher proportion of deaths in the combination arm, toxicity analyses abandoned for reporting bias, every combination patient dropping at least one ECOG point after PRRT before SIRT, and funding from Terumo with two co-authors employed by Terumo. There is no evidence for or against the safety of sequencing radioembolisation and PRRT. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Thermal ablationEXPERTISE Selected oligometastatic complete local treatment, usually four lesions or fewer each under 3 cm; otherwise cytoreduction, symptom control or treatment of a growing dominant lesion.
text: Thermal ablation Evidence C EXPERTISE Selected oligometastatic complete local treatment, usually four lesions or fewer each under 3 cm; otherwise cytoreduction, symptom control or treatment of a growing dominant lesion. Indications Preferred when Safe access, achievable margins, all sites reviewed and a hormone-syndrome plan in place — an upfront local option for suitable oligometastatic disease, or focal salvage. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Separate complete treatment from debulking: there is no established cured fraction, local recurrence per patient was 11% and 22% against per-lesion rates of 6.3% and 7.9%, and long survival after ablation is strongly affected by indolent biology, multimodality salvage and entry criteria that selected the least burdened patients — under 20% liver volume, at most 15 tumours, at most 10 cm. lead: SBRT or ablative radiotherapy can provide local treatment of selected liver targets in well-differentiated NET, particularly where access or anatomy prevents ablation.
text: Reasonable Evidence C SBRT or ablative radiotherapy can provide local treatment of selected liver targets in well-differentiated NET, particularly where access or anatomy prevents ablation. Indications Preferred when An alternative focal therapy, or control of oligoprogression, with the continuing systemic or PRRT strategy coordinated. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Evidence is mainly retrospective and there is no established tumour-specific curative benefit. An exceptional plan to treat all oligometastatic disease is labelled definitive local intent with uncertain cure, not proven curative treatment. Evidence & sources There is no NET-specific series; the matrix entry for this modality rests on mixed-histology data. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Avoid drug-eluting embolics in NET.
text: Avoid Evidence C Avoid drug-eluting embolics in NET. Why Why NCCN NET directly advises against drug-eluting embolics. Retain avoidance using the small primary safety series and RETNET DEB-arm closure; assess liver burden, reserve and prior biliary intervention separately rather than assuming every injury is irreversible or that a safe DEB subgroup is established. Additional cautions Additional cautions NCCN says drug-eluting embolics are associated with increased hepatobiliary toxicity in the NET population and are not recommended. The phase 2 DEB-TACE study stopped on its safety endpoint: 7 of 13 patients (54%) developed a biloma, 6 of them after the first procedure, four needed percutaneous drainage, and two had a prolonged infected hospital course and subsequently died. Evidence & sources The precautionary recommendation rests on small safety series and the early closure of RETNET’s DEB arm. The 13-patient phase 2 series reported bilomas in 54%; technique, bead size, tumour burden and the small denominator limit attribution to the whole device class. Serious hepatobiliary injury may be permanent. The 2018 RETNET paper is a protocol, whereas separate NANETS 2025 conference results report 151 TAE/cTACE patients and hepatic-PFS HR 1.40 (95% CI 0.80–2.46; P=.234). Those results do not establish equivalence or remove the DEB safety signal. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Phase 2 DEB-TACE stopped on safety endpoint: biloma in 7 of 13 (54%), 6 after first procedure; four needed drainage, two later died Single-centre interrupted interim; signal may reflect technique/bead size, not device class

lead: Hepatic arterial infusion has no routine role in this indication.
text: Avoid Evidence D Hepatic arterial infusion has no routine role in this indication. Why Why Consider only within a disease-specific study or as an exceptional expert indication. Additional cautions Additional cautions Do not transfer colorectal or intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma pump evidence across histologies; there is no dedicated NELM data.

lead: Histotripsy is investigational here: trial or institutional registry only.
text: Avoid Evidence D PROTOCOL REGISTRY Histotripsy is investigational here: trial or institutional registry only. Why Why Only with explicit consent about oncologic uncertainty, suitable ultrasound visibility and acoustic access, device-compliant target size and depth, an independent standard-treatment review, and functional-syndrome precautions. Additional cautions Additional cautions FDA device clearance for tumour destruction does not establish survival benefit or equivalence to established ablation, and there is no tumour-specific curative evidence. A bridge-to-transplant use remains protocol-based: a technical response does not establish transplant eligibility. Evidence & sources The HOPE4LIVER one-year update reported local control of 63.4% on the primary assessment against 90% post hoc in 47 patients with 52 tumours of mixed histology. lead: Write a procedure-specific crisis plan with a named owner, available rescue octreotide and immediate haemodynamic treatment, for every functional tumour.
text: Standard Evidence D Write a procedure-specific crisis plan with a named owner, available rescue octreotide and immediate haemodynamic treatment, for every functional tumour. Indications Preferred when Every procedure in a functional patient — surgery, ablation, embolisation and PRRT, with anaesthesia and nuclear medicine determining the precautions for each. Treatment is intravenous octreotide 500 to 1000 micrograms at symptom onset, repeated every 5 minutes until control and escalated to a continuous infusion if refractory. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let a plan live in individual memory; this is a named safety process that fails exactly when it is informal. It is not an evidence question and carries no comparative outcome evidence — audit it for adherence. Evidence & sources Highest risk: midgut primary, high hepatic tumour burden, liver metastases, raised 5-HIAA or chromogranin A, prior carcinoid syndrome including carcinoid heart disease, advanced age, and concurrent histamine-releasing drugs. Crisis usually appears 12 to 48 hours after a first PRRT dose but has followed later doses. The source is a narrative review — no search dates, strings, study selection or quality appraisal are reported — whose management advice rests on case reports and small series, with no consensus recorded on how many boluses precede an infusion, on steroid prophylaxis, or on whether PRRT should be re-attempted after a crisis. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Give short-acting octreotide before embolisation in patients with hormonal syndromes.
text: Standard Evidence C Give short-acting octreotide before embolisation in patients with hormonal syndromes. Indications Preferred when Functional disease going to bland embolisation, conventional TACE or radioembolisation: short-acting octreotide 250 to 500 micrograms subcutaneously, or 50 micrograms intravenously, 1 to 2 hours before the procedure. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The LUTATHERA label calls for withholding short-acting octreotide for at least 24 hours and long-acting SSA for at least 4 weeks before each dose; individualized crisis prophylaxis requires a coordinated nuclear-medicine plan, and no rule defines when prophylaxis is worth that trade-off — decide it explicitly with nuclear medicine rather than by default. Evidence & sources NCCN preserves pre-embolisation octreotide for hormonal syndromes; the roadmap keeps it while refusing the wider claim that prophylaxis prevents crisis. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Assess the syndrome and the heart before hepatic procedures, with joint cardiology and anaesthesia review where carcinoid heart disease is significant.
text: Standard Evidence C Assess the syndrome and the heart before hepatic procedures, with joint cardiology and anaesthesia review where carcinoid heart disease is significant. Indications Preferred when Annual echocardiography once serotonin or 5-HIAA exceeds about five times the upper limit of normal, and a low threshold in anyone with signs or symptoms. NCCN: in significant carcinoid heart disease, valve replacement should be done before liver resection if at all possible. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not take a functional patient to hepatic resection or transplant evaluation with right-heart disease unassessed — NANETS treats significant carcinoid heart disease as a contraindication to hepatic cytoreduction, because raised right-sided pressure increases the risk of liver surgery. Evidence & sources This closes a gap the earlier draft acknowledged. Whether an explicit echocardiography assessment is adopted is alignment area 12 and remains a local approval item. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

text: Reasonable Evidence C Debulking by surgery, interventional radiology or external-beam radiotherapy before a radioligand course is a recognised preventive measure, alongside correction of electrolyte, nutritional and protein deficits. Indications Preferred when High hepatic burden with a midgut primary and an active syndrome, where cytoreduction is justified on its own terms. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Not as a reason to operate on a patient who would not otherwise be a cytoreduction candidate: the evidence is a narrative review and a single retrospective series. lead: For refractory carcinoid diarrhoea with stable imaging, telotristat ethyl rather than raising the analogue dose.
text: Reasonable Evidence B For refractory carcinoid diarrhoea with stable imaging, telotristat ethyl rather than raising the analogue dose. Indications Preferred when Diarrhoea that persists on a standard-dose analogue while imaging is stable — the hormone problem, not the tumour problem. Use the current labelled telotristat ethyl dose of 250 mg orally three times daily with food for carcinoid-syndrome diarrhoea inadequately controlled by SSA. The historical 500 mg three-times-daily trial arm is not the recommended dose and produced no additional primary-endpoint benefit with more adverse reactions. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Escalating the analogue dose for diarrhoea and calling it tumour control; state which problem is being treated.
