Meta-analysis of six retrospective studies, LT vs resection: 5-y OS pooled OR 0.55 (95% CI 0.38–0.81), p=0.002, I²=0%; 1-y 0.67 (0.39–1.15) and 3-y 0.70 (0.42–1.17) NS Smaller tumours in LT arms; one of six propensity-matched; leave-one-out flipped 3-/5-y OS

lead: Differentiation grade and the explant pathological variables carry the most reproducible signal in the transplant literature — but every one of them is measured after the organ is out.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Differentiation grade and the explant pathological variables carry the most reproducible signal in the transplant literature — but every one of them is measured after the organ is out. Indications Preferred when Every candidacy discussion. In the three-centre French cirrhosis cohort, poor differentiation was independently predictive of recurrence in the 2–5 cm subgroup (HR 4.16, 95% CI 1.37–12.66, p=0.01) alongside nodule diameter (HR 1.10, 95% CI 1.02–1.73). In 40 Korean registry recipients, microvascular invasion was the only independent predictor of recurrence-free survival (HR 4.56, 95% CI 1.36–15.22) while perineural invasion (HR 5.14, 95% CI 1.07–24.69) and portal vein tumour thrombosis (HR 13.43, 95% CI 2.17–83.21) predicted worse overall survival — and in that cohort no pre-operative variable predicted anything. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The problem is that all of these are explant variables. Pre-transplant biopsy grading of a tumour with two components is unreliable, the biopsy may sample only one component, and no study has tested whether biopsy grade predicts explant grade in this disease. So this is the right criterion measured at the wrong time, and the page should not pretend otherwise. The hazard ratios above also rest on 45, 19, 4 and 3 patients respectively, with confidence intervals to match. Evidence & sources The 2018 propensity-matched series of 12 recipients, on which the local protocol rests, has now been read in full. Matched 1:3 on explant pathology, its 12 explant-diagnosed recipients had 5-year recurrence-free survival of 42% against 44% (p=0.44; 0.45 in the abstract); matched on pre-transplant characteristics, 42% against 61% (p=0.17) in the results text, although the abstract — and the 2026 overview that quotes it — gives 28% against 61% (p=0.12) for the same 12 patients. The direction of that asymmetry is the whole argument — matched on what you know before transplant, the cHCC-CCA patients trended worse (5-year recurrence 50% against 22%, p=0.07), though no recurrence or survival comparison with matched HCC reached significance — and it points the same way as the 2026 double-matched cohort in the avoid column below. A separate 2026 comparison table reproduces the same series as 12 patients with 1-, 3- and 5-year overall survival of 75%, 54% and 42%. See the limited-evidence section. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Where the local protocol is used, run the induction, restaging and adjuvant structure it specifies, and enter every patient in the prospective database.
text: Reasonable Evidence D PROTOCOL REGISTRY Where the local protocol is used, run the induction, restaging and adjuvant structure it specifies, and enter every patient in the prospective database. Indications Preferred when Protocol candidates at this programme. The CPG requires platinum-based biliary chemotherapy or another standard regimen at the discretion of a protocol-approved oncologist; permits locoregional therapy other than external-beam radiation, but not as the sole pre-transplant therapy except for a solitary tumour under 3 cm; restages every three months; requires full explant histopathology with next-generation sequencing; sets tiered adjuvant therapy; and withdraws steroids rapidly with a view to mTOR-inhibitor conversion at four weeks. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat the induction regimen list as current. It names FOLFOX, FOLFIRI, gemcitabine–capecitabine and gemcitabine–cisplatin and predates every immunotherapy combination now recommended; NCCN's current position for advanced mixed tumours is cisplatin–gemcitabine with either durvalumab or pembrolizumab. See clinical decision 7. Evidence & sources The protocol's own adjuvant tiers have an internal gap: the moderate-risk tier requires a single lesion under 3 cm among its criteria, while the high-risk tier is triggered by a single lesion of 6 cm or more, so a single 4 cm well-differentiated tumour with clear margins and negative nodes falls into neither. Flagged for local approval. Its explant next-generation sequencing requirement is the right test ordered at the wrong time: in the largest genomic series, 34.7% of 150 cHCC-CCA carried a potentially actionable alteration, and a result that arrives on the explant cannot inform the induction regimen. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not list a patient on the strength of the words "regardless of size".
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not list a patient on the strength of the words "regardless of size". Why Why Size is the variable on which the older and newer evidence agree. In the 19-patient multicentre transplant series, tumour size above 3 cm (p=0.038) and lymphatic invasion (p=0.023) were associated with mortality; recurrence occurred in 11 of 17 evaluable patients (64.7%) at a median of 4 months, and 1- and 3-year survival were 57.1% and 38.1% — with 95% confidence intervals of 0.301 to 1 and 0.137 to 1, which is to say those point estimates carry almost no information. The reason that series did so badly is in its baseline data: mean tumour 6.1 cm, 73.7% multinodular, 42.1% with vascular invasion, 36.8% beyond Milan, 10.5% with unsuspected nodal metastases, and 30-day mortality 10.5%. Additional cautions Additional cautions The local CPG's 'regardless of size' is the single widest gap between it and every other document and every dataset: the NLRB guidance route (nonstandard review) sets 3 cm, the ILTS-ILCA intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma statement sets 3 cm, the published series used Milan, and the UNOS analysis of 94 earlier recipients showed 1-, 3- and 5-year survival of 82%, 47% and 40%, similar to cholangiocarcinoma and significantly worse than HCC (86%, 72%, 62%, p=0.002). That UNOS cohort spans 1994 to 2013, records nothing about the tumour, coded only 6.3% as incidental — which the authors state is an undercount — and had recurrence data for just 27 of the 94, among whom 3-year recurrence was 93%. No Cox predictor in it reached significance, which with 94 patients means underpowered rather than absent. Evidence & sources The Spanish matched multicentre study is the one cohort here composed of knowingly abnormal nodules — incidental tumours were excluded by design — and in its 15 mixed HCC-CC patients 5-year survival was 78% against 86% in their matched HCC controls (p=0.9), with recurrence 7% against 4% (p=0.6). It is the most favourable comparison in the literature and it is 15 patients with a non-significant p value, matched on explant pathology that cannot be known at listing. Three exclusions matter: 8 patients beyond UCSF criteria, 16 patients who could not be matched because their disease was more advanced than any available HCC control, and whose 5-year survival was 28% with 51% recurrence, and the incidental cases. Even its uninodular subgroup of 2 cm or less, 12 per arm, showed 62% against 80% 5-year survival (p=0.4). The 27 pure iCCA patients in the same paper had 51% against 93% (p<0.001), so the pooled 42-patient figures should never be quoted. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: UNOS registry, 94 LT recipients: 1-, 3-, 5-y survival 82%, 47%, 40% vs 86%, 72%, 62%, combined HCC-CC vs HCC (p=0.002) 1994–2013, no tumour data; recurrence known in only 27 of 94

Matched LT cohort, 15 mixed HCC-CC vs matched HCC: 5-y survival 78% vs 86% (p=0.9); recurrence 7% vs 4% (p=0.6) 15 patients; matched on explant pathology unknowable at listing; incidental cases excluded

lead: Do not promise long-term graft and patient survival at HCC rates.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not promise long-term graft and patient survival at HCC rates. Why Why Give the long-horizon numbers alongside the five-year ones. In the UNOS registry, 309 cHCC-CCA candidates had the lowest 3-year waitlist mortality (4.6%) and dropout (29.0%) of the three diagnoses compared — adjusted HR 0.33 (95% CI 0.12–0.89) for waitlist mortality and 0.56 (95% CI 0.36–0.86) for dropout — and the worst post-transplant outcomes: 5-year graft survival 58.7% (95% CI 52.2–64.6) and patient survival 60.3% (95% CI 53.7–66.2), falling to 37.6% and 40.3% at 10 years and 25.5% and 27.3% at 15 years, with adjusted hazard ratios of 1.79 (95% CI 1.50–2.13) for graft loss and 1.67 (95% CI 1.41–1.98) for death against HCC. Post-transplant recurrence was 23.0% against 11.3% for HCC (p<0.001) and came soonest in this diagnosis (2.7 ± 3.1 years). Additional cautions Additional cautions A programme's own recent experience may be less favourable than the series it cites. In a matched single-centre cohort of 19 incidentally diagnosed cHCC-CCA recipients among 493 HCC transplants (3.9%), overall survival was 78.9% at 1 year and 23.8% at 3 and 5 years, and the excess hazard survived both matches: against controls matched on pre-transplant variables, overall survival HR 6.47 (95% CI 2.87–14.55) and recurrence-free survival HR 5.55 (95% CI 2.58–11.97); against controls matched on explant pathology, HR 4.67 (95% CI 2.07–10.53) and 3.65 (95% CI 1.70–7.82). Matching on what the explant showed does not explain the disadvantage away. Nine of the 19 died of metastatic adenocarcinoma, which names the cholangiocytic component as the cause of death. All 19 were assumed to be HCC before transplantation and received HCC-directed neoadjuvant treatment — this is the outcome of treating cHCC-CCA as HCC, not of a deliberate transplant decision. Evidence & sources The two findings are not contradictory, and the registry paper settles the question the single-centre series could not: it is the only analysis here with a waitlist denominator, and it shows cHCC-CCA candidates dropping out less often than either HCC or cholangiocarcinoma candidates. So the favourable per-protocol survival in the single-centre literature is not explained by dropout removing the patients who did badly. The deficit is after transplantation, not before it. Two cautions on the same paper: 250 of 278 transplanted patients (89.9%) carried a pre-transplant HCC diagnosis, so the cohort is a coding construct rather than a group known to have this disease at listing; and the reported improvement after MMaT-3 — 5-year graft survival 63.8% (95% CI 50.4–74.5) rising to 76.2% (95% CI 58.9–87.0) — has overlapping intervals, no test of interaction, shorter follow-up in the later era, and no selection data of any kind behind the authors' reading of it as refined selection. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not transplant for cHCC-CCA outside a written protocol with a registry, and do not let "the evidence now supports it" stand in for the sentence a consensus document actually wrote.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not transplant for cHCC-CCA outside a written protocol with a registry, and do not let "the evidence now supports it" stand in for the sentence a consensus document actually wrote. Why Why Read the primary wording before quoting it. The 2024 ILTS-ILCA consensus makes no cHCC-CCA-specific statement at all: its only reference to the entity is that biopsy should be performed in HCC candidates to rule out cholangiocarcinoma or mixed tumours because they affect eligibility, prognosis and treatment. Its 3 cm statement is about intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma in cirrhosis (moderate evidence, moderate strength). Additional cautions Additional cautions And the direction of the literature is not uniform. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 42 observational studies and 1,691 patients, all level 4 evidence, found median 5-year overall survival of 29% after hepatectomy against 41% after transplantation and recurrence of 65% against 54%, with no significant difference in the only 4 directly comparative studies (67 transplant against 227 resection patients) — and then concluded that hepatectomy should be preferred, which its own pooled estimates do not support. That paper is now eight years old and predates the 12-centre analysis, but the group should know that it exists, that it says the opposite, and that pooling single-arm proportions across 42 cohorts from different decades and classification eras does not produce a treatment effect either way. Evidence & sources Graft stewardship in a disease with 15-year patient survival of 27.3% against 45.9% for HCC is an institutional judgement, not an evidence question. It is approval item 1. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Treat the explant or resection specimen as the commonest route to this diagnosis, and build the pathway so that an unexpected result has a defined next step rather than a phone call.
text: Standard Evidence C Treat the explant or resection specimen as the commonest route to this diagnosis, and build the pathway so that an unexpected result has a defined next step rather than a phone call. Indications Preferred when Every programme. In the Korean single-centre transplant series, all 32 cHCC-CC cases were diagnosed incidentally in the explanted liver, 31 of 32 having been pre-diagnosed as HCC, and 12 of 32 (37.5%) had a separate concurrent HCC. In the 40-recipient Korean national registry series, none was identified before transplantation. In the French cirrhosis cohort, all 49 transplant diagnoses were made on the explant — 44 listed for HCC and 5 for decompensated cirrhosis. In the matched single-centre cohort, 19 of 19 were assumed to be HCC pre-transplant and all received HCC-directed neoadjuvant treatment. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat the post-hoc diagnosis as a reason to re-litigate the transplant. It is a reason to re-stage, to intensify surveillance, and to decide adjuvant therapy with the explant variables in hand — and, at a programme level, to improve pre-operative detection. Evidence & sources In the French multicentre cirrhosis series, incidental cHCC-CCA and iCCA of 5 cm or less in transplanted patients had 5-year survival of 69% at 2 cm or less and 65% above 2 cm, with no significant difference between the iCCA and cHCC-CCA patients (p=0.29) — and the two entities are not interchangeable, since the Spanish matched study put 5-year survival at 78% for mixed tumours against 51% for pure iCCA. The international 'very early' study is the clearest statement of how the explant defines these cohorts: 81 intrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas were found among 25,016 transplants at 17 centres, mixed HCC-CCA in the same nodule was excluded by design, 48 were analysed, and 46.7% of its favourable 15-patient group were incidental findings. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Re-stage on the specimen with the AJCC intrahepatic bile duct categories, and report lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, tumour necrosis, component proportion and margin status explicitly.
text: Standard Evidence C Re-stage on the specimen with the AJCC intrahepatic bile duct categories, and report lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, tumour necrosis, component proportion and margin status explicitly. Indications Preferred when Every specimen. These are the variables with the clearest outcome signal and none of them is in a radiological stage. Lymphovascular invasion separated 5-year overall survival of 93.3% from 35.8% in 80 hepatectomy patients, HR 11.35 (95% CI 3.20–40.3). Perineural invasion was present in 49 of 307 patients (16.0%) and carried worse median recurrence-free survival (0.21 against 0.54 years, HR 2.00, p<0.001) and overall survival (1.18 against 2.56 years, HR 2.21, p<0.001). Component proportion separated median overall survival of 3.16 years in HCC-dominant tumours from 1.86 years in CCA-dominant ones among 306 resections. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not accept a report that gives only the two component names. The local CPG already requires complete explant histopathology plus next-generation sequencing, which is the right standard — the gap is that it asks for the sequencing on the explant rather than on the diagnostic specimen, by which point the result cannot inform induction therapy. Evidence & sources Perineural invasion also had a direction effect that is worth knowing: the worst recurrence-free survival was in patients whose perineural invasion involved the HCC component, or was purely intratumoral. These are single-cohort subgroup findings from 307 patients, they have not been replicated, and that paper is one of the items on this page still cited from its abstract rather than from a full-text read. The transplant registry data agree on the variables while adding how thin they are: perineural invasion HR 5.14 (95% CI 1.07–24.69) on 4 patients and portal vein tumour thrombosis HR 13.43 (95% CI 2.17–83.21) on 3. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Adjuvant systemic chemotherapy Two datasets point in different directions and neither is informative. In 75 patients after R0 resection at one centre, the 19 who received adjuvant chemotherapy had better overall survival on Kaplan-Meier (p=0.029) and after 1:2 propensity matching (p=0.0011), with the benefit confined to a nomogram-defined high-risk group (p=0.013; low-risk p=0.084) — a subgroup of 13 treated against 32 untreated patients, from a nomogram with a time-dependent AUC of 0.694 at two years. In 197 resected patients in SEER, median overall survival was 40 months (95% CI 26.4–53.7) without post-operative chemotherapy against 26 months (95% CI 18.6–33.4) with it, but the difference was not significant before matching (HR 1.290, 95% CI 0.850–1.956, p=0.20) or after it (HR 1.063, 95% CI 0.646–1.749, p=0.81).
text: Adjuvant systemic chemotherapy Evidence C Two datasets point in different directions and neither is informative. In 75 patients after R0 resection at one centre, the 19 who received adjuvant chemotherapy had better overall survival on Kaplan-Meier (p=0.029) and after 1:2 propensity matching (p=0.0011), with the benefit confined to a nomogram-defined high-risk group (p=0.013; low-risk p=0.084) — a subgroup of 13 treated against 32 untreated patients, from a nomogram with a time-dependent AUC of 0.694 at two years. In 197 resected patients in SEER, median overall survival was 40 months (95% CI 26.4–53.7) without post-operative chemotherapy against 26 months (95% CI 18.6–33.4) with it, but the difference was not significant before matching (HR 1.290, 95% CI 0.850–1.956, p=0.20) or after it (HR 1.063, 95% CI 0.646–1.749, p=0.81). Indications Preferred when A resected or transplanted patient with high-risk explant features — macrovascular invasion, nodal metastasis, a tumour above 5 cm, lymphovascular or perineural invasion, poor differentiation, or a positive margin — discussed as a shared decision with the numbers above stated. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not present it as established, and do not present the SEER analysis as evidence against adjuvant therapy. Its chemotherapy arm had more advanced disease at baseline — T3–T4 in 25.5% against 15.2% (p=0.044), node-positive in 11.9% against 2.2% (p=0.003) — it excluded 87 transplant recipients, it records no recurrence and no second-line therapy, and its matched confidence interval still admits a 35% relative reduction in mortality. That is an uninformative null, not a negative result. The positive study is 19 treated patients whose own inclusion criteria excluded macrovascular invasion while the final model contains it. No adjuvant trial had ever enrolled this histology until 2025: patients with cHCC-CCA were systematically excluded from the landmark trials in both HCC and biliary tract cancer, so BILCAP, PRODIGE-12, BCAT and ASCOT say nothing about them. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Post-operative adjuvant transarterial chemoembolisation The most consistently positive adjuvant signal in this disease, and the most clearly confined. In the 306-patient four-centre cohort, adjuvant TACE improved early recurrence-free survival only in HCC-dominant tumours (2-year early recurrence-free survival 53.3% against 32.3%, p=0.028) and not in balanced (p=0.276) or CCA-dominant (p=0.433) patients — and even there, overall recurrence-free and overall survival were both non-significant (p=0.068 and p=0.549) on 30 treated patients. In 95 radically resected patients, post-operative TACE was independently associated with better overall survival (HR 0.2, p=0.005) with no confidence interval reported. In 307 patients it improved early recurrence-free survival only in those without perineural invasion (p=0.031).

Indications Preferred when A resected, hepatitis-B-associated, HCC-dominant tumour at a centre that does this routinely, with the patient told the evidence is retrospective, confined to early recurrence, and almost entirely from one population. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Not after transplantation, where the evidence does not exist at all and the risks differ. Not where perineural invasion is present, on the one dataset that examined the interaction. Not in a CCA-dominant tumour, where the only dataset that stratified by component found nothing. lead: Observation with intensive surveillance The honest default where no adjuvant modality has a trial behind it, and where the SEER analysis of post-operative chemotherapy could neither find nor exclude a benefit.
text: Observation with intensive surveillance Evidence D The honest default where no adjuvant modality has a trial behind it, and where the SEER analysis of post-operative chemotherapy could neither find nor exclude a benefit. Indications Preferred when A low-risk explant — single tumour, well or moderately differentiated, no vascular, lymphovascular or perineural invasion, clear margins, negative nodes — and any patient whose recovery will not tolerate adjuvant treatment. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not call it observation and then not observe. Surveillance intensity is the whole of this option's value and it has to be scheduled, not intended. lead: Do not start adjuvant capecitabine on BILCAP's authority, or any biliary adjuvant regimen on the assumption that this histology was in the trial.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not start adjuvant capecitabine on BILCAP's authority, or any biliary adjuvant regimen on the assumption that this histology was in the trial. Why Why If adjuvant systemic therapy is given, give it as an explicit extrapolation, recorded as such, with the regimen chosen for the predominant component and the patient told there is no reported trial — and offer the trial that now exists. A single-arm phase II study of cadonilimab with capecitabine after R0 resection of cHCC-CCA opened in November 2025 (NCT07243951, 75 patients planned); it is the first adjuvant study in this histology, it compares against a historical control rather than a randomised arm, and it excludes patients with prior or planned liver transplantation. Additional cautions Additional cautions cHCC-CCA has been systematically excluded from the landmark adjuvant trials in both HCC and cholangiocarcinoma. Quoting an adjuvant hazard ratio from a biliary trial to a patient with this histology misrepresents what is known. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not change immunosuppression on the explant finding alone without recording it as a decision with a reason.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not change immunosuppression on the explant finding alone without recording it as a decision with a reason. Why Why The local CPG's position — rapid steroid withdrawal, minimised immunosuppression, and consideration of conversion to an mTOR inhibitor at four weeks — is a reasonable one and is what the protocol says to do. Apply it as a protocol step, with the date and the reason in the note. Additional cautions Additional cautions There are no comparative data on immunosuppression strategy after transplantation for cHCC-CCA specifically: the mTOR rationale is borrowed from HCC, and in the 40-recipient Korean registry series everolimus at 1, 6 or 12 months made no difference to survival or recurrence. An unrecorded change made on a pathology report is the kind of decision nobody can audit afterwards. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Cisplatin–gemcitabine plus durvalumab or pembrolizumabPROTOCOL What NCCN names, and now the one option with a direct comparison behind it. Both the Hepatocellular Carcinoma and the Biliary Tract Cancers guidelines state that for histologically proven mixed tumours at advanced stages, cisplatin–gemcitabine with either durvalumab or pembrolizumab is an appropriate first-line choice, on the grounds that these combinations contain agents active in both histologies.
text: Cisplatin–gemcitabine plus durvalumab or pembrolizumab Evidence C PROTOCOL What NCCN names, and now the one option with a direct comparison behind it. Both the Hepatocellular Carcinoma and the Biliary Tract Cancers guidelines state that for histologically proven mixed tumours at advanced stages, cisplatin–gemcitabine with either durvalumab or pembrolizumab is an appropriate first-line choice, on the grounds that these combinations contain agents active in both histologies. Indications Preferred when Most patients, and particularly a CCA-predominant tumour, a raised CA 19-9, or nodal and extrahepatic spread in a biliary pattern. In four Taiwanese centres, 21 patients with cHCC-CCA given first-line durvalumab with gemcitabine–cisplatin were compared with 154 patients with pure cholangiocarcinoma, all slides read jointly by two hepatopathologists: median overall survival 13.8 months (95% CI 2.1–25.6) against 13.3 months (95% CI 9.5–17.1), p=0.60, and after 2:1 propensity matching 13.8 against 14.5 months, p=0.78. Median progression-free survival was 5.3 against 5.1 months, objective response 38.1% against 23.8% after matching (p=0.24) with identical disease control at 66.7%, and histology was not an independent predictor of overall survival (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.42–1.66). Grade 3 or worse toxicity was 57.1% against 42.9% after matching (p=0.30), with no immune-related adverse events in the cHCC-CCA patients and no treatment-related deaths. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Read that comparison for what it is. Twenty-one patients with a confidence interval running from 2.1 to 25.6 months cannot demonstrate equivalence; a p value of 0.60 is a failure to detect a difference, and the hazard ratio admits both a 58% reduction and a 66% increase in mortality. Matching shrank the comparator from 154 to 42, so the matched analysis has 63 patients in total. No patient in it received an HCC regimen, so the comparison that would justify preferring a biliary backbone was never made — and the 21 were chosen for a biliary regimen by their own physicians, almost certainly on cholangiocarcinoma-like imaging or markers that the paper does not report. The older retrospective support is weaker still: in a 101-patient European cohort the 44 treated patients gave median overall survival of 15.5 months with chemotherapy against 5.3 months without, p=0.052 — not significant, not associated with survival on multivariable analysis, with objective response 8% against 5% and progression-free survival 3.0 against 3.2 months, and with 16 of the 19 non-chemotherapy patients on sorafenib. That is chemotherapy against sorafenib, and against a group too unwell for treatment at all. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

Retrospective, 44 treated of 101: median OS 15.5 mo with chemotherapy vs 5.3 mo without, p=0.052 (NS); ORR 8% vs 5%; PFS 3.0 vs 3.2 mo 16 of 19 non-chemotherapy patients on sorafenib; NS on multivariable analysis

lead: An HCC backbone — atezolizumab–bevacizumab, or tremelimumab–durvalumab Reasonable where the tumour is HCC-predominant, where AFP is the raised marker, and where cirrhosis limits chemotherapy tolerance. The genomic argument is real but narrower than it is usually stated: TP53 and TERT promoter alterations predominate and TERT promoter mutation is present in both components of the same tumour, establishing clonal common origin — but in 150 cHCC-CCA against 2,372 HCC, CTNNB1 was under 7% against over 34%, and the iCCA-typical drivers IDH1 (8.0% against 0.3%) and FGFR2 (7.3% against 0.3%) were present and are absent from HCC. This is not simply an HCC.
text: An HCC backbone — atezolizumab–bevacizumab, or tremelimumab–durvalumab Evidence C Reasonable where the tumour is HCC-predominant, where AFP is the raised marker, and where cirrhosis limits chemotherapy tolerance. The genomic argument is real but narrower than it is usually stated: TP53 and TERT promoter alterations predominate and TERT promoter mutation is present in both components of the same tumour, establishing clonal common origin — but in 150 cHCC-CCA against 2,372 HCC, CTNNB1 was under 7% against over 34%, and the iCCA-typical drivers IDH1 (8.0% against 0.3%) and FGFR2 (7.3% against 0.3%) were present and are absent from HCC. This is not simply an HCC. Indications Preferred when The HCC-predominant tumour in a cirrhotic patient, or a patient who cannot take a platinum doublet. In 16 patients given atezolizumab–bevacizumab across 7 French centres, the 9 treated in the first line had median overall survival 13 months, median progression-free survival 3 months and partial response in 3 of 9 (33%). In 21 Japanese patients given first-line HCC-directed therapy at 6 centres, objective response was 33.3% overall with disease control 95.2%, median overall survival 14.9 months (95% CI 9.7–19.3) and median progression-free survival 6.5 months (95% CI 4.9–10.8); by regimen, lenvatinib (n=14) gave 42.9% response and atezolizumab–bevacizumab (n=7) gave 14.3%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Severe gastrointestinal bleeding occurred in 2 of the 16 atezolizumab–bevacizumab patients (12.5%), which is a real signal in a cirrhotic population, and a 33% response rate from 3 responses in 9 patients has a confidence interval of roughly 7% to 70%. Note what the Japanese cohort is: median age 74, 19 of 21 ECOG 0, 18 of 21 Child-Pugh A, and 17 of 21 recurrences after prior local treatment — the fittest advanced population reported here — and no patient in it received a biliary regimen, so it cannot compare the two backbones either. IMbrave150 (HR for death 0.58, 95% CI 0.42–0.79) and HIMALAYA (median overall survival 16.43 against 13.77 months, HR 0.78, 96.02% CI 0.65–0.93) were trials in hepatocellular carcinoma and did not enrol this histology. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Targeted therapy where an alteration is present NCCN states that at progression, molecularly targeted therapies should be considered where the tumour harbours a targetable aberration, and that panel testing should be considered in all advanced mixed tumours.
text: Targeted therapy where an alteration is present Evidence C NCCN states that at progression, molecularly targeted therapies should be considered where the tumour harbours a targetable aberration, and that panel testing should be considered in all advanced mixed tumours. Indications Preferred when Any patient with an actionable result. In the largest genomic series, 52 of 150 cHCC-CCA (34.7%) carried a potentially actionable alteration against 462 of 2,372 HCC (19.5%), comprising IDH1 or IDH2 in 16, FGFR2 in 11, BRCA1 or BRCA2 in 7, ERBB2 in 5, BRAF in 4 and MET in 3. A separate 72-case series found FGFR2 alteration in 26.4% and HER2 immunohistochemistry 3+ in 8.3%, and a machine-learning classification of 73 tumours put potentially actionable alterations at 24.6%, concentrated in the CCA-like group where FGFR2, IDH1 and ARID1A each reached 25%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not expect the target frequencies of pure iCCA, and do not treat the 34.7% as a property of the disease: it rests on 52 patients in a commercial sequencing cohort selected by whose physician ordered profiling, and it bundles approved FGFR and IDH indications with MET and amplification targets that have no liver-cancer data at all. Do not test for mismatch-repair deficiency as the only molecular test — none was found in 24 cHCC-CCA in one series or in 72 in another, and only 2.7% of 150 were tumour-mutational-burden high. And every targeted agent in this setting is used on a basket or extrapolated indication, with no reported trial in this disease. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Genomic cohort: actionable alteration 34.7% (52 of 150) vs 19.5% (462 of 2,372), cHCC-CCA vs HCC; TMB-high only 2.7% Commercial sequencing cohort selected by whose physician ordered profiling

lead: Before systemic therapy: multigene panel and trial screening. The only randomized trial closed with four patients.
text: Standard Evidence C Before systemic therapy: multigene panel and trial screening. The only randomized trial closed with four patients. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Order multigene panel testing in every patient entering systemic therapy, and screen for trial eligibility at the same visit — there are now open trials in this histology, and the only one that ever randomised patients closed with four. Indications Preferred when Every advanced case. No prospective trial in this disease has ever reported, so a trial is often the best available option and the panel result is what opens it. Four studies are currently open or about to open, all single-arm: durvalumab with a single priming dose of tremelimumab plus gemcitabine–cisplatin (NCT06855225, 29 patients, response rate primary, University of Alabama at Birmingham); hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy with camrelizumab and rivoceranib (NCT07105748, TASK-05, 45 patients, recruiting in Shanghai); GEMOX with anlotinib and sintilimab (NCT06033118, 25 patients, Sichuan University, registry status last recorded as unknown); and the adjuvant study of cadonilimab with capecitabine after R0 resection (NCT07243951, 75 patients). A Japanese single-arm study of atezolizumab–bevacizumab in 12 patients (jRCTs031220099) is also reported. Reviews of the retrospective experience put gemcitabine–platinum median overall survival at 10.2–16.2 months with objective response 15–29%, and checkpoint-inhibitor objective response at 20–33%, with roughly 57% of tumours showing an immune-high phenotype and about a quarter carrying a targetable alteration. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not wait for the explant to sequence, which is what the local CPG currently specifies — by then the result cannot inform induction. Do not read the immune-high figure as a predictive biomarker; it is a descriptive finding in 96 patients. And do not read those ranges as pooled estimates: the review that assembles them states plainly that they are the span of two or three cohorts of 7 to 101 patients, with no weighting and no confidence intervals, and that the molecular treatment algorithm it proposes is unvalidated for efficacy. Evidence & sources The correction this page needed most in this assessment is a factual one. It is not true that no prospective trial has ever existed: NCT05211323, a National Cancer Institute randomised phase II comparing gemcitabine–cisplatin–atezolizumab with and without bevacizumab in advanced cHCC-CCA, with progression-free survival as its primary endpoint, opened in December 2022 across 37 US sites against a planned enrolment of 88. It accrued 4 patients, is listed as active but not recruiting with a primary completion date of 20 January 2026, and has posted no results. The accurate statement is that no prospective trial in this disease has ever reported, and that the one randomised attempt failed on accrual — which is the single most important fact for anyone deciding whether to refer a patient to one of the four studies now open. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Combining liver-directed treatment with immune and targeted therapy is a reasonable approach in liver-dominant unresectable disease, on real-world data only.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Combining liver-directed treatment with immune and targeted therapy is a reasonable approach in liver-dominant unresectable disease, on real-world data only. Indications Preferred when Liver-confined or liver-dominant unresectable disease with preserved function. In 51 patients screened from 242 at a single Chinese centre, all Child-Pugh A and ECOG 0–1, median overall survival was 17.8 months (95% CI 12.4–23.2) and median progression-free survival 8.9 months (95% CI 5.8–12.0), with objective response 41.2% by RECIST 1.1 and 56.9% by mRECIST, disease control 78.4%, and grade 3 or worse adverse events in 6 patients (11.8%). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Those are the best numbers on this page and they come from a single-arm retrospective cohort of 51 patients selected from 242, with no comparator — and the 50 patients excluded because they received something other than this combination are precisely the control group it lacks. Eleven of the 51 (21.6%) were downstaged to resection and their median survival was not reached against 17.2 months for the rest (p=0.005), so they are carrying the headline figure. Two-year overall survival was 20.3% against a median of 17.8 months, so the curve falls away sharply. Seven different checkpoint inhibitors and four targeted agents were used across three interventional protocols, so no single regimen was evaluated. Primary disease did better than recurrent disease (median overall survival 21.4 against 11.4 months, p=0.011), and HCC-dominant and iCCA-dominant tumours did not differ in overall or progression-free survival (p=0.835 and p=0.553) at any HCC-component threshold from 20% to 80% — a useful negative finding for the backbone question. Baseline disease was advanced: median largest nodule 8.2 cm, 82.4% multinodular, 51.0% node-positive, 62.7% stage IV. Evidence & sources Grade C on the strength of a single-arm cohort. Nothing here justifies preferring this over a guideline-named regimen outside a protocol or trial. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Re-biopsy at progression where areas of response and progression are discordant, and switch to the regimen appropriate to the component that is progressing.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Re-biopsy at progression where areas of response and progression are discordant, and switch to the regimen appropriate to the component that is progressing. Indications Preferred when A patient still fit for further therapy whose imaging shows one lesion growing while others respond. NCCN recommends considering this, and states that if the recurrence biopsy suggests isolated recurrence of either the HCC or the CCA component, a systemic therapy option appropriate for that component is reasonable. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not assume the recurrence carries the same mix as the primary, and do not assume a single-component recurrence biopsy means the other component has gone — the same sampling problem applies, with CK19 positive in 33% of biopsies against 84% of the matching specimens. No study has measured how often a recurrence biopsy in this disease changes the regimen or whether doing so helps. Evidence & sources This is the one place where the two-component biology is used constructively rather than apologetically. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not choose a tyrosine kinase inhibitor alone as first line on the ground that the tumour is "mostly HCC".
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not choose a tyrosine kinase inhibitor alone as first line on the ground that the tumour is "mostly HCC". Why Why If an HCC backbone is chosen, choose a current one. The non-cytotoxic arm of the 101-patient European cohort was 16 sorafenib patients out of 19, with objective response 5%, median progression-free survival 3.2 months and median overall survival 5.3 months against 15.5 months for chemotherapy (p=0.052). Additional cautions Additional cautions In a 123-patient single-institution experience, gemcitabine–platinum gave a disease control rate of 78.4% against 38.5% for gemcitabine–fluoropyrimidine (p=0.008), and sorafenib only 20% — but read the survival endpoint, because that paper's own overall survival comparison was flatly null: 11.5 months with gemcitabine–platinum against 11.7 months with gemcitabine–fluoropyrimidine, p=0.9686, with sorafenib at 9.6 months. A regimen that doubles disease control and changes survival by nothing is telling you that stable disease here is not durable benefit. Both cohorts are retrospective and neither tested a modern immunotherapy doublet. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Retrospective: non-cytotoxic arm (16 of 19 sorafenib) ORR 5%, median PFS 3.2 mo; median OS 5.3 vs 15.5 mo with chemotherapy, p=0.052 Not significant; no modern immunotherapy doublet tested

lead: Do not quote a trial effect size from biliary tract cancer or from hepatocellular carcinoma as if it applied at full strength here.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not quote a trial effect size from biliary tract cancer or from hepatocellular carcinoma as if it applied at full strength here. Why Why KEYNOTE-966 enrolled 13 mixed HCC–CCA patients (8 pembrolizumab, 5 placebo), but reported no separate treatment effect for them. The overall BTC result (OS 12.7 versus 10.9 months; HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.72–0.95) cannot be presented as a cHCC–CCA-specific effect. HCC and other BTC regimens remain individualized extrapolations in this histology. Additional cautions Additional cautions Name the source population, comparator and the absence of a powered mixed-histology analysis. Thirteen enrolled mixed cases do not establish a histology-specific benefit or a preferred regimen; retain multidisciplinary review and clinical trials. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: KEYNOTE-966 enrolled 13 patients with mixed HCC–CCA; no separate treatment-effect estimate was reported. The overall biliary-tract result is not an established effect estimate for cHCC–CCA.

lead: Record every liver-directed treatment in this disease as borrowed evidence, and expect lower response than in hepatocellular carcinoma.
text: Standard Evidence D Record every liver-directed treatment in this disease as borrowed evidence, and expect lower response than in hepatocellular carcinoma. Indications Preferred when Every case. The reviews that address this question directly reach the same conclusion: liver-directed methods — TACE, percutaneous ethanol injection, hepatic arterial infusion, radioembolisation and ablation — are less effective here than in HCC because of the cholangiocytic component's vascularity and desmoplasia, and transarterial chemoembolisation may be effective in unresectable disease particularly where the tumour is hypervascular. The one dataset that tested vascularity as a selection variable agrees: adjuvant TACE improved early recurrence-free survival only in the HCC-dominant third of 306 resected tumours (53.3% against 32.3% at two years, p=0.028) and not in balanced (p=0.276) or CCA-dominant (p=0.433) patients. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not quote an HCC response rate, a BCLC stage-based algorithm, or an iCCA radioembolisation series as though either applied directly. There is no prospective trial of any liver-directed modality in cHCC-CCA, and the evidence base for this assessment is review-level synthesis of HCC and iCCA experience plus small retrospective cohorts. Both interventional reviews are explicit that essentially all their quantitative material concerns cholangiocarcinoma, and neither distinguishes the hypervascular HCC-dominant tumour that might respond to an arterial therapy from the hypovascular CCA-dominant one that will not. Evidence & sources Grade D is the honest grade for this whole assessment. It is labelled Standard because liver-directed therapy is what gets done, and the page's job is to say what is known about it, not to pretend the modality is unevidenced and then recommend it silently. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: On a transplant pathway, locoregional therapy is the instrument that generates the six months of documented stability the exception requires — plan it as part of the listing strategy, not as treatment in parallel with it.
text: Standard Evidence D On a transplant pathway, locoregional therapy is the instrument that generates the six months of documented stability the exception requires — plan it as part of the listing strategy, not as treatment in parallel with it. Indications Preferred when Every protocol candidate. The OPTN review-board criteria require six months from diagnosis or last treatment with the tumour remaining 3 cm or less, no new lesions and no extrahepatic disease, with imaging every three months; the ILTS-ILCA consensus frames bridging with neoadjuvant therapy as a way of identifying favourable tumour biology, with more than six months of stability or successful downstaging (low evidence, weak strength). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let the locoregional plan and the listing timeline be managed by different people. And note what the consensus statement actually claims: that bridging helps identify favourable biology, not that it improves outcome. Evidence & sources The local CPG permits locoregional therapy other than external-beam radiation — TACE, radiofrequency ablation, Y-90 — but states it should not be the sole pre-transplant therapy except for a solitary tumour under 3 cm. That is the one place where the local document is more conservative than it needs to be and more specific than the evidence; it is also the only written local rule on the subject, so it stands until the group changes it. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Transarterial chemoembolisation The most used modality and the one with the most supporting data, though all of it is retrospective and the benefit is confined. Post-operative adjuvant TACE was independently associated with better overall survival (HR 0.2, p=0.005, no confidence interval reported) in 95 radically resected patients, and in 306 resections it improved early recurrence-free survival only in HCC-dominant tumours, with overall recurrence-free and overall survival both non-significant even there (p=0.068 and p=0.549).
text: Transarterial chemoembolisation Evidence C The most used modality and the one with the most supporting data, though all of it is retrospective and the benefit is confined. Post-operative adjuvant TACE was independently associated with better overall survival (HR 0.2, p=0.005, no confidence interval reported) in 95 radically resected patients, and in 306 resections it improved early recurrence-free survival only in HCC-dominant tumours, with overall recurrence-free and overall survival both non-significant even there (p=0.068 and p=0.549). Indications Preferred when A hypervascular, HCC-predominant, liver-confined tumour with preserved function, and bridging on a transplant pathway. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not use it for a hypovascular, CCA-predominant tumour and expect a response — the quantitative imaging work in this disease shows that a large hypovascular component is what distinguishes cHCC-CCA from HCC in the first place, and the one cohort that stratified adjuvant TACE by component found no signal outside the HCC-dominant group. And in the Taiwan national registry the hazard ratio for TACE was 0.56 in the non-surgical stratum and 1.64 in the surgical one, which is confounding by indication rather than an effect. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Transarterial radioembolisation Covered in both interventional reviews as an option extrapolated from HCC and iCCA experience, with no cHCC-CCA-specific data.
text: Transarterial radioembolisation Evidence D Covered in both interventional reviews as an option extrapolated from HCC and iCCA experience, with no cHCC-CCA-specific data. Indications Preferred when A larger liver-dominant tumour, or one in which the biliary component makes a bland or chemoembolic response unlikely, at a centre with the dosimetry expertise. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid There is no series in this histology to quote. Treat it as protocol or registry territory rather than routine. lead: Thermal ablation Radiofrequency and microwave ablation appear in the interventional reviews, and the local CPG permits them as pre-transplant therapy. Ablation is the modality most defensible for a solitary small tumour.
text: Thermal ablation Evidence D Radiofrequency and microwave ablation appear in the interventional reviews, and the local CPG permits them as pre-transplant therapy. Ablation is the modality most defensible for a solitary small tumour. Indications Preferred when A solitary tumour under 3 cm in a position that allows a margin, in a patient on a transplant pathway or unfit for resection. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Obtain the biopsy before ablation, because the tissue opportunity closes with it — NCCN says so for HCC and the point is sharper here, where the transplant pathway requires biopsy-proven mixed histology. An ablated tumour with no tissue diagnosis cannot enter the exception pathway. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not use external-beam radiation as pre-transplant therapy under the local protocol.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not use external-beam radiation as pre-transplant therapy under the local protocol. Why Why The local CPG excludes external-beam radiation from the locoregional options it permits before transplantation, and that is the local rule. Additional cautions Additional cautions No data support the exclusion in this disease specifically, and no data support the alternative either. The perihilar protocol's experience of radiation-related vascular friability, gastroduodenal ulceration and ischaemic cholangiopathy is the likely origin of the restriction and is a reasonable analogy, but it is an analogy. If the group wants to permit radiotherapy here it needs to say so and record why.

lead: Do not treat a liver-directed response as evidence that the diagnosis was something other than cHCC-CCA.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not treat a liver-directed response as evidence that the diagnosis was something other than cHCC-CCA. Why Why A good embolic response tells you the arterialised component responded. It does not reclassify the tumour, it does not remove the cholangiocytic component, and it does not change the staging system, the nodal question or the surveillance interval. Additional cautions Additional cautions This is a specific trap in a disease whose diagnosis is often provisional: a tumour that behaves like HCC on treatment invites the board to quietly revert to the HCC pathway. The histology, not the response, decides which page you are on. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Surveil at biliary rather than hepatocellular intensity — cross-sectional imaging of the liver and chest with AFP and CA 19-9 every three months for the first two years — because most recurrences happen inside that window.
text: Standard Evidence D Surveil at biliary rather than hepatocellular intensity — cross-sectional imaging of the liver and chest with AFP and CA 19-9 every three months for the first two years — because most recurrences happen inside that window. Indications Preferred when Every resected and transplanted patient. Median recurrence-free survival was 7.27 months in a 95-patient multicentre radical-resection cohort and 5-year recurrence-free survival was 12.2% in a 19-patient single-centre series, against a 5-year overall survival of 44.7% in the same 19 patients — most of these patients recur, and recur early. The contemporary surgical review puts post-operative recurrence above 60%. In the 306-patient component-proportion cohort, extrahepatic or combined recurrence accounted for 26.9% of recurrences in HCC-dominant tumours, 37.2% in balanced and 50.5% in CCA-dominant ones (p=0.043), so the more biliary the tumour the more the surveillance has to look outside the liver. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not run a six-monthly HCC surveillance schedule. Grade D: no study has tested a surveillance interval in this disease, and the three-monthly interval is reasoning from the recurrence timing plus concordance with the NLRB guidance route (nonstandard review)'s own three-monthly imaging requirement. It is an operating rule, not an evidence threshold. Evidence & sources Include the porta hepatis deliberately in the reporting request. The lymph node was the second commonest site of first recurrence in the Japanese resection series, unlike HCC, and where nodal recurrence occurs it concentrates at the hepatic hilum (62.3%) and the portal vein–vena cava region (39.6%) — from 53 patients who had already recurred in nodes, of whom 11 had cHCC-CCA, so that is a map of where to look rather than a measure of how often. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Biopsy a recurrence whose component mix could change the regimen.
text: Standard Evidence C Biopsy a recurrence whose component mix could change the regimen. Indications Preferred when Any recurrence in a patient still fit for systemic therapy, particularly where response is discordant across lesions. NCCN recommends considering repeat biopsy in metastatic or locally advanced recurrence after prior resection or local therapy, to establish the dominant histology — and treating an isolated single-component recurrence with the regimen for that component. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not re-biopsy where the result cannot change the plan, and do not read a single-component recurrence biopsy as proof that only that component remains. The sampling problem of clinical decision 1 applies unchanged: CK19 was positive in 33% of pre-operative biopsies against 84% of the matching specimens. No study has measured biopsy performance at recurrence in this disease. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Local re-treatment of an isolated recurrence Repeat hepatectomy and ablation are both reported in the review literature, and no study has compared local re-treatment with systemic therapy at recurrence in this disease. The nearest signal is from conversion rather than recurrence: in a 51-patient advanced cohort, the 11 downstaged to hepatic resection had a median overall survival not reached against 17.2 months for the rest (p=0.005), which is selection as much as surgery.
text: Local re-treatment of an isolated recurrence Evidence D Repeat hepatectomy and ablation are both reported in the review literature, and no study has compared local re-treatment with systemic therapy at recurrence in this disease. The nearest signal is from conversion rather than recurrence: in a 51-patient advanced cohort, the 11 downstaged to hepatic resection had a median overall survival not reached against 17.2 months for the rest (p=0.005), which is selection as much as surgery. Indications Preferred when A solitary intrahepatic recurrence after a long disease-free interval in a fit patient with adequate remnant — which, given 5-year recurrence-free survival of 12.2% and a median recurrence-free survival measured in months, is an uncommon patient. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not offer repeat local treatment for early multifocal recurrence or for nodal recurrence. Early recurrence in this disease is a statement about biology, and the recurrence-pattern data put the liver and the regional nodes as the two dominant sites. lead: Systemic therapy at recurrence The default for multifocal, nodal or extrahepatic recurrence. This is clinical decision 7, with the component question re-asked on the recurrence biopsy rather than the primary.
text: Systemic therapy at recurrence Evidence C The default for multifocal, nodal or extrahepatic recurrence. This is clinical decision 7, with the component question re-asked on the recurrence biopsy rather than the primary. Indications Preferred when Most recurrences. Recurrent disease does worse than primary disease on the only cohort that separated them — median overall survival 11.4 against 21.4 months, p=0.011 — so the conversation should start from that figure, not from the first-line figures. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not carry over a first-line regimen that has already failed, and do not assume the backbone chosen for the primary is still the right one. lead: Best supportive care The right answer in a patient with poor performance status, decompensated liver function or rapid multifocal progression, and the one this page is least likely to be opened for.
text: Best supportive care Evidence D The right answer in a patient with poor performance status, decompensated liver function or rapid multifocal progression, and the one this page is least likely to be opened for. Indications Preferred when State it as a choice, early, and involve palliative care at the same visit rather than later. In 529 SEER patients the median overall survival was 8 months, and in the Taiwan Cancer Registry 5-year overall survival for this histology was 25.7% across 95,149 primary liver cancers — both whole-registry figures dominated by patients who were never resected, which is the point when the question is whether to treat at all. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not reach it by default after three lines of borrowed therapy in a patient who was never going to tolerate them. And do not quote either registry's treatment hazard ratios in that conversation: the SEER paper reports the surgery hazard ratio as 4.94 in its abstract and 4.18 in its table, and the Taiwan registry's TACE hazard ratio reverses between its surgical and non-surgical strata. lead: Do not call a new nodule a recurrence of one component without tissue, and do not call a second primary a recurrence either.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not call a new nodule a recurrence of one component without tissue, and do not call a second primary a recurrence either. Why Why In the Korean transplant series, 12 of 32 patients (37.5%) had a concurrent separate HCC in the same explant. A new nodule in a cirrhotic remnant liver may be a new HCC rather than recurrent cHCC-CCA, and the two have different implications for what to offer. Additional cautions Additional cautions The labelling matters for the registry as well as for the patient: outcome figures in this disease are already distorted by cohorts that mixed true mixed tumours with separate synchronous primaries, and the 2019 classification explicitly puts the double-cancer and collision types outside the entity. lead: Make the diagnosis on contrast-enhanced MRI, and use a hepatobiliary contrast agent where the question is adenoma versus focal nodular hyperplasia.
text: Standard Evidence C Make the diagnosis on contrast-enhanced MRI, and use a hepatobiliary contrast agent where the question is adenoma versus focal nodular hyperplasia. Indications Preferred when Every patient at presentation. EASL 2016 states that MRI is superior to all other imaging modalities and, because it detects fat and vascular spaces, offers an opportunity to subtype adenomas in up to 80% of cases (evidence level II-2, grade of recommendation 1). The French multisociety guidance adds that hepatobiliary contrast has additional value specifically for focal nodular hyperplasia. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not accept an ultrasound or single-phase CT diagnosis and then counsel on it, and do not assume the diagnosis is secure because somebody resected it. In the multicentre prospective pregnancy cohort, 18 of 66 women (27%) referred with a suspected adenoma under 5 cm turned out to have focal nodular hyperplasia once hepatobiliary-contrast MRI was done — a lesion with no bleeding or malignant risk and no follow-up requirement at all. In the Dutch nationwide audit of 222 resections performed for a presumed adenoma, the postoperative diagnosis differed from the preoperative one in 43% of cases, rising to 70% of lesions under 50 mm and 78% of male patients; focal nodular hyperplasia was the final diagnosis in 21% of the resected sub-50 mm lesions. Independent predictors of a changed diagnosis were lesion under 50 mm (adjusted odds ratio 3.4), male sex (3.7) and absence of hepatobiliary contrast-enhanced MRI (1.8). In the Korean nationwide series of 121 patients with 138 adenomas, hepatocellular adenoma was not suspected at all in 31.6% of the original radiology reports. Evidence & sources Contrast-enhanced ultrasound separates adenoma from focal nodular hyperplasia by the absence of the central spoke-wheel pattern, but EASL is explicit that it is not accurate enough to subtype an adenoma. Fix the measurement convention locally — longest axial diameter on the same sequence each time — because the growth trigger downstream is a 20% change. The Dutch audit is retrospective and selected on having been resected, so it cannot say how often the diagnosis is wrong in a lesion that was watched; the authors note it is plausibly worse, which would strengthen rather than weaken the point. The adjusted odds ratio of 1.8 for absence of hepatobiliary contrast is confounded by era and centre and should not be read as an effect of the agent alone. lead: HNF1A-inactivated (H-HCA) EASL 2016: positive identification of HNF1A-inactivated adenoma is achievable with MRI with more than 90% specificity (evidence level II-2, grade of recommendation 1).
text: HNF1A-inactivated (H-HCA) Evidence C EASL 2016: positive identification of HNF1A-inactivated adenoma is achievable with MRI with more than 90% specificity (evidence level II-2, grade of recommendation 1). Indications Preferred when The lesion with diffuse homogeneous signal dropout on chemical-shift opposed-phase T1, reflecting marked steatosis. Reported MRI sensitivity 87-91% and specificity 89-100% across two series of 50 and 44 adenomas. This is the subtype that lets you lengthen an interval: histological haemorrhage was the lowest of any subgroup at 39%, and no malignant transformation was seen in any HNF1A-inactivated adenoma under 5 cm in a woman (0 of 47). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not read any fatty adenoma as HNF1A-inactivated. Inflammatory adenomas that contain fat drop signal heterogeneously and moderately, and some HNF1A-inactivated adenomas are only mildly steatotic. Germline rather than somatic mutation in 8% of cases means a positive call should prompt a family and diabetes history. lead: Inflammatory (I-HCA) EASL 2016 groups it with HNF1A-inactivated adenoma as identifiable by MRI with more than 90% specificity.
text: Inflammatory (I-HCA) Evidence C EASL 2016 groups it with HNF1A-inactivated adenoma as identifiable by MRI with more than 90% specificity. Indications Preferred when Strong T2 hyperintensity as bright as spleen, diffuse or as a peripheral rim (the atoll sign), with persistent enhancement on the delayed phase using extracellular contrast agents. Sensitivity 85-88%, specificity 88-100% with extracellular agents. Suspect it in obesity, metabolic syndrome or high alcohol intake, with a raised C-reactive protein, GGT and alkaline phosphatase; it is the least often symptomatic subtype at presentation (30%, P<0.0001). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not use a hepatobiliary agent to make this call and expect the same numbers: with gadoxetic acid, sensitivity and specificity for inflammatory subtype fall to 80.9% and 77.3%, and nearly half of inflammatory adenomas are iso- or hyperintense on the hepatobiliary phase, mimicking focal nodular hyperplasia. About half of all beta-catenin-activated adenomas are also inflammatory, so an inflammatory phenotype does not exclude the high-risk driver. lead: Beta-catenin-activated and unclassified EASL 2016 is explicit: identification of beta-catenin-activated adenoma, and its distinction from unclassified adenoma and from hepatocellular carcinoma, is not possible by any imaging technique (evidence level II-2, grade of recommendation 1).
text: Beta-catenin-activated and unclassified Evidence C EASL 2016 is explicit: identification of beta-catenin-activated adenoma, and its distinction from unclassified adenoma and from hepatocellular carcinoma, is not possible by any imaging technique (evidence level II-2, grade of recommendation 1). Indications Preferred when Nothing. If the subtype matters — and this is the subtype that matters most, carrying an odds ratio of 9.3 (95% CI 4.4-20.0) for malignant transformation — it needs tissue or it needs resecting. And tissue alone may not settle it: across 220 adenomas, 373 carcinomas and 17 borderline lesions, only 27% of the 33 beta-catenin-mutated adenomas tested showed the textbook strong homogeneous glutamine synthetase pattern, so immunohistochemical triage under-detects the very subtype it is deployed to find, and those authors recommended mutation screening. The narrative review of the WHO 6th-edition classification says the same: nuclear beta-catenin staining has sensitivity too low to be reliable in routine practice, especially on a biopsy, glutamine synthetase is the usable surrogate, and every inflammatory adenoma should have glutamine synthetase staining to detect an added CTNNB1 mutation. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat heterogeneous T2 signal with a central scar and no chemical-shift dropout as a beta-catenin diagnosis. Gadoxetic acid retention occurs in both inflammatory and beta-catenin adenomas and reflects OATP1B1/B3 expression, not the driver. Unclassified adenomas have no characteristic imaging feature at all. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Sonic hedgehog (shHCA) Described after EASL 2016 and therefore absent from it: a subgroup defined by focal INHBE deletion producing an INHBE-GLI1 fusion, 22 of 533 adenomas (4%) in the reference series, previously counted as unclassified.
text: Sonic hedgehog (shHCA) Evidence C Described after EASL 2016 and therefore absent from it: a subgroup defined by focal INHBE deletion producing an INHBE-GLI1 fusion, 22 of 533 adenomas (4%) in the reference series, previously counted as unclassified. Indications Preferred when Suspect it rather than diagnose it: 100% female, higher BMI, and the only subgroup associated with symptomatic bleeding — 71% versus 14% in every other subgroup, P<0.0001. The obese woman who presents with a bled adenoma is the phenotype. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not expect to find it on MRI; no imaging phenotype has been defined, and no reliable routine immunohistochemical marker exists either. Prostaglandin D synthase is specific but insensitive, and in the study that proposed it was diffusely positive in all 5 sonic hedgehog adenomas tested and negative in the others — a numerator of five. Argininosuccinate synthase 1 is sensitive and not specific: it was proposed as a marker of high bleeding risk but turns out to sit downstream of the INHBE-GLI1 fusion as part of a periportal expression programme, correlating with GLI1 at R=0.75 (P<0.0001), and ASS1 messenger RNA was not associated with histological haemorrhage at all. The review of the WHO 6th-edition classification states plainly that a reliable immunohistochemical marker for routine practice is still lacking and molecular profiling remains the gold standard. Do not use ASS1 as a bleeding-risk score. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Record whether the background liver is at risk for hepatocellular carcinoma, because that one fact decides which pathway this patient belongs on.
text: Standard Evidence D Record whether the background liver is at risk for hepatocellular carcinoma, because that one fact decides which pathway this patient belongs on. Indications Preferred when Cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis B, or current or prior hepatocellular carcinoma. Any of those and this is the HCC pathway from here, assessed on its own terms with LI-RADS and the OPTN imaging criteria; an adenoma in a cirrhotic liver is an unusual enough claim to need expert pathology before it is accepted. Absence of an at-risk background is the usual case and is the reason the HCC imaging criteria cannot be borrowed later. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not carry an adenoma diagnosis forward without this line in the note. The local hepatic adenoma protocol builds its entire malignant-transformation routing on it: because most adenoma-derived carcinoma arises in a non-cirrhotic, non-at-risk liver, OPTN Class 5 classification and LI-RADS do not apply and the lesion cannot be classified on imaging alone.

lead: Biopsy when the imaging is atypical, when malignant transformation is suspected, or when the subtype will change what you do — and not otherwise.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Biopsy when the imaging is atypical, when malignant transformation is suspected, or when the subtype will change what you do — and not otherwise. Indications Preferred when EASL: biopsy may be considered within a benign liver tumour multidisciplinary team to exclude malignancy. ACG 2024: obtaining a biopsy should be reserved for cases in which imaging is inconclusive (strong recommendation, low quality of evidence). The Italian multisociety guideline goes further and recommends biopsy wherever the subtype is not classifiable on imaging, specifically to identify beta-catenin exon 3 and sonic hedgehog adenomas, quoting major complications of image-guided liver biopsy at 0.1-4.6% and of adenoma biopsy specifically at no mortality, 2% major and 10% minor — but it grades that recommendation very low quality (D), conditional. The local hepatic adenoma protocol says the biopsy should target the dominant or most suspicious lesion. In 47 resected adenomas with both preoperative MRI and biopsy, biopsy subtyped correctly in 76.6% (95% CI 61-88) on morphology alone and 81.6% (65-93) where immunohistochemistry was available in 38 of 47, against 85.1% (71-94) for the senior blinded MRI reader and 76.6% (61-88) for the junior one, interobserver kappa 0.85 (0.69-0.97); the two agreed in 74.5% of cases and where they agreed the likelihood ratio for the subtype exceeded 20. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not biopsy reflexively. EASL states plainly that there is no justification for recommending histopathology or molecular subtyping of adenoma as routine clinical practice, and do not biopsy a lesion you have already decided to resect — the resection specimen answers more questions than the needle and a negative needle will not stop the operation. The immunophenotypical markers add most in steatotic lesions and least where tissue is scant. Evidence & sources Two findings in that series matter more than its headline. First, accuracy did not deteriorate in small lesions: for adenomas under 5 cm against those over 5 cm, imaging was correct in 80% versus 87.5% (P=0.45), routine biopsy 66.7% versus 81.3% (P=0.27) and biopsy with immunohistochemistry 75% versus 84.6% (P=0.48), and tumour size did not differ between correctly and incorrectly classified lesions (6.3 versus 6.8 cm, P=0.71) — which removes the main technical objection to subtype-based management of small lesions, and is reported in one sentence that the paper's own conclusion does not carry. Second, only three lesions in the whole series showed beta-catenin activation and none was analysed as a separate category, so the study does not establish that the subtype which should override size can be detected at all; 72% of its lesions were telangiectatic or inflammatory, far above the usual third, which inflates every accuracy figure. Both biopsy and MRI are also reference-standard-limited: truth was the resection specimen, so only lesions someone had decided to resect could enter. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Where tissue exists, ask for the four-antibody panel, and for the CTNNB1 exon and codon when beta-catenin activation is in question.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Where tissue exists, ask for the four-antibody panel, and for the CTNNB1 exon and codon when beta-catenin activation is in question. Indications Preferred when LFABP, glutamine synthetase, beta-catenin and SAA or CRP. In the 533-adenoma molecular series this panel reproduced the major molecular subtypes with sensitivity and specificity of 0.85 to 0.93 depending on the marker. Glutamine synthetase pattern carries real information: strong homogeneous staining goes with the highly activating exon 3 mutants, diffuse heterogeneous staining with a glutamine-synthetase-positive and CD34-negative rim with S45, and faint patchy staining with no nuclear beta-catenin with exon 7/8 alterations, which are not associated with increased malignant risk. The review of the WHO 6th-edition classification sets out the same mapping, and adds that every inflammatory adenoma should be stained for glutamine synthetase because about one in ten carries an added CTNNB1 mutation that no other feature reveals. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat immunohistochemistry as equivalent to sequencing. In the Dutch nationwide series of 66 male adenomas, next-generation sequencing identified 4 beta-catenin-mutated adenomas that neither immunohistochemistry nor expert re-review had found. Across the genotype-phenotype series, only 27% of the 33 beta-catenin-mutated adenomas tested showed the strong homogeneous pattern that the algorithms key on, and S45-mutated adenomas give an intense but heterogeneous pattern that the authors describe as difficult to recognise — their conclusion was that the immunohistochemical criteria must be revised or mutation screening performed. Nuclear beta-catenin has good specificity and insufficient sensitivity, because very few nuclei may stain. Evidence & sources The exon and codon matter downstream: the local transplant protocol's molecular route turns on them, and S45 exon 3 is a genuinely contested category — see the limited-evidence section and the transplant assessment. The classification itself began as three genotype-phenotype groups in 96 lesions, in which carcinoma or a borderline lesion was present in 46% of beta-catenin-mutated tumours and in none of the inflammatory ones (P=0.004); the eight-subgroup version and the immunohistochemical panel are refinements of that original observation. lead: Do not ablate or embolise a small indeterminate lesion before you know what it is.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not ablate or embolise a small indeterminate lesion before you know what it is. Why Why Biopsy it instead, which is EASL's explicit instruction: for smaller indeterminate lesions, ablation without confirmation of diagnosis is not recommended, and biopsy should be considered. Additional cautions Additional cautions Ablation destroys the specimen, and the specimen is how malignant transformation is actually detected in this disease. A small lesion treated without a diagnosis leaves you with neither a diagnosis nor a follow-up rule. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not run an adenoma patient through imaging criteria that were not built for them.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not run an adenoma patient through imaging criteria that were not built for them. Why Why Use the adenoma phenotype described above, and state in the report which subtype criteria were applied and which were not assessable. Additional cautions Additional cautions LI-RADS and OPTN Class 5 classification are defined for patients at risk for hepatocellular carcinoma. Applying them to a young woman with a normal liver generates a category that means nothing and, worse, generates a transplant-pathway assumption that the local protocol specifically corrects.
