lead: Stop oestrogen and androgen exposure, counsel on contraception and pregnancy, and put the advice in writing.
text: Standard Evidence C Stop oestrogen and androgen exposure, counsel on contraception and pregnancy, and put the advice in writing. Indications Preferred when Every patient at diagnosis. EASL: upon adenoma diagnosis, lifestyle changes such as discontinuation of oral contraceptives as well as weight loss should be advised (evidence level II-2, grade of recommendation 1). ACG 2024 is firmer in wording and weaker in evidence: oral contraceptives, hormone-containing intrauterine devices and anabolic steroids are to be avoided (strong recommendation, low quality of evidence). The Italian multisociety guideline is the only one that grades discontinuing oral contraceptives any higher than the rest of its adenoma recommendations — low quality (C) but strength 1, strong — while conceding that no randomised trial compares continuation with discontinuation and that the evidence is small case series. The exposure association is consistent, and recent hormone use within 6 months was independently associated with rupture in the 124-patient multicentre series (odds ratio 4.46, 95% CI 1.49-13.33), an effect of the same order as the size effect in the same model. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not present withdrawal as sufficient, and do not promise it will be quick. In the three-centre US cohort of 187 to 193 patients, 69% showed regression after oral contraceptive cessation, but 47% of that cohort still had a lesion of 5 cm or more and haemorrhage occurred in 10 of 193 (5%) at a median lesion size of 8.7 cm. In the Dutch timing cohort, regression below 5 cm had occurred in only 8.5-15.3% of patients at 26 weeks. Hormone withdrawal also has no demonstrated effect on malignant transformation. Evidence & sources Androgen exposure is not only prescribed. Non-prescribed anabolic steroid use in a man presenting with an adenoma should be asked about directly and recorded, because it clusters with the beta-catenin exon 3 subtype. Ask about alcohol in the same breath and record the quantity: in the 261-patient French multicentre bleeding cohort regular alcohol consumption carried an odds ratio of 9.16 (95% CI 2.47-34.01) for haemorrhage, nine times the effect of a centimetre of diameter, and in the 533-adenoma series alcohol was an independent predictor of malignant transformation at 4.85. Both are modifiable; neither has been pursued as an alternative to resection in any published series. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Treat the weight, and treat it as a tumour intervention rather than as general advice.
text: Standard Evidence D Treat the weight, and treat it as a tumour intervention rather than as general advice. Indications Preferred when Every overweight or obese patient, and every patient with an inflammatory-subtype adenoma. EASL recommends control of body weight alongside stopping oral contraceptives, and reports regression of tumour burden in up to a third of patients complying with lifestyle change, with progression associated with obesity. In the three-centre US cohort, 47% of patients had a lesion of 5 cm or more and 54 of them had adenomatosis, in a population in which metabolic disease was the dominant association. In the Taiwanese series of 45 adenomas, where only 3 women had ever taken oral contraceptives and 58% of patients were male, 75% of the adenomas were of the inflammatory subtype — so in a population without hormone exposure the metabolic driver is what is left. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not promise regression, and do not count it as a treatment effect. The regression figures are uncontrolled before-and-after observations in cohorts where hormone withdrawal happened at the same time, so the weight effect cannot be isolated from the hormone effect — and the untreated comparator is not zero: 58.5% of adenomas over 5 cm fell below 5 cm with no intervention at all, at a median of 104 weeks. Any claimed effect of weight loss has to beat that, and none of the published series is designed to. Evidence & sources Name an owner for the weight plan — bariatric medicine, endocrinology or primary care — the same way you would name an owner for a drain. An unassigned weight plan is the commonest reason a 6-month scan shows nothing has changed. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: After risk-factor modification: assess growth and regression. In women with lesions ≥5 cm, individualize reassessment or intervention over 6–12 months; act earlier for concerning features.
text: Standard Evidence D After risk-factor modification: assess growth and regression. In women with lesions ≥5 cm, individualize reassessment or intervention over 6–12 months; act earlier for concerning features. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Reimage after risk-factor modification and assess the trajectory. In women with lesions ≥5 cm, individualize reassessment and intervention over 6–12 months unless bleeding, concerning growth or suspected malignancy requires earlier action. Indications Preferred when EASL recommends six months of observation after lifestyle change in women, then resection for lesions ≥5 cm or continuing to grow. ACG 2024 allows 6–12 months for an appropriate woman with a lesion ≥5 cm before deciding on treatment; this timing and size statement is an ungraded key concept. Individualize continued observation of a shrinking, otherwise low-risk lesion. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat a lesion still over 5 cm at 6 months as a failed trial. In 194 patients with adenomas larger than 5 cm followed with serial imaging, regression to 5 cm or less had occurred in only 8.5-15.3% at 26 weeks — the exact point at which EASL and ACG advise resection — rising to 23.7-27.1% at 52 weeks, with 69 of 118 (58.5%) regressing below 5 cm eventually at a median of 104 weeks (95% CI 80-128). Time to regression was strongly size-dependent: a median of 63 weeks for lesions under 7 cm, 109 weeks for 7-10 cm and 208 weeks for those over 10 cm (P<0.001). No complication occurred anywhere in that follow-up. A decision point at six months therefore identifies roughly one in six to one in ten of the lesions that will eventually fall below the line, which means the timing of the rule — not only the value of the threshold — drives resections that a longer wait would have avoided. Evidence & sources Read against that, the counter-evidence is thin. The single-institution surgical series that reports no significant regression at six months does not define significant regression and did not look beyond six months, in a literature whose median time to regression is about two years — so the observation arm was never given a fair test before the surgical policy was validated against it. The Dutch cohort has its own problems: 47 of 241 patients were excluded for under six months of follow-up, which removes precisely the patients in whom the guideline rule was applied, and regression is defined as crossing the 5 cm line, so a lesion falling from 12 cm to 6 cm counts as a non-responder. EASL's growth trigger is a diameter increase of 20% or more, taken from RECIST 1.1, which was built for response assessment in solid malignancy and has never been validated in a benign liver lesion; on a 5 cm lesion it is 1 cm, small enough that the measurement convention in the radiology report decides whether the trigger fires. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Extend observation past 12 months in a woman with a typical, non-beta-catenin adenoma that is shrinking.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Extend observation past 12 months in a woman with a typical, non-beta-catenin adenoma that is shrinking. Indications Preferred when The patient whose lesion is falling, whose risk factors are still being modified, and for whom the operation would be major. This is the conclusion the 194-patient cohort's own authors drew: the cut-off in women with typical, non-beta-catenin-activated adenoma could be prolonged to 12 months irrespective of baseline diameter. A PROSPERO-registered meta-analysis of 7 retrospective studies and 699 surveilled patients across Europe and the United States found 88.5% (95% CI 74.9-95.2) stable or regressed, with pooled symptomatic bleeding of 0.5% (95% CI 0.1-3.5) and pooled malignant transformation of 0.8% (95% CI 0.4-1.9) over median follow-up ranging from 2 to 5.8 years. Those two figures are one to two orders of magnitude below the historical references the 5 cm rule was built on — spontaneous bleeding of 20-40% and transformation of 4-10% — and the authors explain the gap: the founding cohorts were small surgical series of 6 to 30 cm lesions in which almost nothing was an incidental finding, and they did not separate histological from symptomatic bleeding. A contemporary 164-patient cohort managed 76.2% of its patients by surveillance and reports rupture in 1.8%, regression in 18.4% and no malignant transformation at all among those watched. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not read 88.5% and 0.5% as the risk of watching any adenoma. In five of the seven pooled studies, lesions were pulled out of the surveillance group by intervention whenever they grew or looked worrying, so these are the outcomes of the lesions that were allowed to remain under observation and not of all adenomas over 5 cm — informative censoring that no random-effects model corrects. Six of the seven carried a moderate to serious risk of bias, their definitions of stability differed (RECIST in four, a 1 cm threshold, regression below 5 cm, or unspecified in the rest), and removing one outlying study moved pooled progression from 11.5% to 18.1%. The confidence interval for symptomatic bleeding runs from 0.1% to 3.5%, a thirty-five-fold range, so the headline figure is far more precise-sounding than the data support; the meta-analysis also overlaps substantially with the individual cohorts cited elsewhere on this page and is not independent of them. The 164-patient cohort has the same problem in a simpler form: zero transformation in a surveillance group chosen by clinicians who judged those lesions low-risk is the expected result of successful selection. Do not extend any of it to a man, a beta-catenin-activated or unclassified lesion, an exophytic lesion, or one that is growing. Evidence & sources EASL's own later intervals, for the lesion that stabilises: stable after 12 months, annual imaging is acceptable; stable or reducing after 5 years, biannual imaging can be proposed; ultrasound is cost-effective and may be preferred for a well-seen lesion. EASL also says there is no robust data on the timeline that defines stable disease. A 2026 narrative review of nonoperative management reaches the same direction of travel — that recent data support extending non-operative management even to lesions over 5 cm, because they can respond to lifestyle intervention — but it is a review of the same retrospective cohorts and adds no new comparative data. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Where the subtype is known and low risk, let it lengthen the interval rather than shorten the operating list.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Where the subtype is known and low risk, let it lengthen the interval rather than shorten the operating list. Indications Preferred when A confidently subtyped HNF1A-inactivated adenoma under 5 cm in a woman. EASL notes that subtyping may be used in some specialist centres to support longer intervals between imaging follow-up, and the molecular series found no malignant transformation in any HNF1A-inactivated adenoma under 5 cm in a woman (0 of 47). The usual technical objection — that subtyping is unreliable in small lesions — is not supported: in the series that measured it, subtype accuracy was 80% below 5 cm against 87.5% above (P=0.45) for imaging and 75% against 84.6% (P=0.48) for biopsy with immunohistochemistry, and lesion size did not differ between correctly and incorrectly classified lesions. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let a reassuring imaging phenotype cancel risk from sex, size, growth or bleeding. Imaging subtype alone is not equivalent to a confirmed molecular diagnosis. Proven beta-catenin activation, particularly a high-risk exon 3 alteration, warrants specialist assessment for resection irrespective of size under EASL/ACG guidance; document the exon/codon and diagnostic certainty. Evidence & sources This asymmetry — subtype may reassure but may not alone commit — is a local safety convention, not a guideline position. It is in the limited-evidence section for that reason. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not accept lifestyle advice as the whole plan in a man, in a proven beta-catenin-activated adenoma, or in a lesion that is growing.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not accept lifestyle advice as the whole plan in a man, in a proven beta-catenin-activated adenoma, or in a lesion that is growing. Why Why Those three go to the resection assessment. EASL recommends resection irrespective of size in men and in any instance of proven beta-catenin mutation (evidence level II-3, grade of recommendation 2). Additional cautions Additional cautions Hormone withdrawal has no demonstrated effect on malignant transformation, and in men the associated condition driving transformation since 2000 has been the metabolic syndrome rather than hormone exposure — so there may be no hormone to withdraw. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not operate on a large adenoma at 6 months without telling the patient what waiting another six months would probably have done.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not operate on a large adenoma at 6 months without telling the patient what waiting another six months would probably have done. Why Why Document the conversation: only 8.5-15.3% of adenomas over 5 cm had fallen below 5 cm at 26 weeks against 58.5% eventually at a median 104 weeks, no complication occurred during that follow-up, and the counter-argument is a surgical series' selection bias rather than a measured hazard of waiting. Additional cautions Additional cautions This is where practice diverges most from the written guideline. In a European expert survey, 48 of 61 analysable respondents (79%) advise against routine resection of a hepatocellular adenoma larger than 5 cm after lifestyle change — a direct majority rejection of the EASL recommendation — and only 31 of 61 (51%) reported having an EASL-compliant benign-liver-tumour multidisciplinary team. Read it with its limits: 61 of 294 invited clinicians responded (21%), the respondents are self-selected specialists at referral centres, and the survey records stated advice rather than observed practice — the same group's own national audit found 20% of resections for presumed adenoma were performed on lesions under 50 mm. Do not pretend the question is closed in either direction. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Expert survey: 79% (48 of 61) advise against routine resection of HCA >5 cm after lifestyle change; 51% (31 of 61) have an EASL-compliant MDT 61 of 294 responded (21%); self-selected referral-centre specialists; stated advice only

lead: Resect, irrespective of size, and treat the lesion as possibly already malignant rather than as a benign tumour with a future risk.
text: Standard Evidence C Resect, irrespective of size, and treat the lesion as possibly already malignant rather than as a benign tumour with a future risk. Indications Preferred when Every male adenoma. EASL: resection or curative treatment is recommended for all adenomas diagnosed in men because of a significantly higher incidence of malignant transformation, irrespective of size (evidence level II-3, grade of recommendation 2); the Italian multisociety guideline says the same at very low quality of evidence (D), conditional. In the 218-patient tertiary series malignant transformation occurred in 4% of women and 47% of men; beta-catenin activation was present in 16 of the 25 transformed adenomas (64%). In the 122-patient, 365-adenoma French surgical series malignant transformation was about ten-fold more frequent in men than in women. In the 533-adenoma molecular series male sex was the second strongest independent predictor of transformation at an odds ratio of 18.9 (95% CI 8.5-44.2), behind only TERT promoter mutation. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not be reassured by a small adenoma in a man, and do not overstate what the evidence for the rule is. The transformed adenomas in the 218-patient series had a median diameter of 10 cm and only 3 of 25 were 5 cm or smaller — and all three of those arose in a liver with fibrosis or iron overload, which argues for the background liver rather than for size. In the 122-patient series the one malignancy under 5 cm was in a man taking steroids, so that paper's own data are consistent with size being irrelevant once sex and androgen exposure are accounted for. Sex and size are therefore not independent in any of the published data, and the irrespective of size rule rests on the sex effect rather than on any observed outcome in small male lesions. Evidence & sources Metabolic syndrome, not hormone exposure, has been the commonest associated condition in men with malignant transformation since 2000, and the number of such men has risen markedly over that period. Androgen exposure concentrated in beta-catenin exon 3 adenomas with or without inflammation (P<0.0001) in the 411-patient molecular series. The male series are small and selected: the 218-patient cohort is a tertiary surgical series in which men with large or suspicious lesions are preferentially referred and operated, so 47% is close to a maximum rather than a population risk, and the finding that half of presumed male adenomas are not adenomas on expert review means part of that 47% may be misclassification of carcinoma as transformed adenoma. The rule may well be right; the number behind it is not a risk estimate. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Send every male adenoma for expert liver pathology review, with sequencing, before you accept the diagnosis.
text: Standard Evidence C Send every male adenoma for expert liver pathology review, with sequencing, before you accept the diagnosis. Indications Preferred when Every male case, including those referred with an outside diagnosis. In the Dutch nationwide series of 66 men from 26 centres, the diagnosis changed after expert revision plus next-generation sequencing in 33 of 66 (50%): the final diagnoses were 20 adenoma, 26 lesion of uncertain malignant potential and 20 hepatocellular carcinoma. Tumour-related mortality tracked the revised diagnosis — 1 of 18 (5.6%) for adenoma, 5 of 14 (35.7%) for uncertain malignant potential and 4 of 9 (44.4%) for carcinoma (P=0.031). The full malignancy panel of glutamine synthetase, glypican-3 and HSP70 had been performed primarily in only 8 of 66 cases (12%), rising to 55 of 66 (83%) after revision. The Dutch resection audit found the same thing prospectively from the other end: male sex independently predicted a change of diagnosis after resection (adjusted odds ratio 3.7), and 78% of male patients resected for a presumed adenoma had their diagnosis changed. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not rely on immunohistochemistry alone: sequencing in that series found 4 beta-catenin-mutated adenomas that neither immunohistochemistry nor expert re-review had identified. The authors' own conclusion was that sequencing may be more important for subtyping than current guidelines indicate. Evidence & sources That 50% reclassification figure comes from a registry-based pathology review with no comparator, selected on the availability of tissue, and is as much a statement about the difficulty of the distinction as about outside laboratories. Note also that the mortality denominators (18, 14 and 9) do not match the final diagnostic groups (20, 26 and 20), so a substantial fraction of patients lacked follow-up and the direction of that loss is not stated; and that only 12% had the standard malignancy panel done originally, which means the pre-revision cohort is not a fair comparator for the post-revision one. The distinction being made — adenoma against well-differentiated carcinoma in a non-cirrhotic liver — is one of the hardest in liver pathology. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
