Resection audit: male sex independently predicted a changed diagnosis after resection (aOR 3.7); 78% of men resected for presumed adenoma reclassified None

lead: ResectionEXPERTISE EASL, ACG 2024 and the Italian 2022 guideline all say resect a male adenoma — the Italian one at very low quality of evidence (D), conditional. The Brazilian surgical series adopted the same rule after using a 4 cm threshold and then a 5 cm threshold in earlier eras, which is itself worth noticing: one institution ran three different cut-offs over one study period, each adopted without new local data, and reported comparable outcomes under all three.
text: Resection Evidence C EXPERTISE EASL, ACG 2024 and the Italian 2022 guideline all say resect a male adenoma — the Italian one at very low quality of evidence (D), conditional. The Brazilian surgical series adopted the same rule after using a 4 cm threshold and then a 5 cm threshold in earlier eras, which is itself worth noticing: one institution ran three different cut-offs over one study period, each adopted without new local data, and reported comparable outcomes under all three. Indications Preferred when Any male patient fit for the operation. It is the only option that produces a specimen, which is how transformation in men is actually detected. In the 134-patient Brazilian series, 124 resections gave 8.1% morbidity and no mortality; malignant transformation was found in 4 of 124 (3.2%), all beta-catenin-activated and all larger than 5 cm. Parenchyma-sparing and laparoscopic approaches should be the default in a young patient with benign disease. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not accept a major hepatectomy without asking whether a parenchyma-sparing resection reaches the same lesion. These are young patients and the indication is benign in most of them. And do not quote the 8.1% morbidity as reassurance without saying that it is reported with no Clavien-Dindo distribution, so the clinical weight of those complications is unknown. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Observation with a sequenced, confidently low-risk subtype Not a guideline position. EASL, ACG and the Italian guideline all recommend resection in men irrespective of size.
text: Observation with a sequenced, confidently low-risk subtype Evidence D Not a guideline position. EASL, ACG and the Italian guideline all recommend resection in men irrespective of size. Indications Preferred when A man with a small, hepatobiliary-contrast-confirmed, sequenced HNF1A-inactivated adenoma with no CTNNB1 alteration, who is a poor operative candidate and accepts close surveillance with a documented reason. There is no cohort that supports this. The full-text read of the male series found no followed, biopsy-only male cohort to cite: what exists is 4 malignant transformations in 27 male adenomas (14.8%), occurring in beta-catenin-inflammatory and unclassified lesions, with androgen receptor staining positive in half of cases and not associated with transformation. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Half of presumed male adenomas are reclassified on expert review, 78% of male resections in the national audit had their diagnosis changed, and transformation in the male pathology series occurred in unclassified as well as beta-catenin lesions — so a subtype-only reassurance in a man is reassurance about a label that is frequently wrong, assigned by a method that misses mutations sequencing finds. Do not offer this as an equivalent option, and do not offer it at all without sequencing and a board decision. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: National audit: diagnosis changed after resection in 78% of male resections

lead: Thermal ablationEXPERTISE No male-specific data exist. EASL positions ablation for smaller lesions as an alternative to resection and as the treatment of choice only in poor surgical candidates.
text: Thermal ablation Evidence D EXPERTISE No male-specific data exist. EASL positions ablation for smaller lesions as an alternative to resection and as the treatment of choice only in poor surgical candidates. Indications Preferred when A small, accessible lesion in a prohibitive operative candidate in whom tissue has already established the subtype and excluded atypia. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Ablation destroys the specimen, and the specimen is how malignant transformation in men is found. Do not ablate a male adenoma you have not biopsied, and record that the trade-off was explained. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Where an androgen exposure can be stopped, stop it — but do not wait on it before operating.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Where an androgen exposure can be stopped, stop it — but do not wait on it before operating. Indications Preferred when Anabolic steroid use for sport or bodybuilding, androgen therapy for aplastic anaemia or paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, and endogenous androgen excess. EASL links the rising male incidence to these exposures, and androgen exposure clusters with the beta-catenin exon 3 subtype. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid There is no regression series for androgen withdrawal comparable to the oral-contraceptive data, and the 6-month observation window EASL grants to women is explicitly not extended to men. Stopping the androgen is harm reduction, not treatment. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not use a normal alpha-fetoprotein to exclude carcinoma in a male adenoma.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not use a normal alpha-fetoprotein to exclude carcinoma in a male adenoma. Why Why Measure it where transformation is a concern, record it, and treat an elevated value as informative in one direction only. The ACMG glycogen storage disease guideline states the same conclusion for a different population: alpha-fetoprotein and carcinoembryonic antigen do not predict malignant transformation and cannot be used for surveillance. Additional cautions Additional cautions The local hepatic adenoma protocol states the rule explicitly: alpha-fetoprotein does not exclude carcinoma when normal. In the male series the discriminating test was expert pathology plus sequencing, not a serum marker. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not treat an androgen-exposed adenoma as though it were an oestrogen-exposed one.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not treat an androgen-exposed adenoma as though it were an oestrogen-exposed one. Why Why Record the exposure, expect the beta-catenin exon 3 subtype, and send for sequencing. Additional cautions Additional cautions The 6-month lifestyle-modification window, the 5 cm threshold and the expectation of regression all come from cohorts that were 85 to 99% female. None of them has been tested in androgen-driven disease, and the one series that reported both sexes found malignant transformation in 47% of men against 4% of women. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Assess resection for persistent size ≥5 cm or growth after risk-factor modification; account for subtype, sex, symptoms, bleeding and suspected malignancy.
text: Standard Evidence D Assess resection for persistent size ≥5 cm or growth after risk-factor modification; account for subtype, sex, symptoms, bleeding and suspected malignancy. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Assess resection for a persistently ≥5 cm or growing adenoma after appropriate risk-factor modification; account for subtype, sex, symptoms, bleeding and suspicion of malignancy. Indications Preferred when EASL: adenomas persistently greater than 5 cm, or increasing in size by 20% or more of diameter as per RECIST, should be considered for resection or curative treatment irrespective of their molecular or histological subtype, because of the risk of haemorrhage; in women resection is indicated for nodules equal to or greater than 5 cm and those continuing to grow (evidence level II-3, grade of recommendation 2). ACG 2024 agrees that lesions of 5 cm or more warrant intervention because of rupture and malignancy risk (conditional recommendation, low quality of evidence). The recommendation stands on this page. What has changed is how it should be described. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not present the number as derived, because it is not, and every document that states it says so in its own grading. EASL calls it the accepted clinically relevant size cut off — accepted, not derived — and supports its central factual premise, that in nearly all cases of spontaneous rupture or haemorrhage the lesion is at least 5 cm, with a single citation; it grades the recommendation at evidence level II-3, non-randomised observational evidence, with recommendation strength 2, its weaker category. The Italian multisociety guideline is the only adenoma guideline built on a formal GRADE Evidence-to-Decision framework with PICO questions, QUADAS-2 and ROBINS-I appraisal and formal voting, and it grades every size-based adenoma recommendation — the 5 cm resection trigger, the resect-all-men rule, the 6-month decision point and the whole surveillance schedule — as very low quality of evidence (D) with strength of recommendation 2, conditional. Where the threshold has been tested directly it has not held: in 261 patients with full molecular subtyping, diameter was modelled continuously and acted as an independent risk factor for bleeding at an odds ratio of only 1.02 per millimetre (95% CI 1.01-1.03, P<0.001), with the authors stating that they did not identify a threshold size; the one study that set out to derive a bleeding cut-point derived 35 mm, not 50 mm; and the series usually cited for the rule fitted its own cut-point at 7 cm and recommended resecting above 4 cm. Do not apply the threshold before the risk-factor trial has run for long enough to mean anything, and do not apply it to a 5.2 cm lesion that has fallen from 8 cm without saying so to the patient. Evidence & sources Graded D here rather than C, and the downgrade is the point: this is a consensus threshold that nobody derived, so it cannot be graded from the design of the cohorts that happen to be consistent with it. Four fifths of responding European experts decline to follow it, and one institution in the published literature ran 4 cm, then 5 cm, then a subtype-and-sex rule across a single study period with comparable outcomes under all three. Keeping the recommendation while grading it D is deliberate: the alternative on offer — subtype-directed management — requires tissue and sequencing that EASL declines to recommend routinely, so a programme cannot simply swap one rule for the other. What it can do is stop describing 5 cm as a risk threshold. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: State where the 5 cm number comes from, and record the position and vascularity of the lesion alongside its diameter.
text: Standard Evidence C State where the 5 cm number comes from, and record the position and vascularity of the lesion alongside its diameter. Indications Preferred when Where the number comes from, said plainly. Three surgical datasets, none of them a test of a threshold. A systematic review of 28 articles and 1,176 patients reported haemorrhage in 315 of 1,160 patients (27.2%) but in only 118 of 748 lesions (15.8%), rupture in 114 of 651 (17.5%), and haemorrhage as the first symptom in 126 of 184 bleeding cases (68.5%); 1,073 of the 1,176 pooled patients (91.2%) had been resected, and the authors explicitly label their figures maximum risks for that reason. A 5-centre series of 124 patients found rupture in 31 (25%) and fitted its size dichotomy at 7 cm, not 5 cm — odds ratio 7.78 (95% CI 2.22-26.32) — alongside recent hormone use at 4.46 (1.49-13.33); malignancy was present in 5 patients (4%) and the smallest malignant adenoma measured 8 cm; the authors then recommended resecting adenomas larger than 4 cm, so three different numbers appear in one paper and the one that entered the guidelines has the least statistical support. A pooled review of 1,635 adenomas gave malignant transformation in 68 (4.2%) overall, 50 of 1,617 (3.1%) in series and 4.5% of the 1,462 resected, with only 3 of the 68 transformations (4.4%) in a tumour under 5 cm and the smallest transformed adenoma in the literature measuring 4 cm. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Read each of those backwards before using it. Every one is a surgical series, so the denominators are patients selected for operation. The per-patient figure (27.2%) and the per-lesion figure (15.8%) differ by nearly twofold, which means a rule derived from per-lesion data and applied per patient is not the same rule — and most citations do not say which they mean. Two thirds of bleeds were the presenting event, so most haemorrhage is unpreventable by surveillance at any threshold. Six of the 13 articles in the systematic review that reported lesion size reported haemorrhage below 5 cm, and the smallest bled lesion in that literature measured 1 cm. The '4.4% below 5 cm' statistic is a proportion of the numerator, not a risk: it says nothing about the probability that a sub-5 cm adenoma transforms, and it is partly a function of how few sub-5 cm adenomas were in the pooled denominator at all, since 89% of the pooled lesions were resected and small lesions generally are not. In the one cohort assembled to derive a bleeding threshold, 7 of 129 adenomas below 35 mm bled (5.4%) against 35 of 66 above it (53%, P<0.001) — but that institution's own protocol used 5 cm to decide which lesions were resected and therefore sectioned, no beta-catenin-activated adenoma was identified in the whole 195-lesion series and 48% were unclassifiable, so it cannot exclude subtype as the real driver of its apparent size effect. In the most favourable modern dataset, haemorrhage occurred in 13% of patients with a lesion of 5 cm or more against 0% below — but on 10 events at a median bleeding size of 8.7 cm, and a zero rate in roughly a hundred patients has an upper 95% bound of about 3%, so the data are compatible with a modest rather than an absent risk below 5 cm and support a cut-point well above 5 cm as readily as 5 cm itself. Evidence & sources The direct tests of the threshold, in one place. In 533 adenomas the 50 mm cut-off separated histological haemorrhage (65% versus 40%, P<0.0001) but did not separate symptomatic bleeding (P=0.29) — and symptomatic bleeding is the outcome the operation is meant to prevent; the malignancy difference did not reach significance either (13.1% versus 7.6%, P=0.053). In 261 patients with full subtyping, size acted continuously at an odds ratio of 1.02 per millimetre (1.01-1.03), roughly a 1.2-fold increase in odds per centimetre, and no threshold could be identified, while sonic hedgehog subtype carried 21.02 (5.05-87.52), regular alcohol 9.16 (2.47-34.01) and beta-catenin exon 7/8 6.47 (1.78-23.55); body-mass index was not associated (P=0.71), and bleeding occurred below 5 cm. The apparently clean size gradient in the 122-patient, 365-adenoma French series — microscopic haemorrhage 0.9%, 19% and 68% and macroscopic 0%, 5% and 24% across the under-2 cm, 2-5 cm and over-5 cm strata — is largely an artefact of the denominator: that series was run under a policy of systematic resection, the sub-2 cm stratum consists almost entirely of incidental microadenomas found inside specimens removed for a different and larger lesion, and the over-5 cm stratum consists of the lesions that prompted the operation, so the two strata are not comparable populations. Counting 365 lesions in 122 patients inflates the small-lesion denominator mechanically, and microscopic haemorrhage found only because the specimen was removed and sectioned is an endpoint that cannot occur in a lesion left in situ. The 124-patient series' own authors recommended operating on asymptomatic adenomas approaching 4 cm; no guideline adopted it. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: ResectionEXPERTISE EASL: the recommended first-line therapy is resection of larger (over 5 cm) or growing lesions, aiming to remove the whole tumour and all risk of malignant transformation.
text: Resection Evidence C EXPERTISE EASL: the recommended first-line therapy is resection of larger (over 5 cm) or growing lesions, aiming to remove the whole tumour and all risk of malignant transformation. Indications Preferred when Unilobar or peripherally placed disease in a fit patient, and any lesion where malignant transformation is a live question — resection is the only option that yields a specimen. In a 134-patient single-centre series, 124 resections gave 8.1% morbidity and no mortality, with malignant transformation found in 4 (3.2%), all beta-catenin-activated and all larger than 5 cm. Parenchyma-sparing and laparoscopic approaches should be the default in a young patient with benign disease; the Italian multisociety guideline grades laparoscopic over open resection at low quality of evidence (C), conditional, on the strength of a Dutch nationwide comparison of 415 resections for benign tumours (59% of them adenoma) in which, after propensity matching, laparoscopy gave a shorter stay (median 4 against 6 days) and lower 30-day overall morbidity (12.0% against 22.4%) but no significant difference in major morbidity (4.8% against 6.4%, p = 0.78). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not accept a major hepatectomy for a lesion that is still shrinking on risk-factor modification, and do not resect a small indeterminate lesion when a biopsy would answer the question first. A fifth of the resections in the Dutch nationwide audit were performed on lesions under 50 mm, 70% of those had their diagnosis changed afterwards and 21% proved to be focal nodular hyperplasia — so the cost of operating early is measurable, and it is measured in operations on lesions that needed nothing. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Dutch nationwide audit: a fifth of resections were on lesions <50 mm; of those, 70% had the diagnosis changed afterwards and 21% proved FNH

lead: Transarterial embolisation EASL positions embolisation for larger lesions as an alternative to resection, but as the treatment of choice only in poor surgical candidates.
text: Transarterial embolisation Evidence C EASL positions embolisation for larger lesions as an alternative to resection, but as the treatment of choice only in poor surgical candidates. Indications Preferred when A large, central or bilobar lesion for which the resection would be major, and the patient who wants to avoid an operation and accepts imaging follow-up afterwards. In the 59-patient cohort the median diameter fell from 76 mm to 48 mm by 5.5 months (P<0.001) and to 45 mm at 27.4 months. In a systematic review covering a pooled literature of 851 patients, 151 of whom had been embolised, surgery was avoided in 41 of 49 electively embolised patients (84%) and in 68 of 151 overall (45%), over a pooled median follow-up of 31 months. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Discuss the mixed elective/emergency cohort explicitly: 6/59 (10%) had major complications; the supplement records 3/36 nonbleeding elective cases and 3/23 bleeding cases. One patient died three months after emergency TAE for haemorrhagic shock, following aspiration pneumonia, with attribution uncertain. Twenty of 59 (34%) later underwent surgery for several indications. Symptoms were reported in 58% before versus 37% within three months (P=.134); durable symptom benefit remains uncertain. Lack of a whole-lesion specimen limits pathological assessment, but some patients had biopsy or previous resection. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Systematic review: surgery avoided in 41 of 49 electively embolised (84%) and 68 of 151 overall (45%); pooled median follow-up 31 mo Elective complications not reported separately; 'surgery avoided' is a process endpoint

lead: Thermal ablationEXPERTISE EASL positions ablation for smaller lesions as an alternative to resection and as the treatment of choice only in poor surgical candidates, and explicitly does not recommend ablation of a smaller indeterminate lesion without a confirmed diagnosis.
text: Thermal ablation Evidence D EXPERTISE EASL positions ablation for smaller lesions as an alternative to resection and as the treatment of choice only in poor surgical candidates, and explicitly does not recommend ablation of a smaller indeterminate lesion without a confirmed diagnosis. Indications Preferred when A small number of small, accessible lesions with the diagnosis already established, particularly where the alternative is a major resection. A stereotactic multiprobe series of 14 patients and 38 adenomas achieved technical efficacy in 97.4% with no major complications across 18 sessions, over a median follow-up of 49.6 months, with disease-free survival of 100% at the first time point and 85.8% thereafter. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Conventional single-probe results are far weaker: in 18 patients and 45 adenomas, primary technical efficacy was achieved in only 26 of 45 (57.8%), and it depended entirely on approach — 79% for open ablation against 31% percutaneously (P=0.013), so the minimally invasive route, the only one that offers an advantage over surgery, failed two times in three. Two major complications occurred in those 18 patients. The stereotactic series is 14 patients at a single specialised centre whose senior author consults for the manufacturer of the navigation platform the technique depends on; a zero complication count in 18 sessions has an upper 95% bound of around 15%, and both series report per-lesion efficacy in patients with multiple nodules, which inflates the denominator. Neither provides tissue, so neither the diagnosis nor the exclusion of a malignant focus is established, and no study compares ablation with resection in this disease. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Continued surveillance Not EASL's position for a lesion persistently over 5 cm, but the position the newer surveillance data support in a selected woman — and the position four fifths of responding European experts say they already take.
text: Continued surveillance Evidence C Not EASL's position for a lesion persistently over 5 cm, but the position the newer surveillance data support in a selected woman — and the position four fifths of responding European experts say they already take. Indications Preferred when A woman with a typical, non-beta-catenin, hepatobiliary-contrast-confirmed adenoma that is falling, where the operation would be major and the risk factors are still being addressed. Only 8.5-15.3% of adenomas over 5 cm have fallen below 5 cm at 26 weeks, against 58.5% eventually at a median of 104 weeks, with no complication documented anywhere in that follow-up — so the six-month trigger is the wrong time to decide. The pooled contemporary surveillance figures are 88.5% stable or regressed (95% CI 74.9-95.2), symptomatic bleeding 0.5% (0.1-3.5) and malignant transformation 0.8% (0.4-1.9); in a 164-patient contemporary cohort, 76.2% were managed by surveillance with rupture in 1.8% and no malignant transformation among those watched. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not extend it to a man, a beta-catenin-activated or unclassified lesion, an exophytic lesion, a lesion with visible arteries, a growing lesion, or a woman who wants to conceive now. The pooled figures come from cohorts already selected as safe to watch, and in five of the seven pooled studies lesions were removed from the surveillance group by intervention as soon as they grew — so the figures describe the lesions that were allowed to stay under observation, not all adenomas over 5 cm. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Where the resection would be major and obesity is driving the disease, consider bariatric referral before hepatectomy.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Where the resection would be major and obesity is driving the disease, consider bariatric referral before hepatectomy. Indications Preferred when The severely obese patient with multiple or large adenomas who is not bleeding and has time. In a three-patient series, body-mass index fell by 31-48% after bariatric surgery and two of the three showed complete regression of the adenoma without any liver-directed intervention. In a pooled review of 4 studies and 7 patients, body-mass index fell from a mean of 41 to 28 (P=0.002) and percentage excess weight loss correlated with reduction in the number of lesions (Spearman rho 0.78, P=0.04) but not significantly with reduction in lesion size (rho 0.46, P=0.29). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Three patients and seven patients, all female, with no comparator and no adjustment for simultaneous hormone withdrawal — and formal correlation testing on seven patients is one observation away from non-significance. The positive finding concerns lesion number; the negative one concerns lesion size, which is the variable every threshold is built on, so the headline does not touch the decision variable. Both are published because the outcome was favourable; a series of non-responders would not have been written up. And the untreated comparator is not zero: 58.5% of adenomas over 5 cm regress below 5 cm with no intervention at all, so any claimed effect of weight loss has to beat that, and none of these studies is designed to. Do not describe bariatric surgery as a treatment for adenoma; describe it as treatment for the driver, with adenoma regression as a plausible consequence observed in single figures of patients. Evidence & sources The same logic applies without an operation: the point is sustained weight loss, by whatever route the patient and the bariatric service agree on. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Pooled case series, 4 studies/7 patients: mean BMI 41 to 28 (P=0.002); excess weight loss correlated with fewer lesions (rho 0.78, P=0.04), not size (rho 0.46, P=0.29) Seven patients, all female, no comparator; lesion size (the decision variable) NS

lead: Where a woman's adenoma sits between 4 and 5 cm, treat the decision as a judgement about subtype, position and trajectory rather than as a threshold.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Where a woman's adenoma sits between 4 and 5 cm, treat the decision as a judgement about subtype, position and trajectory rather than as a threshold. Indications Preferred when The 4.5 cm exophytic lesion in segment III in a woman who wants to conceive, and equally the 4.5 cm lesion with a beta-catenin exon 3 result. Two findings bear on this band directly. First, the only cohort assembled to derive a bleeding cut-point derived 35 mm, with bleeding in 7 of 129 adenomas below 35 mm (5.4%) against 35 of 66 above (53%, P<0.001) — so the band sits above, not below, the only empirically fitted threshold in the literature. Second, in a 164-patient contemporary cohort the 4-5 cm band comprised 26.8% of patients and 22.7% of them regressed, which is the most directly useful datum for this decision and rests on about 11 of 44 patients. Against both, the review of the WHO 6th-edition classification states that beta-catenin exon 3 adenomas are resected or ablated whatever their size, and that sonic hedgehog adenomas carry a high risk of haemorrhage even below 5 cm. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid No guideline endorses operating below 5 cm on position alone. The 35 mm cohort is retrospective, from one centre whose own protocol used 5 cm to decide which lesions were resected, pooled trivial intratumoral blood with peritoneal rupture in its headline comparison, and identified no beta-catenin-activated adenoma at all in 195 lesions with 48% unclassifiable — so it cannot exclude subtype as the real driver. The WHO-review statements are expert assertion: the review cites no cohort quantifying either the exon 3 size-independence or the sub-5 cm sonic hedgehog bleeding risk, and concedes that the markers needed to identify both subtypes are insensitive, non-specific or available only by sequencing. Record the reasoning, present it as a judgement, and take it to the board rather than making it alone. Evidence & sources The earlier draft of this page quoted exophytic position, visible lesional arteries and a segment II-III location with specific effect sizes attributed to the 35 mm cohort. Those specific figures were not carried in the full-text abstraction of that paper and could not be confirmed here, so they have been removed rather than restated; the composite-trigger proposal that rested on them remains in the limited-evidence section and in approval item 7 as a proposal, now graded D, pending someone reading that paper's positional analysis directly. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not report a small focus of haemorrhage inside an adenoma as an indication to operate.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not report a small focus of haemorrhage inside an adenoma as an indication to operate. Why Why Record it, and let size, growth, subtype and sex make the decision. Additional cautions Additional cautions EASL: small foci of haemorrhage within adenomas are often observed and are not an indication for clinical intervention (case series, evidence level 4). Histological bleeding was present in 52% of 533 adenomas while only 14% of patients presented with symptomatic bleeding, so incidental intralesional blood is the rule rather than a warning. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not use a reassuring subtype to withhold curative treatment from a lesion that is persistently over 5 cm or growing.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not use a reassuring subtype to withhold curative treatment from a lesion that is persistently over 5 cm or growing. Why Why Let the subtype lengthen the interval in a lesion below the threshold; once the threshold is crossed, EASL's rule is explicit that it applies irrespective of molecular or histological subtype, because the indication at that point is haemorrhage, not transformation. Note that the WHO 6th-edition classification, as reviewed in 2026, points the other way for one subtype: it states that beta-catenin exon 3 adenomas are resected or ablated whatever their size, which is a size-independent recommendation in the opposite direction — towards treating below 5 cm, not withholding above it. Additional cautions Additional cautions The subtype data stratify malignant transformation well and bleeding less well, but not as poorly as the earlier draft of this page implied. In the 261-patient multivariate bleeding model, sonic hedgehog subtype carried an odds ratio of 21.02 (95% CI 5.05-87.52) and beta-catenin exon 7/8 — the subtype with no increased malignant risk — carried 6.47 (1.78-23.55), against 1.02 per millimetre for diameter. Those confidence intervals are desperately wide and rest on a handful of events, so they identify the right axis without quantifying it usably. The practical problem is availability: sonic hedgehog subtype, the dominant bleeding predictor, cannot be identified on imaging and in practice requires sequencing, so the single most actionable bleeding predictor in the literature is not available in the clinic where the 5 cm decision is made. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Unstable bleeding: blood-product resuscitation, contrast CT and transfer for embolization; embolization precedes resection.
text: Standard Evidence D Unstable bleeding: blood-product resuscitation, contrast CT and transfer for embolization; embolization precedes resection. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Resuscitate with blood products, get a contrast-enhanced CT, and transfer to a centre that can embolise — embolisation, not resection, is the first manoeuvre in the unstable patient. Indications Preferred when Haemodynamic instability with imaging evidence of active bleeding. EASL: a bleeding adenoma with haemodynamic instability should be embolised (evidence level III, grade of recommendation 2); in cases of major haemorrhage, resuscitation with blood products and transfer to a centre where embolisation can be performed to control active bleeding is appropriate. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Emergency major hepatectomy in a shocked young patient with a benign tumour. The review that proposed the acute algorithm makes the same point: standard treatment was surgical resection for both ruptured and unruptured tumours, and the shift to initial conservative management with selective embolisation is the change of the last fifteen years. Evidence & sources Grade D by construction. There is no comparative series of embolisation against emergency resection in ruptured adenoma, and EASL's own grade for this recommendation is evidence level III. It is a sequence convention built on physiology and case series, and the page should not imply more. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Admit and observe the stable patient with contained haemorrhage, and do not operate in the acute phase.
text: Standard Evidence D Admit and observe the stable patient with contained haemorrhage, and do not operate in the acute phase. Indications Preferred when Contained intralesional or intrahepatic bleeding with stable observations. EASL: if clinically evident haemorrhage occurs, admission for close observation and contrast-enhanced CT is appropriate. Operating on a freshly bled adenoma takes more parenchyma than the same operation six weeks later and makes the pathology harder to read. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not discharge on the strength of a stable haemoglobin without a named owner, an interval scan and a plan to exclude malignancy. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Re-image once stable, and treat residual viable lesion as an indication to resect.
text: Standard Evidence C Re-image once stable, and treat residual viable lesion as an indication to resect. Indications Preferred when Every patient who has bled. EASL: residual viable lesion on follow-up imaging is an indication for resection (evidence level III, grade of recommendation 2), and further investigation once stable should be pursued to exclude malignancy and secure appropriate follow-up. In the systematic review of 851 patients, surgery was avoided altogether in 68 of 151 embolised patients (45%), so a substantial proportion need no second procedure — but that proportion is identified by re-imaging, not assumed. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat embolisation as definitive without the follow-up scan. In the 59-patient cohort, 20 of 59 patients (34%) ultimately required surgery despite embolisation, and one patient died three months after emergency TAE for haemorrhagic shock and aspiration pneumonia, with uncertain attribution. Half the embolisations in the systematic review (95 of 196 tumours, 48.5%) were for non-bleeding lesions, so the 45% surgery-avoidance figure mixes acute and elective indications and should not be quoted as the post-rupture figure. Surgery avoided is also a process endpoint and the pooled median follow-up was 31 months — too short to find malignant transformation in a lesion that was never removed. Evidence & sources The interval before re-imaging is not defined by any study. A contrast-enhanced MRI at 6 to 12 weeks, once the haematoma has resolved enough to see the lesion, is the common practice and is a convention. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Systematic review, 851 patients: surgery avoided in 68 of 151 embolised patients (45%) Mixes acute and elective: 48.5% embolised for non-bleeding lesions; median follow-up 31 mo

lead: Send the embolised or resected lesion, and any later specimen, for subtyping — a bled adenoma in an obese woman is where sonic hedgehog adenoma hides.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Send the embolised or resected lesion, and any later specimen, for subtyping — a bled adenoma in an obese woman is where sonic hedgehog adenoma hides. Indications Preferred when Any patient who presents with symptomatic bleeding, particularly an obese woman or a drinker. Sonic hedgehog adenoma was the only subgroup associated with symptomatic bleeding in the 533-adenoma series — 71% versus 14% in every other subgroup — and its 22 of 533 cases (4%) had all previously been counted as unclassified. In the 261-patient multivariate bleeding model the ranking was sonic hedgehog subtype odds ratio 21.02 (95% CI 5.05-87.52), regular alcohol consumption 9.16 (2.47-34.01), beta-catenin exon 7/8 6.47 (1.78-23.55) and diameter 1.02 per millimetre (1.01-1.03); body-mass index was not associated with bleeding at all (P=0.71), which is worth knowing before attributing a bleed to obesity. Bleeding in that cohort occurred in adenomas below 5 cm, including in 2 of the 4 pregnant women. Prostaglandin D synthase is the specific immunohistochemical marker for sonic hedgehog adenoma, but it is insensitive and was assessed in only 5 cases. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not report argininosuccinate synthase 1 as a bleeding-risk score. It was proposed as a marker of adenomas at high risk of haemorrhage; on reanalysis across 408 adenomas its overexpression marks the sonic hedgehog subgroup as part of a periportal expression programme (correlation with GLI1 expression R=0.75, P<0.0001), and ASS1 messenger RNA expression was not associated with any specific clinical feature in 390 adenomas. Evidence & sources Knowing the subtype after a bleed changes the surveillance of the rest of the liver and the counselling about a future pregnancy. It does not retrospectively change the acute management. Read the predictors with their limits: 97% of the 261-patient cohort was operated, bleeding status was ascertained at or before resection so the model predicts prevalent rather than future bleeding, and the two dominant predictors are a subtype that needs sequencing and an exposure that is modifiable — neither of which the 5 cm rule touches. The 5 biopsy-related bleeds excluded from that cohort are the one harm attributable to the diagnostic pathway itself, and a decision model would need them back. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Stable patient, small peripheral/exophytic bleeding lesion, no local IR: limited resection may be an alternative to transfer.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Stable patient, small peripheral/exophytic bleeding lesion, no local IR: limited resection may be an alternative to transfer. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Where the bleeding lesion is exophytic, peripheral and small and the patient is stable in a centre without interventional radiology, a limited resection is a reasonable alternative to transfer. Indications Preferred when A peripherally placed segment II-III or segment VI exophytic lesion, where a non-anatomical resection is quick and the transfer is long. There is no comparative evidence for this at all; it is an availability argument. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not generalise this to a central or large lesion, and do not use it to justify a major hepatectomy in an unstable patient when transfer for embolisation is achievable. The positional bleeding figures the earlier draft of this page cited in support could not be confirmed in the full-text read and have been withdrawn, which leaves this option resting on surgical convenience rather than on evidence. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not embolise a pregnant patient before 24 weeks if a peripheral resection will do.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not embolise a pregnant patient before 24 weeks if a peripheral resection will do. Why Why EASL: prior to 24 weeks, surgery may be preferred, especially for smaller resections located at the periphery of the liver, because the ionising radiation exposure and intravenous contrast agents associated with transarterial embolisation may be harmful to the fetus. Obstetric and fetal-medicine input belongs in the decision. Additional cautions Additional cautions In an exsanguinating patient this reverses: control the bleeding by whichever route is fastest. The rule applies to the planned or semi-urgent case, not to the resuscitation. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not treat a haemorrhage as proof that the lesion was benign.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not treat a haemorrhage as proof that the lesion was benign. Why Why Exclude malignancy once stable, as EASL requires, and review any specimen with expert liver pathology. Additional cautions Additional cautions Bleeding and transformation are not mutually exclusive. In the 533-adenoma series histological haemorrhage was present in 52% of tumours and symptomatic bleeding in 14% of patients, while male sex carried an odds ratio of 18.9 (95% CI 8.5-44.2) and CTNNB1 exon 3 mutation 9.3 (4.4-20.0) for malignant transformation — so the same lesion can do both, and a man who has bled is at the top of both lists. The adenomas that bleed are large, and the adenomas that transform are large, so the two associations are confounded in every series. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Confirm the diagnosis on MRI with a hepatobiliary contrast agent before you counsel her, because a quarter of these lesions are not adenomas.
text: Standard Evidence B Confirm the diagnosis on MRI with a hepatobiliary contrast agent before you counsel her, because a quarter of these lesions are not adenomas. Indications Preferred when Every woman of childbearing age with a suspected adenoma, ideally before pregnancy. In the multicentre prospective cohort, 18 of 66 women (27%) with a suspected adenoma under 5 cm on conventional imaging were shown on hepatobiliary-contrast MRI to have focal nodular hyperplasia instead — a lesion with no haemorrhage risk, no malignant potential and no follow-up requirement. The authors' own conclusion was that the misdiagnosis rate justifies the scan simply to prevent unnecessary anxiety. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not counsel on the strength of an ultrasound or a non-hepatobiliary MRI, and do not perform the confirmatory scan during pregnancy if it can be done before or after — in that study the postpartum scan was used where a definitive diagnosis was lacking at inclusion. The national resection audit found the same error at the other end of the pathway: focal nodular hyperplasia was the final diagnosis in 21% of the resected lesions under 50 mm, and absence of hepatobiliary contrast-enhanced MRI independently predicted a change of diagnosis (adjusted odds ratio 1.8). Evidence & sources This is the one place on the page with prospective multicentre data, and the finding is about diagnosis rather than treatment. Grade B refers to the misclassification rate, not to any management question. Note that the 27% figure also means this cohort is cleaner than routine practice and therefore not representative of it — the women enrolled had all had their diagnosis confirmed on hepatobiliary-contrast MRI, which most surveilled women have not. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Prospective multicentre cohort: 18 of 66 women (27%) with suspected adenoma <5 cm on conventional imaging had FNH on hepatobiliary-contrast MRI Cohort cleaner than routine practice and therefore not representative of it
National resection audit: FNH was the final diagnosis in 21% of resected lesions <50 mm; no hepatobiliary-contrast MRI predicted changed diagnosis, aOR 1.8

lead: An adenoma under 5 cm is not a reason to discourage pregnancy, and is not by itself a reason for caesarean section.
text: Standard Evidence C An adenoma under 5 cm is not a reason to discourage pregnancy, and is not by itself a reason for caesarean section. Indications Preferred when The woman with a hepatobiliary-contrast-confirmed adenoma under 5 cm that is not exophytic and not growing. In 48 such women followed through 51 pregnancies with protocolised ultrasound, growth occurred in 13 of 51 pregnancies (25.5%) with a median increase of 14 mm; no rupture or haemorrhage occurred in any of the 51 pregnancies, and the one lesion that grew beyond 7 cm was embolised. ACG 2024: pregnancy is not generally contraindicated in adenoma under 5 cm (conditional recommendation, low quality of evidence). EASL: in the presence of adenomas under 5 cm that are not exophytic or growing in size, there is no data supporting elective caesarean and vaginal delivery can be pursued. The Italian multisociety guideline sets the pregnancy surveillance schedule at ultrasound at 14, 20, 26, 32 and 38 weeks and at 6-12 weeks postpartum, graded very low quality (D), conditional. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Forty-eight women is the entire prospective evidence base, every lesion in it was under 5 cm, and the study can say nothing about the 5 cm-and-larger lesion — which is exactly where practice diverges most. Zero ruptures in 51 pregnancies has an upper 95% confidence bound of about 7%, so the data license pregnancy in a small adenoma without establishing that the residual risk is negligible. A quarter of pregnancies showed growth, so minimal risk is not the same as no change, and growth was measured by ultrasound while the diagnosis was made by MRI, so the growth figures come from the less reproducible modality. There are no subtype data, so the quarter that grew cannot be characterised and the subtypes that bleed below 5 cm are not identified. Evidence & sources The earlier 12-woman, 17-pregnancy retrospective series reached the same conclusion from weaker data: 4 adenomas grew, one woman had caesarean sections at 36 and 34 weeks for an assumed rupture risk after her largest lesion grew from 32 to 75 mm, one had radiofrequency ablation in the first trimester, and all 17 pregnancies ended well with no rupture. Read its selection: the institutional policy was to treat adenomas of 5 cm or more that did not regress before pregnancy, so the women who reached pregnancy had already been filtered as low-risk, two had been operated and one embolised beforehand, and the same single patient generated two of the three caesareans. Zero events in 17 pregnancies has an upper 95% bound of roughly 20%. The historical comparator those authors cite — 44% maternal and 38% fetal mortality — comes from published case reports of women presenting acutely, the most biased possible control. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Monitor with ultrasound every 6 to 12 weeks through pregnancy and into the early puerperium, with obstetric liaison written into the plan.
text: Standard Evidence C Monitor with ultrasound every 6 to 12 weeks through pregnancy and into the early puerperium, with obstetric liaison written into the plan. Indications Preferred when Every pregnant woman with an adenoma, whatever its size. EASL: adenoma in a pregnant woman requires close follow-up using frequent ultrasound every 6 to 12 weeks to monitor size, and liaising with the obstetric team is essential if the lesion increases in size. The prospective cohort monitored growth with ultrasound throughout pregnancy specifically so that intervention remained possible, and that is what happened in the one patient who needed it. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not stop watching at delivery. In the combined cohort and systematic review of 11 local patients plus 90 patients with 99 pregnancies, 15 adenoma-related haemorrhages occurred: 8 during pregnancy, 2 during labour and 5 postpartum. Maternal death occurred in 5 of those 15 and fetal death in 5 of 15 — but that is the case fatality of the published haemorrhage literature, in which only catastrophic events reach print, and it cannot be used to estimate the consequence of haemorrhage in an unselected pregnancy. The puerperal events are the reason surveillance runs past the birth. Evidence & sources The interval is EASL's, and no study has compared intervals. Ultrasound is the modality because it is repeatable without contrast or ionising radiation; a lesion that becomes hard to see on ultrasound needs a non-contrast MRI rather than a CT. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Resect before conceptionEXPERTISE EASL: in women with large tumours, or in whom adenoma had complicated previous pregnancies, surgical resection may be recommended.
text: Resect before conception Evidence D EXPERTISE EASL: in women with large tumours, or in whom adenoma had complicated previous pregnancies, surgical resection may be recommended. Indications Preferred when The woman with a lesion comfortably over 5 cm, or an exophytic lesion, or a previous pregnancy complicated by the adenoma, who has time before she wants to conceive and in whom the resection is not major. It removes the question rather than managing it. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not impose a major hepatectomy on a young woman whose lesion is still falling on risk-factor modification. Pregnancy should also not be delayed indefinitely for a resection that keeps being deferred — name the date. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Embolise before conception, or during pregnancy if it grows EASL: for growing lesions, embolisation can be considered; prior to 24 weeks surgery may be preferred because ionising radiation and intravenous contrast may be harmful to the fetus.
text: Embolise before conception, or during pregnancy if it grows Evidence C EASL: for growing lesions, embolisation can be considered; prior to 24 weeks surgery may be preferred because ionising radiation and intravenous contrast may be harmful to the fetus. Indications Preferred when A large central lesion for which resection would be major, and the growing lesion in the second half of pregnancy — which is what happened in the single intervention in the prospective cohort, at 26 weeks for a lesion that had passed 70 mm. Multicentre data show the median diameter falling from 76 to 48 mm by a median 5.5 months. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Major complications in 6 of 59 patients (10%) in the non-pregnant multicentre series, symptoms in 58% before versus 37% within three months (P=.134), with long-term symptom benefit uncertain, and viable tissue left behind that EASL would then have you resect if it persists. Before 24 weeks, prefer a peripheral resection where one is feasible. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Multicentre non-pregnant series: median diameter fell from 76 to 48 mm by a median 5.5 mo after embolisation Major complications 6 of 59 (10%); nonrandomized, non-pregnant cohort
Prospective pregnancy cohort: a single intervention, embolisation at 26 weeks for a lesion that had passed 70 mm One intervention only in the cohort

lead: Proceed with close surveillance Not a guideline position for a lesion over 5 cm; EASL's size-based advice is drawn at 5 cm and its pregnancy advice below it.
text: Proceed with close surveillance Evidence C Not a guideline position for a lesion over 5 cm; EASL's size-based advice is drawn at 5 cm and its pregnancy advice below it. Indications Preferred when The woman with a 5 to 6 cm, non-exophytic, non-beta-catenin lesion who wants to conceive now and accepts 6-weekly ultrasound. Of 73 pregnancies in which the adenoma was untreated, 39 (53.4%) remained stable, 11 (15.1%) regressed and 23 (31.5%) grew. All 15 adenoma-related haemorrhages in that pooled literature occurred in lesions of 6.5 cm or larger and none below that size. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The 6.5 cm figure is the smallest size among published haemorrhages, not a derived threshold — it is governed by what gets written up, and a case report of a small adenoma bleeding in pregnancy is far less likely to be published than a dramatic large one. ACG 2024 nonetheless adopts 6.5 cm as a treatment trigger, so a publication-limited minimum has become a criterion in a GRADE guideline. The pooling is itself a problem: a modern institutional cohort is combined with decades of case reports across incompatible eras of imaging and obstetric care, the stability figures use a denominator of 73 against 99 pregnancies reviewed so a quarter lack trajectory data, growth is undefined, and there are no subtype data anywhere — so the paper cannot say whether the bleeding lesions were sonic hedgehog or beta-catenin exon 7/8, the obvious alternative explanation to size. Fatal rupture during pregnancy is reported: one of the six haemorrhages in the 40-patient adenomatosis natural-history cohort was fatal and occurred during pregnancy. Do not present no reported bleed below 6.5 cm as a safe threshold. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not use CT for surveillance in pregnancy.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not use CT for surveillance in pregnancy. Why Why Ultrasound for the interval monitoring, and non-contrast MRI if the lesion cannot be followed sonographically. Additional cautions Additional cautions EASL's reason for preferring surgery to embolisation before 24 weeks is the ionising radiation and intravenous contrast; the same reasoning applies to a surveillance CT, where there is no urgency to justify it. A CT is still the right test in suspected rupture. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not discourage a pregnancy on an unconfirmed diagnosis.
text: Avoid Evidence B Do not discourage a pregnancy on an unconfirmed diagnosis. Why Why Get the hepatobiliary-contrast MRI first; 27% of these referrals turned out to be focal nodular hyperplasia, which carries no restriction at all. Additional cautions Additional cautions Advising against pregnancy, or recommending a hepatectomy, on the basis of a lesion that has not been characterised is the most consequential avoidable error on this page. Expert practice in this disease has already diverged from the written guideline — 48 of 61 responding European experts (79%) advise against routine resection of an adenoma over 5 cm after lifestyle change, and only 31 of 61 (51%) have the benign-liver-tumour multidisciplinary team the guideline assumes — which makes a confident unilateral answer in clinic hard to defend. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Expert survey: 48 of 61 European experts (79%) advise against routine resection of adenoma >5 cm after lifestyle change; only 31 of 61 (51%) have a benign-liver MDT None

lead: Manage by the size and behaviour of the largest lesion, not by the count.
text: Standard Evidence C Manage by the size and behaviour of the largest lesion, not by the count. Indications Preferred when Every patient with multiple adenomas. EASL: the management of patients with multiple adenomas should be based on the size of the largest tumour (evidence level III, grade of recommendation 2), because the clinical presentation and risk of bleeding and malignant transformation do not differ from patients with a single adenoma. In a 122-patient surgical series the risk of complications was not related to the number of adenomas but to size over 5 cm, and especially to the telangiectatic (inflammatory) and unclassified subtypes; steatotic adenomas had a low complication risk. In the 533-adenoma molecular series the rate of haemorrhage or malignant transformation was the same whatever the number of adenomas. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not read manage by the largest as the others do not matter. In the long-term adenomatosis cohort, 87% of patients had subtype-homogeneous nodules, so sampling one nodule generally characterises the others — but the 13% who do not are the reason a single biopsy cannot be treated as a survey of the liver, and that figure comes from the nodules that happened to be sampled, which were not randomly chosen. Evidence & sources A single nodule on imaging was itself associated with malignant transformation in the 533-adenoma series (odds ratio 4.1, 95% CI 1.7-11.7), which is the opposite of the intuition that more lesions mean more danger. Read the long-term adenomatosis data the same way: malignant transformation occurred in 1 of 40 patients (2.5%) over a median 10.6 years, and haemorrhage in 6 of 40 (15%) of whom 5 bled as the presenting event — so surveillance at any threshold would not have prevented most of them. With 40 patients those rates rest on one and six events respectively. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Resect the dominant lesions where the disease is unilobar or where the largest can be cleared — and do not try to clear the liver.
text: Standard Evidence C Resect the dominant lesions where the disease is unilobar or where the largest can be cleared — and do not try to clear the liver. Indications Preferred when Unilobar disease, or widespread disease with one or two lesions that have crossed the size or growth threshold. EASL: hepatic resection might be considered in unilobular disease, and in those cases with more widespread adenoma, resection of the largest adenomas may be an option (evidence level III, grade of recommendation 2). In the 40-patient adenomatosis natural-history cohort, 37 (93%) had surgery at diagnosis and 4 (10%) needed repeat resections over a median 10.6 years of follow-up. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid EASL records that microscopic adenomatous foci escaping radiological detection have been found in resected livers with widespread bilobar disease, so no resection short of hepatectomy makes the liver adenoma-free and none should be presented to the patient that way. Expect to come back: in the 40-patient adenomatosis cohort 4 patients (10%) needed repeat resections over a median 10.6 years. Evidence & sources A 134-patient surgical series reports 8.1% morbidity and no mortality for resection in this disease, without a Clavien-Dindo distribution; repeat resection in a previously operated liver is not that operation. Count on the first operation being the easiest one. And note what the long-term cohort cannot tell you: 37 of 40 patients (93%) had surgery at diagnosis, so its complication rates describe treated disease, and resected nodules leave the risk set without any competing-risk accounting. lead: Look for a germline HNF1A mutation and offer genetic counselling where the picture fits.
text: Standard Evidence C Look for a germline HNF1A mutation and offer genetic counselling where the picture fits. Indications Preferred when A young patient with many adenomas, a family history of liver adenoma, or early-onset non-insulin-dependent diabetes. In the 40-patient long-term adenomatosis cohort, 6 patients (15%) carried germline HNF1A mutations and all 6 of the familial cases did. In the founding genotype-phenotype series, 7 of 44 HNF1A-mutated adenomas (16%) carried one germline and one somatic mutation, and those germline carriers were younger (23 versus 40 years, P=0.0001), had larger tumours (142 versus 69 mm, P=0.02), more nodules (P=0.04) and less oral contraceptive use (P=0.002) — a different disease wearing the same name. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not restrict the search to women, and do not assume small nodules in this setting are safe. In familial HNF1A adenomatosis the disease occurs equally in men and women with the higher bleeding rate in the men, and in the long-term cohort two male patients with familial adenomatosis bled from nodules measuring only 20 mm and 40 mm — among the clearest documented haemorrhages far below the 5 cm line anywhere in this literature, and an argument for subtype and sex rather than for relocating the threshold downwards. Evidence & sources Familial adenomatosis is associated with maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 3, so a fasting glucose and a three-generation family history for diabetes and liver tumours belong in the first clinic visit, and metabolic genetics belongs at the board. lead: Where the number is large but every lesion is small, surveillance is defensible.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Where the number is large but every lesion is small, surveillance is defensible. Indications Preferred when Many small HNF1A-inactivated or inflammatory lesions in a woman, with risk factors being modified and the dominant lesion well under 5 cm. Over a median 10.6 years in the 40-patient cohort, malignant transformation occurred in 1 patient (2.5%) and haemorrhage in 6 (15%), 5 of those at the time of diagnosis; 87% of patients had subtype-homogeneous nodules, so one biopsy generally characterises the liver. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid That cohort was 93% operated at diagnosis, so its complication rates describe treated disease and cannot be read as the natural history of observation, and with 40 patients the 2.5% and 15% rest on one and six events with confidence intervals compatible with most published figures. Set the 2.5% ten-year transformation rate against what the radical alternative costs: in the European registry series of 49 transplants for adenomatosis there were three operative deaths, five retransplantations and three fatal carcinoma recurrences — roughly one patient in eight died of the treatment or its failure. Evidence & sources The pooled contemporary surveillance figures — 88.5% stable or regressed, 0.5% symptomatic bleeding, 0.8% malignant transformation across 699 patients — include multiple-lesion patients but do not report them separately. lead: Transarterial embolisation of the dominant lesions is a reasonable way to reduce burden without taking parenchyma.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Transarterial embolisation of the dominant lesions is a reasonable way to reduce burden without taking parenchyma. Indications Preferred when Bilobar disease where a resection clearing the dominant lesions would be major, and the patient who has already had one resection. In 59 patients the median diameter fell from 76 to 48 mm by a median 5.5 months (P<0.001), and in the 851-patient systematic review elective embolisation avoided surgery in 41 of 49 patients (84%). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Major complications in 6 of 59 (10%) with one death after emergency TAE for haemorrhagic shock and later aspiration pneumonia, with uncertain attribution, 20 of 59 (34%) still requiring surgery, an uncertain symptom effect at three months (58% symptomatic before versus 37% after; P=.134), and viable tissue left behind in a liver that already has lesions you are not treating. EASL reserves embolisation for poor surgical candidates, so using it here is a departure that should be recorded as one. lead: Do not list a patient for transplantation on lesion number.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not list a patient for transplantation on lesion number. Why Why Use the transplant assessment's named routes, every one of which requires something beyond the count. Additional cautions Additional cautions EASL: liver transplantation is not recommended in multiple adenoma, but might be considered in individuals with underlying liver disease (evidence level III, grade of recommendation 2). The 122-patient series drew the conclusion explicitly — because complications were unrelated to the number of adenomas, patients with multiple adenomas do not need liver transplantation. The local hepatic adenoma protocol says the same thing in its own words: lesion number alone does not qualify, and more than 10 lesions is a necessary but not sufficient condition. lead: Do not use the old ten-lesion definition of adenomatosis as though it were a risk category.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not use the old ten-lesion definition of adenomatosis as though it were a risk category. Why Why Record the count, the dominant diameter, the distribution and the subtype, and let the dominant lesion drive management. Additional cautions Additional cautions EASL replaced the term liver adenomatosis with multiple hepatocellular adenomas precisely because precise counting of adenomas by imaging can be challenging and because risk is driven by the size of the largest nodule. The local transplant protocol nevertheless uses more than 10 lesions as one necessary condition of its adenomatosis route — that is a policy threshold inherited from the registry literature, not a risk threshold, and it should be described as one in any narrative that invokes it. lead: In glycogen storage disease, treat metabolic control as the first-line adenoma therapy and keep lifelong imaging surveillance.
text: Standard Evidence C In glycogen storage disease, treat metabolic control as the first-line adenoma therapy and keep lifelong imaging surveillance. Indications Preferred when Every patient with glycogen storage disease type I, III or IV. EASL: in glycogen storage diseases the lifelong risk of adenoma is particularly high, the tumours frequently appear in the second or third decade, nearly half are inflammatory adenomas, and no HNF1A-inactivated adenoma has been observed in this setting; reduction in size and/or number has been observed following optimal metabolic control. The 533-adenoma molecular series confirms both halves of that. The ACMG practice guideline for glycogen storage disease type I puts numbers to the burden: 70-80% of patients over the age of 25 have at least one hepatic adenoma, progression defined as growth or increase in number occurs in about 50%, and the mean age at adenoma presentation is 14.8 years — so these are decisions made in children and adolescents. Chromosome 6p gain or 6q loss is present in about 60% of GSD Ia adenomas. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not import the general adenoma surveillance interval or the general resection threshold, and do not expect a serum marker to help: the ACMG guideline states that alpha-fetoprotein and carcinoembryonic antigen do not predict malignant transformation and cannot be used for surveillance, which leaves imaging size as the only monitored variable and reimports the 5 cm convention into a population in which it was never tested and in which adenomas are multiple from adolescence. EASL's own interval here is annual ultrasound from 0 to 10 years and biannual beyond 10 years; the GSD type I surveillance table uses liver ultrasound every 12 to 24 months to age 16 and then CT, ultrasound or contrast MRI every 6 to 12 months from age 16, earlier in those who already have adenomas. And weigh the operation differently: 53.1% of the 99 published liver transplants for hepatic adenoma were in glycogen storage disease patients, and metabolic decompensation, renal disease and the neutropenia of type Ib change the operative calculus entirely. Evidence & sources Get metabolic genetics into the room. The local hepatic adenoma protocol requires it for glycogen storage disease cases and requires glycogen storage disease therapy to be optimised and renal, metabolic and systemic manifestations assessed before transplantation is considered. Note the status of the guidance you are following: the ACMG document states explicitly that its recommendations are considered expert opinion, applies no recommendation grading to its adenoma sections, gives the 50% progression figure without a time base, and predates both the sonic hedgehog subtype and the exon-specific beta-catenin gradient — so a near-universal complication of a rare disease is being managed by convention borrowed from cohorts of young women on oral contraceptives. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: In a congenital portosystemic shunt, define the anatomy and ask whether the shunt can be closed before you touch the nodule.
text: Standard Evidence D In a congenital portosystemic shunt, define the anatomy and ask whether the shunt can be closed before you touch the nodule. Indications Preferred when Any patient, and especially any child, with Abernethy malformation or another congenital extrahepatic portosystemic shunt. Nodules in this setting span focal nodular hyperplasia, adenoma and carcinoma, and resection can impede a future shunt occlusion procedure — which is the argument for defining the vascular anatomy first. The local hepatic adenoma protocol requires exactly this: define the Abernethy anatomy and assess whether shunt closure or another vascular intervention is feasible before transplantation. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The evidence that shunt closure shrinks the nodule is one paediatric case report, and it does not show regression: an HNF1A-inactivated adenoma fell from 11.5 cm to 10 cm four months after closure, a 13% change in diameter that does not meet the RECIST threshold for response and sits within the range of between-scan measurement variability, in a lesion that remained far above any size at which management would change. Do not present shunt closure as an established adenoma treatment; present it as the intervention that addresses the cause, to be assessed by a service that performs them. And do not assume the nodule is benign — carcinoma occurs in this setting, and adenomas arising in vascular liver disease are reported to behave atypically with higher transformation risk. Evidence & sources Ruling out a congenital portosystemic shunt in a child with a liver tumour is itself a reason to look at the portal vein deliberately rather than incidentally; a hypoplastic portal vein is present in most cases. lead: In vascular liver disease, raise your suspicion of beta-catenin activation and of carcinoma, and biopsy the nodule with a full immunohistochemical profile.
text: Standard Evidence C In vascular liver disease, raise your suspicion of beta-catenin activation and of carcinoma, and biopsy the nodule with a full immunohistochemical profile. Indications Preferred when Budd-Chiari syndrome, portal vein thrombosis, obliterative portal venopathy and other vascular liver disease. Patients with liver vascular disease developed beta-catenin exon 3 adenomas significantly more often in the 411-patient series (P=0.04), and fibrosis in the non-tumour liver was itself associated with malignant transformation (odds ratio 3.8, 95% CI 1.1-11.4). Imaging follow-up protocols for these patients should be designed to identify an adenoma early and distinguish it from a large regenerative nodule, and every biopsied hepatocellular lesion should get the full immunohistochemical panel. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not try to separate adenoma from a large regenerative nodule and from carcinoma on imaging alone in a Budd-Chiari liver — the three overlap and the stakes differ completely. And read the evidence honestly: this rests on a single subgroup P value of 0.04 in a cross-sectional series, plus case reports. It is a reason to biopsy and to look harder, not a quantified risk. Evidence & sources Nodular regenerative hyperplasia is explicitly outside EASL's benign-tumour guideline and is covered separately in the non-cirrhotic portal hypertension literature; do not manage it from this page. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Record the rarer associations, but do not invent management rules for them.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Record the rarer associations, but do not invent management rules for them. Indications Preferred when Iron overload from beta-thalassaemia or haemochromatosis, McCune-Albright syndrome, familial adenoma with maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 3, and endogenous androgen excess states such as polycystic ovary syndrome and Klinefelter syndrome. EASL lists these as rarer associations with implications for management, and recording them is how a cluster is eventually recognised. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid There is no subtype, surveillance or threshold data for any of them beyond case reports. Manage the adenoma by sex, size, growth and subtype, and manage the association on its own terms. Evidence & sources In an unusual association, the registry entry is the deliverable. Nothing will be learned about these settings from single cases that are not recorded. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: A paediatric or adolescent presentation belongs with the metabolic and vascular services from the first visit, not after the adenoma workup fails.
text: Reasonable Evidence D A paediatric or adolescent presentation belongs with the metabolic and vascular services from the first visit, not after the adenoma workup fails. Indications Preferred when Adenoma under 18. The underlying diagnosis is far more likely to be glycogen storage disease, a congenital portosystemic shunt or germline HNF1A disease than sporadic hormone-related adenoma: the mean age at adenoma presentation in glycogen storage disease type I is 14.8 years, the published congenital portosystemic shunt case was a 9-year-old, and in the long-term adenomatosis cohort all 6 familial cases carried germline HNF1A mutations with germline carriers presenting at a median 23 years against 40 for the rest. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not apply adult hormone-withdrawal and 5 cm logic to a child. None of the threshold data include children, and in glycogen storage disease the lesions appear in the second or third decade against a background that is itself the problem. lead: Do not resect a glycogen storage disease adenoma before the metabolic team has had a run at it, unless the lesion itself forces your hand.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not resect a glycogen storage disease adenoma before the metabolic team has had a run at it, unless the lesion itself forces your hand. Why Why Size, growth or suspected transformation still force the operation. Short of that, optimise control and reimage, because reduction in size and number following optimal metabolic control is a reported phenomenon in this specific setting. Additional cautions Additional cautions The regression claim rests on case series within a rare disease and is not a treatment effect established against a comparator. It justifies a trial of control before an operation in a stable patient; it does not justify deferring an operation in a growing or atypical lesion. lead: Do not assume an adenoma in a syndromic patient behaves like a sporadic one.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not assume an adenoma in a syndromic patient behaves like a sporadic one. Why Why Record the syndrome, expect the subtype distribution to differ, and set the surveillance interval from the syndrome rather than from the adenoma. Additional cautions Additional cautions The subtype distribution genuinely differs: never HNF1A-inactivated in glycogenosis, enriched for inflammatory there, enriched for beta-catenin exon 3 in vascular liver disease, and in familial HNF1A adenomatosis equally distributed between the sexes with the higher bleeding rate in men. Every one of those breaks an assumption the sporadic pathway is built on. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Accept that transformation is usually diagnosed on the specimen rather than on surveillance imaging, and let that shape the decision to resect.
text: Standard Evidence C Accept that transformation is usually diagnosed on the specimen rather than on surveillance imaging, and let that shape the decision to resect. Indications Preferred when Any high-risk lesion. In the 218-patient series, 25 patients had malignant transformation; the median diameter of the transformed adenomas was 10 cm, only 3 of the 25 were 5 cm or smaller, and all three of those arose in a liver with fibrosis or iron overload. In the male pathology series, malignant transformation occurred in 4 of 27 adenomas (14.8%), in beta-catenin-inflammatory and unclassified lesions. The pooled figure across 1,635 adenomas is 68 transformations (4.2%), with only 3 of those 68 (4.4%) in a tumour under 5 cm and the smallest transformed adenoma in the literature measuring 4 cm. The practical consequence is that imaging surveillance of a high-risk lesion is not a transformation-detection strategy; resection is. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not offer surveillance as a way of catching transformation early in a beta-catenin-activated adenoma or in a man. And do not read the size association in reverse. In the 533-adenoma molecular series the 50 mm cut-off did not significantly separate malignant transformation (13.1% versus 7.6%, P=0.053), so a small high-risk lesion is not safe merely for being small. The '4.4% below 5 cm' statistic is a proportion of the numerator and not a risk, and it is partly an artefact of how few sub-5 cm adenomas entered the pooled denominator at all; the review it comes from carries three mutually inconsistent denominators (1,635 in the abstract, 1,617 in the table and 1,568 in the discussion), pools case reports with series, and its authors conclude that the 5 cm treatment recommendation is open for debate and that over 95% of patients resected above it are unnecessarily exposed to a procedure with reported morbidity up to 27% and mortality up to 3%. The Taiwanese series contributes the clearest counter-examples: 2 of its 6 malignant transformations occurred in adenomas of 3.5 cm and 4.4 cm, both beta-catenin-activated. Evidence & sources Beware the confounding that makes the threshold look validated. In the 164-patient contemporary cohort all six patients who developed carcinoma had lesions of 5 cm or larger — but every one of those six was also beta-catenin-activated or inflammatory, so size and subtype are completely confounded in six events and the paper cannot separate them. The same pattern recurs: in the 134-patient surgical series all four transformations were both beta-catenin-activated and over 5 cm, and in the 218-patient series beta-catenin activation was present in 16 of 25 transformed adenomas. Transformation is also ascertained on the resection specimen, so a lesion resected for being large is more likely to have a small malignant focus found — verification bias working in the same direction as the size association being tested. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
