lead: A multiphase contrast study is the characterising test, and the phases and the agent depend on the question — say which question you are asking when you order it.
text: Standard Evidence C A multiphase contrast study is the characterising test, and the phases and the agent depend on the question — say which question you are asking when you order it. Indications Preferred when Every solid lesion the index study left unresolved. The technical minimum, stated by the ACR Appropriateness Criteria and applying equally to CT, MRI and contrast-enhanced ultrasound, is at least two dynamic phases — late arterial and portal venous. The ACR white paper prefers MRI over CT for characterisation on three grounds: better assessment of internal features, more reliable assessment of enhancement, and no ionising radiation. EASL 2025 prefers CT or MRI over contrast-enhanced ultrasound as the first-line non-invasive test in at-risk patients because of higher sensitivity (LoE 3, strong recommendation). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not read 'MRI is preferred' as a measured advantage. The ACR Appropriateness Criteria rate contrast-enhanced ultrasound, multiphase CT and contrast-enhanced MRI as equivalent and usually appropriate alternatives for an indeterminate lesion larger than 1 cm, both in a normal liver and in known chronic liver disease, and they do so on narrative accuracy ranges from different studies in different populations with no head-to-head data and no equivalence testing. The same document's own text cites specificity for contrast-enhanced CT in ultrasound-detected lesions as 38-82%, and one cited MRI study at 43% specificity for an exact diagnosis. A pathway that reads only the rating table never sees the 38%. And do not order 'MRI liver' and leave the agent to chance — the two guidelines ask for different agents for different questions, and that choice cannot be made by the scheduler. Evidence & sources Where contrast is contraindicated, say what the unenhanced study can and cannot do rather than treating it as the characterising test. Note that the ACR Appropriateness Criteria and the ACR white paper, from the same organisation, use incompatible risk taxonomies: the white paper merges low and average risk into one low-risk tier, while the Appropriateness Criteria split high risk into chronic liver disease versus known extrahepatic malignancy. A pathway using both has to reconcile them, and this page does so by treating the liver-disease fork at clinical decision 0 as primary. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Contrast-enhanced ultrasound characterises a solid lesion in real time and is the right test when the question is vascular pattern rather than anatomy.
text: Standard Evidence B Contrast-enhanced ultrasound characterises a solid lesion in real time and is the right test when the question is vascular pattern rather than anatomy. Indications Preferred when The lesion that is unclear after greyscale and Doppler ultrasound, the patient who cannot have gadolinium or iodinated contrast, and the small focal nodular hyperplasia where EASL puts CEUS ahead of MRI. The WFUMB guideline's single level-1 strong recommendation is for exactly this situation — contrast-enhanced ultrasound as the first-line technique for an incidentally detected indeterminate focal liver lesion at ultrasound in a non-cirrhotic liver without history or clinical suspicion of malignancy. In the DEGUM multicentre study of 1,349 patients at 14 hospitals with a hepatic lesion lacking a definite diagnosis on B-mode and power Doppler, overall accuracy against a reference standard that was histology in more than 75% of cases was 90.3%: 723 of 755 malignant lesions correctly assessed (sensitivity 95.8%) and 476 of 573 benign lesions (specificity 83.1%), with positive predictive value 95.4% and negative predictive value 95.7%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Carry both halves of that result and the limits of the recommendation behind it. Specificity was 83.1% — CEUS over-calls benign lesions as suspicious far more often than it misses cancer. In the companion analysis, 92 of the 1,349 lesions (6.8%) could not be definitively diagnosed by CEUS at all, mostly benign ones; the CEUS diagnosis was wrong in 39 lesions; and 8 lesions called benign by CEUS proved malignant — three histologically proven HCCs called adenoma, two called focal nodular hyperplasia that were an HCC and a metastasis, two called haemangioma that were an HCC and a metastasis, and one called benign that was a lymphoma. The WFUMB level-1 grade is asserted rather than demonstrated: no randomised comparison of CEUS-first against MRI-first for this lesion is cited, the supporting text is a block citation of roughly twenty studies with no pooled estimate or quality appraisal, and the guideline grades the same lesion in a patient with suspected malignancy as level 2 and only a weak recommendation — the higher-stakes scenario getting the weaker grade with no explanation. Evidence & sources WFUMB in cooperation with EFSUMB, AFSUMB, AIUM and FLAUS updated the liver CEUS recommendations in 2020; that document, not the DEGUM study, is the protocol source, and it is the source to read on dose, mechanical index and the artefacts that cause mischaracterisation. Operator dependence is the unquantified variable: the guideline addresses it only through a training recommendation at its lowest evidence level, reports no interobserver agreement anywhere, and more than twenty of its authors declare relationships with the contrast or scanner manufacturers whose products the recommendations require. The DEGUM accuracy came from 14 centres using a standardised protocol, and CEUS LI-RADS category agreement is the lowest of any modality at kappa 0.30-0.39. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Multicentre diagnostic study, 1,349 patients: accuracy 90.3%; sensitivity 95.8% (723 of 755), specificity 83.1% (476 of 573); PPV 95.4%, NPV 95.7% Specificity 83.1%: over-calls benign lesions; 8 called benign by CEUS proved malignant

lead: In an at-risk liver, read the CEUS against CEUS LI-RADS v2017 criteria, not against the CT/MRI criteria — the washout timing and intensity are different and that is the whole point of the separate algorithm.
text: Standard Evidence C In an at-risk liver, read the CEUS against CEUS LI-RADS v2017 criteria, not against the CT/MRI criteria — the washout timing and intensity are different and that is the whole point of the separate algorithm. Indications Preferred when The cirrhotic or chronic hepatitis B patient whose nodule is being worked up by ultrasound. EASL 2025 gives the CEUS criterion explicitly — non-rim arterial hyperenhancement with late-onset washout (later than 60 seconds) of mild intensity (LoE 1). In a meta-analysis of 10 studies, 5,543 patients and 6,124 lesions including 4,492 HCCs, 97% (95-98) of CEUS LR-5 observations were HCC, and CEUS LR-5 had sensitivity 0.76 (0.70-0.81), specificity 0.95 (0.91-0.97) and accuracy 0.82 (0.75-0.88) for HCC. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The categories are not interchangeable between modalities, and the evidence that they are not is weaker than the page previously implied. In a 43-study comparison, CEUS LR-3 was 21% HCC against 35% for CT/MRI LR-3 (p=0.02) and CEUS LR-M was 56% HCC against 33% (p=0.01), with non-HCC malignancy in LR-M 35% against 58% (p=0.01) — but few paired studies exist, so these are comparisons between different populations with different HCC prevalence and different reference standards, presented with p-values as though they were head-to-head tests. Heterogeneity across the pooled proportions is I-squared 78-93%, the authors concede meta-regression could not explain it, and the LR-3 proportion itself moves from 14% in Asian to 32% in non-Asian studies, which shows these are population artefacts rather than properties of the categories. The two meta-analyses this page used to make the point come from the same Tianjin department, share authors, grants and included studies, were published two months apart, and report CEUS LR-M as 44% and 56% HCC from largely the same primary literature — they are one body of work, not independent corroboration. Evidence & sources CEUS LI-RADS remains at v2017 while CT/MRI LI-RADS is at v2018, and the diagnostic versions are not synchronised. For a CT or MRI observation that is LR-3 or non-characterizable, the prospective evidence that CEUS resolves it comes from one multicentre sub-analysis of 75 observations in 68 patients who were 97.1% cirrhotic — see clinical decision 6, where the figures and their limits are set out. That study licenses nothing about a lesion in a liver that is not at risk. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Meta-analysis, 10 studies, 6,124 lesions: CEUS LR-5 97% (95–98) HCC; sensitivity 0.76 (0.70–0.81), specificity 0.95 (0.91–0.97) Same Tianjin department as the companion meta-analysis; not independent
Meta-analysis, 43 studies, CEUS vs CT/MRI: LR-3 HCC 21% vs 35% (p=0.02); LR-M HCC 56% vs 33% (p=0.01) Few paired studies: between-population comparisons; I-squared 78-93%

lead: MRI with an extracellular gadolinium agentPROTOCOL EASL 2025: extracellular contrast agents should be favoured over gadoxetic acid for the non-invasive diagnosis of HCC using MRI (LoE 1, strong recommendation, consensus). The ACR white paper likewise prefers gadolinium blood-pool agents generally.
text: MRI with an extracellular gadolinium agent Evidence B PROTOCOL EASL 2025: extracellular contrast agents should be favoured over gadoxetic acid for the non-invasive diagnosis of HCC using MRI (LoE 1, strong recommendation, consensus). The ACR white paper likewise prefers gadolinium blood-pool agents generally. Indications Preferred when The at-risk liver, where the diagnosis turns on true washout in the portal venous or delayed phase, and the haemangioma or focal nodular hyperplasia where delayed-phase fill-in and a delayed-enhancing central scar are the diagnostic features. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid It will not answer the adenoma-versus-focal-nodular-hyperplasia question, which needs hepatocyte uptake. Evidence & sources The individual-patient-data meta-analysis that would have settled the agent question could not: only one contributing study made a direct within-observation comparison of extracellular against hepatobiliary agents, and the pooled dataset was skewed toward extracellular agents, so no comparative estimate exists. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: MRI with gadoxetate disodium (hepatobiliary agent)PROTOCOL The ACR white paper recommends gadoxetate disodium specifically to distinguish focal nodular hyperplasia from hepatocellular adenoma, because focal nodular hyperplasia takes up the agent on the hepatobiliary phase and adenoma was thought not to. The white paper flags the question as important especially above 3 cm and subcapsular — a threshold its own 2010 predecessor set at 4 cm, with no new evidence cited for the change.
text: MRI with gadoxetate disodium (hepatobiliary agent) Evidence C PROTOCOL The ACR white paper recommends gadoxetate disodium specifically to distinguish focal nodular hyperplasia from hepatocellular adenoma, because focal nodular hyperplasia takes up the agent on the hepatobiliary phase and adenoma was thought not to. The white paper flags the question as important especially above 3 cm and subcapsular — a threshold its own 2010 predecessor set at 4 cm, with no new evidence cited for the change. Indications Preferred when A solid hepatocellular lesion in a young woman in a normal liver, where the fork is focal nodular hyperplasia (discharge) versus adenoma (the HCA pathway). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Two separate problems, and the first needs stating precisely because this page previously stated it loosely. In a meta-analysis of 28 studies, 364 patients and 410 subtyped adenomas, hepatobiliary-phase iso- or hyperintensity was present in 14% of all adenomas (95% CI 4-26%), in 0% of HNF1A-inactivated adenomas (0-2%), 14% of inflammatory (2-31%), 11% of unclassified (0-29%) and 59% of beta-catenin-activated adenomas (26-88%). Sensitivity and specificity for separating focal nodular hyperplasia from all adenoma subtypes together were 99% (57-100%) and 89% (82-94%); the much-quoted 65% specificity (44-80%) applies only once HNF1A-inactivated and inflammatory adenomas have already been excluded, so it is the specificity against an enriched residual population and not a measured property of the test in an unselected lesion. Second, in an at-risk liver EASL 2025 states that hypointensity on the transitional or hepatobiliary phase is an ancillary finding favouring malignancy in general, not the equivalent of washout, and that the agent carries a risk of respiratory motion artefact in the arterial phase — the phase the HCC diagnosis depends on. Evidence & sources The B-HCA estimate rests on 33 lesions, 16 of the 28 included studies are case reports or small series, and no sensitivity analysis excluding them was performed — a case report of a beta-catenin adenoma gets written because it was hepatobiliary-phase hyperintense and surprised someone. The pairwise comparison that would matter most clinically, beta-catenin against inflammatory adenoma, did not separate them. The direction is clear and the precision is poor. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Meta-analysis (28 studies): FNH vs all adenomas sensitivity 99% (57–100), specificity 89% (82–94); HBP iso/hyperintensity in 59% (26–88) of β-catenin, 0% of HNF1A HCA β-catenin estimate on 33 lesions; 16 of 28 studies case reports or small series

lead: Where the index study is adequate and the lesion has distinctly benign features, order nothing.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Where the index study is adequate and the lesion has distinctly benign features, order nothing. Indications Preferred when The ACR benign-feature list on non-contrast or portal-venous-phase CT is a sharp margin with homogeneous low attenuation at or below 20 HU, or the characteristic appearance of haemangioma, focal nodular hyperplasia, focal fatty sparing or deposition, or a perfusion change. Any of those needs no follow-up regardless of risk category, and the first two of the white paper's four core recommendations say exactly that. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not apply the list to a lesion with ill-defined margins, heterogeneous density, mural thickening or nodularity, thick septa, or intermediate-to-high attenuation above 20 HU on portal venous phase with pseudoenhancement excluded. Those features require prompt MRI, not reassurance. And do not mistake the lists for measurements: sharp versus ill-defined margin, homogeneous versus heterogeneous density, thick versus thin septa and the judgement of whether pseudoenhancement is present are all reader calls on which the whole algorithm pivots, and no interobserver agreement is reported for any of them anywhere in either white paper. The 2010 document's own benign-feature footnote permits 'sharp but irregular margins' while its suspicious-feature footnote lists 'ill-defined margins', leaving irregular-but-sharp to the reader. Evidence & sources Grade D, downgraded from C after the full-text read. This is a consensus feature list with no derivation and no reproducibility data, in a document whose committee states that its process meets no specific formal national standard and that its content should not be considered standard of care. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not use FDG PET/CT routinely to characterize an incidental liver lesion; reserve it for selected oncology questions.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not use FDG PET/CT routinely to characterize an incidental liver lesion; reserve it for selected oncology questions. Why Why Use it to answer a distribution question in a patient with a known extrahepatic primary and a lesion larger than 1 cm found on non-contrast or single-phase imaging, which is the one scenario of eight that the ACR Appropriateness Criteria rate usually appropriate. Additional cautions Additional cautions Per-lesion sensitivity for colorectal liver metastases was 81.4% (95% CI 66.5-90.6), statistically indistinguishable from MRI at 80.3%, and the FDG PET/CT data specifically came down to one per-lesion data set. The white paper's own claim is modest — PET may preclude biopsy in some patients with lesions larger than 1 cm — and the Appropriateness Criteria rate PET usually not appropriate in a normal liver on the stated ground that no relevant literature supports it there. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Meta-analysis, per-lesion sensitivity for CRLM: FDG PET 81.4% (95% CI 66.5–90.6) vs MRI 80.3%, not significantly different FDG PET/CT data came from one per-lesion data set

lead: Do not repeat the same inadequate study with the same protocol.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not repeat the same inadequate study with the same protocol. Why Why Name the deficiency — missing arterial phase, missing delayed phase, aggressive dose reduction, no contrast — and order the study that fixes it. Additional cautions Additional cautions A second single-phase CT answers nothing and is the commonest wasted step in this pathway. The local master workup CPG requires the multidisciplinary team to document whether repeat imaging is needed when image quality or protocol is inadequate, rather than proceeding on a study that cannot support the decision. lead: In a normal liver, a hyperechoic lesion under 3 cm with a sharp margin, posterior acoustic enhancement and no halo sign is a haemangioma on ultrasound alone, and no contrast study is needed.
text: Standard Evidence C In a normal liver, a hyperechoic lesion under 3 cm with a sharp margin, posterior acoustic enhancement and no halo sign is a haemangioma on ultrasound alone, and no contrast study is needed. Indications Preferred when The asymptomatic patient with no liver disease and no cancer. This is EASL's recommendation at evidence level II-2, grade of recommendation 1, and the prior probability is consistent with it — haemangioma was the third commonest of five pre-specified benign findings in 45,319 university-hospital ultrasound examinations, 1,640 cases, mean size 20.1 mm, after focal fatty sparing (2,839, 6.26%) and cysts (2,631, 5.81%). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid EASL draws the line itself: in oncology patients or in those with underlying liver disease, contrast-enhanced imaging is required (II-2, grade 1). The ultrasound-only rule does not cross into either of those populations. And do not treat the prevalence as a fixed quantity — EASL's own figure for haemangioma is a range of 0.4% to 20% of the general population, around 5% in imaging series and up to 20% at autopsy, and the 45,319-patient series reports its haemangioma rate as 3.3% in the abstract and 3.62% in the results table and Table 3, of which only the latter matches 1,640 of 45,319. Evidence & sources Discharge rule: because of its benign course, imaging follow-up is not required for a typical haemangioma (II-2, grade 1), and pregnancy and oral contraceptives are not contraindicated (III, grade 2). Conservative management is appropriate for typical cases (II-2, grade 1). Worth knowing when quoting the grades: not one recommendation anywhere in that guideline rests on evidence level I or II-1, so there is no randomised or controlled evidence behind any of it, and there is no stated search strategy, database or date range underneath the GRADE labels. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Where ultrasound is atypical, diagnose the haemangioma on MRI — peripheral and globular arterial enhancement with central fill-in on delayed phases, strong T2 hyperintensity, high apparent diffusion coefficient — and then discharge it.
text: Standard Evidence C Where ultrasound is atypical, diagnose the haemangioma on MRI — peripheral and globular arterial enhancement with central fill-in on delayed phases, strong T2 hyperintensity, high apparent diffusion coefficient — and then discharge it. Indications Preferred when Rapidly filling and giant haemangiomas, the two commonest atypias, are both readily diagnosed on MRI. EASL reports MRI sensitivity and specificity for haemangioma above 90%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Know the named pitfalls. High-flow haemangiomas imaged with gadoxetic acid can show relatively low signal against liver on the three-minute equilibrium phase — a pseudo-washout that mimics a hypervascular tumour; the discriminators are very strong T2 signal and arterial-phase enhancement. Cystic, pedunculated, fluid-fluid-level, calcified, hyalinised or very slowly filling haemangiomas are the rare group in which imaging including MRI is explicitly less reliable, and small haemangiomas may show uniform flash filling that the ACR algorithm treats differently by risk category. Evidence & sources Size does not create follow-up. EASL states there is no relationship between haemangioma size and complications, and little relationship between symptoms and lesion characteristics; no randomised trial shows resection better than conservative management. Kasabach-Merritt syndrome, a growing lesion, or symptoms from compression are the referral triggers (III, grade 1). Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Focal nodular hyperplasia can be diagnosed with nearly 100% specificity when the typical features are seen in combination, and a typical lesion needs no follow-up at all unless there is underlying vascular liver disease.
text: Standard Evidence C Focal nodular hyperplasia can be diagnosed with nearly 100% specificity when the typical features are seen in combination, and a typical lesion needs no follow-up at all unless there is underlying vascular liver disease. Indications Preferred when The young woman with a lobulated, homogeneous, arterially enhancing lesion with a T2-bright central scar that enhances late. EASL: CEUS, CT or MRI can diagnose focal nodular hyperplasia with nearly 100% specificity when typical features are seen in combination (II-2, grade 1); MRI has the highest overall performance, and CEUS the highest accuracy below 3 cm (II-2, grade 1). It is also an uncommon incidental finding — 81 cases (0.18%) in 45,319 hospital ultrasound examinations, against 19 (0.04%) for adenoma — so an incidental hepatocellular lesion is far more often focal nodular hyperplasia than adenoma, but neither is a random discovery. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The sensitivity is the weak half: MRI sensitivity is 70-80% and lower in small lesions where the central scar is usually absent, so a lesion without the full feature set is neither excluded as focal nodular hyperplasia nor diagnosed as it. EASL's rule is that in atypical cases, liver biopsy is indicated. Steatotic focal nodular hyperplasia mimics adenoma and is commoner in a steatotic liver; strong T2 hyperintensity, a pseudocapsule and washout are the other recognised atypias. Be careful with the two prevalence figures as well: in that series both focal nodular hyperplasia and adenoma required confirmation by CEUS, MRI or histology while cysts, haemangiomas and fatty sparing were accepted on B-mode alone, and the mean confirmed lesion sizes were 51.6 mm and 39.0 mm — far larger than a typical incidental lesion. Asymmetric ascertainment of the rare entities is the likeliest reason both figures came in roughly tenfold below every prior series, including EASL's own 0.4-3% at autopsy and 0.03% clinically relevant for focal nodular hyperplasia. Evidence & sources Discharge rule: where the diagnosis is firm and the patient asymptomatic, follow-up imaging is not required and the patient can be discharged (III, grade 2). There is no indication to discontinue oral contraceptives and no need for follow-up during pregnancy. Treatment is not recommended (II-3, grade 2). The 'nearly 100% specificity' claim carries no pooled estimate and no confidence interval in the guideline. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Where the hepatocellular lesion cannot be separated from adenoma on an extracellular-agent study, add a hepatobiliary-phase study — but grade the result by what it can and cannot exclude.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Where the hepatocellular lesion cannot be separated from adenoma on an extracellular-agent study, add a hepatobiliary-phase study — but grade the result by what it can and cannot exclude. Indications Preferred when The indeterminate hepatocellular lesion where the fork is discharge versus the HCA pathway. EASL reports that hepatobiliary agents raise sensitivity for focal nodular hyperplasia to about 90%, with sensitivity and specificity for separating it from adenoma of 92–96.9% and 91–100% in the primary studies. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid EASL itself flags that the supporting meta-analysis rested on few, heterogeneous studies at high risk of bias, and the subsequent subtype-stratified meta-analysis shows where the specificity goes. Hepatobiliary-phase iso- or hyperintensity occurs in 0% of HNF1A-inactivated adenomas (95% CI 0-2%), 14% of inflammatory (2-31%) and 59% of beta-catenin-activated adenomas (26-88%). Specificity for focal nodular hyperplasia against all adenoma subtypes together is 89% (82-94%); it falls to 65% (44-80%) only against beta-catenin-activated and unclassified adenoma, after conventional MRI has already excluded the two commoner subtypes. State it that way round. Either way, a hepatobiliary-phase iso-intense lesion does not exclude the adenoma subtype with the highest malignant potential, and the paired sensitivity figures of 99% carry intervals of 57-100% and 53-100%, which are not measurements. Evidence & sources The authors' own explanation is that the low prevalence of beta-catenin-activated adenoma produced the earlier high performance figures. Thirty-three beta-catenin-activated adenomas across 28 studies, 16 of which were case reports or small series, is a thin basis for a 59% estimate, and all four studies supplying the diagnostic-performance figures were case-control in design and marked high risk of bias for patient selection — so the specificity numbers are functions of the sampling as much as of the test. It is the direction, not the precision, that matters for the discharge decision. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: HBP iso/hyperintensity: HNF1A 0% (95% CI 0–2), inflammatory 14% (2–31), β-catenin 59% (26–88); FNH specificity vs all HCA 89%, vs β-catenin/unclassified 65% Thirty-three β-catenin adenomas across 28 studies; accuracy studies case-control, high bias

EASL-reported: HBP agents raise FNH sensitivity to ~90%; FNH vs adenoma sensitivity 92–96.9%, specificity 91–100% (primary studies) Supporting meta-analysis: few, heterogeneous studies at high risk of bias

lead: Where focal nodular hyperplasia is multiple, look for the setting rather than counting the lesions.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Where focal nodular hyperplasia is multiple, look for the setting rather than counting the lesions. Indications Preferred when Focal nodular hyperplasia is multiple in 20-30% of cases and associated with liver haemangioma in 20%. Multiple lesions should prompt a search for an underlying vascular liver disease — Budd-Chiari syndrome, obliterative portal venopathy or porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, portal vein agenesis — in which EASL's own discharge rule no longer applies. The reason is quantitative: imaging displays hepatic nodules in 60-80% of patients with Budd-Chiari syndrome, usually under 4 cm, frequently more than ten, hypervascular and disseminated throughout a non-cirrhotic liver. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat multiplicity as evidence of malignancy, and do not discharge multiple focal nodular hyperplasia without asking why there are several. But do not read the 60-80% as a post-test probability either: it is the prevalence of nodules among patients already known to have Budd-Chiari syndrome, and neither guideline reports the inverse — the probability of underlying vascular disease given multiple hypervascular nodules in a non-cirrhotic liver. That conditional, which is the one a radiologist needs, does not exist in either document. Evidence & sources EASL's wording is precise: for a lesion typical of focal nodular hyperplasia follow-up is not necessary, unless there is underlying vascular liver disease (III, grade 2). It does not say what the interval should be in that case, and neither does this page. Grade D, downgraded from C: the rule is a III / grade 2 recommendation on one side and a superseded 2015 vascular-disease guideline on the other. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not biopsy a typical haemangioma, and do not biopsy a typical focal nodular hyperplasia.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not biopsy a typical haemangioma, and do not biopsy a typical focal nodular hyperplasia. Why Why Diagnose on imaging, name the features, discharge. Where the diagnosis genuinely cannot be reached on imaging, EASL accepts percutaneous biopsy of a haemangioma provided a cuff of normal parenchyma lies between the capsule and the lesion margin, reporting an overall diagnostic accuracy of 96%. Additional cautions Additional cautions The procedure is not free, it does not alter management in a typical lesion, and both EASL recommendations state that these are invasive procedures with risk that should only be pursued after consideration by an experienced multidisciplinary team. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Guideline-quoted: percutaneous haemangioma biopsy with a normal-parenchyma cuff, overall diagnostic accuracy 96% Only where imaging cannot reach the diagnosis; invasive, needs experienced MDT review

lead: Do not attach a surveillance interval to a typical haemangioma or focal nodular hyperplasia because the lesion is large.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not attach a surveillance interval to a typical haemangioma or focal nodular hyperplasia because the lesion is large. Why Why Discharge, with a plain explanation that the lesion may change size and that a slow incidental increase is not a cause for concern where the diagnosis is solid. Additional cautions Additional cautions EASL states that haemangiomas may change size during long-term follow-up with no relationship between size and complications, and that focal nodular hyperplasia is stable over time in the vast majority of cases. Size-triggered surveillance of these two lesions generates scans without generating decisions. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Focal fat and focal fat sparing in a characteristic location with no vessel displacement and no mass effect are definitively characterised on the study in front of you and need no follow-up.
text: Standard Evidence C Focal fat and focal fat sparing in a characteristic location with no vessel displacement and no mass effect are definitively characterised on the study in front of you and need no follow-up. Indications Preferred when The commonest finding of all — focal fatty sparing was the single largest contributor to the 15.1% benign-finding rate in 45,319 university-hospital ultrasound examinations, 2,839 cases (6.26%), mean size 20.6 mm, every one of them solitary and every one of them in the segment IV and gallbladder-bed location. It is a pseudolesion rather than a tumour, which is part of why that 15.1% figure cannot be read as a lesion prevalence. The ACR white paper states that the characteristic locations enable definitive characterisation without further follow-up, naming the region near the falciform ligament and the gallbladder fossa. The pattern review adds the diagnostic features: the distribution is heterogeneous or non-uniform, the margin may be geometric, and traversing vessels are not displaced. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Know the patterns that do not look like this. Multinodular and perivascular fat accumulation are specifically described as mimicking neoplastic, inflammatory or vascular conditions, and patchy foci of normal parenchyma in an otherwise fatty liver can be a genuinely difficult problem. Where the pattern is nodular rather than geometric, treat it as unresolved and go to clinical decision 3. Evidence & sources Chemical-shift or fat-fraction MRI settles the question directly when it matters; opposed-phase signal loss confirms fat. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: A transient hepatic attenuation or intensity difference is a perfusion phenomenon, not a mass: recognise it by its peripheral location, wedge shape and single-phase behaviour, and report no follow-up.
text: Standard Evidence C A transient hepatic attenuation or intensity difference is a perfusion phenomenon, not a mass: recognise it by its peripheral location, wedge shape and single-phase behaviour, and report no follow-up. Indications Preferred when The peripheral wedge of altered enhancement on the arterial phase that is invisible on the portal venous phase. The white paper's position is that characteristic locations and enhancement features allow definitive recognition and that these require no follow-up. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid A true lesion can sit at the apex of a perfusion abnormality, particularly in an at-risk liver, and a uniformly flash-filling observation is treated differently by risk category — in a high-risk patient the white paper advises MRI routinely for flash-filling lesions because of a higher probability of malignancy, while noting that in cirrhosis the majority of small wedge-shaped hypervascular lesions remain benign. Evidence & sources The phrase to avoid in a report is 'cannot exclude a lesion' when the finding is confined to one phase and has no counterpart on any other sequence. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: For a nodule without arterial hyperenhancement in an at-risk liver, assign the full LI-RADS category using all major and ancillary features; absence of hyperenhancement does not establish a benign or dysplastic nodule.
text: Standard Evidence C For a nodule without arterial hyperenhancement in an at-risk liver, assign the full LI-RADS category using all major and ancillary features; absence of hyperenhancement does not establish a benign or dysplastic nodule. Indications Preferred when Classic benign findings can be LR-1 or LR-2. Other observations without arterial hyperenhancement may be LR-3 or LR-4, depending on size and the remaining features. LR-3 generally receives repeat or alternative diagnostic imaging in 3–6 months; LR-4 warrants multidisciplinary diagnostic planning, which may include biopsy. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not describe either category as benign to the patient, and do not treat the numbers as precise. In the pooled systematic review, 13% (95% CI 8-22) of LR-2 and 38% (31-45) of LR-3 observations were confirmed HCC, and 14% (9-21) and 40% (31-50) respectively were confirmed malignant — a 3-to-6-month interval on a 38% probability is a watch, not reassurance. The authors explicitly label the LR-2 estimate provisional and at high risk of bias, and it rests on 223 observations for HCC and 162 for malignancy. Evidence & sources Two cautions on how the category is reached. The feature that most often lifts a nodule out of LR-2 or LR-3 on a follow-up study is threshold growth, and the 2022 individual-patient-data meta-analysis found no association between threshold growth and HCC (OR 1.6, 95% CI 0.8-3.4) — assessable in only 452 of 4,434 observations, and reported a second time in the same paper as 1.6 (0.7-3.6). Enhancing capsule is weak too, OR 2.4 (1.7-3.5), and reached significance in only one of the three analysis cohorts. Downgraded from B to C: every figure here comes from retrospective cohorts with structural verification bias. A cirrhotic liver with a nodule is, by definition, a liver that needs surveillance anyway; the surveillance programme and the nodule's follow-up interval should be one plan with one owner, not two. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Pooled review: confirmed HCC in 13% (95% CI 8–22) of LR-2 and 38% (31–45) of LR-3; confirmed malignant 14% (9–21) and 40% (31–50) LR-2 estimate provisional, high risk of bias; 223 observations

IPD meta-analysis: threshold growth not associated with HCC, OR 1.6 (95% CI 0.8–3.4), assessable in 452 of 4,434; enhancing capsule OR 2.4 (1.7–3.5) Capsule significant in one of three cohorts; retrospective, verification bias

lead: Vascular liver disorder with regenerative/FNH-like nodules: follow vascular-liver-disease guidance and team-set intervals, not LI-RADS intervals.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Vascular liver disorder with regenerative/FNH-like nodules: follow vascular-liver-disease guidance and team-set intervals, not LI-RADS intervals. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × In a liver with a vascular disorder, treat regenerative and focal-nodular-hyperplasia-like nodules as a specific entity to be managed under the vascular-liver-disease guideline, with an interval set by the multidisciplinary team rather than copied from LI-RADS. Indications Preferred when Budd-Chiari syndrome, obliterative portal venopathy, congenital portosystemic shunt, cardiac congestion, and what is now called porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder or non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis. These livers generate multiple arterially hyperenhancing benign nodules, LI-RADS explicitly excludes them from its population, and EASL's benign-tumour guideline removes its own no-follow-up rule for focal nodular hyperplasia in this setting. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Neither guideline states an interval for this situation. Setting one is a local decision and should be recorded as such rather than presented as guideline-derived. One thing has changed since this page was drafted and it changes what a report can safely say: the 2026 multisociety consensus makes nodular regenerative hyperplasia one of three major histological criteria for porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder, alongside muscularised portal venules and portal venule stenosis in 50% or more of portal tracts. Nodular regenerative hyperplasia is therefore no longer a benign nodular tumour to reassure a patient about; it is a marker of a vascular disorder, and EASL's benign-tumour guideline had already placed it outside its own scope on exactly that ground. Evidence & sources Grade D, and labelled as an operating rule rather than a result. Take the 2026 consensus for what it is: liver biopsy is mandatory for the diagnosis (95% agreement) with adequacy set at a 15 mm specimen including one fragment of 10 mm or more, but the criteria were derived in 88 European patients who all had specific signs of portal hypertension while the definition permits diagnosis without portal hypertension — which is exactly the patient an incidental nodular liver produces — a major criterion needs a sensitivity of only 0.10 provided specificity exceeds 0.95, and the diagnostic score was fitted to votes on 36 hypothetical scenarios and then shown to reproduce those votes, which is arithmetic consistency rather than diagnostic validity. The consensus says nothing about how incidentally detected nodular regenerative hyperplasia should be handled, and nothing about the harms of biopsying incidental nodularity. The EASL vascular-liver guidance this page otherwise relies on is the 2015 edition, superseded by a 2026 edition not obtained for this page. See the limited-evidence section and the approvals list. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Where a pseudolesion cannot be distinguished from a mass on the available study, re-image on the modality that answers the mechanism rather than repeating the one that raised the question.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Where a pseudolesion cannot be distinguished from a mass on the available study, re-image on the modality that answers the mechanism rather than repeating the one that raised the question. Indications Preferred when Chemical-shift MRI for a suspected fat phenomenon; a properly phased multiphase study for a suspected perfusion phenomenon. Both answer a mechanism question that a second unenhanced CT cannot. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not put a pseudolesion into a surveillance programme because the index study was ambiguous. Resolve it once. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not biopsy a geometric area of altered attenuation in a fatty liver.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not biopsy a geometric area of altered attenuation in a fatty liver. Why Why Confirm with chemical-shift imaging and report it as a fat phenomenon. Additional cautions Additional cautions The histology comes back as liver, the patient has had a procedure for nothing, and the next clinician reads the result as an inadequate sample. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not call a sub-centimetre nodule in a cirrhotic liver benign.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not call a sub-centimetre nodule in a cirrhotic liver benign. Why Why Assign the LI-RADS category, state the category's own management interval, and make sure the surveillance programme owns it. Additional cautions Additional cautions LR-1 is the only category in which no malignancy was found in the pooled review. LR-2 at 13% (95% CI 8-22) HCC and LR-3 at 38% (31-45) are not benign. The systematic review's authors do argue those figures indicate the need for a more active management strategy than the categories currently recommend — but they also call the LR-2 estimate provisional and at high risk of bias two paragraphs earlier, so this page states the number and does not adopt the recommendation. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Pooled review: HCC in 13% (95% CI 8–22) of LR-2 and 38% (31–45) of LR-3; no malignancy found only in LR-1 Authors call the LR-2 estimate provisional and at high risk of bias

lead: Decide before you set an interval what a stable repeat scan will change, and write that down.
text: Standard Evidence D Decide before you set an interval what a stable repeat scan will change, and write that down. Indications Preferred when Every indeterminate lesion. If the answer is that stability discharges the patient, say so and name the interval. If the answer is that stability changes nothing because the lesion will be resected either way, go to clinical decision 7 or clinical decision 8 now. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid An interval set without a stopping rule becomes indefinite surveillance. The ACR Incidental Findings Committee exists because of exactly this cascade — its founding paper describes the inclination to evaluate incidental findings as driven by physician and patient unwillingness to accept uncertainty, and names the potentially injurious and expensive cascade of tests and procedures as the harm. Evidence & sources Grade D by construction. No trial compares interval strategies for the indeterminate liver lesion, and this is an operating rule the programme chooses. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: A new sub-centimetre lesion in a patient with cancer, cirrhosis or other hepatic risk factors gets MRI at 3 to 6 months; the same lesion in a patient with no risk factor gets nothing.
text: Standard Evidence D A new sub-centimetre lesion in a patient with cancer, cirrhosis or other hepatic risk factors gets MRI at 3 to 6 months; the same lesion in a patient with no risk factor gets nothing. Indications Preferred when Apply the ACR CT-incidental algorithm to its intended population. A low-risk lesion <1 cm generally needs no further workup, but suspicious features may justify MRI. A high-risk lesion <1 cm generally receives MRI in 3–6 months, with surveillance CT an alternative in the appropriate oncology setting. Exactly 1.0 cm enters the 1.0–1.5 cm branch. The separate ACR Appropriateness Criteria also depend on how the lesion was first detected. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Four honest qualifications, and the first is the most important. Every number in this rule is a convention. The small-lesion stratum was 0.5 cm in the 2010 white paper and 1 cm in 2017; the interval was 6 months and became 3 to 6 months; the three risk tiers became two; the focal-nodular-hyperplasia-versus-adenoma threshold moved from 4 cm to 3 cm. Four thresholds changed in seven years with no new evidence cited and the same subcommittee chair on both occasions, and the committee states that its consensus process meets no specific formal national standard and that its content should not be considered standard of care. Second, the test being ordered is not reliable at that size: per-lesion sensitivity for colorectal metastases below 10 mm was 60.2% for MRI and 47.3% for CT. Third, in the 2,978-patient cancer cohort, 8.2% of small lesions were followed for under 6 months, remained stable and were still classed indeterminate — so a 3-month repeat often resolves nothing. Fourth, the white paper permits the radiologist to deviate from the under-1-cm rule even in low-risk patients when a lesion has suspicious features, in which case MRI is suggested. Evidence & sources Growth over a year is concerning; growth over a shorter timeframe is more urgent. That is the white paper's wording and it is a judgement, not a threshold — and growth was deliberately left out of the algorithm altogether because thresholds vary by risk category, then reinserted as narrative advice. Downgraded from C to D: an underived consensus threshold is grade D however firmly it is stated. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: A lesion that exists on one modality and not on another is a finding about the two studies, not about the liver — reconcile the studies before you work up the lesion.
text: Standard Evidence D A lesion that exists on one modality and not on another is a finding about the two studies, not about the liver — reconcile the studies before you work up the lesion. Indications Preferred when Compare the actual images side by side with the radiologist, not the two reports. Check phase timing, slice thickness, dose, breath-hold position, field of view and whether the segment was covered at all. Most one-modality lesions resolve as a timing or coverage difference, a perfusion phenomenon, or a lesion that one modality cannot show. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid There is no literature that quantifies how often a one-modality-only liver lesion proves malignant, and targeted searching does not find one — this page should not imply there is. What is documented is that even with a standardised protocol and a histological reference standard in a 1,349-patient multicentre study, 6.8% of lesions that were unclear on greyscale ultrasound could not be definitively diagnosed by contrast-enhanced ultrasound either, and most of those were benign. Residual uncertainty is normal and is not by itself a reason to escalate. Evidence & sources The local master workup CPG requires baseline and restaging studies used for selection to be available for central review with the priors, and requires the team to document whether repeat imaging is needed when the protocol was inadequate. Reconciliation is a named step, not an informal courtesy. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Where the lesion is LR-3 or LR-4 in an at-risk liver, use the category's own management pathway and put the case in front of the board rather than inventing a plan.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Where the lesion is LR-3 or LR-4 in an at-risk liver, use the category's own management pathway and put the case in front of the board rather than inventing a plan. Indications Preferred when LI-RADS v2018 specifies repeat or alternative diagnostic imaging in 3 to 6 months for LR-3, and multidisciplinary discussion with consideration of biopsy or shorter-interval imaging for LR-4. The pooled malignancy figures justify the difference — 40% (95% CI 31-50) of LR-3 and 80% (75-85) of LR-4 observations were confirmed malignant. Where the unresolved observation is in a cirrhotic liver, contrast-enhanced ultrasound is a reasonable next step before an interval is set: in a prospective multicentre cohort of 75 CT/MRI-indeterminate observations in 68 patients, CEUS re-categorised 25 of 75 (33.3%) with a management change that was correct in 24 of 25 (96.0%), and avoided follow-up imaging altogether in 21 of 75 (28.0%). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat LR-4 as a diagnosis and do not treat it as benign. It is 74% (67-80) HCC and 80% malignant in pooled retrospective data with acknowledged verification bias, which is exactly the range in which a board decision beats an algorithm. And do not over-read the CEUS study. Its population was 97.1% cirrhotic with 23.5% having a personal history of HCC, enrolled because a lesion had already been found — the baseline risk in that cohort was 25.9% HCC for a CT/MRI LR-3 observation and 52.4% for a non-characterizable one. In a liver that is not at risk the same appearances carry a far lower probability and none of those predictive values holds. The quoted 100% positive and negative predictive values rest on 7, 7, 6 and 1 observations with no confidence interval anywhere in the paper — 7 of 7 has an exact interval of roughly 59-100%. CEUS readers could see the CT or MRI in most cases, the reference standard was follow-up CT or MRI in 72% of observations, persistently LR-3 nodules at one year were counted non-malignant, and 74.1% of LR-3 observations remained indeterminate after CEUS. The study was funded in part by the manufacturer of the contrast agent. Evidence & sources An LR-M or mixed-phenotype observation needs diagnostic clarification at decision 8, often including tissue, rather than routine interval follow-up alone. HCC remains in the differential; route to a disease-specific treatment pathway after clarification. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Where an interval is chosen, name the owner, the date and the modality in the record, and close the loop in the registry.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Where an interval is chosen, name the owner, the date and the modality in the record, and close the loop in the registry. Indications Preferred when Every deferred lesion. The failure this prevents is the common one: an interval recommended in a radiology report that no clinician owns. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not leave the interval in the impression of a report as the only record of it. The local master workup CPG requires an assigned owner and due date for any conditional or incomplete disposition, and requires that such a case not be presented as approved.

lead: Do not keep re-imaging a lesion when the answer will not change management.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not keep re-imaging a lesion when the answer will not change management. Why Why Either resolve it with tissue, or resect it, or discharge it, and say which. Additional cautions Additional cautions Repeated imaging of a stable indeterminate lesion is the pathway's commonest source of a year's delay. The ACR's founding incidental-findings paper puts standardisation forward precisely to limit cost and reduce risk to patients from this cascade. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not resolve diagnostic uncertainty by escalating to a more invasive test before the cheaper one has been done properly.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not resolve diagnostic uncertainty by escalating to a more invasive test before the cheaper one has been done properly. Why Why An adequate multiphase MRI with the right agent, read against the right criteria, resolves most of these. Biopsy follows a failed adequate study, not a failed inadequate one. Additional cautions Additional cautions The ACR algorithm reserves direct biopsy for large, highly suspicious lesions in high-risk patients and otherwise recommends prompt MRI at minimum. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Suspected pCCA: do not perform transperitoneal or primary-tumor needle biopsy until the transplant pathway has been reviewed (local safety rule).
text: Standard Evidence D Suspected pCCA: do not perform transperitoneal or primary-tumor needle biopsy until the transplant pathway has been reviewed (local safety rule). Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Do not perform a transperitoneal or primary-tumour needle biopsy in a patient with suspected perihilar cholangiocarcinoma until the transplant pathway has been reviewed — this is the local programme's written safety rule and it is not a weighing of evidence. Indications Preferred when Any central, periductal or hilar lesion with biliary dilatation above it. The local Master Workup and Staging CPG carries this as its one critical safety rule, requires suspected perihilar disease to be flagged before any primary-tumour biopsy at the safety-screen step, requires regional-node sampling to follow the perihilar protocol, and requires the biopsy route to be documented for all cholangiocarcinoma candidates. From here the case is the perihilar cholangiocarcinoma pathway, which carries the route rules in full. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The supporting data are retrospective, small, and asymmetrically evidenced. Of 191 patients in a neoadjuvant-plus-transplant protocol, 16 had a transperitoneal fine-needle aspiration of the primary elsewhere; of the 6 whose aspirate was positive for adenocarcinoma, 5 of 6 (83%) had peritoneal metastases at operative staging, against 8% (14 of 175) in those not biopsied, p=0.0097. The 9 patients with non-diagnostic aspirates had no metastases — which means the excess fell entirely on diagnostic aspirates and reverse causation is not excluded. Six patients is not a measured seeding rate. Note the asymmetry in the surgical literature too: the seeding risk that justifies the prohibition is asserted with no rate and no denominator anywhere, while the competing harm is quantified — about 15% of patients resected for apparent perihilar cholangiocarcinoma prove on final pathology to have benign disease, a figure the review states twice from a single citation with no denominator or interval of its own. Evidence & sources The surgical review of this disease states the general position plainly: biopsy is typically avoided because of the risk of seeding metastases and the low yield of a bile duct brush, it is contraindicated outright in a transplant candidate, and a negative brushing or biopsy should not exclude the diagnosis or delay treatment. Read the review for what it is — a narrative paper by hepatobiliary and transplant surgeons with no search strategy, no quality appraisal and survival figures drawn entirely from uncontrolled surgical series — and take the safety rule from the local CPG rather than from it. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not biopsy a lesion you are going to resect anyway.
text: Standard Evidence C Do not biopsy a lesion you are going to resect anyway. Indications Preferred when The resectable colorectal liver metastasis in a patient with a confirmed colorectal primary, the resectable solitary mass in a fit patient where the operation is the same whatever the histology shows, and the lesion whose imaging phenotype and clinical context leave no competing diagnosis that would change the plan. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The quantitative case rests on two different kinds of evidence and they are not equally strong. For colorectal metastases, 17 of 90 biopsied patients (19%) had needle-track deposits and 4-year survival was 32.5% against 46.7%, p=0.008 — in a retrospective comparison in which every biopsy was done at a referring hospital, synchronous disease was present in 61% of the biopsied against 26% of the non-biopsied (p<0.001) with no multivariable adjustment, and the denominator is conditioned on having reached a resection. For hepatocellular carcinoma, a meta-analysis of 8 observational studies put needle-track seeding at 2.7% per patient (95% CI 1.8-4.0) or 0.9% per patient per year (0.6-1.3), with no case demonstrably affecting survival — but seven of the eight studies were retrospective, the largest and only prospective one found zero events in 239 patients, median follow-up in several series was shorter than the 17-month median time to seeding, and the abstract misstates its own units by a factor of 100. Do not quote one number for both diseases. Evidence & sources Procedural harm is quoted inconsistently across every source this page uses, and the group should know that before it writes a consent line. The ACR white paper gives morbidity of about 0.5% and mortality about 0.05% and prefers core biopsy over fine-needle aspiration; the same committee's 2010 document gave morbidity of 2.0% to 4.8%, with no explanation for the revision. The AASLD position paper gives severe bleeding at 1 in 2,500 to 1 in 10,000 and mortality at about 1 in 10,000 — but explicitly for the intercostal percutaneous approach in diffuse non-focal disease, while noting that death from bleeding may be greater after biopsy of a malignant lesion — and gives tumour seeding as 0.13% from one study, twenty-fold below the pooled HCC figure. If the route under discussion is endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy, a meta-analysis of 99 studies and 9,303 patients puts the overall adverse-event rate at 1.8% but the liver subgroup at 14.0% (95% CI 7.7-24.0) — on 133 patients in 4 studies with 18 events, 13 of which were abdominal pain, 3 bleeds and one suspected death from anticoagulant interruption that the paper's own conclusion denies occurred. No source in this depot reports comparable harm figures for the competing routes, which is a local approval item rather than a finding. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
