HCC meta-analysis of 8 observational studies: seeding 2.7% per patient (95% CI 1.8–4.0), 0.9% per patient per year (0.6–1.3); no case shown to affect survival Seven of eight retrospective; sole prospective study had zero events in 239
EUS-guided FNB meta-analysis, 99 studies/9,303 patients: overall adverse events 1.8%; liver subgroup 14.0% (95% CI 7.7–24.0) Liver subgroup 133 patients in 4 studies, 18 events (13 abdominal pain)

lead: Biopsy is the right move when imaging criteria cannot be applied or have failed, and the result will change the plan — and in a liver that is not at risk, that is the guideline position rather than a fallback.
text: Standard Evidence B Biopsy is the right move when imaging criteria cannot be applied or have failed, and the result will change the plan — and in a liver that is not at risk, that is the guideline position rather than a fallback. Indications Preferred when The indeterminate solid lesion in a non-cirrhotic liver; the lesion that remains indeterminate after an adequate multiphase MRI; the at-risk patient whose observation does not meet LR-5. EASL 2025 states that HCC diagnosis should be confirmed by tumour biopsy when the non-invasive imaging-based diagnostic criteria are not met (LoE 1), and that in patients without cirrhosis, chronic HBV or a history of HCC the diagnosis must be confirmed by biopsy. The ACR white paper's indication is the same shape — when MRI cannot confirm the diagnosis and the knowledge would alter management. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not biopsy to document a diagnosis nobody will act on. And do not biopsy without agreeing the specimen priorities first — the local CPG requires tissue priorities to be defined before limited material is consumed, in the order diagnostic confirmation, required biomarkers, broad sequencing, research, and tumour-informed circulating-tumour-DNA assay creation. Evidence & sources Route, platelet count, coagulation, ascites and the choice between percutaneous, transjugular and laparoscopic access are governed by the AASLD liver biopsy position paper and by local interventional radiology policy. EASL 2025 also asks that, if a biopsy is obtained, prognostic features including tumour differentiation and WHO subtype be reported (LoE 1, strong recommendation). Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Where the lesion is hepatocellular and the question is which adenoma subtype, accept that biopsy answers a question imaging increasingly cannot, and send the case to the HCA pathway with the subtype question stated.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Where the lesion is hepatocellular and the question is which adenoma subtype, accept that biopsy answers a question imaging increasingly cannot, and send the case to the HCA pathway with the subtype question stated. Indications Preferred when A hepatobiliary-phase iso-intense hepatocellular lesion in a normal liver, where 59% (95% CI 26-88%) of beta-catenin-activated adenomas show that same appearance and the hepatobiliary phase cannot separate beta-catenin-activated from inflammatory adenoma at all. The subtype decides risk, and this is the HCA pathway from here. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not biopsy a lesion that is already going to be resected on size or sex criteria — the explant or resection specimen answers the subtype question without a needle. Evidence & sources The ACR white paper's own subtype summary — inflammatory adenoma carrying the greatest haemorrhage risk and beta-catenin-activated adenoma the greatest malignancy risk — is the reason the subtype matters. EASL goes further and states that beta-catenin-activated adenoma cannot be identified, or distinguished from unclassified adenoma or from HCC, by any imaging technique, while simultaneously making a proven beta-catenin mutation an indication for resection. That circularity is the reason the question reaches a needle at all, and the HCA pathway carries it. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Where the result will not change management but the diagnosis is needed for a trial, a registry or a protocol, say that is the reason.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Where the result will not change management but the diagnosis is needed for a trial, a registry or a protocol, say that is the reason. Indications Preferred when Protocol-mandated tissue, molecular profiling for a named systemic therapy decision, or the assay-creation requirement for tumour-informed circulating tumour DNA. Naming the reason makes the risk-benefit explicit and makes the consent accurate. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not fold a protocol-driven biopsy into the clinical indication. They have different thresholds and different consent conversations. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not biopsy before the destination has been named.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not biopsy before the destination has been named. Why Why Resection, transplant pathway, systemic therapy or discharge — one of those, written down, before the needle. Additional cautions Additional cautions A biopsy obtained for convenience is the commonest way a curative option is lost in this pathway, and the local CPG's safety screen exists to catch it. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not accept a non-diagnostic result as reassurance.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not accept a non-diagnostic result as reassurance. Why Why Decide in advance what a negative or non-diagnostic result will change. If the answer is nothing, the patient needs a destination decision, not another needle. Additional cautions Additional cautions In the perihilar series the 9 non-diagnostic aspirates had no metastases while 5 of 6 diagnostic ones did — the same procedure, two entirely different implications — and the yield of brush cytology and biopsy in biliary strictures is low enough that the surgical review states plainly a negative result should not exclude the diagnosis or delay treatment. The same holds for a small nodule: in the one prospective series inside the hepatocellular-carcinoma seeding meta-analysis, 294 nodules of 2 cm or less were biopsied, 49 (17%) yielded no diagnosis, and 29 of those (10% of the whole series) later proved to be HCC that the aspirate had missed — 8 inadequate samples, 11 read as regenerative and 10 as dysplastic. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: An LR-5 observation in an at-risk liver is hepatocellular carcinoma and this is the HCC pathway from here — including the transplant question, which that page opens.
text: Standard Evidence C An LR-5 observation in an at-risk liver is hepatocellular carcinoma and this is the HCC pathway from here — including the transplant question, which that page opens. Indications Preferred when Every LR-5 observation. 94% (95% CI 92-96) of pooled LR-5 observations were confirmed HCC and 97% (95-99) were confirmed malignant, which is what justifies treating without tissue in this population and nowhere else. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid 6% of pooled LR-5 observations were not HCC and 3% were not malignant, and the pooled data are retrospective with acknowledged verification and incorporation bias. The size of that bias has been measured: in a 43-study meta-analysis, the CT/MRI LR-5 HCC proportion was 92.3% where pathology was the reference standard against 97% where a composite imaging standard was used (p=0.01), and for LR-4 it was 63.4% against 81.2% (p=0.03) — so between 5 and 18 percentage points of the headline figures come from confirming HCC partly by its LR-5 appearance on another modality. LR-5 is not a histological diagnosis, and a lesion with an atypical clinical context deserves the board's attention before a treatment commitment. Downgraded from B to C for that reason. Evidence & sources The local master workup CPG sets the staging bundle for this destination: multiphasic liver CT or MRI, chest CT, alpha-fetoprotein, and assessment of LI-RADS and OPTN class and vascular invasion, with biopsy only when imaging is atypical or a mixed or intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma diagnosis is suspected and the multidisciplinary team agrees. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: An LR-M observation is probably or definitely malignant but is not specific for HCC. Clarify the diagnosis before choosing the HCC, iCCA, mixed-tumour or metastatic treatment pathway.
text: Standard Evidence C An LR-M observation is probably or definitely malignant but is not specific for HCC. Clarify the diagnosis before choosing the HCC, iCCA, mixed-tumour or metastatic treatment pathway. Indications Preferred when The differential includes iCCA, combined HCC–CCA and atypical HCC. Historical pooled CT/MRI categories reported 93% malignancy and 36% HCC in LR-M; these are selected, earlier-version cohorts rather than a histologic diagnosis for the individual patient. Discuss tissue sampling and the safest route in the multidisciplinary team. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid LR-M is not a diagnosis of cholangiocarcinoma, and on contrast-enhanced ultrasound the mix is different again — but less precisely than this page previously said. In a meta-analysis of 1,046 CEUS LR-M observations, 54% (44-65) were HCC and 40% (28-53) non-HCC malignancy, with heterogeneity of I-squared 84% and 88%; the widely quoted 94% malignant is the arithmetic sum of those two separately pooled proportions, carries no confidence interval anywhere, and does not match the raw counts, which give 1,011 of 1,046 or 96.7%. Removing a single case-control study moves the HCC proportion from 54% to 59% and halves the heterogeneity, 31% of the non-HCC malignancies have no specified diagnosis, and the non-HCC proportion is 35% in Asian and hepatitis-B-dominant studies against 54% in Western ones. The direction is reliable — a CEUS LR-M carries a materially higher chance of being HCC than a CT or MRI LR-M — and the numbers are not. Tissue decides, and clinical decision 7 governs the route by which it is obtained. Note too the surgical position: no imaging feature is unique to intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, so a peripherally enhancing mass in a non-cirrhotic liver cannot be called cholangiocarcinoma, metastasis or HCC on imaging alone. Evidence & sources Washout timing is the practical discriminator at the scanner. In a 320-patient subanalysis, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma showed early portal-venous washout in the tumour centre in 85.8% of cases against 49.8% for HCC, initial peripheral enhancement in 85.7% against 61%, and late-phase hypoenhancement in 92.9% against 75%; cirrhosis was present in 76.9% of the HCC patients and 16.7% of the cholangiocarcinoma patients. That subanalysis is one of the papers on this page still read from its abstract only. Downgraded from B to C. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Meta-analysis, 1,046 CEUS LR-M observations: HCC 54% (44–65), non-HCC malignancy 40% (28–53); I² 84% and 88% Quoted 94% malignant is an unpooled sum; 31% of non-HCC malignancies unspecified

lead: Route confirmed colorectal liver metastases to CRLM and confirmed neuroendocrine liver disease to NELM. A hepatocellular lesion in a normal liver requires positive assessment for HCA and exclusion of HCC; exclusion of FNH alone does not diagnose HCA.
text: Standard Evidence D Route confirmed colorectal liver metastases to CRLM and confirmed neuroendocrine liver disease to NELM. A hepatocellular lesion in a normal liver requires positive assessment for HCA and exclusion of HCC; exclusion of FNH alone does not diagnose HCA. Indications Preferred when As soon as the primary or the entity is established. Each destination page carries its own resectability criteria, its own sequencing and its own biopsy rules, and routing early is how those rules get applied rather than discovered late. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Early cancer-roadmap referral does not require the colorectal primary already resected or extrahepatic disease absent; those factors affect treatment and transplant assessment later. Confirm the likely origin, and obtain expert pathology review of neuroendocrine grade and differentiation when relevant. Evidence & sources Hepatic epithelioid haemangioendothelioma is in the programme's scope but has no page in this set; the local CPG requires expert pathology review for it because of diagnostic overlap, and it goes to the board as its own case. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Where the lesion looks hepatocellular but the liver is normal and the patient is male, or the lesion is over 5 cm, route to the HCA pathway with those features stated rather than attempting to resolve the subtype here.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Where the lesion looks hepatocellular but the liver is normal and the patient is male, or the lesion is over 5 cm, route to the HCA pathway with those features stated rather than attempting to resolve the subtype here. Indications Preferred when When HCA is suspected, obtain appropriate imaging and expert review, with tissue where it will change management. Excluding FNH alone does not establish HCA; exclude HCC and other mimics before definitive treatment routing. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not discharge a hepatocellular lesion as focal nodular hyperplasia on hepatobiliary-phase uptake alone when the clinical context is wrong for it. Specificity against all adenoma subtypes together is 89% (95% CI 82-94), and 65% (44-80) against beta-catenin-activated and unclassified adenoma once the commoner subtypes have been excluded on conventional MRI — and 59% of beta-catenin-activated adenomas, the subtype with the highest malignant potential, take up the agent. Evidence & sources Incidental adenoma is rare — 19 cases, 0.04%, in 45,319 hospital ultrasound examinations, with a mean confirmed size of 39.0 mm and confirmation required by CEUS, MRI or histology — so an incidental hepatocellular lesion that is not focal nodular hyperplasia deserves a second look at the history, particularly oestrogen and androgen exposure and glycogen storage disease. EASL's own figure for adenoma prevalence is 0.001-0.004%, three to four orders of magnitude lower, and neither document reconciles with the other. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Where the lesion cannot be assigned to a single destination, send it to the board as an unassigned case with the competing possibilities named, rather than entering it on the closest-looking page.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Where the lesion cannot be assigned to a single destination, send it to the board as an unassigned case with the competing possibilities named, rather than entering it on the closest-looking page. Indications Preferred when The mass with both hepatocellular and cholangiocytic features, the discordant marker profile, the lesion whose phenotype changed between studies. The cHCC-CCA pathway exists for the first of these and should be named explicitly. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not assign an LR-M observation to HCC or cholangiocarcinoma treatment from the category alone. Establish the likely histology and extent through multidisciplinary review and appropriate sampling. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not route a patient out of this page without a named destination, a named owner and a date.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not route a patient out of this page without a named destination, a named owner and a date. Why Why One destination page, one owner, one date, recorded in the conference note alongside the staging adequacy and the allocation classification, as the local CPG's minimum conference note requires. Additional cautions Additional cautions A recommendation to 'refer to hepatobiliary' with no named destination is how a patient re-enters this pathway six months later at the same assessment.

lead: Do not discharge a patient from this page without telling them, in writing, what the lesion is and that no follow-up is needed.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not discharge a patient from this page without telling them, in writing, what the lesion is and that no follow-up is needed. Why Why A discharge letter that names the entity, states the criteria it met, and says explicitly that no further imaging is required. Additional cautions Additional cautions An unexplained benign finding is re-investigated by the next clinician who sees the report. The discharge rule only works if it is communicated. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Obtain adequate pancreas-protocol cross-sectional imaging when the referral study cannot stage the tumour: contrast CT is preferred, and high-quality contrast MRI is an accepted alternative.
text: Standard Evidence C Obtain adequate pancreas-protocol cross-sectional imaging when the referral study cannot stage the tumour: contrast CT is preferred, and high-quality contrast MRI is an accepted alternative. Indications Preferred when Every patient referred with an outside scan. NCCN reports that re-imaging patients who arrived with a non-pancreas-protocol CT changed the stage and the management in 56% of cases at a single institution, and that where CT showed a resectable tumour 70% to 85% of patients went on to resection. Both figures are NCCN's citation of single-institution series and are not in the reporting-template paper this item is referenced to. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not accept thick sections, positive oral contrast or a single post-contrast phase. Neutral oral contrast only, because positive contrast degrades the 3D and maximum-intensity-projection reformats that show the vessels. Sections as thin as the scanner allows, under 3 mm and preferably submillimetre, reconstructed at 2–3 mm with multiplanar reformats. Evidence & sources Accuracy decays with time because the disease moves: NCCN prefers imaging within four weeks of surgery; reassess timing in context rather than using it as an absolute initial-review exclusion. Sensitivity for small hepatic and peritoneal deposits is limited however good the protocol is, and protocol quality is not the whole of the problem — in SWOG S1505, 43 of 146 patients centrally reviewed (29%) did not meet the trial's own resectability criteria, 51% of them for arterial interface and 65% for suspicion of distant disease, and adding a mandatory site radiologist checklist moved that only from 33% to 26%. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Report it against the Society of Abdominal Radiology and American Pancreatic Association template, in degrees of vessel contact — not in adjectives.
text: Standard Evidence D Report it against the Society of Abdominal Radiology and American Pancreatic Association template, in degrees of vessel contact — not in adjectives. Indications Preferred when Every staging report. The template covers morphology (appearance in the parenchymal phase, size, location relative to the SMV, duct and biliary cut-off), the arterial evaluation (celiac axis, SMA, common hepatic artery, with vessel contact, soft-tissue contact, hazy attenuation or stranding, focal narrowing and contour irregularity), the venous evaluation (main portal vein and SMV, thrombus, collaterals) and the extrapancreatic evaluation (liver lesions, peritoneal or omental nodules, ascites, suspicious nodes). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Words like abutment, encasement and involvement are defined in the template by degree — 180 degrees or less of circumferential contact is abutment, more than 180 degrees is encasement — so a report that uses them without the degrees cannot be mapped onto the resectability categories and forces the board to re-read the scan. Evidence & sources Downgraded to D on the full-text read. The template is expert consensus from a single meeting at the American Pancreatic Association annual meeting in November 2011, with no Delphi process, no voting, no reported level of agreement, no described literature search and no validation of any kind — the paper does not show that using it changes report completeness, inter-reader agreement, board decisions, resection rates or margins, and reports no inter-reader reproducibility for measuring circumferential contact, which is the measurement the whole template rests on. Variant arterial anatomy — accessory or replaced right hepatic artery, replaced common hepatic artery, and the origin of the replaced or accessory vessel — must still be named whether or not it is in contact, because it changes the operation. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Offer genetic counselling and germline testing to every patient with pancreatic adenocarcinoma, regardless of family history.
text: Standard Evidence C Offer genetic counselling and germline testing to every patient with pancreatic adenocarcinoma, regardless of family history. Indications Preferred when At diagnosis, in parallel with staging, so a result exists before systemic therapy choices are made. In 3,030 patients with pancreatic adenocarcinoma enrolled in the Mayo Clinic pancreas registry between 2000 and 2016, deleterious germline variants in six genes were found in 5.5% overall — CDKN2A (OR 12.33, 95% CI 5.43–25.61), TP53 (6.70, 2.52–14.95), MLH1 (6.66, 1.94–17.53), BRCA2 (6.20, 4.62–8.17), ATM (5.71, 4.38–7.33) and BRCA1 (2.58, 1.54–4.05). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not use family history to select who is tested. In the same cohort the yield was 7.9% with a family history of pancreatic cancer and 5.2% without — a difference far too small to triage on. But do not quote 5.5% as the proportion with an actionable result either: the figure is driven mostly by ATM and BRCA2, and of the six genes only BRCA1/2 has a randomised treatment consequence in this disease, with MLH1 acting through mismatch-repair status rather than through the gene itself. Evidence & sources Downgraded to C on the full-text read. This is a clinic-based case series at a tertiary referral centre compared with race and ethnicity matched public sequencing databases (ExAC non-TCGA and gnomAD) rather than with a recruited control group, so it is exposed to differential variant calling and coverage between cases and controls; the CDKN2A and MLH1 intervals rest on a handful of carriers each, and multiplicity across 21 genes and several subgroup strata is not controlled. It is a prevalence and association study: it does not estimate penetrance, carriage was not associated with overall survival (HR 0.86, P=.09), and it does not show that testing changes outcomes. A germline result still drives cascade testing of relatives, which is a separate benefit from the treatment decision. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Registry case series (n=3,030): deleterious germline variants in six genes in 5.5%; 7.9% with vs 5.2% without family history Compared with public databases, not recruited controls; 5.5% is not the actionable proportion

lead: Treat CA 19-9 as a baseline measurement whose value depends on the bilirubin and the patient's Lewis antigen status, not as a diagnostic test.
text: Standard Evidence C Treat CA 19-9 as a baseline measurement whose value depends on the bilirubin and the patient's Lewis antigen status, not as a diagnostic test. Indications Preferred when Measure baseline CA 19-9 with the bilirubin recorded. If drainage is indicated, prefer reassessment after adequate decompression and improvement in bilirubin. A predrainage value may still be obtained, with its limited interpretation documented. Use serial values alongside imaging and clinical response. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid An elevated CA 19-9 does not indicate cancer or advanced disease — it rises with biliary obstruction, cholangitis and benign or malignant inflammation. It is undetectable in Lewis-antigen-negative individuals, in whom NCCN suggests obtaining CEA and CA-125 instead. Evidence & sources NCCN grades surveillance CA 19-9 after resection as category 2B, and states there are no data that a rising marker leads to earlier intervention or better outcomes. Treat the two uses — baseline and surveillance — as separate questions. The one place CA 19-9 has randomised-adjacent support is as a response measure: ESMO's 2023 guideline cites a pooled analysis of 17 studies and 2,242 patients in which a fall of more than 50% or normalisation after neoadjuvant treatment was associated with better overall survival (P<0.0001). Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Use high-quality pancreas-protocol contrast MRI as an alternative to CT when appropriate, and as a problem-solving study for indeterminate findings.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Use high-quality pancreas-protocol contrast MRI as an alternative to CT when appropriate, and as a problem-solving study for indeterminate findings. Indications Preferred when Three situations: a CT-indeterminate liver lesion, a suspected tumour not visible on CT (the isoattenuating tumour, which the template asks to be reported as non-measurable), and iodinated contrast allergy. The protocol is axial T2 single-shot fast spin echo, in- and opposed-phase gradient echo, fat-suppressed T2, diffusion-weighted imaging, dynamic post-contrast 3D fat-suppressed gradient echo in pancreatic, portal venous and equilibrium phases at 2–3 mm, and coronal MRCP under 3 mm. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Ensure the MRI adequately assesses arterial and venous relationships and distant disease. If both iodinated and gadolinium contrast are contraindicated, individualize noncontrast imaging and supplementary assessment with radiology.

lead: FDG-PET/CT or PET/MRI after the pancreas-protocol CT in patients with high-risk features, to look for extrapancreatic metastases.
text: Reasonable Evidence C FDG-PET/CT or PET/MRI after the pancreas-protocol CT in patients with high-risk features, to look for extrapancreatic metastases. Indications Preferred when NCCN defines high-risk features as equivocal or indeterminate imaging findings, markedly elevated CA 19-9, a large primary tumour, or large regional lymph nodes. PET before and after starting neoadjuvant therapy also gives the metabolic arm of the three-metric response assessment. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid It is not a substitute for high-quality contrast-enhanced CT and does not belong in routine staging. Order it to answer a question, and name the question. Evidence & sources Use PET selectively for staging when its result would change the treatment plan; it does not replace pancreas-protocol cross-sectional imaging. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: EUS in selected cases where it is complementary to CT — but not as a routine staging tool.
text: Reasonable Evidence C EUS in selected cases where it is complementary to CT — but not as a routine staging tool. Indications Preferred when Separating a benign from a malignant stricture, evaluating a periampullary mass, and characterising a cystic lesion. Across 20 studies and 726 cases, EUS had sensitivity 0.72 and specificity 0.90 for T1–2 and 0.90 and 0.72 for T3–4. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The T-stage figures are not good enough to overturn a protocol CT, and the procedure is operator dependent. Where EUS is being done anyway, combine it with ERCP in one anaesthetic — see the tissue and drainage assessment. Evidence & sources The sensitivity and specificity figures are carried in the NCCN discussion text supplied to this page, not in any paper read in full for this depot; the primary reports were not retrieved. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not let a stent be placed before the staging scan in a patient who is not septic and whose bilirubin is not rising.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not let a stent be placed before the staging scan in a patient who is not septic and whose bilirubin is not rising. Why Why Where urgent decompression is unavoidable, document why, and complete pancreas-protocol imaging promptly afterwards. Additional cautions Additional cautions Drainage is not routinely recommended before planned upfront surgery, so a stent placed for convenience adds a procedure, its complications, and a degraded baseline CA 19-9, for no benefit.

lead: Do not call a scan negative for metastases and treat that as proof.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not call a scan negative for metastases and treat that as proof. Why Why Say what the scan can and cannot exclude, and decide at the board whether staging laparoscopy or PET is worth adding in this patient. Additional cautions Additional cautions CT sensitivity for small hepatic and peritoneal metastases is limited, and the resectability criteria are deliberately built to favour specificity over sensitivity so that no resectable patient is denied an operation. That design means occult metastatic disease is expected, not surprising.

lead: Multidisciplinary staging by vessel-contact criteria: exactly one of resectable, borderline resectable, locally advanced or metastatic.
text: Standard Evidence D Multidisciplinary staging by vessel-contact criteria: exactly one of resectable, borderline resectable, locally advanced or metastatic. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Place the patient in exactly one of resectable, borderline resectable, locally advanced or metastatic, by consensus at a multidisciplinary meeting, using the stated degrees of contact. Indications Preferred when Every non-metastatic patient, before any treatment is offered, because every later assessment on this page hangs off which box was ticked. The thresholds are in the quick reference. NCCN is explicit that decisions about resectability status should be made in consensus at multidisciplinary meetings, and ESMO's 2023 guideline asks for the anatomical NCCN criteria to be read alongside the biological and conditional features of the International Association of Pancreatology consensus [III, B], with board discussion in an expert centre [III, A]. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat the thresholds as biologically derived. The 180-degree cut-point was adopted into the Society of Abdominal Radiology and American Pancreatic Association consensus reporting statement from the NCCN criteria of the time rather than derived or validated in it, no outcome study derived it, no inter-reader reproducibility data for measuring circumferential contact were presented with it, and the criteria for resectable disease were deliberately written to favour specificity over sensitivity so that a potentially resectable patient is not denied an operation. They are a shared language, not a prognostic model. Evidence & sources Downgraded to D: the category is assigned against a consensus threshold nobody derived. It is also assigned less reliably than the page previously implied. In SWOG S1505, which required formal surgical consultation plus a resectability checklist at 20-plus experienced US centres, central radiology review found 43 of 146 patients (29%) did not meet the trial's resectability criteria — 22 (51%) had arterial interface, 15 (35%) venous interface of 180 degrees or more and 28 (65%) suspicion of distant disease — and all of them had already started protocol therapy. After neoadjuvant therapy, solid tumour contact may be replaced by increased hazy density or stranding around the peripancreatic vessels; NCCN asks for this to be reported on both the staging and the follow-up scans so that the two are comparable. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Central radiology review: 43 of 146 (29%) did not meet resectability criteria; arterial interface 22 (51%), venous ≥180° 15 (35%), suspected distant disease 28 (65%) All had already started protocol therapy despite surgical consultation and checklist

lead: A distant metastasis, including a non-regional nodal metastasis, rules out upfront resection regardless of how favourable the local anatomy is.
text: Standard Evidence C A distant metastasis, including a non-regional nodal metastasis, rules out upfront resection regardless of how favourable the local anatomy is. Indications Preferred when State this at the board before the anatomy is discussed, so the discussion does not drift into an operative plan for a stage IV patient. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let a technically beautiful local picture pull a metastatic patient toward resection. NCCN's footnote is unambiguous: distant metastasis, regardless of anatomic resectability, implies disease that should not be treated with upfront resection.

lead: Positive cytology from washings taken at laparoscopy or laparotomy is equivalent to M1 disease — and if a resection has already been done, the patient is treated for M1 disease.
text: Standard Evidence C Positive cytology from washings taken at laparoscopy or laparotomy is equivalent to M1 disease — and if a resection has already been done, the patient is treated for M1 disease. Indications Preferred when Send washings whenever the abdomen is entered for staging or resection, and record the result in the operative note so the oncologist does not have to ask for it. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat a positive washing as a technical curiosity in an otherwise successful resection. It changes the postoperative pathway from adjuvant to metastatic.

lead: Selective staging laparoscopy, with intraoperative ultrasound as an adjunct, where occult metastatic disease is suspected on imaging or clinical grounds.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Selective staging laparoscopy, with intraoperative ultrasound as an adjunct, where occult metastatic disease is suspected on imaging or clinical grounds. Indications Preferred when Body and tail lesions, equivocal peritoneal or hepatic findings, markedly elevated CA 19-9, and before committing a patient to a long neoadjuvant course. Avoiding an unnecessary laparotomy is achievable in an estimated 23% of patients planned for curative-intent surgery. In a prospective review of 838 patients judged resectable on imaging, 14% were unresectable at laparoscopy — 21% when only pancreatic adenocarcinoma was counted. Preoperative CA 19-9 above 100 U/mL, or above 215 U/mL, is associated with a greater likelihood of a positive finding. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid NCCN does not regard staging laparoscopy as a substitute for poor-quality preoperative imaging, and routine use remains controversial. Its yield depends entirely on how good the CT was and how likely metastatic disease is in that patient. Evidence & sources The concern that laparoscopy promotes trocar-site recurrence and peritoneal progression rests on clinical observation and on animal and in vitro data; the one retrospective study addressing it (n=235) found no significant association with poor outcomes. That is weak evidence in both directions. Laparoscopy can be repeated after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, before planned chemoradiation or surgery. Note that in PREOPANC staging laparoscopy was mandatory in the neoadjuvant arm (114 of 119) and discretionary in the surgery arm, and 13 of the 28 patients who never started neoadjuvant treatment were found metastatic at that laparoscopy — which is both a demonstration of its yield and the reason that trial's R0 and nodal comparisons are not symmetrical. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: PREOPANC: staging laparoscopy in 114 of 119 neoadjuvant-arm pts, discretionary in surgery arm; 13 of 28 never starting neoadjuvant therapy were metastatic at it Mandatory in one arm only, so the trial's R0 and nodal comparisons are asymmetric

lead: Use the term locally advanced only at the time of initial diagnosis, and say so when you use it.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Use the term locally advanced only at the time of initial diagnosis, and say so when you use it. Indications Preferred when NCCN states the term should only be used at diagnosis, that locally advanced does not imply unresectable tumour, and that once any neoadjuvant therapy has been delivered the criteria for resection should be based on the biological response to treatment. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid A label applied at diagnosis and never revisited is the commonest way a patient who could have been operated on is not. Where there is a response, a second opinion at a centre with expertise in vascular resection and reconstruction is recommended even if the tumour is still called technically unresectable.

lead: Do not close the case on one radiologist's word unresectable.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not close the case on one radiologist's word unresectable. Why Why Send it to the board with the degrees of contact, and record who agreed the category and on what date. Additional cautions Additional cautions This is a sequence and governance error rather than a judgement call: the guideline requires multidisciplinary consensus, and a single-reader determination removes the patient from every curative assessment without one.

lead: Do not re-stage off a post-neoadjuvant scan alone and declare the operation off.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not re-stage off a post-neoadjuvant scan alone and declare the operation off. Why Why Judge response on at least two of three metrics — radiologic, biochemical, metabolic — and explore if there is no extrapancreatic progression. Additional cautions Additional cautions Retrospective studies show that radiographic response does not correlate with pathologic response or with margin-negative resection in borderline resectable disease, and that imaging characteristics are an unreliable indicator of resectability after neoadjuvant therapy. NCCN's own instruction is that if no apparent tumour shrinkage is seen and there is no extrapancreatic progression, surgery should still be attempted.

lead: High suspicion with planned upfront resection: biopsy confirmation is unnecessary; a nondiagnostic biopsy should not delay surgery.
text: Standard Evidence C High suspicion with planned upfront resection: biopsy confirmation is unnecessary; a nondiagnostic biopsy should not delay surgery. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × In a patient going straight to resection with a high clinical suspicion, do not wait for tissue — biopsy proof of malignancy is not required before resection, and a non-diagnostic biopsy should not delay it. Indications Preferred when A pancreas-protocol CT showing a resectable mass with no alternative explanation, in a fit patient, where the operative plan would not change whatever the needle showed. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not carry this permission into any other setting. A pathologic diagnosis is necessary before neoadjuvant therapy, and for locally advanced, borderline resectable and metastatic disease — which is to say for almost everybody who is not going directly to theatre. Evidence & sources Treated as a licence to skip tissue in a borderline resectable patient, this becomes the error that starts chemotherapy without a diagnosis. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: EUS-guided needle biopsy with a latest-generation core needle is the preferred route, and the extra passes are taken at the same sitting and banked.
text: Standard Evidence C EUS-guided needle biopsy with a latest-generation core needle is the preferred route, and the extra passes are taken at the same sitting and banked. Indications Preferred when Every patient who needs tissue and has non-metastatic disease. NCCN prefers EUS over CT-guided biopsy for better diagnostic yield, better safety, and potentially lower risk of peritoneal seeding than the percutaneous approach. Two extra needle passes beyond the diagnostic passes should be taken where safe and feasible and stored for future next-generation sequencing. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Biopsy the lesion that will give the highest stage — a liver deposit, not the primary, if both are there — and use image-guided biopsy rather than EUS for liver lesions suspicious for metastasis. Sampling only the primary in a patient with a liver lesion wastes the procedure. Evidence & sources In metastatic disease, obtaining enough tissue for sequencing is part of the indication, not an afterthought. The seeding argument for EUS over the percutaneous route is NCCN's wording — potentially lower risk — and is not a measured rate. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: When a jaundiced patient needs both tissue sampling and biliary drainage, consider EUS biopsy and ERCP during the same anaesthesia session.
text: Standard Evidence D When a jaundiced patient needs both tissue sampling and biliary drainage, consider EUS biopsy and ERCP during the same anaesthesia session. Indications Preferred when Best practice per NCCN in obstructive jaundice. It saves a procedure, a sedation and usually a week. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not split them between services and dates by default; that is how patients accumulate procedures and lose weeks before any treatment starts.

lead: No routine drainage before imminent surgery. Drain for cholangitis/fever, severe symptomatic jaundice or delayed surgery, including neoadjuvant therapy.
text: Standard Evidence B No routine drainage before imminent surgery. Drain for cholangitis/fever, severe symptomatic jaundice or delayed surgery, including neoadjuvant therapy. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Biliary drainage is not routinely recommended before an operation that is about to happen — drain for cholangitis or fever, for severely symptomatic jaundice, or because surgery is being delayed, including for neoadjuvant therapy. Indications Preferred when Where drainage is indicated it is best accomplished with an endoscopically placed stent. For a jaundiced patient going on to neoadjuvant therapy, decompression is necessary before therapy starts; NCCN describes it as well tolerated with minimal increase in perioperative morbidity, and ESMO recommends endoscopic drainage where bilirubin exceeds 250 micromol/L in patients with cholangitis, those planned for neoadjuvant treatment, or those whose surgery will be delayed beyond 2 weeks [I, B]. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Routine drainage before an imminent operation causes harm: in a multicentre randomised trial of 202 patients with obstructive jaundice from pancreatic head cancer, serious complications within 120 days occurred in 75 of 102 (74%) of the stented group versus 37 of 94 (39%) with surgery alone, relative risk for surgery alone 0.54 (95% CI 0.41–0.71), P<0.001. Complications attributable to drainage occurred in 47 of 102 (46%) versus 2 of 94 (2%) — cholangitis in 27 (26%), stent exchange needed in 31 (30%), occlusion in 15 (15%), pancreatitis in 7 (7%). Evidence & sources Both halves of that trial matter, and so do its boundaries. Surgical complications did not differ significantly (35 of 94 [37%] versus 48 of 102 [47%], RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.57–1.11), nor did mortality from a protocol-specified complication (4 [4%] versus 9 [9%], RR 0.48, 0.15–1.51) or resection rate (67% versus 56%, P=0.11) — so the excess was in drainage-related events and readmissions rather than in the operation, and the trial does not show that drainage makes a pancreatoduodenectomy safer or less safe. Three limits decide how far it travels. It used plastic stents left for 4 to 6 weeks, which is where the cholangitis and exchange rates come from; bilirubin was capped at 250 micromol/L, excluding the most deeply jaundiced; and neoadjuvant chemotherapy was an exclusion criterion, so the trial says nothing about bridging a patient through months of preoperative treatment, which is now the commonest reason to stent. Its control arm also required an operation within one week of diagnosis, guaranteed by dedicated theatre capacity at all 13 hospitals — a unit that cannot deliver that has not got the comparator the trial tested, and delay without drainage is not what was studied. Overall mortality in the trial was 7%, at centres required to perform only 10 resections a year, and 15 of 196 patients (8%) did not have adenocarcinoma on final pathology. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Preoperative stenting vs surgery alone: serious complications within 120 days 74% vs 39%; RR (surgery alone) 0.54 (95% CI 0.41–0.71), P<0.001 Plastic stents; bilirubin ≤250 µmol/L; neoadjuvant therapy excluded; surgical complications NS

lead: Choose the stent for the diagnostic state the patient is in, and keep it as short as feasible.
text: Standard Evidence D Choose the stent for the diagnostic state the patient is in, and keep it as short as feasible. Indications Preferred when Self-expanding metal stents are preferable to plastic. If the tissue diagnosis is not certain, use a fully covered SEMS, because it can be removed or exchanged — and it can be removed for better EUS visualisation if the biopsy has to be repeated, then replaced. Once the diagnosis is confirmed, a non-removable partially covered or bare SEMS may be used, since migration is less frequent. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Plastic stents are for palliation in patients with a predicted survival of less than 3 months. A long stent, or an uncovered metal stent placed before the diagnosis is settled, removes options for no gain. Evidence & sources Downgraded to D: no comparative trial supports any of this. NCCN notes stents are an evolving technology, that any stent can occlude, that covered stents may give more durable patency because they prevent tumour ingrowth but may migrate, and that there are no obvious differences between covered and uncovered stents. Partially covered stents were introduced for this reason and still migrate in a substantial number of patients. The one randomised trial of preoperative drainage in this depot used plastic stents only, so the preference for metal rests on practice rather than on a comparison. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: CT-guided biopsy where EUS-guided biopsy is not feasible.
text: Reasonable Evidence D CT-guided biopsy where EUS-guided biopsy is not feasible. Indications Preferred when A patient who cannot have EUS, or in whom the target is not reachable endosonographically. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid It is second choice in non-metastatic disease on yield, safety and the seeding question, so do not reach for it first out of scheduling convenience.

lead: Percutaneous biliary drainage, or EUS-guided biliary drainage at a high-volume centre, after a failed ERCP.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Percutaneous biliary drainage, or EUS-guided biliary drainage at a high-volume centre, after a failed ERCP. Indications Preferred when NCCN's sequence is to reattempt ERCP at a high-volume centre first, then consider a percutaneous drain, with EUS-guided drainage as an alternative at a high-volume centre. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not move straight to a percutaneous drain after one failed attempt at a low-volume unit. [EXPERTISE]

lead: A pancreatic duct stent, in the specific circumstance of persistent pancreatitis from pancreatic duct obstruction that is preventing other therapy.
text: Reasonable Evidence D A pancreatic duct stent, in the specific circumstance of persistent pancreatitis from pancreatic duct obstruction that is preventing other therapy. Indications Preferred when NCCN lists this as indicated in special circumstances only. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Not part of routine preoperative preparation, and not a treatment for pain.

lead: Do not interpret a CA 19-9 measured during obstructive jaundice as an unconfounded tumour baseline.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not interpret a CA 19-9 measured during obstructive jaundice as an unconfounded tumour baseline. Why Why Draw it after adequate biliary drainage, with liver function tests, and record the bilirubin beside it. Additional cautions Additional cautions Biliary obstruction and cholangitis both raise CA 19-9, so a pre-drainage value cannot be compared with a post-treatment value or used to triage toward staging laparoscopy. This matters more than it used to, because the response assessment that decides on an operation after neoadjuvant therapy uses CA 19-9 as one of its three metrics and is interpretable only against a baseline drawn in a decompressed patient.

lead: Do not keep re-biopsying a resectable mass you intend to resect.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not keep re-biopsying a resectable mass you intend to resect. Why Why Decide in advance what a negative result would change. If the answer is nothing, the patient needs a theatre date, not another needle. Additional cautions Additional cautions Each attempt costs a procedure, a delay and the currency of the 4-week staging scan, and NCCN explicitly says a non-diagnostic biopsy should not delay resection when suspicion is high.

lead: Upfront resection, then adjuvant mFOLFIRINOXEXPERTISE NCCN's stated standard approach in resectable disease has been upfront surgery followed by postoperative treatment, and ESMO's 2023 guideline goes further: neoadjuvant therapy is not recommended for resectable PC due to limited phase III evidence, except in the context of clinical trials — graded [II, E], a recommendation against. No randomised trial has shown a neoadjuvant strategy to be superior in anatomically resectable disease.
text: Upfront resection, then adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX Evidence B EXPERTISE NCCN's stated standard approach in resectable disease has been upfront surgery followed by postoperative treatment, and ESMO's 2023 guideline goes further: neoadjuvant therapy is not recommended for resectable PC due to limited phase III evidence, except in the context of clinical trials — graded [II, E], a recommendation against. No randomised trial has shown a neoadjuvant strategy to be superior in anatomically resectable disease. Indications Preferred when A fit patient with resectable anatomy and no high-risk features, where adjuvant chemotherapy can realistically be delivered. The meta-analysis of nine randomised trials (1,194 patients) found no overall survival benefit for neoadjuvant treatment in the resectable subgroup, hazard ratio 0.90 (95% CI 0.63–1.28), while finding one in the borderline resectable subgroup, 0.60 (0.38–0.96) — but the test for a difference between those subgroups was not significant (p=0.081), so the split this page is organised around is a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated effect. On mature 5-year data the adjuvant arm of this strategy delivers median overall survival 53.5 months (95% CI 43.5–58.4) against 35.5 months (30.1–40.3) for gemcitabine, hazard ratio 0.68 (0.54–0.85), P=.001. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not read upfront surgery as surgery alone, and do not overstate the attrition argument. NCCN and PRODIGE-24's own authors put the proportion of resected patients who never receive adjuvant chemotherapy at up to 30%, and that is the strongest argument for the other sequence — but the randomised data do not show that neoadjuvant sequencing fixes it: pooled across the nine trials, the proportion starting adjuvant therapy was no different (57.7% versus 55.6%, RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.76–1.12, p=0.353). Committing to this option still means committing to a named plan for who delivers chemotherapy and when. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Mature 5-y data, adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX vs gemcitabine: median OS 53.5 (95% CI 43.5–58.4) vs 35.5 mo (30.1–40.3); HR 0.68 (0.54–0.85), P=.001 Up to 30% of resected patients never receive adjuvant chemotherapy

Nine RCTs (n=1,194), neoadjuvant vs upfront surgery: OS HR 0.90 (95% CI 0.63–1.28) resectable, 0.60 (0.38–0.96) borderline; subgroup difference p=0.081, NS Proportion starting adjuvant therapy no different, RR 0.92 (95% CI 0.76–1.12)

lead: Neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX, then surgery PREOPANC-2 (n=369 modified intention to treat, 19 Dutch centres) compared eight cycles of full-dose neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX followed by surgery and no adjuvant treatment against the PREOPANC chemoradiotherapy regimen followed by four cycles of adjuvant gemcitabine: median overall survival 21.9 months (95% CI 17.7–27.0) versus 21.3 months (16.8–25.5), hazard ratio 0.88 (0.69–1.13), p=0.32. The trial's conclusion, and NCCN's, is that either regimen may be considered in resectable or borderline resectable disease.
text: Neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX, then surgery Evidence B PREOPANC-2 (n=369 modified intention to treat, 19 Dutch centres) compared eight cycles of full-dose neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX followed by surgery and no adjuvant treatment against the PREOPANC chemoradiotherapy regimen followed by four cycles of adjuvant gemcitabine: median overall survival 21.9 months (95% CI 17.7–27.0) versus 21.3 months (16.8–25.5), hazard ratio 0.88 (0.69–1.13), p=0.32. The trial's conclusion, and NCCN's, is that either regimen may be considered in resectable or borderline resectable disease. Indications Preferred when A fit patient with high-risk features, or one in whom the board judges that selecting out occult metastatic disease before a major operation is worth the resection-rate cost — occult metastatic disease was found at surgery in 12 of 156 (8%) after FOLFIRINOX versus 25 of 166 (15%) after chemoradiotherapy, a post hoc comparison. PREOPANC-2 is the trial that justifies using FOLFIRINOX rather than chemoradiotherapy if a neoadjuvant route is chosen, and it is a failed superiority trial, not a win and not a demonstration of equivalence: the confidence interval reaches 1.13, so a 12% relative benefit for FOLFIRINOX is not excluded, and the one significant secondary endpoint went the other way (ypN0 58% versus 47%, p=0.0073, with ypN2 in 20% versus 7%). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid NORPACT-1 is the only randomised trial of neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX against upfront surgery restricted to resectable pancreatic head cancer, and its primary endpoint was significant in favour of upfront surgery: 18-month survival 60% (95% CI 49–71) versus 73% (62–84), p=0.032, with median overall survival 25.1 months (17.2–34.9) versus 38.5 months (27.6–not reached), hazard ratio 1.52 (1.00–2.33), log-rank p=0.050 by intention to treat. Grade 3 or worse events occurred in 42 of 73 (58%) versus 19 of 47 (40%). Read it as a failure to show benefit, not as evidence of harm: it is a phase 2 trial designed at a two-sided alpha of 0.15, nothing is significant per protocol (18-month p=0.14; hazard ratio 1.46, 0.99–2.17, p=0.058), and its delivery failed — 16 of 77 (21%) allocated to neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX never received it and all 16 went straight to resection, only 37 of the 61 who started (61%) completed four cycles, and 16 (26%) received one or two. Evidence & sources Two further things decide how much weight NORPACT-1 can carry. Its control arm is the only partly modern comparator in the whole neoadjuvant literature, and only partly: 19 of 44 resected control patients (43%) actually received adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX and 25 of 44 a gemcitabine-based regimen, with mFOLFIRINOX permitted only after an August 2018 amendment. And its 38.5-month control-arm median far exceeds every comparable upfront-surgery arm (14.3 months in PREOPANC), so the headline comparison is driven as much by an unusually good control arm in 63 patients with 28 deaths as by a poor experimental one. Eleven patients (8%) had final pathology other than PDAC, including 3 distal cholangiocarcinomas and 2 pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours in the upfront arm, and they remain in the intention-to-treat denominator. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: mITT n=369, neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX vs CRT + adjuvant gemcitabine: median OS 21.9 vs 21.3 mo, HR 0.88 (CI 0.69–1.13), p=0.32; superiority not shown Failed superiority, not equivalence; FOLFIRINOX arm received no adjuvant treatment

Neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX vs upfront surgery: primary 18-mo survival 60% vs 73%, p=0.032 (ITT); median OS 25.1 vs 38.5 mo, HR 1.52 (1.00–2.33) Phase 2 at two-sided alpha 0.15; 21% never received FOLFIRINOX; read as no benefit, not harm

lead: Neoadjuvant gemcitabine-based chemoradiotherapy, then surgery, then adjuvant gemcitabine The PREOPANC regimen: three cycles of gemcitabine with 36 Gy in 15 fractions during the second cycle, surgery, then four cycles of adjuvant gemcitabine. The long-term analysis of PREOPANC (n=246, median follow-up 59 months, 210 of 246 patients dead) gave an overall survival hazard ratio of 0.73 (95% CI 0.56–0.96), p=0.025, in resectable and borderline resectable disease combined.
text: Neoadjuvant gemcitabine-based chemoradiotherapy, then surgery, then adjuvant gemcitabine Evidence B The PREOPANC regimen: three cycles of gemcitabine with 36 Gy in 15 fractions during the second cycle, surgery, then four cycles of adjuvant gemcitabine. The long-term analysis of PREOPANC (n=246, median follow-up 59 months, 210 of 246 patients dead) gave an overall survival hazard ratio of 0.73 (95% CI 0.56–0.96), p=0.025, in resectable and borderline resectable disease combined. Indications Preferred when Where the board has decided on a neoadjuvant route and wants the regimen with a positive randomised comparison against upfront surgery. PREOPANC-2 found no survival difference between this and FOLFIRINOX, so either is defensible, and this is the regimen to prefer where FOLFIRINOX is not tolerable. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Read both reports and note what the comparator was. The initial primary analysis was not significant — median overall survival 16.0 versus 14.3 months, hazard ratio 0.78 (0.58–1.05), p=0.096 — and the resection rate was lower, 61% versus 72%, p=0.058. The difference in medians in the long-term analysis is 1.4 months (15.7 versus 14.3); what separates is the tail, with 5-year survival 20.5% (14.2–29.8) versus 6.5% (3.1–13.7). The adjuvant comparator in both arms was gemcitabine monotherapy, and in the upfront-surgery arm only 65 of 127 patients (51%) received any chemotherapy at all — so the trial compares a front-loaded strategy with a control arm half of which was never treated systemically, and it does not answer today's question. Evidence & sources Three further qualifications from the full text. The primary endpoint moved from negative to positive at a second look with no prespecified plan for that analysis and no multiplicity adjustment, so the nominal p=0.025 should be read in that light. A 1.4-month median difference alongside a 14-point difference at 5 years means the hazards are far from proportional, yet a single hazard ratio is quoted. And the subgroup the page relies on is not established: in the long-term analysis the resectable subgroup was non-significant (hazard ratio 0.79, 0.54–1.16, P=.23) and the borderline resectable subgroup significant (0.67, 0.45–0.99, P=.045), with no significant interaction across any of seven prespecified subgroups. Twenty-eight of 119 patients (24%) never started the neoadjuvant regimen, staging laparoscopy was mandatory only in that arm, and WHO performance status 0 was recorded in 58% of the neoadjuvant arm against 39% of the surgery arm without adjustment in the primary model. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Enrolment in Alliance A021806, or another randomised trialREGISTRY A021806 is the phase 3 trial that asks this exact question in resectable disease — perioperative versus adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX, enrolment 358, primary endpoint overall survival from randomisation. As of 6 October 2026 its registry record (NCT04340141) shows it active and not recruiting, with primary completion scheduled for December 2028 and no results posted.
text: Enrolment in Alliance A021806, or another randomised trial Evidence D REGISTRY A021806 is the phase 3 trial that asks this exact question in resectable disease — perioperative versus adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX, enrolment 358, primary endpoint overall survival from randomisation. As of 6 October 2026 its registry record (NCT04340141) shows it active and not recruiting, with primary completion scheduled for December 2028 and no results posted. Indications Preferred when The honest position in resectable disease is that the sequencing question is open, so offer a trial wherever one is available. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not cite A021806 as evidence for either sequence, in either direction. Nothing has been published; what is known of it comes from a trials-in-progress abstract and the registry entry. A page that lists it among the trials that showed something is wrong.

lead: Whichever sequence is chosen, write down before the operation who delivers the chemotherapy, when it starts, and who restages before it does.
text: Standard Evidence D Whichever sequence is chosen, write down before the operation who delivers the chemotherapy, when it starts, and who restages before it does. Indications Preferred when Every resectable patient. The one claim both camps accept is that a substantial minority of resected patients never get timely adjuvant therapy at the intended dose — NCCN and PRODIGE-24's authors put it at up to 30% — which is a system failure rather than a biological one and is fixable by naming an owner. What the trials do not show is that giving chemotherapy first solves it: across the nine randomised trials the proportion starting adjuvant therapy was the same either way (57.7% versus 55.6%, p=0.353). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid An operative note that ends at the skin, with the oncology referral left to be made after discharge. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy for a resectable tumour that has high-risk features, named in the note.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Neoadjuvant chemotherapy for a resectable tumour that has high-risk features, named in the note. Indications Preferred when NCCN allows neoadjuvant therapy in resectable disease, especially with high-risk features, which it defines as equivocal or indeterminate imaging findings, markedly elevated CA 19-9, a large primary tumour, or large regional lymph nodes. The rationale is selection: treating micrometastatic disease earlier, and identifying surgical futility before an operation rather than after it. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not present it as evidence based in this group. The pooled resectable subgroup shows no overall survival benefit (HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.63–1.28), none of the randomised trials was restricted to high-risk resectable disease, ESMO recommends against neoadjuvant therapy in resectable disease outside a trial at [II, E], and NCCN itself says there is limited evidence to recommend specific neoadjuvant regimens outside a clinical trial and that panel practice varies. Evidence & sources Downgraded to D on the full-text read: this is a guideline permission with no trial behind it in the population named. Two numbers set the price. Pooled across the nine trials, neoadjuvant treatment lowered the resection rate (72.6% versus 80.6%, RR 0.94, 0.89–0.99) and roughly doubled serious adverse events (56.1% versus 27.0%) — though the published risk ratio for that harm, 1.92 with a reported 95% CI of 1.28 to 1.89, does not contain its own point estimate in either the abstract or the table, so the magnitude as published cannot be relied on even though its direction is clear. If this route is taken, tissue is mandatory first, and the response assessment in the borderline resectable assessment applies — including the rule that a patient with no shrinkage but no extrapancreatic progression is still explored. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Resectable subgroup OS HR 0.90 (95% CI 0.63–1.28); pooled nine RCTs, with vs without neoadjuvant: resection 72.6 vs 80.6%, RR 0.94 (0.89–0.99); serious AEs 56.1 vs 27.0% Published SAE RR 1.92 (95% CI 1.28–1.89) excludes its point estimate; no high-risk-only trial

lead: Perioperative chemotherapy as studied in SWOG S1505 — mFOLFIRINOX or nab-paclitaxel with gemcitabine, given before and after resection — only with its result stated.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Perioperative chemotherapy as studied in SWOG S1505 — mFOLFIRINOX or nab-paclitaxel with gemcitabine, given before and after resection — only with its result stated. Indications Preferred when A randomised phase 2 pick-the-winner trial in resectable disease, designed to select a regimen for further study, with 147 patients enrolled and 102 eligible and evaluable after central radiology review. Preoperative chemotherapy was started by 96% of each arm and completed by 84% and 85%; 40 of 55 (73%) and 33 of 47 (70%) underwent resection; R0 was achieved in 34 of 40 (85%) and 28 of 33 (85%) of those resected. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid It selected no winner and cleared no bar. Both arms missed the primary endpoint: 2-year overall survival 47% (95% CI 31–61), P=.15 with mFOLFIRINOX and 48% (31–63), P=.14 with nab-paclitaxel and gemcitabine, against a prespecified historical threshold of 40%, so the between-arm comparison was never performed. Median overall survival was 23.2 and 23.6 months. Do not quote the completion figure the way this page previously did: only 31 of 40 (78% of those resected, 56% of eligible patients) and 26 of 33 (79%, 55%) started postoperative chemotherapy, and all treatment was completed by 49% and 40% — 16 of the 73 patients who had surgery (22%) could not start adjuvant chemotherapy at all. Pathologic complete or major response was 10 of 40 (25%) and 14 of 33 (42%), in resected-only denominators. Evidence & sources Downgraded from B to C. There is no randomised control arm: both arms were tested against a historical 2-year survival of 40% drawn from adjuvant trials, whose populations were selected after surviving surgery and recovering, so the comparison is biased against a strategy randomised at diagnosis and the failure to beat 40% is not evidence that perioperative chemotherapy is worse. Nobody in the trial received upfront surgery followed by adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX. Forty-five of 147 randomised patients (31%) were removed from the analysed population, 43 of them for failing central radiology review, after they had already received protocol therapy. Age was capped at 75 and performance status at Zubrod 0–1. Its most durable contribution is the misclassification finding in the resectability assessment, not a survival result. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: PAXG — cisplatin, nab-paclitaxel, capecitabine and gemcitabine — as a neoadjuvant option in certain circumstances only.
text: Reasonable Evidence B PAXG — cisplatin, nab-paclitaxel, capecitabine and gemcitabine — as a neoadjuvant option in certain circumstances only. Indications Preferred when A randomised phase 3 trial across 17 Italian academic hospitals (n=260) in pathologically confirmed resectable or borderline resectable disease found median event-free survival 16.0 versus 10.2 months against mFOLFIRINOX, hazard ratio 0.63 (0.47–0.84), p=0.0018. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The endpoint was event-free survival, not overall survival, and NCCN added it as useful in certain circumstances specifically because not all centres have experience with the regimen. Do not adopt a four-drug regimen on an event-free survival result at a centre that has never given it. Evidence & sources The citation for this trial is carried only in the NCCN discussion text supplied to this page; the primary report was not retrieved for this depot and was not read in full, so neither the event-free survival figure nor the hazard ratio has been checked against the published paper. Read it before the regimen is used. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not use chemoradiotherapy as the primary neoadjuvant modality in place of multiagent chemotherapy — but do not overstate what the trials show about it either.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not use chemoradiotherapy as the primary neoadjuvant modality in place of multiagent chemotherapy — but do not overstate what the trials show about it either. Why Why Multiagent systemic chemotherapy remains the initial choice in the neoadjuvant setting per NCCN. Chemoradiation is sometimes added after chemotherapy, and its role and necessity remain poorly defined. Additional cautions Additional cautions Alliance A021501, in borderline resectable disease, closed its mFOLFIRINOX-plus-hypofractionated-radiotherapy arm early for futility when only 10 of the first 30 evaluable patients (33%) achieved R0 resection against a threshold of 12, versus 17 of 30 (57%) with mFOLFIRINOX alone. The mFOLFIRINOX arm met its primary endpoint against a historical benchmark (18-month survival 66.7%, 95% CI 56.1–79.4, median overall survival 29.8 months, 21.1–36.6) and the radiotherapy arm did not (47.3%, 35.8–62.5; median 17.1 months, 12.8–24.4). Retrospective comparisons suggest radiation may improve local control with no survival difference — that is the most that can be claimed for it. Evidence & sources Downgraded from B to C, because A021501's design forbids the comparison this item rests on. Each arm was tested against a historical 18-month survival rate of 50% assembled by the investigators from series published 2004–2015, at a one-sided alpha of 0.07; the protocol permitted a between-arm comparison only if both arms were promising, and arm 2 was not, so every arm-versus-arm figure is descriptive and the radiotherapy arm was stopped on a surrogate before its survival data matured. The denominators of 65 and 55 are evaluable patients who initiated treatment, not the 70 and 56 randomised; 16 of arm 1's 70 patients were registered sequentially without randomisation after arm 2 closed; and 15 of 55 arm 2 patients (27%) never received the radiotherapy that defines their arm. Pancreatectomy was completed in only 32 of 65 (49%) and 19 of 55 (35%). PREOPANC-2 cuts directly against a strong version of this recommendation: it found neoadjuvant gemcitabine-based chemoradiotherapy and neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX indistinguishable on overall survival (21.3 versus 21.9 months, HR 0.88, p=0.32). Doses studied for neoadjuvant chemoradiation are 36 Gy in 2.4 Gy fractions, 45–56 Gy in 1.8–2.2 Gy fractions, and 33–50 Gy in 5 fractions. SBRT after modern multiagent chemotherapy appears feasible without excess surgical complications in experienced centres, but NCCN states further study is needed before it is recommended in borderline resectable disease. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

Neoadjuvant gemcitabine-based CRT vs neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX: OS 21.3 vs 21.9 mo, HR 0.88, p=0.32, no significant difference

lead: Do not start neoadjuvant therapy without a tissue diagnosis.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not start neoadjuvant therapy without a tissue diagnosis. Why Why Tissue first, in the same anaesthetic as the drainage if the patient is jaundiced. Additional cautions Additional cautions The permission to operate without tissue applies only to going directly to resection. Once a patient is given chemotherapy, a wrong diagnosis is treated for months before anyone notices.

lead: Do not deliver a neoadjuvant course that is not coordinated with the centre that will do the operation.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not deliver a neoadjuvant course that is not coordinated with the centre that will do the operation. Why Why NCCN's wording is that when feasible, treatment should be performed at or coordinated through a high-volume centre, and that determinations of resectability after neoadjuvant therapy should be made individually in a multidisciplinary setting. Additional cautions Additional cautions A patient who completes chemotherapy locally and is only then referred arrives with a scan that is weeks old, no baseline PET, and a CA 19-9 drawn while jaundiced — which makes the response assessment impossible to do properly. [EXPERTISE]

lead: Multiagent neoadjuvant chemotherapy first, then restage and re-ask the resectability question — this is where the randomised evidence for the neoadjuvant route is strongest.
text: Standard Evidence C Multiagent neoadjuvant chemotherapy first, then restage and re-ask the resectability question — this is where the randomised evidence for the neoadjuvant route is strongest. Indications Preferred when A fit borderline resectable patient with a tissue diagnosis. In the pooled analysis of nine randomised trials, the borderline resectable subgroup showed an overall survival benefit for neoadjuvant treatment, hazard ratio 0.60 (95% CI 0.38–0.96), against none in the resectable subgroup, 0.90 (0.63–1.28). In the long-term PREOPANC analysis the borderline resectable subgroup was the only significant one, hazard ratio 0.67 (0.45–0.99), P=.045. In ESPAC5, 1-year overall survival was 39% (95% CI 24–61) with immediate surgery, 78% (60–100) with gemcitabine plus capecitabine, 84% (70–100) with FOLFIRINOX and 60% (37–97) with capecitabine-based chemoradiotherapy, p=0.0028, with pooled neoadjuvant versus surgery hazard ratio 0.29 (0.14–0.60), p=0.0052. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid State the limits in the same breath, because they are large. ESPAC5 randomised 90 patients against a target of 100 and analysed 86; its primary endpoints were recruitment rate and resection rate and both were negative — recruitment ran at 2.16 patients per month across 16 sites, and resection occurred in 21 of 31 (68%) after immediate surgery versus 30 of 55 (55%) after neoadjuvant therapy, p=0.33, numerically favouring immediate surgery, with R0 resection in 3 of 21 (14%) versus 7 of 30 (23%), p=0.49. Follow-up was capped at 12 months and there were 31 deaths in the whole trial. The control arm's median CA 19-9 was 802 kU/L against 322 to 623 kU/L in the neoadjuvant arms, an unadjusted and strongly prognostic imbalance in a trial with 16 to 31 patients per arm. Of the 43 patients who received adjuvant therapy anywhere in the trial, 41 (95%) got gemcitabine or gemcitabine plus capecitabine and only 2 (5%) got modified FOLFIRINOX. Evidence & sources Downgraded from B to C on the full-text read. The resectable-versus-borderline split that this assessment depends on is not statistically established: the between-subgroup test in the pooled analysis was not significant (p=0.081), PREOPANC's interaction test was not significant in either report, and PREOPANC-2 found no treatment-effect heterogeneity in any subgroup (all interaction p at or above 0.23). The pooled estimate is also unstable — it depends on post hoc removal of NORPACT-1 and the pooled ESPAC5 chemotherapy comparison as outliers, which drops the only trial whose control arm partly resembles current practice and collapses heterogeneity from I² 55.8% to 0% by construction. ESPAC5's own internals cut against its mechanism: the chemoradiotherapy arm had the best pathology (37% R0, 25% node positive) and the worst neoadjuvant survival, and the authors note the survival benefit was unrelated to the resection rate. Disease-free survival from surgery was 33% (19–58) after immediate surgery and 59% (46–74) after the combined neoadjuvant arms, hazard ratio 0.53 (0.28–0.98), reported as p=0.016 in the abstract and p=0.043 in the results text. Grade 3 or worse adverse events occurred in 2 of 28 (7%) after immediate surgery and 17 of 50 (34%) after neoadjuvant therapy. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
