lead: Olaparib maintenance, for germline BRCA1/2 after platinum The POLO trial (n=154 randomised 3:2 from 3,315 screened) randomised patients with metastatic disease and a germline BRCA1/2 mutation who had not progressed after at least 16 weeks of first-line platinum-based therapy to olaparib or placebo. Median progression-free survival by blinded independent central review was 7.4 versus 3.8 months, hazard ratio 0.53 (95% CI 0.35–0.82), P=0.004.
text: Olaparib maintenance, for germline BRCA1/2 after platinum Evidence B The POLO trial (n=154 randomised 3:2 from 3,315 screened) randomised patients with metastatic disease and a germline BRCA1/2 mutation who had not progressed after at least 16 weeks of first-line platinum-based therapy to olaparib or placebo. Median progression-free survival by blinded independent central review was 7.4 versus 3.8 months, hazard ratio 0.53 (95% CI 0.35–0.82), P=0.004. Indications Preferred when Exactly that population: germline BRCA1/2, platinum-exposed, no progression at 16 weeks. This is the clearest reason to have the germline result early. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Say the other half. At the interim analysis, at 46% data maturity against a final analysis planned at 69%, there was no overall survival difference — 18.9 versus 18.1 months, hazard ratio 0.91 (0.56–1.46), P=0.68 — there was no difference in health-related quality of life (between-group difference in global health status −2.47, 95% CI −7.27 to 2.33), and grade 3 or worse adverse events were more frequent with olaparib, 40% versus 23%. Objective response was 23% versus 12%, and time to second progression was also non-significant (HR 0.76, 0.46–1.23). Evidence & sources Downgraded from A to B. The comparator was placebo, not maintenance chemotherapy or a de-escalated fluoropyrimidine, so the trial establishes that olaparib beats stopping treatment, not that it beats continuing anything — which is the comparison the 16-week decision actually faces. Only 154 of 3,315 screened patients (4.6%) were randomised, and the conditioning step (germline testing plus four months of platinum without progression) is itself the strongest prognostic selection in the trial: a placebo-arm median of 18.1 months in metastatic pancreatic cancer is far above the 6 to 11 months typical of the disease, so these numbers are not comparable with those from unselected trials. Nine placebo patients (15%) received a PARP inhibitor after progression, cited as biasing overall survival toward the null without a sensitivity analysis. The sponsor funded the trial and supplied the companion diagnostic. The page previously quoted the placebo-arm median as 16.1 months; the published figure is 18.1. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Olaparib vs placebo: median PFS 7.4 vs 3.8 mo, HR 0.53 (95% CI 0.35–0.82), P=0.004; interim OS 18.9 vs 18.1 mo, HR 0.91 (0.56–1.46), P=0.68 Placebo comparator, not maintenance chemotherapy; only 154 of 3,315 screened randomised

lead: Pembrolizumab or dostarlimab, for MSI-high or dMMR disease Separate MSI-high/dMMR eligibility from the TMB-high indication. Under the FDA update of 16 October 2026, pembrolizumab for TMB-H solid tumours requires ≥13 mut/Mb by an FDA-authorized test, progression after prior treatment and no satisfactory alternative. The prior ≥10 threshold is historical. Check the applicable current label for each agent.
text: Pembrolizumab or dostarlimab, for MSI-high or dMMR disease Evidence D Separate MSI-high/dMMR eligibility from the TMB-high indication. Under the FDA update of 16 October 2026, pembrolizumab for TMB-H solid tumours requires ≥13 mut/Mb by an FDA-authorized test, progression after prior treatment and no satisfactory alternative. The prior ≥10 threshold is historical. Check the applicable current label for each agent. Indications Preferred when The small minority of pancreatic tumours that are MSI-high or mismatch-repair deficient. It is the one alteration on this list that can produce a durable response. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not test for it late. A patient who has exhausted chemotherapy before anyone checked mismatch repair status has lost the opportunity, and the frequency in PDAC is low enough that nobody finds it by clinical suspicion. Graded D because no trial in pancreatic cancer supports either agent: both are tumour-agnostic approvals carried here through the NCCN listing, and no primary report was retrieved or read in full for this depot.

lead: Sotorasib or adagrasib, for KRAS G12C NCCN lists both as subsequent therapy options at any performance status. KRAS p.G12C occurs in approximately 1 to 2% of pancreatic cancers.
text: Sotorasib or adagrasib, for KRAS G12C Evidence D NCCN lists both as subsequent therapy options at any performance status. KRAS p.G12C occurs in approximately 1 to 2% of pancreatic cancers. Indications Preferred when A previously treated patient with a G12C mutation where daraxonrasib is unavailable. Sotorasib in the pooled phase 1–2 CodeBreaK 100 pancreatic cohort (n=38, all previously treated, about 79% with two or more prior lines): centrally confirmed objective response in 8 of 38 (21%, 95% CI 10–37) with no complete responses, median progression-free survival 4.0 months (2.8–5.6), median overall survival 6.9 months (5.0–9.1). Adagrasib in the KRYSTAL-1 phase 2 non-lung, non-colorectal cohort: objective response in 7 of 21 pancreatic patients (33.3%) by blinded central review, median progression-free survival 5.4 months, median overall survival 8.0 months. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Downgraded to D, and correct the denominators: these are single-arm results in 38 and 21 pancreatic patients, not in the larger numbers this page previously implied. The sotorasib cohort had no prespecified response benchmark and no hypothesis test at all, so there is no threshold it could have failed, and its 10% to 37% confidence interval is compatible with the under-10% historical second-line benchmark the authors invoke. Adagrasib's prespecified 10% null applies to the pooled tumour-agnostic cohort, not to the pancreatic subgroup, and six patients counted as evaluable by investigators were excluded by central review for having no measurable disease at baseline, moving the denominator in the favourable direction. Median overall survival of 6.9 and 8.0 months in third-line-or-later populations with ECOG 0–1 and a life expectancy requirement is indistinguishable from the natural history of those populations. The allele covers 1% to 2% of the disease, and neither report gives a screening denominator. Do not present them as comparable to the RASolute 302 result. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Single-arm phase 1–2, sotorasib, pancreatic cohort n=38: ORR 8/38 (21%, 95% CI 10–37), no CR; median PFS 4.0 mo (2.8–5.6), median OS 6.9 mo (5.0–9.1) No prespecified response benchmark or hypothesis test; CI compatible with <10% benchmark

Single-arm phase 2 subgroup, adagrasib, pancreatic n=21: ORR 7/21 (33.3%) by blinded central review; median PFS 5.4 mo, median OS 8.0 mo The 10% null applies to the pooled cohort, not this subgroup; six excluded by central review

lead: Zenocutuzumab, for NRG1 fusions NCCN lists zenocutuzumab-zbco as a subsequent therapy option for NRG1 fusion-positive disease at performance status 0–2. In the eNRGy basket trial, 36 of 158 patients in the primary efficacy population had pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, and all 36 were KRAS wild-type: 15 of 36 (42%, 95% CI 25–59) responded by investigator assessment and 16 of 36 (44%, 28–62) by blinded independent central review, with median duration of response 7.4 months (4.0–11.2) investigator-assessed and 9.1 months centrally. Twenty-four of 31 pancreatic patients with baseline data (77%) had a CA 19-9 fall of at least 50%.
text: Zenocutuzumab, for NRG1 fusions Evidence D NCCN lists zenocutuzumab-zbco as a subsequent therapy option for NRG1 fusion-positive disease at performance status 0–2. In the eNRGy basket trial, 36 of 158 patients in the primary efficacy population had pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, and all 36 were KRAS wild-type: 15 of 36 (42%, 95% CI 25–59) responded by investigator assessment and 16 of 36 (44%, 28–62) by blinded independent central review, with median duration of response 7.4 months (4.0–11.2) investigator-assessed and 9.1 months centrally. Twenty-four of 31 pancreatic patients with baseline data (77%) had a CA 19-9 fall of at least 50%. Indications Preferred when A patient with KRAS wild-type disease, where NRG1 fusions are enriched — in a single-institution series the median age of 10 patients with a detectable NRG1 fusion was 48.5 years, and KRAS wild-type status is the practical trigger to look. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Downgraded to D. Single-arm, 36 pancreatic patients inside a basket trial sized only for the pooled estimate, with a 95% CI of 25% to 59% that cannot distinguish a major advance from a modest one. No progression-free or overall survival is reported for the pancreatic subgroup, so no survival claim can be derived from it. The primary endpoint was investigator-assessed response in an open-label trial with blinded central review only as a secondary endpoint, and the primary efficacy population is a post-enrolment construct — 204 treated patients become 158 evaluable, with exclusions for short follow-up falling disproportionately on early progressors. Only 9 of 47 responses across the whole trial were ongoing at a median follow-up of 7.1 months. Adverse events were mostly grade 1 or 2 with treatment-related grade 3–4 in 7%, so the risk is low — but NRG1 fusions occur in well under 1% of PDAC, no screening denominator is given, and the sponsor designed the trial, analysed the data and drafted the manuscript. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Single-arm basket, PDAC subset (n=36, all KRAS wild-type): ORR 42% (95% CI 25–59) investigator, 44% (28–62) central review; median response duration 7.4 mo No PFS or OS for pancreatic subgroup; open-label; NRG1 fusions in under 1% of PDAC

lead: An NTRK, RET, BRAF or FGFR-directed agent, by alteration NCCN lists entrectinib, larotrectinib or repotrectinib for NTRK fusion-positive disease; selpercatinib for RET fusions (11 pancreatic patients, at least half with an objective response); dabrafenib with trametinib for BRAF V600E, with ORR 38–47% across the NCI-MATCH subprotocol and the ROAR basket trial; and erdafitinib for FGFR alterations, with response in 10 of 18 pancreatic patients (56%) in RAGNAR.
text: An NTRK, RET, BRAF or FGFR-directed agent, by alteration Evidence D NCCN lists entrectinib, larotrectinib or repotrectinib for NTRK fusion-positive disease; selpercatinib for RET fusions (11 pancreatic patients, at least half with an objective response); dabrafenib with trametinib for BRAF V600E, with ORR 38–47% across the NCI-MATCH subprotocol and the ROAR basket trial; and erdafitinib for FGFR alterations, with response in 10 of 18 pancreatic patients (56%) in RAGNAR. Indications Preferred when Rare alterations where the alternative is further cytotoxic chemotherapy in a previously treated patient. Each is a basket-trial or subgroup result in single-digit to low-double-digit pancreatic numbers. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Downgraded to D: none of these reports was retrieved or read in full for this depot, and all the figures are carried in the NCCN listing supplied to this page. Do not treat the gene as the target. The pancreatic subsets in these trials are tiny — one patient with pancreatic cancer in the larotrectinib analysis, two of three responders among pancreatic patients in the entrectinib trials — and response rates from mixed-tumour baskets do not transfer cleanly to this disease.

lead: A chemotherapy holiday or maintenance therapy for a patient doing well on first-line treatment.
text: Reasonable Evidence D A chemotherapy holiday or maintenance therapy for a patient doing well on first-line treatment. Indications Preferred when NCCN offers either for patients who do well on initial therapy. Set the reassessment interval and the trigger for restarting when the holiday begins. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not drift into a holiday without a date for the next scan.

lead: Rucaparib maintenance for germline or somatic BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 variants, as a second option after platinum.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Rucaparib maintenance for germline or somatic BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 variants, as a second option after platinum. Indications Preferred when A phase 2 trial of maintenance rucaparib after at least 16 weeks of platinum-based chemotherapy in advanced disease with germline or somatic pathogenic variants in BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 reported median progression-free survival of 13.1 months and median duration of response 17.3 months, with no new safety signal. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Downgraded to D: single-arm phase 2 with no control, and the primary report was not retrieved or read in full for this depot — the figures are carried in the NCCN discussion text supplied to this page. The 13.1-month progression-free survival figure cannot be compared with POLO's 7.4 months. Its one advantage over the POLO population is that it included somatic as well as germline variants and PALB2.

lead: After progression on gemcitabine-based therapy, consider liposomal irinotecan with fluorouracil/leucovorin for a suitable patient.
text: Reasonable Evidence A After progression on gemcitabine-based therapy, consider liposomal irinotecan with fluorouracil/leucovorin for a suitable patient. Indications Preferred when In NAPOLI-1, 117 combination patients versus 119 concurrent 5-FU/leucovorin controls had median OS 6.1 versus 4.2 months, HR 0.67 (95% CI 0.49–0.92). The trial selected patients with KPS ≥70 and adequate liver function. Reassess performance status, bilirubin/drainage, prior treatment and goals. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The evidence does not establish immediate reuse after irinotecan-containing FOLFIRINOX or NALIRIFOX. Liposomal irinotecan is not interchangeable with conventional irinotecan; use the actual product label and pharmacy-verified dosing. Continue symptom-directed care and consider trials or supportive care when further cytotoxic therapy is unsuitable. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not treat metastatic pancreatic cancer without a tissue diagnosis.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not treat metastatic pancreatic cancer without a tissue diagnosis. Why Why Biopsy the lesion that gives the highest stage, with image guidance for liver lesions, and bank material for sequencing at the same sitting. Additional cautions Additional cautions NCCN requires a pathologic diagnosis before systemic therapy in metastatic disease. Treating on imaging alone commits a patient to months of cytotoxic therapy on an assumption.

lead: Do not offer prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin routinely.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not offer prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin routinely. Why Why Treat established venous thromboembolism, and keep a low threshold for investigating it — the risk in pancreatic cancer is substantially raised. Additional cautions Additional cautions CONKO-004 showed that prophylactic enoxaparin lowered symptomatic venous thromboembolism (hazard ratio 0.40, 95% CI 0.19–0.83, P=0.01, n=160 versus 152) but progression-free and overall survival did not differ. NCCN does not recommend prophylactic LMWH at this time, citing the absence of a survival effect. Graded D because the trial was not retrieved or read in full for this depot; the figures are carried in the NCCN discussion text supplied to this page.

lead: Do not resect the primary tumour, or a metastasis, for metastatic disease outside a prospective protocol.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not resect the primary tumour, or a metastasis, for metastatic disease outside a prospective protocol. Why Why NCCN's wording is the ceiling of what can be said: in select rare cases, surgery can be considered in patients with a sustained and deep response to systemic therapy, ideally at high-volume centres, and patients with indolent or oligometastatic disease should be referred to a high-volume centre for evaluation. Additional cautions Additional cautions Evidence for resection of metastatic PDAC remains retrospective and highly selected; do not present it as established curative treatment.

lead: Do not let the molecular report arrive after it can be used.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not let the molecular report arrive after it can be used. Why Why Order profiling at the first visit, bank the extra passes at the index biopsy, and name the person who chases the result. Additional cautions Additional cautions This is an operational failure, not a clinical judgement, and it is the one that most often costs a patient a targeted option in this disease — including the two options on this page with randomised support.

lead: Report differentiation, exact Ki-67 and mitotic rate per 2 mm² when assessable. Record specimen adequacy; a reliable Ki-67-based grade can be used when mitotic counting is not possible.
text: Standard Evidence B Report differentiation, exact Ki-67 and mitotic rate per 2 mm² when assessable. Record specimen adequacy; a reliable Ki-67-based grade can be used when mitotic counting is not possible. Indications Preferred when Every specimen, primary or metastatic, biopsy or resection, with at least 500 assessable tumour cells and no crush artefact. Ki-67 is counted in the hot spot of highest nuclear labelling; the mitotic rate is counted in the areas of highest density, per 2 mm², which equals 10 high-power fields at 40× with a 0.5 mm ocular field. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not accept a report that says "neuroendocrine tumour" or "neuroendocrine carcinoma" without a grade and without the parameters used to assign it. NCCN states plainly that such a report is inadequate for prognostication and therapy and inappropriate for pathology reporting. Evidence & sources Where mitotic rate and Ki-67 give different grades, the higher grade is assigned. Where several blocks are available, stain the block with the highest mitotic index and grade on the highest index; with synchronous specimens from several sites, stain at least one block from each. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Separate a well-differentiated grade 3 tumour from a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma before any treatment decision — they are different diseases that share a Ki-67 range.
text: Standard Evidence C Separate a well-differentiated grade 3 tumour from a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma before any treatment decision — they are different diseases that share a Ki-67 range. Indications Preferred when Any pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasm with Ki-67 above 20%. In 31 well-differentiated tumours with a morphologically apparent high-grade component, 21 of them pancreatic, median disease-specific survival was 55 months (range 16-119), with 2-year and 5-year survival of 88-89% and 48-49%. The institutional comparators were 162 months for low and intermediate grade pancreatic well-differentiated tumours (2-year and 5-year 97% and 90%) and 16 months for pancreatic poorly differentiated carcinoma (24% and 24%), p<0.001. Genotype separates them: a DAXX, ATRX or MEN1 mutation was present in 35 of 63 (57%) low and intermediate grade tumours and in 3 of 4 sequenced transformed tumours against 0 of 28 carcinomas; Rb protein was lost in 0% of well-differentiated tumours of any grade against 59% of carcinomas; and p53 immunoreactivity was abnormal in 0% against 56%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not route a well-differentiated G3 tumour down a small-cell carcinoma pathway, and do not treat a poorly differentiated carcinoma as a NET because the Ki-67 happens to be 25%. NANETS reports a multi-institutional pathological review in which only 44 of 107 resected pancreatic tumours originally called poorly differentiated carcinoma actually were; that review is not in this page's full-text depot and the figure is quoted as NANETS states it. Evidence & sources Read the survival contrast carefully. In the stage-matched analysis restricted to stage IV, pancreatic grade 1-2 well-differentiated tumours and those with a high-grade component showed no statistically significant difference in disease-specific survival, and both did far better than poorly differentiated carcinoma (median 61 against 16 months, p<0.001; hazard ratios 0.17 and 0.16 against carcinoma as reference). The 55-against-162-month comparison is unmatched, and it is the one the abstract leads with. The 31 cases were assembled by searching two pathology archives for grade discrepancy, so the series cannot say how often this happens, the genotype contrast rests on four prospectively sequenced tumours against literature controls, and 6 of the 31 were biopsies only in which the coexisting lower-grade component was inferred from clinical history rather than seen. In challenging cases, particularly in the pancreas, NCCN lists Rb, p53, p16, ATRX and DAXX as an optional panel to help distinguish G3 NET from carcinoma, read together with the clinical, functional-imaging and molecular picture. See clinical decision 8 for what each diagnosis then means. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Treat a grade obtained from a needle biopsy as a floor, not a fact — biopsy systematically understates grade in G2 disease.
text: Standard Evidence C Treat a grade obtained from a needle biopsy as a floor, not a fact — biopsy systematically understates grade in G2 disease. Indications Preferred when Any observation-versus-resection decision that rests on grade. In 46 tumours sampled by EUS-FNA at one centre, 33 of which were resected and available for comparison, agreement between readers was excellent within each modality (Pearson r-squared 0.93 on cytology and 0.94 on the resection specimen, both p<0.001, with no grade disagreement between readers) - but agreement between cytological and histological grade was poor: kappa 0.21 (p=0.09), rising only to 0.24 (p=0.06) when restricted to the 27 cases with at least 200 cells counted, and no better at a 5% cut-off than at 2%. Cytology under-graded systematically: 10 of 14 histological G2 tumours (71%) were called cytological G1, and histological Ki-67 averaged 1.3 times the cytological value. Cytological grade still separated the worst group - actuarial progression-free survival 10 plus or minus 4 months for cytological G3 against 29 plus or minus 7 for G2 and 68 plus or minus 10 for G1 (p<0.0001) - but cytological G1 and G2 did not differ for progression-free or overall survival. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not promise a patient that a G1 biopsy means a G1 tumour. NANETS reports agreement of tumour grade between EUS-FNA cytology and the resection specimen in under 50% of G2 and G3 cases, and areas with Ki-67 of 2% or less were common even within G2 tumours. The only prospective study of fine-needle core biopsy in non-functional tumours found 83% concordance, in 30 patients; that study is quoted from the NANETS text and is not in this page's full-text depot. Evidence & sources Two cautions on the study itself. The four cytological G3 patients who drive the significant survival separation were all locally advanced, node-positive or metastatic at diagnosis, so cytological G3 may be marking stage rather than grade; and the concordance analysis could only include the resected tumours, so nothing in it describes how cytology performs in the small lesions actually being watched. Progression-free survival was also calculated independently of whether the tumour was removed, mixing resected and unresected patients in the same curves. Where additional tissue is needed for immunohistochemistry, add core biopsy to aspiration where it is available. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Guideline-reported (NANETS): grade agreement between EUS-FNA cytology and resection specimen in under 50% of G2 and G3 cases Ki-67 ≤2% areas common even within G2 tumours (intratumoral heterogeneity)

lead: For a small incidental suspected nonfunctioning pNET, discuss whether tissue confirmation will change observation or treatment; ENETS recommends confirmation where possible.
text: Reasonable Evidence D For a small incidental suspected nonfunctioning pNET, discuss whether tissue confirmation will change observation or treatment; ENETS recommends confirmation where possible. Indications Preferred when An asymptomatic sub-centimetre lesion with characteristic arterial enhancement where the plan is surveillance whatever the grade. NANETS states that in such patients biopsy is not routinely necessary to confirm the diagnosis before deciding to observe. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not skip tissue when the diagnosis is genuinely in question, when grade would change the plan, or when the lesion is 1-2 cm and the observe-or-resect decision is live - that is exactly the decision grade is meant to inform. And know that the guidelines disagree here. ENETS 2023, read in full, states that a suspected nonfunctioning tumour under 2 cm with positive somatostatin-receptor imaging should be confirmed histologically or cytologically where possible (level 3 evidence, grade B), and notes DAXX and ATRX loss and alternative lengthening of telomeres as independent adverse prognostic factors particularly in tumours of 2 cm or less. The 2025 MEN1 recommendations go the other way again and find no role for routine EUS-guided biopsy in that syndrome. See the limited-evidence section and approval 11. Evidence & sources The ASPEN study required a positive fine-needle aspirate or biopsy, or a positive 68Ga-labelled DOTA PET, before enrolment - but in practice 170 of its 500 patients (34%) never had an aspirate, it was negative in a further 45 (9%), and grade was not evaluable in 68 of the 285 who did have one (23.9%). So its reassuring surveillance figures come from a population in which the diagnosis was often established by receptor PET alone and in which the surveillance arm has no histological characterisation at all. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Order molecular profiling where the disease is locoregionally unresectable or metastatic and the patient is a candidate for systemic therapy.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Order molecular profiling where the disease is locoregionally unresectable or metastatic and the patient is a candidate for systemic therapy. Indications Preferred when Tumour tissue is preferred; circulating tumour DNA is an option when tissue testing is not feasible. ENETS encourages molecular profiling in neuroendocrine carcinoma specifically, to identify new targets, while saying plainly that the targets are not yet established. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not profile a small localised G1 tumour that is going to be observed or enucleated: nothing in the result changes that decision, and there is no established targeted therapy in this setting. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not let a hormone immunostain decide whether the tumour is functional.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not let a hormone immunostain decide whether the tumour is functional. Why Why Functional status is a clinical syndrome plus biochemical evidence of inappropriately raised hormone — that is the ENETS definition and it is what clinical decision 3 works from. Additional cautions Additional cautions NCCN states that hormone staining by immunohistochemistry is not helpful and that a positive stain does not mean there is a functional tumour. Chasing a positive insulin stain in an asymptomatic normoglycaemic patient produces an operation nobody needed. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not accept the diagnostic label "carcinoma with neuroendocrine features".
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not accept the diagnostic label "carcinoma with neuroendocrine features". Why Why Ask for a definite WHO classification. Where the histology is genuinely ambiguous the report should say so, recommend clinical correlation and recommend a broad next-generation sequencing panel. Additional cautions Additional cautions Adenocarcinomas of the GI tract often express neuroendocrine markers patchily with no survival or management significance, and that patchy expression is a common route into the wrong pathway. In higher-grade pancreatic neoplasms, trypsin, chymotrypsin and BCL10 help exclude an acinar cell carcinoma expressing neuroendocrine markers.

lead: If staging shows hepatic metastases, the hepatic disease is the NELM pathway from here — this page covers the primary only.
text: Standard Evidence D If staging shows hepatic metastases, the hepatic disease is the NELM pathway from here — this page covers the primary only. Indications Preferred when Hand off at this assessment, by name, as soon as liver deposits are seen. The NELM page carries hepatic tumour burden and distribution, cytoreduction thresholds, liver-directed modality choice, systemic sequencing for grade 1–2 and high-grade disease, carcinoid-crisis precautions and the transplant question. It also carries the decision about resecting the pancreatic primary when liver metastases are present, where NANETS reached no consensus and the majority view was that resection may help only in selected circumstances. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not make the primary-resection decision in metastatic disease on this page. Two specific warnings travel with the patient: NCCN states that pancreatoduodenectomy in metastatic disease is usually not curative and affects liver-directed therapy long term, and that liver-directed therapies for hepatic metastases after pancreatoduodenectomy carry an increased risk of cholangitis and liver abscess. That makes the sequence a joint decision between this assessment and the NELM pathway, not a pancreatic one. Evidence & sources Locoregionally advanced unresectable disease without liver metastases is also outside this page's scope: it is a systemic-therapy decision and NCCN's pancreatic NET systemic principles apply. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Use somatostatin-receptor PET rather than octreotide scintigraphy, and read it together with multiphase contrast CT or MRI in the same sitting where the scanner allows it.
text: Standard Evidence C Use somatostatin-receptor PET rather than octreotide scintigraphy, and read it together with multiphase contrast CT or MRI in the same sitting where the scanner allows it. Indications Preferred when Staging where occult metastatic disease would change the operation, and localising a primary in a patient who presents with metastases. In a prospective single-centre study of 131 patients imaged with all three modalities and read independently and blind, 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT detected 847 of 891 lesions, 95.1% (95% CI 92.4-96.8), against 404 of 891, 45.3% (37.9-52.9), for anatomic imaging and 275 of 891, 30.9% (25.0-37.5), for 111In-pentetreotide SPECT/CT (p<0.001 for both comparisons), and the PET changed the management recommendation in 43 of 131 patients (32.8%). A previously unknown primary was found in 4 of 14 patients (28.6%). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not read the PET alone. Contrast CT or MRI is what identifies the receptor-negative deposits, and NCCN requires the two together. Acceptable tracers are 68Ga-DOTATATE, 68Ga-DOTATOC and 64Cu-DOTATATE; a lesion counts as receptor-positive when uptake exceeds liver, and the modified Krenning score runs 0 none, 1 very low, 2 at or below liver, 3 above liver, 4 above spleen. Evidence & sources Grade C, downgraded on the full-text read, and the detection figures have to be read against their reference standard. The denominator of 891 lesions is the union of lesions seen on any of the three tests, which structurally pushes the most sensitive modality toward 100% and the others downward. In the 25 patients (19%) who were operated and so had histology, per-lesion true positives fell to 72 of 113 (63.7%) for the PET, 44 of 113 (38.9%) for CT or MRI and 25 of 113 (22.1%) for SPECT/CT - and all 38 histologically proven lesions missed by every imaging test were nodal metastases. Only 110 of the 891 lesions were pancreatic, the cohort was enriched for MEN1 and VHL by inclusion criterion, change in management was adjudicated unblinded by the team that ordered the scans, and there are no follow-up or outcome data. Receptor PET is not a surveillance test: NCCN states that somatostatin-receptor imaging and FDG-PET are not recommended for routine surveillance, and the SNMMI/EANM standard adds that a rise or fall in lesional uptake must not be read as response or progression the way it would be with other tracers. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Record the main pancreatic duct calibre, any calcification and whether the lesion is cystic — all three carry information that size does not.
text: Standard Evidence D Record the main pancreatic duct calibre, any calcification and whether the lesion is cystic — all three carry information that size does not. Indications Preferred when Every lesion being considered for observation. In 981 patients resected for well-differentiated tumours at eight centres, calcification was present in 122 of 697 assessable patients (18%) and a predominantly cystic appearance in 120 of 702 (17%). Calcified tumours were larger (3.2 against 2.0 cm, p=0.001) and more often had Ki-67 of 3% or more (47% against 33%, p=0.029), lymphovascular invasion (42% against 27%, p=0.005), nodal metastasis (36% against 24%, p=0.011), distant metastasis (13% against 4%, p<0.001) and metastasis on preoperative imaging (17% against 7%, p=0.001). Cystic tumours were less often node positive (12% against 30%, p<0.001). Five-year recurrence-free survival was 66% with calcification against 79% without (p=0.002) and 83% for cystic against 73% for solid (p=0.033); in the four-way comparison it was 91% for cystic without calcification (n=89), 77% for solid without calcification (n=494), 69% for solid with calcification and 67% for cystic with calcification (n=16), p=0.043. A dilated duct is the ASPEN study's single strongest stated warning sign. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not call a calcified lesion low risk because it measures 1.4 cm, and do not treat a dilated duct as incidental - see the flagged disagreement at clinical decision 4. Equally, do not convert either feature into a threshold. This is information for the board to weigh alongside grade and growth, not a rule. Evidence & sources Grade D, downgraded on the full-text read. Calcification's independent hazard ratio was 11.5 with a 95% confidence interval of 1.1 to 125.0 at p=0.043, in a Cox model that also returned 25.2 (4.4-142.9) for nodal and 33.0 (4.4-249.3) for distant metastasis - the signature of far too few recurrence events for the covariates entered, with no event count reported anywhere in the paper. Cystic morphology, one of its two headline features, was not independently prognostic at all (HR 1.6, 0.2-14.3, p=0.69), although the abstract presents both as usable for stratification. Imaging was classified from radiology report wording rather than by central re-read, across eight institutions and seventeen years of changing technique; 28-29% of the cohort has no data on the two exposures of interest and the analysis is complete-case with no imputation; median follow-up was 35 months in a disease that recurs at a median of 4 to 7 years; the cystic-and-calcified cell that anchors the four-way comparison contains 16 patients; and no patient in the cohort was observed, which the authors concede before recommending the features for the observation decision anyway. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Where a G2 or higher tumour has had both a receptor PET and an FDG-PET, record and report the pair together - a discordant result carries prognostic information that grade alone does not.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Where a G2 or higher tumour has had both a receptor PET and an FDG-PET, record and report the pair together - a discordant result carries prognostic information that grade alone does not. Indications Preferred when The NETPET grade summarises the pair on the single lesion that is most FDG-avid relative to its receptor uptake, plus the burden of such lesions. In the 62-patient derivation cohort, median overall survival was not reached for receptor-positive, FDG-negative disease (P1) or for the mixed group (P2-4) and was 11 months for significant FDG-positive, receptor-negative disease (P5), p=0.0018. In a 319-patient three-centre cohort, median overall survival was 101.8, 46.5 and 11.5 months and median time to progression 25.5, 16.7 and 6.6 months across the same three strata (both p<0.001), with the score independent of histological grade on multivariable analysis (HR 2.376, 95% CI 1.682-3.357, p<0.001) and grade independent of the score (HR 1.615, 1.192-2.187, p=0.002). Inter-rater kappa was 0.8 and intra-rater kappa 0.9. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not use NETPET alone to decide an operation on a localized primary. The cohorts involved metastatic or unresectable disease, with only 39% and 36% pancreatic primaries and no pancreas-specific analysis. The validation centres had published earlier series, but patient overlap with those series is unquantified. Treatment was not adjusted for. SSTR-positive disease across P1–P4 may be eligible for PRRT; FDG positivity does not by itself exclude it, so treatment access cannot be attributed only to P1. These data support prognosis, not a validated treatment threshold or a localized-primary resection rule. Evidence & sources The SNMMI/EANM procedure standard makes the same point more cautiously: FDG positivity is not rare in G1 and G2 tumours and predicts progression and prognosis more strongly than tumour grade, and combining the two scans can identify the highest-grade, most aggressive lesion and direct a biopsy to it. What no source gives is what to do with the result in a localised primary. See the limited-evidence section. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Derivation cohort (n=62): median OS not reached for P1 (receptor+/FDG−) or P2-4 (mixed) vs 11 mo for P5 (FDG+/receptor−), p=0.0018 Metastatic/unresectable only; no pancreas subgroup; treatment not modelled

Validation cohort (n=319): median OS 101.8, 46.5 and 11.5 mo for P1, P2-4 and P5 (p<0.001); score independent of grade, HR 2.376 (95% CI 1.682–3.357) Partly re-analysis: two of three validation centres supplied derivation data

lead: Do not operate on uncinate-process or tail uptake seen on a somatostatin-receptor PET without a lesion on dedicated pancreas-protocol CT or MRI.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not operate on uncinate-process or tail uptake seen on a somatostatin-receptor PET without a lesion on dedicated pancreas-protocol CT or MRI. Why Why When pancreatic uptake is seen, obtain pancreas-protocol contrast CT to establish whether there is an underlying lesion at all. Additional cautions Additional cautions Physiological pancreatic uptake is described in over half of patients imaged with receptor PET, there is substantial overlap between physiological and malignant activity, and uptake alone cannot characterise a pancreatic finding. The SNMMI/EANM procedure standard says the same and goes no further: physiologically increased uptake in the pancreatic head and uncinate process occurs in a large proportion of patients and overlaps substantially with the standardised uptake values of true lesions in that region, and the standard offers no decision rule beyond correlating with multiphase CT or MRI and following the patient up. Receptor PET also cannot distinguish a splenule or an intrapancreatic splenule from a small tumour - both take up as avidly as spleen - and should not be used to try. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not use somatostatin-receptor imaging to stage a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma as a matter of routine.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not use somatostatin-receptor imaging to stage a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma as a matter of routine. Why Why Multiphasic CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis, with brain imaging and FDG-PET as appropriate, is the staging package NCCN sets for this disease. Additional cautions Additional cautions NCCN states that receptor-based imaging is not part of the routine evaluation of poorly differentiated carcinoma. A negative receptor scan in that setting answers a question nobody needed to ask and delays treatment that is time-critical.

lead: For appropriate sporadic, localized functioning tumours, the hormonal syndrome can justify resection irrespective of size. MEN1-associated gastrinoma requires individualized hereditary and endocrine assessment.
text: Standard Evidence C For appropriate sporadic, localized functioning tumours, the hormonal syndrome can justify resection irrespective of size. MEN1-associated gastrinoma requires individualized hereditary and endocrine assessment. Indications Preferred when Every localised functional tumour without distant metastases, where resection serves both symptom control and cure. Malignant potential runs from 5–15% for insulinoma to 60–90% for gastrinoma, glucagonoma and tumours secreting VIP, PTHrP or ectopic ACTH, so for everything except insulinoma the operation is an oncologic one. Resection of a localised insulinoma gives a 98% biochemical cure rate with a 6% chance of recurrence at 10 years. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not apply the small-nonfunctional observation rule to a functional tumour. NCCN's resection requirement for glucagonoma, VIPoma and somatostatinoma is total removal with negative margins, including adjacent organs where involved, with regional nodes — pancreatoduodenectomy for the head, distal pancreatectomy with or without splenectomy for body and tail. Evidence & sources Biochemical cure for apparently sporadic gastrinoma is 60% immediately after resection and 30-40% at 5 years, with 15-year disease-free survival of 15%, so "cured" means something different in each syndrome and should be said in those terms. For gastrinoma the strongest datum for operating is not randomised: on prospective NIH, UCSF and Stanford protocols, 160 patients who had a standardised exploration were compared with 35 who met the same criteria but did not have surgery. A gastrinoma was found and removed in 150 of 160 (94%), 51% were disease-free immediately and 41% at last follow-up. Liver metastases developed in 8 of 160 (5%) against 10 of 35 (29%), p=0.0002; death from any cause in 34 of 160 (21%) against 19 of 35 (54%), p=0.0002; disease-related death in 2 of 160 (1%) against 8 of 35 (23%), p=0.00001; and 15-year disease-related survival from first admission was 98% against 74%. Those 35 controls were not randomly formed - 19 refused after consulting their own physician, 10 had MEN1 with no lesion above 2.5 cm and 5 had comorbidity - non-disease mortality was numerically higher in them (31% against 20%, p=0.18), the surgical arm's disease-related figure rests on 2 deaths, cause of death was adjudicated unblinded by the operating investigators, and the controls were imaged every 6 to 12 months against yearly evaluation in the operated patients. Almost every primary was duodenal or nodal, so none of this transfers to an incidental non-functional pancreatic tumour. See the limited-evidence section and approval 4. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Gastrinoma, non-randomised: surgery (160) vs no surgery (35): liver metastases 5% vs 29%, p=0.0002; disease-related death 1% vs 23%, p=0.00001 Controls not randomised (19 refused surgery); cause of death adjudicated unblinded

lead: Confirm and stabilize the hormonal syndrome; interpret gastrin with PPI exposure and maintain acid suppression when withdrawal would be unsafe.
text: Standard Evidence D Confirm and stabilize the hormonal syndrome; interpret gastrin with PPI exposure and maintain acid suppression when withdrawal would be unsafe. Indications Preferred when Serum gastrin ideally drawn fasting and off a proton-pump inhibitor for more than a week. Where there are overt clinical symptoms of gastrinoma or a risk of complications, NCCN says to continue the acid suppression and interpret the gastrin with that in mind rather than stop it. Consider endocrinology involvement to establish the endocrine diagnosis. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not diagnose gastrinoma from hypergastrinaemia on a PPI alone. If acid suppression cannot safely be withdrawn, specialist assessment may use the clinical syndrome, imaging and appropriate tissue sampling while excluding other causes. Assess hereditary features and arrange genetic evaluation when indicated; do not delay necessary acid suppression. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: For insulinoma, choose the operation by tumour location and main-duct proximity: enucleation for suitable superficial lesions, spleen-preserving distal resection for appropriate deep distal lesions, and a head-specific operation for deep head lesions.
text: Standard Evidence C For insulinoma, choose the operation by tumour location and main-duct proximity: enucleation for suitable superficial lesions, spleen-preserving distal resection for appropriate deep distal lesions, and a head-specific operation for deep head lesions. Indications Preferred when Insulinomas are highly symptomatic and rarely malignant, which is exactly the setting in which NCCN and NANETS place enucleation. Ninety per cent pursue an indolent course. Where splenic vessels are involved by a larger tumour, splenectomy is performed; otherwise spleen preservation should be considered. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not enucleate a lesion within 2-3 mm of the main pancreatic duct, and do not enucleate a tumour large enough to carry nodal risk - see clinical decision 5 for the trade. And cost the fistula honestly: in a pooled analysis of 22 non-randomised comparative studies (432 enucleations against 716 standard resections), pancreatic fistula occurred in 25.5% after enucleation against 19.7% after standard resection, OR 2.09 (95% CI 1.41-3.11), p<0.001, and OR 1.93 (1.14-3.27) for clinically relevant grade B or C disease; the excess lost significance only in the four studies performing more than 20 enucleations in total and at least 4 a year. Vaccinate against pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae b and meningococcus at least 14 days before any operation that might include splenectomy. Evidence & sources A formal lymphadenectomy is not part of the operation for a benign insulinoma. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Stabilize the hormonal syndrome while localization and definitive treatment are planned.
text: Standard Evidence D Stabilize the hormonal syndrome while localization and definitive treatment are planned. Indications Preferred when Coordinate endocrinology and the treating team: prevent and treat insulinoma hypoglycaemia; maintain acid suppression for gastrinoma; replace fluids and electrolytes in VIPoma; address syndrome-specific metabolic and thrombotic risks. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Severe hypoglycaemia, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, bleeding or other acute complications require urgent clinical care rather than waiting for the tumour board. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Unlocalized insulinoma after CT/MRI and EUS: GLP-1 receptor imaging or arterial stimulation with venous sampling, not another anatomic study.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Unlocalized insulinoma after CT/MRI and EUS: GLP-1 receptor imaging or arterial stimulation with venous sampling, not another anatomic study. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Where contrast CT or MRI and endoscopic ultrasound have not found the insulinoma, the next test is GLP-1 receptor imaging or arterial stimulation with venous sampling, not another anatomic study. Indications Preferred when In a prospective randomised crossover study at one centre, 52 consecutive adults with biochemically proven endogenous hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia had 68Ga-DOTA-exendin-4 PET/CT, 111In-DOTA-exendin-4 SPECT/CT and a standardised 3T MRI within 3 to 4 days, each read independently by three blinded readers, with surgery, histology and postoperative glucose normalisation as the reference standard. Among the 38 who reached surgery with conclusive histology, accuracy was 93.9% (95% CI 87.8-97.5) for GLP-1 receptor PET/CT, 67.5% (58.1-76.0) for the SPECT, 67.6% (58.0-76.1) for the study MRI and 40.0% (23.9-57.9) for the prior external CT or MRI (all comparisons p<0.01 except SPECT against study MRI, p=1.0); reader agreement was 89.5%, 75.7% and 71.1%. Histology confirmed a benign insulinoma in 36 of 38 at a median size of 12 mm (range 5-23) and 37 of 38 normalised their glucose after surgery. ENETS recommends GLP-1 receptor imaging or arterial calcium stimulation with venous sampling when contrast CT or MRI and endoscopic ultrasound are negative. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Read the accuracy figures for what they are. Fourteen of the 52 enrolled patients are absent from that denominator precisely because imaging was negative or discordant or surgery was declined, which is the classic verification bias of an imaging study with a surgical reference standard and which the authors concede inflates sensitivity - the PET showed a suspicious lesion in only 78.8% of all 52 patients. Inclusion required a pathological fasting test, so specificity and negative predictive value cannot be estimated at all. The 40% figure for prior external imaging is an artefact of why these patients were referred, not a general estimate, and that arm was read once at the referring centre against three blinded readers for the index test. GLP-1 receptor expression falls to 4 of 11 (36%) in malignant insulinoma, where 73% express somatostatin receptor 2 instead, so a negative exendin scan in a patient who looks malignant is uninformative. The tracer is not licensed for routine clinical use. Evidence & sources The supporting review is a narrative one by the group that developed, labelled and validated the tracer, with no systematic search, no risk-of-bias appraisal and a comparative sensitivity table that places studies with different reference standards, referral filters and lesion sizes side by side. It does record the practical traps worth knowing: physiological uptake in duodenal Brunner's glands is always present and can be mistaken for an insulinoma, and high renal uptake can mask a lesion in the tail. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Prospective crossover, 38 with surgery: accuracy GLP-1R PET/CT 93.9% (95% CI 87.8–97.5) vs SPECT 67.5% vs study MRI 67.6% vs prior CT/MRI 40.0% Verification bias: fourteen of 52 excluded (negative/discordant imaging); specificity not estimable

lead: Where the lesion is resectable but the patient is not a surgical candidate, EUS-guided ablation at a centre with expertise is an option for insulinoma.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Where the lesion is resectable but the patient is not a surgical candidate, EUS-guided ablation at a centre with expertise is an option for insulinoma. Indications Preferred when NCCN lists this for highly selected cases only. Stabilise first with diet, diazoxide at 3 to 8 mg/kg per day in three or four divided doses, or everolimus. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Nonrandomized comparative evidence exists. ERASING matched 89 EUS-RFA and 89 surgical patients: symptom control was 95.5% versus 100%, with repeat ablation counted as success and shorter RFA follow-up (23 versus 37 months). This does not establish durable oncologic equivalence. Reserve ablation for appropriately selected patients after expert multidisciplinary review. [EXPERTISE] Evidence & sources Correct the metabolic consequences of the syndrome before operating: potassium, magnesium and bicarbonate and dehydration in a VIPoma, glucose in an insulinoma. Glucagonoma carries a described hypercoagulable state and NCCN allows consideration of perioperative anticoagulation. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Avoid an unmonitored start of a somatostatin analogue for insulinoma: hypoglycaemia can worsen.
text: Avoid Evidence C Avoid an unmonitored start of a somatostatin analogue for insulinoma: hypoglycaemia can worsen. Why Why Stabilize with diet and appropriate medical therapy. ENETS supports a monitored short-acting octreotide trial before long-acting treatment; NCCN emphasizes receptor-positive disease. Specialist review should reconcile receptor findings and the clinical response. Additional cautions Additional cautions Suppression of counterregulatory hormones may worsen hypoglycaemia even when an antitumour effect is possible. Monitor glucose and symptoms closely during a short-acting trial; do not infer safe long-acting treatment from receptor imaging alone. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not rely on prophylactic octreotide to prevent an intraoperative crisis.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not rely on prophylactic octreotide to prevent an intraoperative crisis. Why Why Have vasopressors and fluid immediately available and give them without waiting. The crisis plan, the rescue drug in the room and the carcinoid-heart-disease assessment are set out in the NELM pathway's functional-syndrome assessment, which applies unchanged to a patient coming for a pancreatic operation. Additional cautions Additional cautions NCCN states that prophylactic octreotide is likely ineffective in preventing intraoperative carcinoid crisis and that intraoperative administration should not delay vasopressor use and fluid administration. NANETS calls the role of analogues in preventing crisis in pancreatic NET undefined. Also remember cholecystectomy at the index operation where long-term analogue therapy is anticipated, because of the raised risk of biliary symptoms and cholecystitis. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Observation is an option for an asymptomatic, low-grade, nonfunctioning tumour ≤1 cm without main pancreatic duct dilation; consider tissue confirmation where possible and document diagnostic confidence.
text: Standard Evidence D Observation is an option for an asymptomatic, low-grade, nonfunctioning tumour ≤1 cm without main pancreatic duct dilation; consider tissue confirmation where possible and document diagnostic confidence. Indications Preferred when A sub-centimetre lesion with the imaging phenotype of a neuroendocrine tumour in a patient who will be followed. At 1 cm the guidelines agree: NCCN permits observation for small, low-grade, incidentally discovered non-functional tumours and routes 1 cm or less straight to observation; NANETS calls initial observation without a plan for immediate resection an acceptable strategy for an asymptomatic tumour under 1 cm; and ENETS 2023, now read in full, states that an asymptomatic nonfunctioning tumour of 1 cm or less without main pancreatic duct dilation should undergo active surveillance (level 3 evidence, grade B). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not observe a patient who will not return for imaging, and do not observe a lesion you have not characterised on a dedicated pancreas-protocol study. Observation is a programme with dates, not a decision to do nothing. And do not state, as the first draft of this page did from the abstract, that ENETS considers observation for lesions no larger than 2 cm. It does not. ENETS observes 1 cm or less, personalises the band above 1 cm up to 2 cm to the resection that would be required and the patient's comorbidities, and strongly recommends surgery for any nonfunctioning tumour larger than 2 cm or with main pancreatic duct dilation - all three positions at level 3 evidence, grade B. Evidence & sources Grade D, downgraded on the full-text read. Neither 1 cm nor 2 cm was derived from data. NCCN's own supporting citations for the observation footnote are the three cohorts in the next item and nothing stronger; ENETS's surgical thresholds carry level 3 evidence while its strongest wording is reserved for the threshold above which it operates; and the only systematic comparison of surgery against surveillance for lesions of 2 cm or less that exists anywhere - 37 of 3,048 screened publications, 1,814 patients, carried out for the 2025 MEN1 recommendations - found no difference in metastasis or mortality, at low to very low GRADE certainty. The recommendation to observe a sub-centimetre lesion is reasonable and near-universal. It is not derived, and it should not be offered to a patient as though it were. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Guideline systematic review (MEN1; 37 studies, 1,814 patients): no difference in metastasis or mortality, surgery vs surveillance, ≤2 cm Low to very low GRADE certainty; done for MEN1 recommendations

lead: Observation evidence is nonrandomized: short prospective follow-up and a retrospective size-matched comparison with resection.
text: Standard Evidence C Observation evidence is nonrandomized: short prospective follow-up and a retrospective size-matched comparison with resection. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Explain that observation evidence is nonrandomized: prospective cohorts have short follow-up, and Sadot provides a retrospective size-matched observation-versus-resection comparison. Indications Preferred when Every observation conversation, and every tumour board that uses the 2 cm line. The three studies NCCN cites are these, as their full texts report them. Sadot 2016 is a single-centre matched case-control study at one tertiary referral centre, 1993-2013, of sporadic incidentally discovered stage I-II tumours, and its inclusion band was 3 cm or less rather than 2 cm: median size was 1.2 cm (IQR 0.8-1.7) in the observed group and 1.4 cm (1-2) in the resected, and 87% were T1. Of 464 patients reviewed, 104 recommended for observation were matched one-to-one on initial tumour size by a blinded statistician to 77 resected without a period of surveillance, and compared by intention to treat. Median tumour size in the observation group was unchanged at 1.2 cm from first to last imaging (p=0.7) - but the individual trajectories differed: 53 of 104 (51%) grew, 19 (18%) were static and 32 (31%) shrank. Twenty-six of 104 (25%) crossed over to resection at a median of 30 months (range 7-135), for patient preference in 10 (38%), increasing size in 8 (31%), physician preference in 7 (27%) and new duct dilatation in 1 (4%); none had developed symptoms. No observed patient developed radiographic locoregional or distant metastases and nobody in either arm died of disease. In the resected arm 72 of 77 (95%) were G1, 1 was node positive, margins were positive in 9 (12%), and 5 (6%) recurred at a median of 5.1 years (range 2.9-8.1). Operative harm was substantial: any grade 3 complication in 16 of 77 (21%), a grade 3 leak-related complication in 13 (17%), median stay 7 days. PANDORA is the Dutch Pancreatic Cancer Group's nationwide prospective watchful-waiting cohort of 76 patients with a non-functional tumour of 2 cm or less, enrolled 2017-2020, median follow-up 17 months (IQR 8-35). Sixty-eight of 76 (89%) showed no sign of progression; 8 (11%) grew by more than 0.5 cm per year, of whom 2 ended above 2.0 cm, and none of the 8 developed symptoms. Six patients (8%) were operated during follow-up. One of them, who grew from 1.8 to 2.6 cm in a year, had two enlarged nodes on 68Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT and an unexpected peritoneal deposit at operation: final pathology was a 2.0 cm tumour with Ki-67 5-10%, two positive nodes and confirmed peritoneal metastasis, with two new nodes 11 months later requiring a somatostatin analogue. Four patients died, all of non-tumour causes. ASPEN is the largest: a prospective, non-randomised, international cohort of 500 patients at 41 centres, 406 under surveillance and 94 resected, with treatment left to the referring centre, median follow-up 25 months (IQR 16-35). Mean radiological size was 13.2 mm (SD 4.1) - 12.9 mm under surveillance against 14.8 mm in the surgical group, p<0.010. Nine of 406 surveillance patients (2%) came to surgery during follow-up: 4 for increasing size, 3 for increasing duct dilatation, 2 by preference. Distant metastases were present in 4 of 500 (0.8%), all at diagnosis and all operated, and the only recurrence recorded during follow-up was in one of those same patients. Severe complications occurred in 13% of the resected with no deaths. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not present any of this as proof of safety, and do not present it as a comparison of strategies, because not one of the three performs one. Sadot's inclusion criterion was under 3 cm, so the paper most often cited for the 2 cm threshold never tested that threshold; its evidence concerns lesions of about a centimetre and it is silent about the 2-3 cm range it nominally covers. A quarter of its observation arm had the very operation the paper argues can be avoided, and they remain in that arm by intention to treat, so part of the arm's clean oncological record was purchased with surgery. The patients genuinely never operated were followed a median of 33 months (IQR 11-72) against 57 months after resection (p<0.001), while the recurrences in the resected arm appeared at a median of 5.1 years - the observation arm was not watched long enough to experience the event the paper reports as absent. The metastasis-free survival advantage for observation, 99% (97-100) against 88% (79-96), p=0.01, is an artefact of the endpoint and not a finding: a resected patient can be recorded as recurring while an unresected patient with stable imaging cannot, so the two arms are not at risk of the same events, and in the observation-only against resection comparison the difference disappears (metastasis-free survival p=0.08, overall survival p=0.3). Matching was on initial size alone: the observation group was significantly older (median 63 against 59, p=0.04; 65 against 59 in the never-operated subgroup, p=0.001), 36 of 104 (35%) never had a tissue diagnosis at all, and 11 of 181 (6%) died of other or unknown causes with no competing-risk analysis. Fifty-one per cent of observed tumours did grow, a fact submerged beneath an unchanged median. ASPEN's 20% rate of aggressive histology - its most quoted number - comes entirely from the 94 patients who were resected, and that group was selected by radiological size over 10 mm (OR 1.9, p=0.030), a main pancreatic duct over 3 mm (OR 3.4, p<0.001), age 64 or under (OR 2.5, p<0.001), enrolment at a surgical centre (OR 2.0, p=0.012) and a HADS anxiety score of 4-6 (OR 2.0, p=0.029). It therefore cannot describe the prevalence of aggressive biology among sub-2 cm lesions and certainly not among the 406 who were watched. Follow-up was 25 months in a disease measured in decades, crossover was 2%, allocation was by the treating centre rather than randomised, and no outcome comparison between the two strategies was performed at all. The metastasis rate is printed in the paper as 0.08 per cent when 4 of 500 is 0.8 per cent - a tenfold typographical understatement of the key safety signal, uncorrected. A third of patients never had a fine-needle aspirate and grade was not evaluable in a quarter of those who did, so the surveillance arm has no histological characterisation and the extent of under-staging in it is unmeasurable. The study was funded by ENETS, whose guideline recommending surveillance is the hypothesis under test, and senior authors wrote that guideline. In PANDORA, six of the eight patients who met the protocol's own criterion for resection refused the operation and elected to continue watchful waiting, so the protocol was in effect not tested and the cohort's benign course reflects patient choice. Protocol adherence was poor: only 17 of 76 (22%) had the scheduled 3-month endoscopic ultrasound, 19 (25%) had only one imaging modality at diagnosis against a protocol requiring two, and 21 (28%) and 11 (15%) had no imaging at all at 6 and 12 months. Eligibility excluded patients with malignant tumour features - exactly the population whose risk determines whether waiting is safe. And one lesion resected for diagnostic uncertainty proved to be an intravascular pyogenic granuloma and not a neuroendocrine tumour at all, which means some surveilled lesions may not be either. Evidence & sources The nearest thing to a comparison of the two strategies is negative. The 2025 MEN1 best-practice exercise ran a systematic review of surgery against active surveillance for nonfunctioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours of 2 cm or less: across 37 of 3,048 screened publications - 27 retrospective series, 1 prospective cohort and 9 case series - covering 1,814 patients, combined metastatic disease and mortality rates did not differ between the two strategies, at low to very low GRADE certainty and with low precision. The panel notes that surgery in those series was indicated by growth on serial imaging, so the effect of surgery may be understated. That review is in MEN1, where the gland carries a field defect, lesions are multiple and patients are decades younger, so it does not transfer to sporadic disease - but it is the only systematic comparison in existence at this size, and it found nothing. The same panel then recommended a more cautious approach anyway, on expert judgement rather than on the evidence it had convened to produce, which is a defensible clinical position and should not be quoted as evidence-based. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Matched case-control (104 observed, 77 resected): no metastases if observed, no disease deaths; 25% crossed over at median 30 mo; resection grade 3 complications 21% Inclusion ≤3 cm, not 2 cm; never-operated followed median 33 mo vs 57 mo after resection

Prospective watchful-waiting cohort, 76 tumours ≤2 cm, median follow-up 17 mo: 89% no progression, 11% grew >0.5 cm/y, 8% operated Six of eight meeting resection criterion declined surgery; poor protocol adherence

Prospective cohort, 500 (406 surveillance, 94 resected), median follow-up 25 mo: 2% of surveilled came to surgery; metastases 4 of 500 (0.8%), all at diagnosis Non-randomised, no strategy comparison; 20% aggressive histology is from the resected only

Guideline systematic review (MEN1), 37 publications, 1,814 patients: metastatic disease and mortality did not differ, surgery vs surveillance, ≤2 cm Low to very low GRADE certainty; MEN1 only, not sporadic disease

lead: Set the surveillance programme in writing at the moment observation is chosen, using the post-resection schedule.
text: Standard Evidence D Set the surveillance programme in writing at the moment observation is chosen, using the post-resection schedule. Indications Preferred when NCCN states that its surveillance recommendations apply to cases where observation has been chosen: history and examination with multiphasic abdomen with or without pelvis CT or MRI at 12 weeks to 12 months, then every 6 to 12 months to a maximum of 10 years, then as clinically indicated, with chest CT as clinically indicated and earlier imaging if symptoms develop. Use the same modality and contrast agent each time so that growth is measurable rather than inferred - ENETS makes the same point explicitly, that imaging modality, contrast type, contrast timing and tracer should not be changed during follow-up. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Routine surveillance uses CT or MRI. SSTR PET and FDG PET are reserved for defined clinical questions. Reassess for growth, duct dilation, symptoms or other progression; not every operation in the observation cohorts was triggered by growth. Evidence & sources Grade D, and the borrowed schedule is now known to disagree with its own source. The published follow-up recommendations for completely resected gastroenteropancreatic tumours - a 22-member RAND/UCLA panel scoring 193 scenarios against an evidence base of 6 eligible studies plus two then-unpublished cohorts - recommend for a resected pancreatic tumour consultation with triple-phase CT or MRI yearly for 3 years, then every 1 to 2 years to a total of 10 years, deliberately de-intensifying the first three years relative to NCCN, ENETS, ESMO and NANETS while extending surveillance past ten. They also recommend no follow-up at all for a grade 1, node-negative pancreatic tumour smaller than 2 cm. That exemption is expert opinion at a 75% agreement threshold, in a dataset whose cumulative recurrence was 33.5% at 5 years and 48.5% at 10 and whose median time to pancreatic recurrence was 7.2 years, and node-negative in a small tumour usually means few or no nodes were taken. It applies to resected patients and not to observed ones, and this page does not adopt it - but the group should know that the schedule it borrows is contradicted by the paper it is borrowed from. ENETS 2023 sets a third schedule again, imaging at 3 to 6 months after curative resection, then every 6 to 12 months for 5 years, every 12 to 24 months for 10 years after the first five years (the ENETS wording) and then every 5 years, at level 5 evidence graded B, with patients told to expect at least 20 years and possibly lifelong surveillance. See approval 13. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Define in advance what counts as growth, record a rate rather than a size, and say plainly that no growth threshold in use has been derived.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Define in advance what counts as growth, record a rate rather than a size, and say plainly that no growth threshold in use has been derived. Indications Preferred when Two thresholds are in circulation and the board should pick one and write it down. PANDORA used growth of more than 0.5 cm per year as its protocol trigger, and 8 of 76 patients (11%) met it at a median of 17 months. The 2025 MEN1 recommendations use growth of under 1 mm per year as the point at which the imaging interval may be lengthened to every 1 to 2 years, at 92% panel agreement, with intervals individualised to the observed growth rate and the absolute size. In ASPEN, increasing size was the stated indication for surgery in only 4 of the 406 surveillance patients, against patient preference in 42 of 94 operated patients and centre preference in 37. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not present either number as biological - neither has any cited derivation. One millimetre a year lies below the measurement reproducibility of serial cross-sectional imaging of a small pancreatic lesion across different scanners and readers, and will generate both false stability and false progression. Half a centimetre a year is no better founded: in PANDORA the 8 patients who met it had a mean size at last follow-up of still only 1.2 cm (SD 0.7), and only 2 of them ever crossed 2.0 cm, so the threshold was detecting measurement variation as much as growth. What makes either threshold usable at all is the same modality, the same contrast agent and the same measurement convention every time, which is the one part of this that is entirely within the programme's control. Evidence & sources Record the measurement in the body of the note, in millimetres, naming the phase and sequence it was made on. A growth rate that cannot be recomputed from the chart is not a growth rate. See approval 12. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Surveillance cohort: growth >0.5 cm/y trigger met by 8/76 (11%) at median 17 mo; their mean size at last follow-up 1.2 cm; only 2 crossed 2.0 cm Threshold has no cited derivation; likely detects measurement variation as much as growth
Surveillance registry: size increase was the surgical indication in only 4 of 406 surveillance patients; patient preference in 42 of 94 operated, centre in 37

lead: For a nonfunctioning tumour >1 to ≤2 cm, choose observation or resection individually with the multidisciplinary team.
text: Reasonable Evidence C For a nonfunctioning tumour >1 to ≤2 cm, choose observation or resection individually with the multidisciplinary team. Indications Preferred when Consider grade and diagnostic confidence, symptoms, interval growth, main-duct dilation, imaging evidence of invasion or nodes, hereditary context, patient fitness and preference, and the pancreatic operation required. Document a surveillance schedule when observing. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Main-duct dilation, concerning growth, higher grade, invasion, nodal disease or symptoms should prompt reassessment for treatment; 2 cm is not a guarantee of benign behavior. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not treat 2 cm as a biological boundary.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not treat 2 cm as a biological boundary. Why Why Use it as the point at which the conversation changes, and decide with grade, growth rate, duct calibre, calcification, location, age and comorbidity. Additional cautions Additional cautions The number does not survive a receiver-operating-characteristic analysis: in 5,172 SEER patients with pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms, 1,760 of them 2 cm or less, the cutoff best associated with aggressive behaviour was 2.50 cm - area under the curve 0.769 (95% CI 0.755-0.782), sensitivity 81.3%, specificity 63.3% - and in that same dataset a size of 1-2 cm against 1 cm or less was not prognostic for overall survival (HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.65-1.31, p=0.652) while it did predict who was offered an operation (OR 1.60, 1.20-2.12, p=0.001). Below the line, metastatic potential is real rather than absent: 4 of 500 ASPEN patients (0.8%) had distant metastases at diagnosis. And in the National Cancer Data Base, among 1,854 non-functional tumours of 2 cm or less, 303 (29%) presented with regional nodal metastases and 180 (10%) with distant metastases, with nodal involvement failing to fall at the smallest sizes - 33% among the 94 tumours of 0.5 cm or less - while distant metastasis did rise with size (10.5% at 0.5 cm or less, 8.5% at 0.5-1.0 cm, 14.2% at 1-2 cm, p=0.02). Nodal risk may also not be uniform across populations: see the limited-evidence section and approval 3. Evidence & sources Do not read any of these in the other direction either. None of them shows that resecting a small tumour saves a life, and each carries a defect that points the same way. The 33% nodal figure for tumours of 5 mm or less rests on a band of 94 patients, in a variable missing in 45% of that cohort, with no confidence interval given; and the National Cancer Data Base by design records only tumours assigned a malignant behaviour code, which removes exactly the indolent small lesions a surveillance policy is about, so 29% and 10% are a ceiling for a selected malignant subset rather than estimates for an incidental lesion. The paper's own authors say the registry may overestimate the malignant potential of small tumours, and it carries no Ki-67, no mitotic rate and no disease-specific survival. The SEER cutoff of 2.50 cm was derived and reported in the same dataset with no validation, against a composite "aggressiveness" outcome assembled from poor differentiation, nodal involvement, liver involvement and advanced stage - variables mathematically entangled with size and with each other, so size was guaranteed to predict the composite - and a specificity of 63% would be unusable at the bedside. In that same analysis, surgery was associated with better overall survival both before and after propensity matching while cancer-specific survival was comparable after matching, which is the signature of confounding by comorbidity rather than a treatment effect: SEER cannot distinguish a patient enrolled in planned surveillance from one never offered an operation, and before matching that arm was older (65 or over in 52.8% against 36.1%) with seven times the rate of liver involvement (7.0% against 1.0%). There is no imaging follow-up, no growth rate and no crossover anywhere in it, so despite its title it has no purchase on surveillance as a strategy. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

ASPEN, tumours ≤2 cm: distant metastases at diagnosis in 4 of 500 patients (0.8%) Shows metastatic potential only; no evidence that resecting small tumours saves lives

lead: Do not let an observation decision be made without naming who owns the next scan and when it is due.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not let an observation decision be made without naming who owns the next scan and when it is due. Why Why One owner, one date, one named modality, recorded in the board output. A patient told "we will keep an eye on it" is not under surveillance. Additional cautions Additional cautions In ASPEN, patient preference was the stated reason for surgery in 42 of 94 cases (45%) and centre preference in 37 (39%) - 84% between them - duct dilatation in 11 (12%) and distant metastases in 4 (4%); a HADS anxiety score of 4-6 was independently associated with operating (OR 2.0, p=0.029) and enrolment at a surgical centre doubled the odds (OR 2.0, p=0.012). Unowned surveillance converts into an operation driven by accumulated anxiety and local culture rather than by tumour behaviour. The PANDORA quality-of-life finding is about the moment of entry rather than the experience of waiting: at baseline, patients scored worse than the reference population for emotional functioning (83.9 against 89.0, p=0.042), insomnia (22.9 against 14.0, p=0.046), dyspnoea (18.8 against 7.1, p=0.004) and nausea and vomiting (6.9 against 2.7, p=0.037), and its authors call the result too premature to interpret. Either way the psychological cost is measurable at the start of surveillance and should be addressed there rather than absorbed - three of PANDORA's six operations had no protocol indication at all, two of them for fear of progression and one because the surgeon did not support watchful waiting. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
