lead: Standard oncologic surgery — distal pancreatectomy with or without splenectomy, or pancreatoduodenectomy — is the operation for most resectable non-metastatic tumours.
text: Standard Evidence C Standard oncologic surgery — distal pancreatectomy with or without splenectomy, or pancreatoduodenectomy — is the operation for most resectable non-metastatic tumours. Indications Preferred when Tumours larger than 2 cm, malignant-appearing tumours, and functional tumours other than insulinoma. For a tumour larger than 2 cm or malignant-appearing, NCCN requires total removal with negative margins including adjacent organs where involved, together with regional nodes: pancreatoduodenectomy for the head, distal pancreatectomy with or without splenectomy or a spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy for body and tail. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not choose the operation from the size alone — position relative to the main pancreatic duct and the nodal question decide it. Splenectomy is generally included, but spleen preservation should be considered for a benign insulinoma; vaccinate at least 14 days before where splenectomy is possible. Evidence & sources Outcome context from the largest resected series, 3,851 patients in the National Cancer Data Base, 1985-2004: 5-year overall survival 59.3% and 10-year 37.7%, relative survival 65.7% and 47.8%, median follow-up 51 months. The independent predictors were age (55-75 HR 1.57, 95% CI 1.28-1.91; over 75 HR 3.04, 2.17-4.25), a nonfunctional tumour (HR 1.45, 1.06-1.97), high-grade histology (HR 2.03, 1.41-2.92), liver metastases (HR 1.71, 1.36-2.14) and other distant metastases (HR 3.78, 1.51-9.43), with pancreatoduodenectomy against distal pancreatectomy also adverse (HR 1.63, 1.03-2.57, p=0.04). Tumour size was not an independent predictor in any parameterisation, nor were nodal status (HR 1.18, 0.96-1.45, p=0.12), margins (gross positive HR 1.72, 0.95-3.12, p=0.08), chemotherapy, radiotherapy or hospital volume. Read the size result carefully before importing it into the observation decision: only 19% of that cohort's tumours were 2 cm or less, 171 tumours a pathologist had coded benign were excluded by design, grade was missing in 43.5% and size in about 22% with no sensitivity analysis, and the resulting prognostic score was derived and tested in the same 836 complete-case patients with a concordance index of 0.63 (0.59-0.67) - barely above the 0.5 of chance. The paper cannot be used to argue that size is irrelevant to whether to resect a 1 cm incidental lesion. The adverse coefficient for pancreatoduodenectomy is far more plausibly perioperative mortality and tumour location than an effect of the operation, which the authors concede while retaining it. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Aim for a negative margin, but do not extend the resection to get a wider one.
text: Standard Evidence C Aim for a negative margin, but do not extend the resection to get a wider one. Indications Preferred when NANETS' position is that resection with negative margins should be the goal but that no data support more aggressive resection to obtain wider surgical margins in this disease, which is what makes enucleation legitimate in selected patients. In the 3,851-patient National Cancer Data Base series, margin status was not an independent predictor of survival on multivariable analysis - a grossly positive margin carried HR 1.72 (95% CI 0.95-3.12, p=0.08) - although univariately well or moderately differentiated tumours did far better than poorly differentiated ones (5-year survival 63.9% against 28.3%, p<0.0001). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not use a 1 mm margin as a reason for a bigger operation. NANETS reports an 8-centre review of 1,020 resected patients in which R1 (margin 1 mm or less) occurred in 15% and 10-year recurrence-free survival fell to 47% from 63% (HR 1.8, p=0.02) while 10-year overall survival was unchanged at 71.1% against 71.8% (p=0.392), with grade, perineural invasion and vascular invasion significant for overall survival on multivariable analysis and margin status not. That series is not in this page's full-text depot and the figures are quoted as NANETS states them; the three-centre cohort that is in the depot reports R1 in 32 of 211 (15%), significant univariately and dropping out on backward selection. Evidence & sources What does predict recurrence is biology. In 211 curatively resected G1 and G2 non-functional tumours at three high-volume European centres, followed a median of 51 months, 35 (17%) recurred at a median of 43 months (IQR 23-62), 91% of them within 5 years and 69% in the pancreatic remnant; 5- and 10-year disease-specific survival were 98% and 84% and overall survival 91% and 68%. The independent predictors of recurrence within 5 years were grade 2 (HR 4.07, 95% CI 1.87-8.84, p<0.001), positive lymph nodes (HR 2.44, 1.17-5.09, p=0.017) and perineural invasion (HR 2.38, 1.11-5.10, p=0.026); tumour size, R1 and vascular invasion were significant univariately and dropped out on backward selection. Of 107 patients with none of the three factors, 2 recurred. Operative harm in that cohort was substantial too: major complications in 58 of 211 (27%) and grade B or C pancreatic fistula in 46 (22%). All three score components are postoperative findings, so the instrument says nothing about whether to operate - see clinical decision 9 for what it can and cannot do. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

NANETS-quoted 8-centre series (n=1,020): R1 (≤1 mm) in 15%; 10-y RFS 47% with R1 vs 63% without (HR 1.8, p=0.02); 10-y OS did not differ (p=0.392) Series not in full-text depot; figures as NANETS states them

lead: Small, superficial tumor clear of the main duct: consider enucleation/central pancreatectomy at an experienced center, with the nodal question settled before incision.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Small, superficial tumor clear of the main duct: consider enucleation/central pancreatectomy at an experienced center, with the nodal question settled before incision. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Enucleation and central pancreatectomy are legitimate for a small, superficial tumour clear of the main duct - at a centre doing enough of them, and with the nodal question settled before the incision. Indications Preferred when A tumour clear of the main pancreatic duct by more than 2 to 3 mm in a patient for whom preserving parenchyma matters. In a random-effects meta-analysis of 22 observational comparative studies (1,148 patients: 432 enucleations against 716 standard resections, 388 of them distal pancreatectomies and 328 pancreatoduodenectomies), enucleation gave less endocrine insufficiency (risk difference -0.08, 95% CI -0.12 to -0.04, p<0.001, I-squared 0%) and less exocrine insufficiency (-0.17, -0.31 to -0.04, p=0.01, I-squared 86%), 298 mL less blood loss (p<0.001), 78.4 minutes less operating time (p<0.001) and a stay shorter by 1.31 days (-2.55 to -0.06, p=0.04), with no difference in mortality (OR 1.49, 0.54-4.15), overall complications (OR 1.08, 0.68-1.73) or reoperation (OR 0.97, 0.46-2.04). ENETS adds the context: curative resection of a nonfunctioning tumour carries 5-year survival of 70-80%, and pancreatic resection carries morbidity up to 50% and mortality up to 3% even in high-volume centres. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid It costs fistula. Pancreatic fistula occurred in 25.5% after enucleation against 19.7% after standard resection, OR 2.09 (1.41-3.11), p<0.001, holding in the subset using the ISGPF definition (OR 2.15, 1.30-3.57) and for clinically relevant grade B or C disease (OR 1.93, 1.14-3.27, p=0.01, I-squared 0%). The excess lost significance only in the four studies performing more than 20 enucleations in total and at least 4 a year (OR 1.72, 0.87-3.38, p=0.12), which makes this a volume-conditional operation - see approval 5. And do not choose it to avoid a lymphadenectomy the tumour warrants: the review states plainly that it cannot address whether enucleation without lymphadenectomy is oncologically adequate, which is the question a surveillance pathway actually needs answered. Evidence & sources Grade C. No randomised trial exists; all 22 studies were observational, mean methodological quality was 13 of a possible 27 on a modified Downs and Black checklist, only one of the 22 reported information on principal confounders, and only 4 performed more than 20 enucleations. The operations were chosen for anatomically different lesions and the review concedes it cannot tell whether the standard-resection patients were ever enucleation candidates, so part of every difference is lesion size and position rather than the operation. Indications pooled insulinoma, non-functioning tumours, serous and mucinous cystadenoma, IPMN and chronic pancreatitis, so no result is specific to a neuroendocrine tumour; the hospital-stay result is acknowledged to be driven by between-country practice; and the volume threshold was defined by the review's own authors and inserted into the quality checklist, so the least pre-specified analysis is the one carried into the conclusion. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Minimally invasive and robotic approaches are reasonable for distal pancreatectomy and in experienced hands for central pancreatectomy.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Minimally invasive and robotic approaches are reasonable for distal pancreatectomy and in experienced hands for central pancreatectomy. Indications Preferred when NCCN suggests considering minimally invasive resection for a distal insulinoma. For central pancreatectomy, a laparoscopic-versus-open comparison reported shorter stay, less blood loss, earlier return to diet and better long-term quality of life, and a randomised trial of robot-assisted versus open central pancreatectomy reported shorter stay, reduced operative time, less blood loss, a lower clinical fistula rate and faster recovery. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let the approach dictate the oncologic operation. A spleen-preserving laparoscopic distal pancreatectomy that cannot deliver the nodal count the tumour warrants is the wrong operation done elegantly. Neither of the central-pancreatectomy comparisons above is in this page's full-text depot; both are quoted as NANETS reports them, neither was powered for an oncologic endpoint, and ENETS notes separately that robust data on minimally invasive pancreatoduodenectomy in this disease are lacking. [EXPERTISE] Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not use neoadjuvant therapy outside a trial or a specific downstaging intention.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not use neoadjuvant therapy outside a trial or a specific downstaging intention. Why Why NANETS states that the efficacy of neoadjuvant therapy for resectable or borderline-resectable disease remains unclear and that randomised trials are needed, while allowing it as an option for downstaging selected patients with advanced or metastatic disease, especially before cytoreductive surgery — which is the NELM pathway's territory. Additional cautions Additional cautions The supporting data are a retrospective MD Anderson series in which 29 of 356 patients with localised disease received 5-fluorouracil, doxorubicin and streptozocin, 48% went on to pancreatectomy and median overall survival was 112 months in the resected against 41 months in the unresected - a comparison of patients selected by their response. A propensity-matched NCDB study of 301 patients receiving perioperative systemic therapy against 301 having surgery alone found no difference for neoadjuvant therapy (P=0.21) and worse survival in the adjuvant group (P=0.037), with the agents not recorded. Neither series is in this page's full-text depot; both are quoted as NANETS and NCCN report them. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Guideline-quoted retrospective: neoadjuvant series (n=29) 48% resected, OS 112 vs 41 mo, resected vs unresected; matched NCDB, neoadjuvant vs surgery alone NS (P=0.21) Response-selected comparison; quoted secondhand; adjuvant worse in NCDB (P=0.037)

lead: Do not book a pancreatoduodenectomy for a tumour you have not finished staging.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not book a pancreatoduodenectomy for a tumour you have not finished staging. Why Why Liver and nodal status, duct calibre and receptor status before the operating list, not after. A receptor PET that finds an occult liver deposit converts this into the NELM pathway and changes which operation — if any — is right. Additional cautions Additional cautions NCCN's warning is explicit: a Whipple in metastatic disease is usually not curative and compromises later liver-directed therapy, and liver-directed therapy after a Whipple carries increased risk of cholangitis and liver abscess. That is an irreversible cost imposed on a patient whose disease is going to be managed hepatically for years.

lead: Where a formal pancreatoduodenectomy or distal pancreatectomy is being done, retrieve 11 to 15 nodes for accurate nodal staging.
text: Standard Evidence D Where a formal pancreatoduodenectomy or distal pancreatectomy is being done, retrieve 11 to 15 nodes for accurate nodal staging. Indications Preferred when Every oncologic resection. The count is derived rather than tested, and it is not derived in this disease. NANETS reports that compared with 1-5 and 6-10 nodes, examining 11-15 raised the likelihood of finding a nodal metastasis 2.3-fold and 1.5-fold respectively, while 16-20 or more than 20 added nothing; the primary study behind that figure is not in this page's full-text depot, and NANETS itself states that unlike gastric and colon cancer there is no universally accepted minimum node number for prognostication here. With a standard pancreatoduodenectomy or a distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy the count is usually not difficult to achieve. ENETS 2023 draws the line differently again: routine lymphadenectomy for tumours over 3 cm and case-by-case for 2-3 cm, on the ground that no preoperative test accurately predicts nodal involvement. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not present the node count as a therapeutic intervention. In the National Cancer Data Base series of 1,854 non-functional tumours of 2 cm or less, 999 of which were resected, 72.8% had a lymphadenectomy with a median of 8 nodes examined and 27% had no node examined at all; after adjustment there was no 2-year or 5-year survival difference between patients who did and did not have one, and no difference by type of resection (p=0.16). NANETS additionally reports a SEER analysis of 981 patients finding no survival advantage from sampling 10 or more nodes, a study not in this page's depot. The count is a staging instrument. Evidence & sources Nodal status does carry prognostic weight, and the reading of it has to be exact. In 136 operated patients with locoregional disease at one unit, 133 of whom had nodes resected, 50 (37.6%) were node positive with a mean of 13.7 plus or minus 11.5 nodes retrieved, and median disease-free survival was 4.5 against 14.6 years (log-rank p<0.0001), with 5- and 10-year disease-free survival 48.2% and 32.1% against 86.8% and 70.8%. Overall survival did not reach significance: 77.1% and 55.4% against 91.3% and 74.6%, log-rank 0.1. The frequency of nodal metastasis rose with tumour size above 1.5 cm (OR 4.7, 95% CI 1.81-12.35, p=0.002), head location against body and tail (OR 2.8, 1.3-5.8, p=0.007), Ki-67 above 20% (OR 6.7, 1.6-27.3, p=0.008) and lymphovascular invasion (OR 3.6, 1.5-8.6, p=0.004) - but on multivariable analysis no variable independently predicted nodal metastasis at all, those odds ratios were fitted on incomplete and varying subsets (lymphovascular invasion known in 97 of 136, Ki-67 in 121, grade in 112), and median nodes examined were 15 for head against 8 for body and tail (p=0.0002), so part of the location effect is a detection effect. Grade D for the 11-to-15 target: a borrowed number supported by a study this page has not read, in a cohort where no preoperative variable independently predicted the thing the count is for. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: NANETS-reported: 11–15 nodes examined vs 1–5 and 6–10 raised likelihood of finding nodal metastasis 2.3- and 1.5-fold; 16–20 or >20 added nothing Primary study not in depot; count borrowed, not derived in this disease
NCDB, NF tumours ≤2 cm (999 resected): lymphadenectomy in 72.8%, median 8 nodes; no adjusted 2- or 5-y survival difference with vs without

lead: Where a parenchyma-sparing operation is planned for a tumour of 2 cm or less, remove any node that looks suspicious on imaging and consider sampling even when imaging is negative.
text: Standard Evidence D Where a parenchyma-sparing operation is planned for a tumour of 2 cm or less, remove any node that looks suspicious on imaging and consider sampling even when imaging is negative. Indications Preferred when That is NANETS' recommendation verbatim, and the reason is that preoperative variables cannot exclude nodal disease. In the 136-patient series, multivariable analysis identified no independent predictor of nodal metastasis, and on the probability plot even the smallest pancreatic head tumours carried a nodal risk whose lower 95% bound sat just under 20%, with the smallest body and tail tumours estimated near 20% and a lower bound of 8.8%. Nodal metastasis was present in 2 of 17 tumours of 1 cm or less (12%) and 5 of 38 of 1.5 cm or less (13%). NANETS reports nodal metastasis in 12.9% to 27.3% of tumours of 2 cm or less, regardless of location. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat a spleen-preserving or central resection as nodally adequate by default. For body and tail lesions that means attention to the hepatic artery, celiac axis and splenic artery nodes; for head lesions, the posterior pancreatic and portocaval nodes. Whether removing them changes survival has not been established. And read the low-risk estimates for what they are: 2 of 17 patients carries a confidence interval running from roughly 2% to 36%, which can neither support nor refute any size threshold, and every patient in that cohort was operated at a unit that states its own institutional bias toward complete oncological resection - so the favourable small lesions that would populate a low-risk tail are structurally absent from the dataset, which the authors acknowledge before drawing a management conclusion from it anyway. Evidence & sources Nodal risk may not be uniform across populations. In a multi-institutional resected cohort from the US Neuroendocrine Tumor Study Group and a National Cancer Database validation cohort, nodal metastasis in tumours under 2 cm was 7 of 30 (23%) in Black patients against 8 of 151 (5%) in white patients, and 54 of 258 (21%) against 188 of 1,596 (12%), both p<0.01, with no racial difference in any larger size band; tumour size as a continuous variable predicted nodal metastasis in white patients only. The finding below 1 cm did not replicate - 2 of 8 (25%) against 0 of 33 (0%), p<0.01, in the first dataset but 7 of 67 (10%) against 31 of 354 (9%), p=0.66, in the validation. Every patient in both cohorts was resected with nodes removed, the two datasets overlap institutionally because the study group's own institutions report to the national database, grade was excluded from one and unavailable in the other, and no measure of insurance, income, referral delay or access to imaging was available. See the limited-evidence section and approval 3. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: NANETS-reported: nodal metastasis in 12.9% to 27.3% of tumours of 2 cm or less, regardless of location Guideline-quoted range; survival benefit of removing these nodes not established

lead: A pragmatic position: take the nodes because it makes the next decision possible, not because it treats the cancer.
text: Reasonable Evidence D A pragmatic position: take the nodes because it makes the next decision possible, not because it treats the cancer. Indications Preferred when NANETS puts it this way — reducing tumour burden through lymphadenectomy, or at the very least removing suspicious nodes seen on imaging or at exploration, is likely to facilitate future management. Nodal metastasis is one of the three independent predictors in the published recurrence score, so a patient whose nodal status is unknown cannot be risk-stratified for surveillance intensity afterwards. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not inflate this into a survival claim. The relationship between nodal metastasis and survival is genuinely inconsistent across series, and the reasons are structural: small numbers, inconsistent nodal sampling and pathological assessment, and follow-up too short for an indolent disease. NANETS reports a 326-patient cohort in which overall survival did not differ by nodal status at 2.7 years of follow-up and did differ significantly at 11 years; that paper is not in this page's depot. The one nodal cohort read in full here makes the same point in its own data and in the other direction: nodal status predicted disease-free survival strongly and overall survival not at all (log-rank 0.1), and its authors argue that the overall-survival result will become significant with longer follow-up rather than reporting the result they obtained, then use the disease-free finding to justify routine lymphadenectomy. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Extended lymphadenectomy has no established place.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Extended lymphadenectomy has no established place. Indications Preferred when Take the regional basin that the standard operation delivers and stop there. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid No survival benefit of extended dissection has been established, and unlike gastric and colon cancer there is no universally accepted minimum node number for prognostication in this disease — the 11 to 15 figure is borrowed from the pancreatic adenocarcinoma literature. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not convert a planned enucleation into a Whipple intraoperatively to obtain nodes.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not convert a planned enucleation into a Whipple intraoperatively to obtain nodes. Why Why Decide the operation, and therefore the nodal strategy, at the board and before the incision. If the nodal question is live enough to need a formal resection, plan one. Additional cautions Additional cautions The extent of resection has not been shown to change survival in small non-functional tumours: in 1,854 National Cancer Data Base patients with tumours of 2 cm or less, unadjusted 5-year overall survival after excluding metastatic and medically inoperable patients was 83.0% (95% CI 74.0-89.1) after partial pancreatectomy, 72.3% (60.4-81.2) after pancreatoduodenectomy and 86.0% (66.8-94.5) after total pancreatectomy, and after adjustment there was no difference in the risk of death across surgery types (p=0.16) and none with or without regional lymphadenectomy. Escalating the operation in theatre accepts added morbidity in exchange for information. Evidence & sources Grade D. That survival analysis collapses 1,854 patients to 366 by requiring a diagnosis before 2006 and a known surgery type, nodes examined differed systematically by operation (63% of partial pancreatectomies against 89% of pancreatoduodenectomies and 75% of total pancreatectomies), and the registry records only tumours assigned a malignant behaviour code. The same analysis reports 27.6% 5-year survival with no surgery against 83.0% with partial pancreatectomy - a contrast between groups that differed in age (median 63 against 56-57), in poor differentiation (29.9% against 1.8-5.2%), in distant metastases (42.1% against 1.1-2.0%) and in treatment at an academic centre, which the authors concede in the discussion while retaining it in the abstract. It should not be quoted as an argument for operating. The same paper also reports a 15% relative reduction in the risk of death for each later calendar year of diagnosis during a window in which resection rates and metastasis rates did not change, which is far more plausibly stage migration from incidental detection than improving care. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Registry (NCDB), tumours ≤2 cm: unadjusted 5-y OS 83.0% partial, 72.3% PD, 86.0% total pancreatectomy; adjusted, no difference by surgery type (p=0.16) Survival analysis on only 366 of 1,854; nodes examined differed by operation

lead: Send for genetic evaluation rather than assuming a solitary tumour is sporadic.
text: Standard Evidence C Send for genetic evaluation rather than assuming a solitary tumour is sporadic. Indications Preferred when NCCN recommends genetic risk evaluation and testing for gastrinoma, multifocal tumours, parathyroid disease before 30 or multigland disease, clinical suspicion of MEN1, and a mutation on tumour genomic testing with germline implications; it says to consider testing for a duodenal or pancreatic NET at any age. Studies of unselected patients have identified germline variants in 16% to 21% of cases, from relatively small cohorts. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let the result arrive after the operation. In MEN1 the lesion you can see is usually not the only lesion, and the finding changes the operation, its extent and its timing — not just the counselling. Evidence & sources The MEN1 recommendations were comprehensively revised in 2025, and the revision read in full for this page produced 55 recommendations: 52 Delphi consensus statements from an expert panel in 22 countries, plus 3 from systematic reviews that found only 37 of 3,048 screened publications usable, covering 1,814 patients, with all three resulting recommendations rated low or very low certainty by GRADE. Use that document or the separate AACE consensus statement rather than a pre-2021 source for the surveillance schedule. The AACE statement is cited on this page from its abstract only - its full text was not obtained - so every numeric criterion attributed to it must be confirmed against the published paper before use. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: MEN1: treatment depends on syndrome, size, growth and hereditary context. Insulinoma usually needs treatment; gastrinoma surgery is individualized. Small nonfunctioning lesions may be observed.
text: Standard Evidence D MEN1: treatment depends on syndrome, size, growth and hereditary context. Insulinoma usually needs treatment; gastrinoma surgery is individualized. Small nonfunctioning lesions may be observed. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × In MEN1, individualize treatment by functional syndrome and hereditary context. Symptomatic insulinoma generally requires treatment; MEN1 gastrinoma timing and extent remain controversial. Nonfunctioning lesions may be observed when small, with resection considered for size, growth and other concerning features. Surgery will not clear the inherited risk. Indications Preferred when NANETS: nonfunctional tumours under 1 cm can be observed and tumours over 2 cm should generally be resected; functional tumours should be removed where there is a dominant lesion. AACE 2025, from its abstract: functioning tumours resected regardless of size, nonfunctioning observed below 20 mm and strongly considered for resection above 20 mm or on significant growth under surveillance, with parenchyma-sparing surgery preferred. The 2025 best-practice recommendations say surgery should be considered for a growing nonfunctioning tumour and for one larger than 2 cm, with the indication settled by multidisciplinary discussion and shared decision making; ENETS 2023 observes 2 cm or less and advises resection above 2 cm (level 2, grade B), with 2-3 cm and any G2 tumour decided case by case. NCCN adds relatively rapid growth over 6 to 12 months as a third trigger alongside size and refractory symptoms. The threshold traces to a 108-patient cohort drawn from 579 registered MEN1 patients, in which nonfunctioning pancreatic tumours were the commonest pancreaticoduodenal lesion with a penetrance of 3% at age 20, 34% at 50 and 53% at 80, a mean size of 21 plus or minus 18 mm and a mean of 2.9 plus or minus 2.3 tumours per patient. Metastasis rose with size - 1 of 25 (4%) at 10 mm or less, 4 of 40 (10%) at 11-20 mm, 2 of 11 (18%) at 21-30 mm and 9 of 21 (43%) above 30 mm, Spearman 0.33, p<0.01 - and life expectancy was 68.5 years (95% CI 64-72.9) against 77.1 (74.4-79.9) for MEN1 patients without a pancreatic tumour, p<0.01. The authors concluded against routine surgery at or below 20 mm. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not plan an operation intended to be definitive. Microadenomas make complete clearance unachievable, local intrapancreatic recurrence unrelated to margins is reported as high as 50%, and the residual pancreas and duodenum remain at risk because the predisposition does not go away - in that same cohort, 2 of 32 curatively resected patients were reoperated for new tumours. It remains unclear from the literature whether an extensive partial resection reduces malignant progression or prevents new tumours in the remnant. Evidence & sources Grade D, downgraded on the full-text read. The 20 mm cut point was never derived: its two lowest strata are 1 of 25 and 4 of 40 patients whose confidence intervals overlap entirely, metastasis was imaging-defined in 60% of cases in a paper that itself cites evidence that a quarter of radiographically node-negative MEN1 patients have occult metastases at operation, mean follow-up after diagnosis was 4.3 plus or minus 3.3 years in a disease whose victims died at a mean age of 43, and the cohort spans 1956 to 2003 with prospective registration only from 1997, so penetrance and metastasis are estimated from different populations. The same paper's comparison of 32 curatively operated patients against 66 unoperated found no difference in metastasis (16% against 11%, p=0.5), death from the tumour (3.1% against 3%, p=0.99) or progression (22% against 12%, p=0.32) and no separation of the survival curves - an underpowered null, not evidence of equivalence, in groups that differed in follow-up and in mean size (30.2 against 16.3 mm, p=0.01). The 2025 systematic review reaches the same place from the other direction: across 37 studies and 1,814 patients, surgery and active surveillance for lesions of 2 cm or less produced no difference in metastasis or mortality at low to very low certainty. The 2025 recommendations add a surveillance schedule for a newly diagnosed lesion of 2 cm or less - repeat imaging at 6 to 12 months, again after 12 months if stable, then every 1 to 2 years if growth stays under 1 mm per year (92% agreement) - and a somatostatin-receptor PET for every patient planned for duodenopancreatic surgery (100% agreement). Hypergastrinaemia in MEN1 usually comes from small, multiple duodenal gastrinomas rather than from a pancreatic tumour, which is why NANETS allows medical management in many of these patients. Outcomes after surgery are good - 5-year overall survival 90-100% for functional and 65-100% for nonfunctional tumours - in a selected population. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: In von Hippel-Lindau, use three factors rather than size alone: size 3 cm or more, doubling time under 500 days, and a germline exon 3 mutation.
text: Standard Evidence D In von Hippel-Lindau, use three factors rather than size alone: size 3 cm or more, doubling time under 500 days, and a germline exon 3 mutation. Indications Preferred when NANETS: a patient with a tumour under 3 cm, doubling time over 500 days and a mutation outside exon 3 can be safely observed with imaging every 1 to 2 years; one high-risk factor means considering surgery or imaging at 6 to 12 month intervals; two or more means strongly considering resection. The derivation is a prospective NIH protocol in which 633 VHL patients were screened and 108 (17%) had a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour - none functional by hormone level or symptom - of whom 9 (8.3%) developed metastases and 2 died of them, 1.4% of everyone screened, over a median follow-up of 53 months. A primary larger than 3 cm was present in 6 of the 9 with metastases (67%) against 19 of 99 without (19%), p=0.0046; an exon 3 germline mutation in 7 of 9 (78%) against 32 of 98 (46%), p=0.01; and mean tumour doubling time was 337 days (range 180-463) against 2,628 days (103-9,614), p<0.0001. All 9 metastatic patients met at least two of the three criteria and 6 met all three, while among the 54 assessable patients without metastases 5 met two, 20 met one and 29 met none. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not transfer the sporadic 2 cm threshold to VHL - the malignant potential is lower and the observation ceiling is correspondingly higher. Equally, do not assume every solid pancreatic lesion in a VHL patient is a neuroendocrine tumour: NANETS reports that about half of VHL patients develop benign pancreatic cysts, serous cystadenomas or haemangioblastomas, which need no intervention unless symptomatic or causing pancreatitis or biliary compression. Evidence & sources Grade D, downgraded on the full-text read. The three-criterion rule was derived from 9 metastatic events and then declared to capture all 9, so its perfect sensitivity is a tautology of the derivation rather than a finding, with no independent or temporal validation attempted. Doubling time, the criterion with the largest apparent separation, was computable in all 9 metastatic patients but in only 54 of 99 without metastases, and patients with visibly growing lesions are imaged more often, so the exposure and the ability to measure it are entangled and 45 patients are simply absent from the stratification table. Sixty-nine of the 108 lesions were never resected and their diagnosis rests on CT or MRI appearance alone, which the senior author conceded in discussion could include microcystic adenomas. The 3 cm cut point was carried over from the group's own earlier publications and was never tested against 1 or 2 cm within the dataset - a discussant asked exactly that and was told the analysis had not been done - and the study dates are internally inconsistent between abstract and methods. There is no Ki-67, grade or differentiation datum anywhere in the series. Receptor PET is useful here specifically: differentiating a microcystic adenoma from a small tumour is difficult on CT and MRI in VHL, and receptor PET can resolve it. NANETS reports that these tumours cluster in the head and uncinate process (52%) against body (21%) and tail (28%). Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Prospective NIH: metastases 9/108 VHL PNETs (8.3%); metastatic vs not: >3 cm 67 vs 19% (p=0.0046), exon 3 78 vs 46% (p=0.01), doubling time 337 vs 2,628 days Rule derived from 9 events, no validation; doubling time missing in 45 without metastases

lead: A somatostatin analogue is a reasonable antiproliferative option for MEN1-related tumours under 2 cm, on prospective but non-randomised evidence.
text: Reasonable Evidence D A somatostatin analogue is a reasonable antiproliferative option for MEN1-related tumours under 2 cm, on prospective but non-randomised evidence. Indications Preferred when A MEN1 patient with one or more sub-2 cm tumours in whom the aim is to delay or avoid pancreatic surgery. In a prospective observational study at one Italian centre - 23 patients given lanreotide autogel 120 mg every 28 days and 19 continuing active surveillance, 91 lesions in all at a mean size of 6.8 plus or minus 3.4 mm, median follow-up 73 months (range 24-84) - median progression-free survival was not reached with lanreotide against 40 months under surveillance (p<0.001). On treatment there were 4 objective responses (17.4%), 15 stable (65.2%) and 4 progressing (17.4%); under surveillance 13 of 19 (68.4%) progressed and 6 (31.6%) were stable. Toxicity was minimal: one grade 1 diarrhoea and two cases of asymptomatic biliary stone disease, with no dose reduction or interruption. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Treatment was chosen rather than allocated - lanreotide was proposed to every included patient as an alternative to surveillance - and the paper reports no comparison of comorbidity, disease burden, prior surgery or stated reason for the choice, so the arms differ by whatever disposes a patient to accept monthly injections for six years. The lanreotide arm also carried more tumours per patient at baseline (p=0.038), and patient-level progression-free survival is mixed with lesion-level response counting (22 of 62 treated lesions shrank against 0 of 29) with no adjustment for clustering of lesions within patients. Forty-two patients generated 17 radiological progression events in total, assessed unblinded with no central read, under a definition that counts a 20% size increase in a 7 mm lesion. Everything that matters was indistinguishable: liver metastases in 1 patient per arm, operations in 2 of 23 against 5 of 19, and no deaths. Do not extend it to sporadic small tumours, where there is no comparable evidence, no guideline support, and ENETS states explicitly that no evidence supports somatostatin analogues for controlling the progression of a small nonfunctioning tumour under surveillance. Evidence & sources Grade D, downgraded on the full-text read. This is still the only prospective evaluation of analogues in MEN1-related tumours and it is cited by NCCN. The international consensus statement on the pancreas in MEN1 remains the fuller reference for how functioning and nonfunctioning duodenopancreatic disease is managed in this syndrome; it is cited on this page from its abstract only, its full text was not obtained, and the 2025 best-practice recommendations should be read alongside it. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Belzutifan may be considered for a resectable tumour in a patient with a germline VHL alteration, individualised, and is not a substitute for an operation.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Belzutifan may be considered for a resectable tumour in a patient with a germline VHL alteration, individualised, and is not a substitute for an operation. Indications Preferred when NCCN allows consideration of belzutifan for resectable tumours in germline VHL disease, with the decision individualised for small resectable lesions. The supporting trial is a phase 2, open-label, single-group study of 61 patients at 11 centres, all given belzutifan 120 mg daily, whose primary endpoint was objective response in renal cell carcinoma. After a median follow-up of 21.8 months the renal response rate was 49% (95% CI 36-62), all partial, with 24-month progression-free survival 96% (87-99). All 61 patients had pancreatic lesions, of which 47 (77%) responded including 6 complete responses; among the 22 patients who had pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours specifically, 20 (91%) had a confirmed response including 3 complete responses, at a median baseline target size of 21 mm (range 10-52) and a median time to response of 5.5 months. Central nervous system haemangioblastomas responded in 15 of 50 (30%). No patient underwent pancreatic surgery during the trial. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Read the pancreatic figure for what it is: 20 of 22 patients, a secondary endpoint of a single-arm industry-sponsored trial with no comparator, no pre-specified statistical plan for it, no multiplicity control across the several organ systems assessed and no histological confirmation that each measured lesion was a neuroendocrine tumour rather than a serous cystadenoma - the two were deliberately measured together in the larger 77% figure. Eligibility required no renal tumour above 3 cm, no metastases and performance status 0 or 1, so the cohort is the fittest and least advanced end of the VHL population. Anaemia occurred in 90% of patients, grade 3 in 8%, with 20% needing erythropoiesis-stimulating agents and 7% transfusion, and fatigue in 66%; every patient's haemoglobin fell by at least 1.9 g/dL in the first 13 weeks. Twenty-two months of exposure cannot establish durability, cumulative harm or resistance in a drug that might be taken for decades. Nothing here applies to sporadic disease, where the driving lesion is not VHL loss. NCCN states that data for larger tumours, locally advanced unresectable tumours and distant disease are extremely limited and that trials are ongoing. [PAYER] Evidence & sources One correction from the full-text read: the first draft of this page said the trial does not report a response rate for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours separately. It does - 20 of 22 (91%), which ENETS quotes as 90.9%. The comparison of 327 lifetime tumour-reduction procedures before treatment against 3 afterwards is not a like-for-like rate; the authors' own figure records 64 procedures in the preceding 2.5 years, which is. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: MEN4, NF1 and tuberous sclerosis: manage on clinical judgement, and say that is what you are doing.
text: Reasonable Evidence D MEN4, NF1 and tuberous sclerosis: manage on clinical judgement, and say that is what you are doing. Indications Preferred when Pancreatic tumours are rare in NF1 and tuberous sclerosis, and in tuberous sclerosis they are typically small, well-differentiated and often functional, in the body or tail, with insulin-secreting tumours common; resection of a functional tumour to cure the hormone excess is indicated when safe. MEN4 is newly described, penetrance estimates and surveillance guidelines are not available, and NCCN allows following the MEN1 surveillance recommendations given the clinical overlap. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not present any of this as evidence based. By 2012 only 10 tuberous-sclerosis-associated pancreatic NETs had been reported, and NANETS states that no evidence-based surveillance or treatment recommendation can be made. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not operate for a hormonal syndrome in MEN1 on the assumption that the biggest visible tumour is the source.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not operate for a hormonal syndrome in MEN1 on the assumption that the biggest visible tumour is the source. Why Why Attempt preoperative localisation of the functional tumour specifically, and use intraoperative ultrasonography routinely. Refer to a high-volume endocrine surgery centre. Additional cautions Additional cautions NANETS warns that multiplicity makes definitive preoperative determination that the dominant tumour is the source of hormone overproduction difficult, and that hypergastrinaemia in MEN1 much more often arises from duodenal gastrinomas than from pancreatic tumours. Resecting the dominant nodule and finding the syndrome unchanged is a recognised outcome. [EXPERTISE] Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not use a VHL tumour's location in the head as a reason to resect it earlier.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not use a VHL tumour's location in the head as a reason to resect it earlier. Why Why Decide on size, doubling time and mutation; let location decide only which operation is performed. Additional cautions Additional cautions The earlier proposal of a 2 cm threshold in the head and 3 cm in the body and tail was motivated by a wish to avoid a future pancreatoduodenectomy, not by biology. NANETS states that there is no evidence of any difference in biological behaviour by anatomic location and therefore no evidence that size criteria should be influenced by it — see the flagged item below. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: A localised well-differentiated G3 tumour is evaluated for resection with regional lymphadenectomy, after multidisciplinary review, with a clinical trial preferred where one exists.
text: Standard Evidence C A localised well-differentiated G3 tumour is evaluated for resection with regional lymphadenectomy, after multidisciplinary review, with a clinical trial preferred where one exists. Indications Preferred when NCCN's locoregional G3 page offers clinical trial as the preferred option, or resection with regional lymphadenectomy if appropriate after multidisciplinary review, or neoadjuvant systemic therapy case by case where the Ki-67 is 55% or above. NANETS: patients with high-grade well-differentiated tumours should be evaluated for resection if localised, in the context of multimodal therapy. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Be honest about what resection achieves here. In 310 resected patients, the 24 with G3 tumours had 5-year overall survival of 20% (relative risk 13.56 against G1) compared with 91% for G1 and 71% for G2; among the G3 patients, those without metastases reached 43% at 5 years and those with metastases 0% (35% at 2 years). In 119 high-grade tumours from 10 Nordic centres, 85% were metastatic at diagnosis; of 14 resected patients without metastases, 13 developed metastases and the fourteenth a local recurrence, at a median of 7 months. Evidence & sources The 310-patient and 119-patient resected series quoted above are taken from the NANETS consensus text and are not in this page's full-text depot. The 305-patient Nordic study of advanced gastrointestinal neuroendocrine carcinoma that is in the depot concerns unresectable disease and bears on this assessment only through its prognostic findings: median survival was 11 months (95% CI 9.4-12.6) with palliative chemotherapy and 1 month (0.3-1.8) with best supportive care, but the untreated group was twelve years older with 52% at performance status 3-4, so that contrast is late referral rather than a treatment effect. Pancreatic primaries, 71 of the 305, had the longest median survival of any site - 15 months against 8 for colonic, p=0.01 across sites - and were more often receptor-positive (46% against 0-25%, p=0.001). Performance status dominated the final model: median survival 18 months at PS 0, 12 at PS 1 and 5 at PS 2, alongside primary site, platelets below 400 and a normal lactate dehydrogenase. There is no role for adjuvant therapy here outside a trial. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Observational, unresectable GI NEC (n=305): median survival 11 mo (95% CI 9.4–12.6) vs 1 mo, palliative chemo vs best supportive care; pancreatic 15 vs colonic 8 mo Untreated group older, 52% PS 3–4: late referral, not treatment effect; unresectable disease

lead: For poorly differentiated pancreatic NEC, prioritize multidisciplinary systemic-treatment assessment; selected localized disease may still warrant consideration of R0 surgery.
text: Standard Evidence C For poorly differentiated pancreatic NEC, prioritize multidisciplinary systemic-treatment assessment; selected localized disease may still warrant consideration of R0 surgery. Indications Preferred when NANETS 2020 generally advises against resection of pancreatic NEC. ENETS 2023 permits selected localized disease to be considered for surgery after thorough staging, with perioperative treatment discussed. Differentiation informs care but is not the sole determinant: integrate stage, anatomy, fitness and expected benefit. Metastatic NEC generally follows a systemic-therapy pathway. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not read the two guidelines as agreeing. NANETS is close to absolute; ENETS leaves a door open for genuinely localised disease after thorough imaging. Where they do agree is that cytoreduction of liver metastases is not indicated in this histology because of high relapse rates and poor survival, and that chemotherapy comes first. Evidence & sources Molecular profiling can identify treatment-relevant alterations. Biomarker-unselected immunotherapy has limited activity. Keep poorly differentiated NEC separate from well-differentiated NET G3 and do not use a Ki-67 threshold alone to choose between them. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Treat the Ki-67 55% split as a prompt for discussion rather than a decision rule - it is not independently prognostic in the study that produced it.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Treat the Ki-67 55% split as a prompt for discussion rather than a decision rule - it is not independently prognostic in the study that produced it. Indications Preferred when NCCN offers neoadjuvant systemic therapy case by case where the Ki-67 is 55% or above. The cut point comes from 305 patients with advanced gastrointestinal neuroendocrine carcinoma at twelve Nordic centres, in whom the first-line response rate to platinum was 15% below 55% against 42% at or above it (p<0.001). Platinum schedule made no difference to response or survival, small-cell and non-small-cell morphology made no difference either (median survival 12 against 11 months), and later lines retained activity - second-line response 18%, third-line 7%, platinum reintroduction after a break 15%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not use 55% to decide an operation. The cut point was derived by receiver-operating-characteristic analysis in 42 randomly selected patients and then applied to the rest of the same cohort with no external validation; median survival was longer below it, not above it (14 against 10 months, p<0.001, with 30-month survival 23% against 7%); and it dropped out of both the full and the final multivariable models because of its strong association with primary site, so the paper's signature marker is not independently prognostic in its own analysis - a point the abstract does not convey. Ki-67 was read by many pathologists in several countries with no central review, and response was assessed by RECIST 1.0 from radiological reports rather than from measured target lesions. The regression producing the final model ran on 170 of 252 chemotherapy patients. Evidence & sources What the model did retain was performance status (PS 0 odds ratio 0.24, 0.14-0.42, p<0.001), primary tumour site (p=0.007), platelets below 400 x 10^9 (0.47, 0.31-0.72) and a normal lactate dehydrogenase (0.50, 0.32-0.78). See approval 6. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Cohort n=305: platinum response 15% (Ki-67 <55%) vs 42% (≥55%), p<0.001; median survival 14 vs 10 mo (<55% vs ≥55%), p<0.001 Cut point from ROC in 42 patients, unvalidated; not independently prognostic

lead: In a mixed neuroendocrine–non-neuroendocrine neoplasm, have each component diagnosed and graded, and stage by the non-neuroendocrine counterpart.
text: Reasonable Evidence D In a mixed neuroendocrine–non-neuroendocrine neoplasm, have each component diagnosed and graded, and stage by the non-neuroendocrine counterpart. Indications Preferred when NCCN requires each component to be diagnosed and graded separately where the smaller component is at least 30% of the tumour mass. Extrapulmonary carcinomas, including these mixed neoplasms, are staged according to the organ-specific criteria for their non-neuroendocrine counterpart — for the pancreas, that means adenocarcinoma staging. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid There is no pathway for this entity. NCCN calls management controversial and notes that chemotherapy regimens directed at the non-neuroendocrine component may be considered. Do not pretend a decision rule exists. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not route a high-grade tumour to a pathway on the Ki-67 alone.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not route a high-grade tumour to a pathway on the Ki-67 alone. Why Why Differentiation first, then grade. NCCN says it in the plainest terms available: not all high-grade neoplasms with Ki-67 above 20% are poorly differentiated. Additional cautions Additional cautions Treating a well-differentiated G3 tumour as a small-cell carcinoma costs a patient a potentially curative operation - median disease-specific survival in well-differentiated tumours with a morphologically apparent high-grade component was 55 months (range 16-119), with 2-year and 5-year survival 88-89% and 48-49%, against 16 months and 24% and 24% for true pancreatic poorly differentiated carcinoma. Treating a carcinoma as a NET costs weeks that patient does not have. NCCN's own statement is that advanced carcinoma patients should be considered for chemotherapy without delay. Evidence & sources Two cautions from the full-text read. First, the 55-against-16-month contrast is unmatched: once stage IV was matched, pancreatic grade 1-2 tumours and those with a high-grade component did not differ significantly in disease-specific survival, and both did far better than poorly differentiated carcinoma (median 61 against 16 months, p<0.001), which is the result most corrosive to a sharp prognostic split between the first two. The first draft of this page gave 11 months for the carcinoma comparator; the paper's figure is 16. Second, the Ki-67 55% cut point NCCN uses is not independently prognostic in its own derivation study - see the reasonable-alternative item above and approval 6. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: For resected well-differentiated NET G3, adjuvant systemic therapy is not established; assess clinical-trial eligibility.
text: Avoid Evidence D For resected well-differentiated NET G3, adjuvant systemic therapy is not established; assess clinical-trial eligibility. Why Why Do not generalize this NET statement to poorly differentiated NEC. For selected resected localized NEC, ENETS allows discussion of adjuvant platinum-based therapy within multidisciplinary care. Additional cautions Additional cautions The temptation is strong because relapse is near-universal, but nothing establishes benefit, and the only comparative data in this disease — propensity-matched NCDB — found worse survival in the adjuvant group (P=0.037). Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: There is no established adjuvant therapy after resection of a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour — say so rather than offering something.
text: Standard Evidence C There is no established adjuvant therapy after resection of a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour — say so rather than offering something. Indications Preferred when For resected well-differentiated pNET, no routine adjuvant systemic treatment is established. Consider trials after checking current eligibility and an accessible site. SWOG S2104 (NCT05040360) tests CAPTEM versus observation in a selected higher-risk population, including 14–120 days after resection, Ki-67 3–55% and Zaidi recurrence-risk score ≥3; it is not available to every resected patient. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not improvise. The only comparative data are a propensity-matched NCDB analysis of 301 patients receiving perioperative systemic therapy against 301 having surgery alone, in which the adjuvant group did worse (P=0.037) - a result that is almost certainly selection rather than harm, since the agents were not recorded, but which does not support treating. That analysis is quoted from the NANETS and NCCN text and is not in this page's full-text depot. Evidence & sources Somatostatin analogues are not adjuvant therapy. Their antiproliferative evidence is in advanced disease, the only prospective study in small tumours is in MEN1 and was not randomised (see clinical decision 7), and ENETS states plainly that no evidence supports somatostatin analogues for controlling the progression of a small nonfunctioning tumour under surveillance. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Follow the schedule: imaging at 12 weeks to 12 months, then every 6 to 12 months to a maximum of 10 years, then as clinically indicated.
text: Standard Evidence D Follow the schedule: imaging at 12 weeks to 12 months, then every 6 to 12 months to a maximum of 10 years, then as clinically indicated. Indications Preferred when History and examination, multiphasic abdomen with or without pelvis CT or MRI, chest CT as clinically indicated, and biochemical markers for functional tumours as clinically indicated. Earlier if symptoms. Use the same modality and contrast agent each time. For high-grade disease the interval is shorter: every 12 to 24 weeks for 2 years, then every 6 to 12 months for up to 10 years depending on biology and Ki-67. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Receptor-based imaging and FDG-PET are not recommended for routine surveillance. Do not stop at 5 years in a G2 or node-positive patient: recurrences appear at a median of 5.1 years after resection of small tumours in the matched case-control series, at a median of 43 months in the three-centre European cohort of G1-G2 non-functional tumours, and at a median of 7.2 years for pancreatic primaries in the Ontario population cohort behind the published follow-up recommendations, where cumulative recurrence reached 33.5% at 5 years and 48.5% at 10. Ten-year overall survival after resection is 37.7% across the whole resected National Cancer Data Base population. ENETS tells patients to expect at least 20 years of surveillance and possibly lifelong. The tail of this disease is long. Evidence & sources This schedule is consensus, not trial-derived, and the three consensus sources disagree with one another. NCCN starts at 12 weeks to 12 months and runs to a maximum of 10 years. ENETS 2023 starts at 3 to 6 months; SSTR PET is considered if no pretherapeutic scan was obtained or when clinically indicated, alongside morphological imaging, then every 6 to 12 months for 5 years, every 12 to 24 months for 10 years after the first five years (the ENETS wording) and then every 5 years, at level 5 evidence graded B in the guidance's own framework. The RAND/UCLA follow-up recommendations for completely resected gastroenteropancreatic tumours deliberately de-intensify the first three years - yearly imaging for 3 years, then every 1 to 2 years to 10, with the decision to continue or stop discussed with the patient at 10 - while extending beyond 10, and exempt a grade 1, node-negative pancreatic tumour under 2 cm from follow-up altogether. That exemption came from a 22-member panel at a 75% agreement threshold, over an evidence base of 6 eligible studies plus two then-unpublished cohorts that carried no grade, stage or margin data - the very variables the recommendations stratify on. It is not adopted here. All three agree on one thing: no serum or urine biomarker has a routine role, and an isolated rise in chromogranin A is not an indication to change treatment without radiological progression. See approval 13. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Risk-stratify the surveillance intensity on grade, nodal status and perineural invasion rather than on size.
text: Standard Evidence D Risk-stratify the surveillance intensity on grade, nodal status and perineural invasion rather than on size. Indications Preferred when In 211 curatively resected G1 and G2 non-functional tumours at three high-volume European centres, followed a median of 51 months, 35 (17%) recurred at a median of 43 months (IQR 23-62), 91% within 5 years and 69% in the pancreatic remnant; 5- and 10-year disease-specific survival were 98% and 84% and overall survival 91% and 68%. The independent predictors of recurrence within 5 years were grade 2 (HR 4.07, 95% CI 1.87-8.84, p<0.001), lymph node metastasis (HR 2.44, 1.17-5.09, p=0.017) and perineural invasion (HR 2.38, 1.11-5.10, p=0.026), and the resulting score discriminated well internally (Harrell c-statistic 0.81, 95% CI 0.75-0.87) and calibrated adequately (Hosmer-Lemeshow chi-square 11.25, p=0.258). Of 107 patients with none of the three factors, 2 recurred. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Grade D on the full-text read, and the score has not been shown to add to grading: WHO grade alone gave a c-statistic of 0.72 (0.64-0.79) and the difference between the two was p=0.059, so by the paper's own test it is not better than grade. Its cut-off of 24 was selected by receiver-operating-characteristic analysis in the same data by both Youden index and log-rank, so 91% sensitivity is optimistic by construction and 62% specificity does not discriminate clinically. External validation was still ongoing at publication and the authors chose to publish without it. All three components are postoperative findings, so the instrument cannot inform whether to operate, only how often to scan afterwards. Imaging intensity during follow-up was explicitly keyed to chromogranin A, grade and nodal status, so the score's predictors also predicted the chance of detecting a recurrence - a surveillance bias the authors note and do not adjust for. The cohort excluded MEN1, VHL, grade 3 and all metastatic disease, so the 17% recurrence rate and the 2-of-107 figure apply to a cleaner population than clinic presents. In the sub-2 cm subgroup, which is what any size threshold needs, there were 4 recurrence events in 84 patients and the univariable hazard ratios span two orders of magnitude (perineural invasion 30.7, 95% CI 3.19-295.74); no multivariable model was possible and none should be inferred. The work was funded by Ipsen and its stated purpose is to identify high-risk patients for future adjuvant therapy trials. Evidence & sources In MEN1 the remnant is the problem rather than the margin: local intrapancreatic recurrence unrelated to margin status is reported as high as 50%, so a MEN1 patient's surveillance is lifelong and is about new disease, not about this operation. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: When hepatic metastases appear, this becomes the NELM pathway — hand the patient over by name and keep the pancreatic history with them.
text: Standard Evidence D When hepatic metastases appear, this becomes the NELM pathway — hand the patient over by name and keep the pancreatic history with them. Indications Preferred when The NELM page is where hepatic burden and distribution, cytoreduction thresholds, liver-directed modality selection, systemic sequencing, carcinoid-crisis precautions and the transplant question live. Two facts from this page travel with the patient and change what that page can offer: whether a pancreatoduodenectomy has been done, because liver-directed therapy afterwards carries an increased risk of cholangitis and liver abscess; and whether a cholecystectomy was performed, because long-term somatostatin analogue therapy raises the risk of biliary symptoms and cholecystitis. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not start systemic therapy for hepatic metastases on this page. Do not restage with a pancreas-only protocol. And do not let a transplant-relevant patient be committed to a pancreatic reoperation before the NELM page's transplant assessment has been asked, since Milan-NET criteria require the primary to have been resected with all extrahepatic disease and a documented disease-free interval. Evidence & sources Resection of recurrent locoregional disease, an isolated distant metastasis, or a previously unresectable tumour that has regressed should be considered for selected patients with adequate performance status — that is NCCN's position and it is the one circumstance where this page and the NELM page are deciding the same operation together. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Receptor PET has a defined place in follow-up, and it is not routine imaging.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Receptor PET has a defined place in follow-up, and it is not routine imaging. Indications Preferred when The appropriate-use indications NANETS reproduces are three: monitoring disease seen predominantly on receptor PET; restaging at clinical or biochemical progression without progression on conventional imaging; and a new indeterminate lesion on conventional imaging with unclear progression. Where disease is visible on both and conventional imaging is stable, intermittent PET every 2 to 3 years may help; where the tumour is readily seen on CT or MRI, receptor PET is not needed for monitoring. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The supporting evidence is thin and mostly expert opinion. NANETS reports that in 63 patients imaged after resection sensitivity and specificity for recurrence were 92% and 80%, and that in a 143-patient multicentre follow-up cohort receptor imaging detected 75.8% (132 of 174) of new lesions and 29.3% (51 of 174) that CT had missed, being judged useful in 73.4% of patients - but "useful" was defined as changing a subsequent action, not as changing an outcome, and neither series is in this page's full-text depot. The SNMMI/EANM procedure standard, which is, gives no guidance at all on whether or how to use receptor PET in a small pancreatic lesion under surveillance, and warns that an increase or decrease in lesional uptake must not be taken as an indicator of response or progression the way it would be with other radiotracers - which removes the obvious use. The standard also carries no systematic review, no evidence grading and no strength-of-recommendation scheme, so a prospective trial and a package insert carry equal weight in it. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Manage the sequelae of the operation as part of follow-up, not as someone else's problem.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Manage the sequelae of the operation as part of follow-up, not as someone else's problem. Indications Preferred when New endocrine and exocrine insufficiency is the commonest durable harm of this pathway and it is measurable. In a random-effects meta-analysis of 22 observational comparative studies (1,148 patients: 432 enucleations against 716 standard resections), enucleation gave less endocrine insufficiency (risk difference -0.08, 95% CI -0.12 to -0.04, p<0.001, I-squared 0%) and less exocrine insufficiency (-0.17, -0.31 to -0.04, p=0.01, I-squared 86%). NANETS adds that after central pancreatectomy endocrine and exocrine insufficiency rates were 4% and 5% against 24% and 17% after distal pancreatectomy and 17% and 29% after pancreatoduodenectomy. Screen for both, and for pancreatic exocrine deficiency in anyone on long-term analogue therapy. ENETS adds the late iatrogenic harms to screen for after systemic treatment: renal dysfunction after streptozotocin or peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, heart failure after sunitinib or doxorubicin, and marrow effects after radionuclide therapy or alkylating agents. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not count a resection a success on imaging alone in a patient who now has diabetes they did not have, for a tumour that might have been observed. And do not read the functional advantage as an effect of the operation alone: the review concedes it cannot tell whether the standard-resection patients were ever enucleation candidates, the indications pooled are insulinoma, non-functioning tumours, serous and mucinous cystadenoma, IPMN and chronic pancreatitis, mean methodological quality was 13 of a possible 27, only one of the 22 studies reported information on principal confounders, and the exocrine result carries I-squared 86% across 5 studies with no standardised definition or timing of assessment. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Consensus-reported endocrine/exocrine insufficiency 4%/5% vs 24%/17% vs 17%/29%, central pancreatectomy vs distal pancreatectomy vs pancreatoduodenectomy

lead: Do not surveil an observed primary less carefully than a resected one.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not surveil an observed primary less carefully than a resected one. Why Why NCCN applies the same surveillance schedule to patients in whom observation was chosen. The whole safety case for observation rests on detecting growth, and the crossover rates in the published cohorts are the mechanism by which that case holds, or fails to: 26 of 104 (25%) over a median of 30 months in the matched case-control series, 9 of 406 (2%) over 25 months in ASPEN, and 6 of 76 (8%) over 17 months in PANDORA. Read each of them as the full text reports it. In the first, the crossovers stay in the observation arm by intention to treat, so part of that arm's clean record was bought with the operation the paper argues can be avoided. In PANDORA, six of the eight patients who met the protocol's own resection criterion refused the operation, so the protocol was never tested. And in ASPEN only 4 of 406 surveillance patients came to surgery for growth at all. Additional cautions Additional cautions An observed tumour with no owner and no interval is not being observed. This is the single most likely way for this pathway to fail a patient. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: ASPEN surveillance: crossover to surgery 9 of 406 (2%) over 25 mo; only 4 of 406 operated for growth
PANDORA: crossover to resection 6 of 76 (8%) over 17 mo; six of eight meeting the resection criterion refused surgery Protocol's own resection criterion was never tested

lead: Do not use routine FDG-PET or receptor PET as a surveillance scan.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not use routine FDG-PET or receptor PET as a surveillance scan. Why Why Multiphasic CT or MRI on the schedule above, with the functional scans reserved for the three appropriate-use situations. Additional cautions Additional cautions NCCN states that receptor-based imaging and FDG-PET are not recommended for routine surveillance. Receptor PET also has not been shown to add significantly to conventional imaging for assessing response to peptide receptor radionuclide therapy. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: MRI/MRCP: characterize the cyst and record main duct diameter in mm; 5-/10-mm thresholds affect management.
text: Standard Evidence C MRI/MRCP: characterize the cyst and record main duct diameter in mm; 5-/10-mm thresholds affect management. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Characterise the cyst on MRI with MRCP and write the main pancreatic duct diameter down in millimetres, because the 5 mm and 10 mm duct thresholds are what separate surveillance from an operation. Indications Preferred when Every incidental or symptomatic pancreatic cyst at first presentation. ACG names MRCP the preferred modality for pancreatic cyst surveillance; Kyoto 2024 builds its whole algorithm on duct diameter and on the height and enhancement of a mural nodule, so a report that omits those measurements cannot be acted on. Reported accuracy for naming the cyst type is 40 to 50% for MRI, CT and EUS without aspiration per ACG and 40 to 95% for MRI and 40 to 81% for CT per the European guideline; for benign against malignant, 55 to 76%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not accept a report that says 'cystic lesion of the pancreas, recommend follow-up' with no duct diameter, no nodule height and no comment on communication with the duct. That report cannot be placed anywhere on this page. Evidence & sources Duct communication is the single most useful discriminator in practice but is not by itself diagnostic: a mucinous cystic neoplasm does not communicate, a branch-duct IPMN does, and both are mucinous. Kyoto 2024 is explicit that the classification of mixed IPMN remains ambiguous between imaging and pathology definitions and left the categories unchanged. The measurements are what this assessment asks for; the thresholds applied to them are consensus lines and are argued at clinical decision 2. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: ACG-quoted accuracy for naming cyst type: 40 to 50% for MRI, CT and EUS without aspiration
European guideline-quoted cyst-type accuracy: 40 to 95% for MRI, 40 to 81% for CT

lead: Main-duct IPMN Segmental or diffuse dilatation of the main pancreatic duct of 5 mm or more without an obstructing cause. Kyoto 2024 makes a duct of 10 mm or more a high-risk stigma and a duct of 5 to 9 mm a worrisome feature. The 5 mm definition is Fukuoka 2012's, lowered from the 10 mm used at Sendai in 2006 to raise radiological sensitivity, and Fukuoka 2012 cited no study comparing outcomes above and below the new line.
text: Main-duct IPMN Evidence C Segmental or diffuse dilatation of the main pancreatic duct of 5 mm or more without an obstructing cause. Kyoto 2024 makes a duct of 10 mm or more a high-risk stigma and a duct of 5 to 9 mm a worrisome feature. The 5 mm definition is Fukuoka 2012's, lowered from the 10 mm used at Sendai in 2006 to raise radiological sensitivity, and Fukuoka 2012 cited no study comparing outcomes above and below the new line. Indications Preferred when Treat as a surgical disease until proved otherwise. Kyoto 2024 reports mean rates in resected main-duct specimens of 62% (range 36 to 100%) for high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma and 43% (11 to 81%) for invasive carcinoma alone. Fukuoka 2012 pooled 3,568 resected IPMNs and reported more than 62.2% and 43.6% for the main-duct subset; Sendai 2006 pooled nine smaller resected series and reported 70% (57 to 92%) and 43% (23 to 57%). NCCN quotes about 62% and recommends resection in operable patients with a main-duct IPMN of 10 mm or more. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Every one of those percentages is the prevalence of malignancy in specimens that were taken out, so they describe the yield of past operating decisions and not the risk in the cyst in front of you. Four guideline generations have carried them forward without supplying a denominator: Sendai 2006 made the recommendation to resect all main-duct IPMN with no data at all on what happens to an unresected one, and there are still none. Do not quote 62% to a patient in clinic as their personal risk. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Guideline-reported, resected main-duct IPMN: HGD or invasive mean 62% (range 36–100%); invasive alone 43% (11–81%) Prevalence in resected specimens, not the risk in an unresected cyst
Guideline-pooled, nine resected series: main-duct HGD or invasive 70% (57–92%), invasive 43% (23–57%) Resected-specimen prevalence; no data on unresected main-duct IPMN

lead: Branch-duct IPMN Cystic dilatation of side branches of more than 5 mm communicating with a non-dilated main duct. The commonest incidental finding — Kyoto 2024 puts about 80% of incidentally discovered cysts in this category — and the population every surveillance schedule on this page was written for.
text: Branch-duct IPMN Evidence C Cystic dilatation of side branches of more than 5 mm communicating with a non-dilated main duct. The commonest incidental finding — Kyoto 2024 puts about 80% of incidentally discovered cysts in this category — and the population every surveillance schedule on this page was written for. Indications Preferred when Risk-stratify rather than operate. Resected-series rates in Kyoto 2024 are 31% (15 to 48%) for high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma and 19% (6 to 38%) for invasive carcinoma, and Kyoto 2024 now adds, in the same paragraph, that given the large number of unresected indolent branch-duct lesions the real rate across all branch-duct IPMNs is much lower — without saying how much lower, or supplying the denominator that would make the figure usable. In surveillance cohorts the numbers are an order of magnitude smaller: in 1,404 branch-duct IPMNs followed at the University of Tokyo the cumulative incidence of pancreatic carcinoma was 3.3% at 5 years, 6.6% at 10 and 15.0% at 15, an annual rate of about 0.7%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not read 'branch duct' as 'benign', and do not read the Tokyo figures as an unselected natural history either: that cohort excluded any lesion with a mural nodule or a duct of 10 mm or more at diagnosis, and anyone diagnosed with carcinoma or resected within 6 months, which strips prevalent disease out of the numerator while keeping its risk factors in the denominator. Within it, 30 of 68 carcinomas were concomitant ductal adenocarcinoma arising elsewhere in the gland, and cyst size and duct diameter predicted the IPMN-derived cancers (subdistribution hazard ratio 1.85 per 10 mm, 95% CI 1.38 to 2.48) but not the concomitant ones (P=.60) — so watching the cyst does not watch the whole pancreas. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Kyoto 2024, resected series: HGD or invasive carcinoma 31% (15 to 48%), invasive carcinoma 19% (6 to 38%) Kyoto notes the real rate across all BD-IPMN is much lower, without a denominator

Surveillance cohort, 1,404 BD-IPMN: cumulative pancreatic carcinoma 3.3% at 5 y, 6.6% at 10 y, 15.0% at 15 y; about 0.7%/y Excluded mural nodule, duct ≥10 mm, early resection; 30 of 68 cancers concomitant PDAC

lead: Mixed-type IPMN Both a dilated main duct and communicating branch-duct cysts. Kyoto 2024 states plainly that it is difficult to assign significance to this category and left it unchanged from 2017.
text: Mixed-type IPMN Evidence D Both a dilated main duct and communicating branch-duct cysts. Kyoto 2024 states plainly that it is difficult to assign significance to this category and left it unchanged from 2017. Indications Preferred when Manage by its highest-risk component — in practice as a main-duct IPMN, which is what the European guideline recommends at GRADE 2C on the ground that mixed-type carries comparable risk. That is the convention, not a result. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not use the label to split the difference between surveillance and resection. There is no interval schedule and no resection threshold specific to mixed-type disease in any of the four guidelines. The category is also an artefact of a definition change nobody followed through: Fukuoka 2012 lowered the main-duct threshold to more than 5 mm, which enlarged the mixed group, recorded that enlargement as a classification problem, and never addressed what it meant for management. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Say out loud how confident the imaging diagnosis actually is, because it is wrong often enough to change the conversation.
text: Standard Evidence C Say out loud how confident the imaging diagnosis actually is, because it is wrong often enough to change the conversation. Indications Preferred when Every cyst discussed at the board.
