Additional cautions Additional cautions That means 63 of 115 resections (54.8%) removed a lesion that did not need removing — a premalignant cyst without high-grade dysplasia or malignancy in 40.8% and a cyst with no malignant potential in 13.9% — in an operation with real mortality. Any programme that does not know its own figure is assuming it is better than published. In the same cohort 22 patients (19.1%) had died at a median of 15 months after surgery, with no 30-day deaths, and that mortality is nowhere related to pathology or indication. Evidence & sources Read the benchmark with its construction before adopting it as a target. 'Justified' is the authors' own composite and counts any neuroendocrine tumour, any solid pseudopapillary neoplasm and any symptom improvement, none of which is an endpoint any of the four guidelines was designed to hit, so 45% is not strictly a guideline performance figure. The three-guideline comparison in the same paper is structurally one-sided: the cohort was selected for resection by the IAP and European criteria, so those two cannot be measured as missing anything, while the AGA criteria are scored on a population they never selected. Applying AGA strictly would have avoided 21 of 75 resections (28%) against 8 (11%) for IAP and 7 (9%) for the European guideline, but would have missed 4 of 33 patients (12%) with high-grade dysplasia or malignancy against none missed by the other two — and those 4 are two lesions, a 15 mm main-duct IPMN and a 23 mm side-branch IPMN with a nodule, each counted once as malignant and once as high-grade dysplasia. The independent test of the AGA rule in a consecutive aspiration cohort found 62% sensitivity, 79% specificity, 57% positive and 82% negative predictive value, from 13 events among 41 verified patients with no confidence intervals reported, main-duct IPMN excluded, and the criteria applied at aspiration rather than on MRI — which the authors say makes 62% an overestimate of the rule's real performance. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Single-centre, 115 resections: justified in 52 (45.2%), unneeded in 63 (54.8%); strict AGA would avoid 28% of resections but miss 4 of 33 (12%) HGD/cancer 'Justified' is the authors' composite; cohort selected by IAP/European criteria

Consecutive aspiration cohort, 41 verified patients: AGA criteria sensitivity 62%, specificity 79%, PPV 57%, NPV 82% 13 events, no CIs; applied at aspiration not MRI; authors say 62% is an overestimate

lead: Do not offer prophylactic total pancreatectomy for a pancreatic cyst.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not offer prophylactic total pancreatectomy for a pancreatic cyst. Why Why Kyoto 2024: prophylactic total pancreatectomy is not recommended because of its endocrine and exocrine metabolic consequences, but the possibility of total pancreatectomy should be discussed with all patients before an operation that might require it. Kyoto adds that multifocality does not raise the risk of high-grade dysplasia or carcinoma, so a multifocal branch-duct IPMN is managed by its highest-risk lesion and only that lesion is resected. Additional cautions Additional cautions The systematic review that underpins the shared-decision material found no studies at all of prophylactic total pancreatectomy — two papers mention the concept — so the 25% major morbidity, 6% 30-day mortality, 33% exocrine insufficiency, 18% endocrine-related readmission and 1.8% hypoglycaemia-related mortality are figures for total pancreatectomy for all indications pooled together, in patients mostly operated for disease rather than prophylaxis. The programme that proposes it rests on 35 patients in 7 series for the minimally invasive approach, with a reported 0% mortality whose upper 95% bound is about 10%, and quotes patients a 2 to 5% operative mortality against its own pooled 6%. The 60% lifetime risk on the other side of that decision table is the prevalence of malignancy in resected main-duct specimens, so both sides of the comparison are measured on incompatible scales. Evidence & sources An international survey of 97 experts split 41% for surveillance and 59% for intervention on the precise indication those tables encode, and 46% of those favouring intervention would do a total pancreatectomy. There is no evidence base for doing this prophylactically, only an evidence base for what it costs. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do an oncological resection with regional lymphadenectomy where invasive carcinoma is suspected, and a parenchyma-sparing operation where it is not.
text: Standard Evidence C Do an oncological resection with regional lymphadenectomy where invasive carcinoma is suspected, and a parenchyma-sparing operation where it is not. Indications Preferred when Kyoto 2024: radical pancreatectomy with lymph node dissection should be performed when invasive carcinoma is suspected; a branch-duct IPMN can usually be completely removed by partial pancreatectomy, and organ-preserving approaches such as middle pancreatectomy or spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy are acceptable when suspicion of invasive carcinoma is low, with minimally invasive approaches acceptable. The European guideline recommends pancreatoduodenectomy with frozen section of the margins when the whole duct is dilated, and standard oncological resection with lymphadenectomy and splenectomy for any mucinous cystic neoplasm with imaging features of high-grade dysplasia or cancer. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not do a parenchyma-sparing operation in a patient with a high-risk stigma suggesting invasion, because it forfeits the nodes and the margin. Do not add a lymphadenectomy to an enucleation for a low-suspicion lesion either — it adds morbidity for no staging benefit in a lesion that is not expected to be invasive. Evidence & sources [EXPERTISE] If the resection specimen contains invasive carcinoma, the postoperative pathway is that of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma — this is the PDAC pathway from here for staging and adjuvant therapy. Kyoto 2024 notes that chemotherapy and radiotherapy for IPMN with invasive carcinoma have not been established for lack of high-quality evidence and that most physicians use PDAC regimens; in the largest resected series, adjuvant therapy given to 35 of 84 patients with invasive IPMN (42%) did not reduce recurrence. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Take an intraoperative frozen section of the duct transection margin, and act on it by grade.
text: Standard Evidence C Take an intraoperative frozen section of the duct transection margin, and act on it by grade. Indications Preferred when Kyoto 2024 recommends intraoperative frozen section to rule out unexpected main-duct involvement at the cut margin. Normal epithelium or low-grade dysplasia at the margin: no additional resection. High-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma at the margin: additional resection recommended. The practice has usable data behind it: in 412 resected IPMNs frozen section was sent in 276 (69%), was negative in 210 (76%), low or intermediate grade in 44 (16%), high grade in 11 (4%) and invasive in 11 (4%); 15 of those 22 (68.2%) had the resection extended, 9 to total pancreatectomy; it changed the planned operation in 38 of 276 cases (13.7%) and final pathology confirmed the frozen reading in 96.3%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid An absence of epithelial cells at the transection margin — a denuded duct — is explicitly not equivalent to a negative margin in Kyoto 2024, and additional resection should be considered where feasible. Do not let a 'no epithelium seen' report close the case. Sendai 2006 made the same point twenty years ago and added that negative margins do not assure absence of neoplasia, because of multifocality and skip lesions. Evidence & sources The evidence on what low-grade dysplasia at the margin means is genuinely mixed and Kyoto's systematic review group concluded there were insufficient data to recommend additional resection for it. The figure most often quoted for high-grade dysplasia at the margin — a hazard ratio of 20.9 for recurrence of non-invasive IPMN, P=.03 — comes from 10 margin-positive patients and is reported without a confidence interval, so it should not be carried into practice as an effect size. The margin is nonetheless one of the recurrence predictors that replicates in direction: 25% recurrence with IPMN at the margin against 14% with a negative margin (P=.008), and earlier, at a median of 37 against 48 months. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Parenchyma-sparing resectionEXPERTISE Kyoto 2024 accepts middle pancreatectomy or spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy where suspicion of invasive carcinoma is low; the European guideline accepts non-oncological or spleen-preserving resection for low-risk mucinous cystic neoplasms at GRADE 2C.
text: Parenchyma-sparing resection Evidence C EXPERTISE Kyoto 2024 accepts middle pancreatectomy or spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy where suspicion of invasive carcinoma is low; the European guideline accepts non-oncological or spleen-preserving resection for low-risk mucinous cystic neoplasms at GRADE 2C. Indications Preferred when A localised branch-duct lesion in the neck or body of a young patient, where preserving endocrine and exocrine function over decades is worth something. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Not where invasion is suspected, and not where the remnant it leaves will be impossible to surveil. Central pancreatectomy has a high pancreatic fistula rate, and in the largest resected series recurrence of non-invasive IPMN was 22% after middle pancreatectomy against 7% after pancreatoduodenectomy and 6% after distal pancreatectomy (P=.016) — a difference that could reflect the operation or the selection of patients for it, with no adjustment attempted. Preserving pancreatic tissue may increase the complication risk; discuss both outcomes. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Standard oncological partial pancreatectomy The default for a lesion requiring resection where invasive carcinoma is suspected or cannot be excluded.
text: Standard oncological partial pancreatectomy Evidence C The default for a lesion requiring resection where invasive carcinoma is suspected or cannot be excluded. Indications Preferred when Most resections on this page. It gives the margin and the nodes, and the frozen-section protocol above applies to it. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not choose it reflexively for a small, confidently non-invasive lesion in a young patient without discussing a parenchyma-sparing alternative. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Total pancreatectomyEXPERTISE Kyoto 2024: not recommended prophylactically, but the possibility should be discussed with all patients; and leaving high-grade dysplasia at the margin may be appropriate to avoid a total pancreatectomy, particularly in older or frail patients, and where invasive cancer is already present, since prognosis is then dictated by the invasive component. The European guideline reserves it for a distal mural nodule or familial pancreatic cancer, and advises against it where an IPMN-associated invasive carcinoma in the head will determine prognosis.
text: Total pancreatectomy Evidence C EXPERTISE Kyoto 2024: not recommended prophylactically, but the possibility should be discussed with all patients; and leaving high-grade dysplasia at the margin may be appropriate to avoid a total pancreatectomy, particularly in older or frail patients, and where invasive cancer is already present, since prognosis is then dictated by the invasive component. The European guideline reserves it for a distal mural nodule or familial pancreatic cancer, and advises against it where an IPMN-associated invasive carcinoma in the head will determine prognosis. Indications Preferred when Diffuse main-duct involvement where a partial resection cannot clear high-grade disease, in a patient who understands and accepts an apancreatic state. Discussed before the operation, never decided for the first time intraoperatively. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Twenty-five per cent major morbidity and 6% 30-day mortality (95% CI 4 to 8%) across 52 studies and 3,570 patients, exocrine insufficiency symptoms in 33% over a median 33 months, readmission for endocrine-related morbidity in 49 of 273 (18%) over a median 38 months, hypoglycaemia-related mortality in 10 of 568 (1.8%), lifelong insulin dependence and a mean global health status of 75 on a 0 to 100 scale. There are no studies of prophylactic total pancreatectomy in main-duct or mixed IPMN at all, so this is a decision taken without comparative evidence either way, and the patient-facing decision tables built for it quote 2 to 5% operative mortality rather than the 6% their own review produced. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not accept a denuded duct margin as clear.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not accept a denuded duct margin as clear. Why Why Ask the pathologist for epithelium. Where the margin is denuded and further resection is feasible, Kyoto 2024 says it should be considered. Additional cautions Additional cautions This is a labelling problem with a surgical consequence: a report that says no dysplasia at the margin, when it means no epithelium at the margin, closes a case that is still open. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not commit to an extent of resection that was never discussed with the patient.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not commit to an extent of resection that was never discussed with the patient. Why Why Kyoto 2024 requires that the possibility of total pancreatectomy be put to every patient facing a resection in which it could arise. Do that in clinic, with the morbidity and mortality numbers, and document it. Additional cautions Additional cautions An apancreatic state decided intraoperatively without a prior conversation is a consent failure, and it is not corrected by the operation having been oncologically correct. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Kyoto 2024 schedule Cyst under 20 mm: first follow-up at 6 months, then every 18 months if stable. 20 to under 30 mm: 6 months twice, then every 12 months if stable. 30 mm or more: every 6 months. Graded SIGN 2+, recommendation B.
text: Kyoto 2024 schedule Evidence C Cyst under 20 mm: first follow-up at 6 months, then every 18 months if stable. 20 to under 30 mm: 6 months twice, then every 12 months if stable. 30 mm or more: every 6 months. Graded SIGN 2+, recommendation B. Indications Preferred when The spine of this page, and the only one of the four with published data under its size bands: pooled progression to worrisome features was 4.8% at a median of 54 months for lesions under 10 mm, 10% at 55 months for 10 to 20 mm and 48.8% at a median of 23 months for 20 to 30 mm. Its intervals are the most generous for small cysts of any guideline that keeps surveilling them. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Two limits. It is an IPMN guideline and nothing else — no schedule for mucinous cystic neoplasms, serous cystadenomas or cystic neuroendocrine tumours — so a programme adopting it still has to borrow the non-IPMN intervals from elsewhere. And its 30 mm band has validation evidence against it: in the 3,336-patient cohort that validated the rest of the criteria, long-term risk was stratified at 20 mm but not at 30 mm, the subdistribution hazard ratio being 2.07 (95% CI 1.38 to 3.10) for 20 to 29 mm and 1.75 (1.00 to 3.08) for 30 mm or more. The band that triggers the most imaging is the one that did not separate. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Guideline-pooled data: progression to worrisome features 4.8% at median 54 mo (<10 mm), 10% at 55 mo (10–20 mm), 48.8% at median 23 mo (20–30 mm) IPMN only; its 30 mm band did not separate risk in validation
Validation cohort, 3,336 pts: risk stratified at 20 mm, not 30 mm; SHR 2.07 (95% CI 1.38–3.10) for 20–29 mm, 1.75 (1.00–3.08) for ≥30 mm

lead: ACG 2018 schedule Escalating with size, as published in full: under 1 cm, MRI every 2 years for 4 years; 1 to 2 cm, MRI yearly for 3 years then every 2 years for 4 years; 2 to 3 cm, MRI or EUS every 6 to 12 months for 3 years then yearly for 4 years; over 3 cm, MRI alternating with EUS every 6 months for 3 years then alternating yearly for 4 years, with multidisciplinary referral. Lengthening may be considered once stability is documented. New or worsening diabetes, or growth of more than 3 mm per year, prompts a short-interval MRI or EUS with or without aspiration.
text: ACG 2018 schedule Evidence D Escalating with size, as published in full: under 1 cm, MRI every 2 years for 4 years; 1 to 2 cm, MRI yearly for 3 years then every 2 years for 4 years; 2 to 3 cm, MRI or EUS every 6 to 12 months for 3 years then yearly for 4 years; over 3 cm, MRI alternating with EUS every 6 months for 3 years then alternating yearly for 4 years, with multidisciplinary referral. Lengthening may be considered once stability is documented. New or worsening diabetes, or growth of more than 3 mm per year, prompts a short-interval MRI or EUS with or without aspiration. Indications Preferred when The most commonly used schedule in US practice and the one most radiologists will recognise. ACG names MRCP the preferred modality and accepts EUS where MRI is unavailable. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Conditional recommendation on very low quality evidence, by ACG's own grading of all 20 of its recommendations, and the guideline states that there are very little data on whether intervals can be extended and none to guide stopping by age. It also excludes from scope patients with a strong family history of pancreatic cancer or a predisposing germline mutation, which is the group in whom surveillance is most likely to be worthwhile. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: European 2018 schedule MRI preferred; 6-monthly in the first year, then yearly thereafter when no risk factors are present, and 6-monthly for patients with a relative indication, the elderly and those with severe comorbidity — the same for IPMN and for mucinous cystic neoplasms under 40 mm. Follow-up continues for life while the patient is fit for surgery. Graded 1B with strong agreement.
text: European 2018 schedule Evidence D MRI preferred; 6-monthly in the first year, then yearly thereafter when no risk factors are present, and 6-monthly for patients with a relative indication, the elderly and those with severe comorbidity — the same for IPMN and for mucinous cystic neoplasms under 40 mm. Follow-up continues for life while the patient is fit for surgery. Graded 1B with strong agreement. Indications Preferred when The simplest schedule to run and audit, because it does not branch on size, and the only one that covers the non-IPMN cysts as well. Its own rationale is that the risk of IPMN progression increases over time, with progression of branch-duct IPMN expected in about 10 to 15% over 3 to 5 years, and it asks for the whole gland to be covered because of the risk of a new cancer elsewhere. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid It is the most imaging-intensive of the four for a small stable cyst — yearly, indefinitely — and that cost is not matched by any demonstrated outcome advantage. The GRADE 1B label should not be read as high-quality evidence either: the single comorbidity study the guideline cites in support of lifelong follow-up reports that patients with a Charlson-age index of 7 or more have an elevenfold risk of comorbidity-related death within 3 years and that only 6% die of malignant IPMN, which argues against the recommendation it accompanies. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Guideline-cited comorbidity study: Charlson-age index ≥7, elevenfold risk of comorbidity-related death within 3 y; only 6% die of malignant IPMN Single study, and it argues against the lifelong follow-up it is cited to support

lead: AGA 2015 schedule For cysts under 3 cm without a solid component or a dilated duct: MRI at 1 year, then every 2 years, for a total of 5 years. EUS-FNA only when at least two of three high-risk features are present — size 3 cm or more, a dilated main duct, or an associated solid component.
text: AGA 2015 schedule Evidence D For cysts under 3 cm without a solid component or a dilated duct: MRI at 1 year, then every 2 years, for a total of 5 years. EUS-FNA only when at least two of three high-risk features are present — size 3 cm or more, a dilated main duct, or an associated solid component. Indications Preferred when The least intensive schedule, and the only one with an explicit endpoint. Every recommendation in it is graded conditional on very low quality evidence by the AGA itself. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not adopt it without stating what it misses and what it is built on. The AGA says in its own text that the 1-year-then-2-year interval 'is not based on any evidence but is believed to be reasonable', that there are no data on the effect of multiple high-risk features, and that a dilated main duct was retained as a high-risk feature although its own review of unselected cysts found no significant association with malignancy. Applied to 225 consecutive patients having EUS-FNA, the criteria detected advanced neoplasia with 62% sensitivity, 79% specificity, 57% positive and 82% negative predictive value and missed 5 of 11 IPMNs harbouring adenocarcinoma or high-grade dysplasia (45%) — figures resting on 13 events among 41 verified patients, with no confidence intervals, main-duct IPMN excluded, and the criteria applied at aspiration rather than on MRI, which the authors say makes 62% an overestimate. Applied in retrospect to 75 resected suspected IPMNs, they would have avoided 21 resections (28%) but missed 4 of 33 patients (12%) with high-grade dysplasia or malignancy — effectively two lesions — against none missed by the IAP or European criteria, in a cohort those two guidelines had selected. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: 225 consecutive EUS-FNA pts: AGA criteria advanced-neoplasia sensitivity 62%, specificity 79%, PPV 57%, NPV 82%; missed 5 of 11 IPMNs with HGD/cancer 13 events in 41 verified, no CIs; main-duct IPMN excluded; authors: 62% an overestimate

lead: Use MRI with MRCP as the surveillance modality wherever it is available, and keep the same modality for the life of the surveillance.
text: Standard Evidence C Use MRI with MRCP as the surveillance modality wherever it is available, and keep the same modality for the life of the surveillance. Indications Preferred when ACG names MRCP the preferred modality for pancreatic cyst surveillance and accepts EUS as the primary tool where MRI is unavailable; the European guideline prefers MRI at GRADE 2C for its sensitivity to duct communication, mural nodules, septations and multifocality and because repeated CT radiation carries its own risk, reserving CT for calcification, staging and postoperative recurrence; Kyoto 2024 writes its intervals as CT or MRI and reports that MDCT, MRI and EUS are equivalent for diagnosing high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not alternate modality for convenience. A size difference between a CT in one year and an MRI the next is not reliably a size difference, and growth is a worrisome feature in Kyoto 2024 at 2.5 mm per year — well inside the disagreement between two modalities. Note also that neither Kyoto nor the European guideline can recommend a specific MRI or CT protocol: the European guideline says so explicitly, for want of comparative studies. Evidence & sources The cost of the commitment now has published numbers, and they are not reassuring in either direction. Up to $3.6 million is spent on cyst surveillance per cancer detected in the United States, with no appreciable change in cyst-related pancreatic adenocarcinoma mortality over two decades of rising expenditure; one Markov model of IAP 2017 surveillance against no surveillance in a 60-year-old with an asymptomatic 25 mm cyst returned an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of $171,143 per quality-adjusted life-year, while an earlier model of 2006 consensus surveillance in a 60-year-old returned $20,096 per QALY — two models differing in cyst size, guideline, era and assumptions, which the review that prints both does not reconcile. Sendai 2006, Fukuoka 2012, Fukuoka 2017, Kyoto 2024, ACG 2018 and the European 2018 guideline contain no cost analysis at all, and ACG and AGA both state that none exists. This is not a reason to under-image a patient; it is a reason for the programme to know how many scans it is committing to. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Alternate MRI with EUS in the cyst of 2 cm or more, where the question is a mural nodule rather than size.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Alternate MRI with EUS in the cyst of 2 cm or more, where the question is a mural nodule rather than size. Indications Preferred when ACG brings EUS into the schedule at 2 to 3 cm; Fukuoka 2017 alternated MRI with EUS at 2 to 3 cm and every 3 to 6 months above 3 cm. EUS is the modality Kyoto names for confirming a mural nodule and measuring its height, and the 5 mm nodule threshold is the single most consequential measurement on this page. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not add EUS to a schedule for a small stable cyst — it adds a sedated procedure to each cycle without changing the question. And do not let an EUS report that omits the nodule measurement count as an EUS. Evidence & sources [EXPERTISE] Inter-operator variation in nodule measurement is not published and is not audited anywhere; a programme that makes operative decisions on a 5 mm EUS threshold should know who is measuring. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Consider earlier resection in young, fit patients facing decades of surveillance; explain that surveillance duration motivates this choice.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Consider earlier resection in young, fit patients facing decades of surveillance; explain that surveillance duration motivates this choice. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Consider earlier resection in a young fit patient facing decades of surveillance, and say that the argument is about the duration of the commitment rather than about the cyst. Indications Preferred when Fukuoka 2012 said surgery should be strongly considered in young fit patients with a cyst above 3 cm, and Fukuoka 2017 that patients under 65 with cysts over 2 cm may still be candidates. The supporting observation is that risk accumulates rather than plateaus: cumulative incidence of pancreatic carcinoma was 3.3% at 5 years, 6.6% at 10 and 15.0% at 15 in 1,404 branch-duct IPMNs, and Kyoto 2024 states that its own option to discontinue surveillance does not apply to younger patients with branch-duct IPMN, because the risk appears cumulative over time. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Kyoto 2024 Figure 3 includes young, surgically fit patients among those in whom surgery may be considered. This is an individualized discussion, not a mandate to resect solely for age or cyst size. No randomized comparison establishes that early resection is better than continued surveillance in young patients; weigh cumulative cancer risk, operative harm and long-term pancreatic function. Evidence & sources This argument cuts both ways. The same young patient has the most years in which to suffer the long-term consequences of a pancreatectomy, and the most years in which a remnant can produce a new lesion: after resection of 130 non-invasive IPMNs the 1-, 5- and 10-year risks of a new IPMN were 4%, 25% and 62%, with invasive IPMN in 0%, 7% and 38% by 10 years. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not run surveillance without a named owner and a recall system that fails loudly.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not run surveillance without a named owner and a recall system that fails loudly. Why Why One owner per patient, an interval recorded in the record rather than in a letter, and a report that lists overdue patients by name every month. Additional cautions Additional cautions Every schedule on this page assumes the scan happens. A surveillance programme whose default failure mode is silent is not safer than no programme — it is a programme that carries the cost and generates the reassurance without the benefit. This is an operational requirement, grade D, and is audited for adherence rather than for effect.

lead: Do not mix the four schedules, taking the generous interval from one and the stopping rule from another.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not mix the four schedules, taking the generous interval from one and the stopping rule from another. Why Why Adopt one schedule whole, note the deviations deliberately, and record which version and which date. Additional cautions Additional cautions Each of the four is internally coherent: AGA's long intervals go with its 5-year stop, the European guideline's short intervals go with lifelong follow-up, and Kyoto's 18-month interval for a small cyst goes with its conditional 5-year discontinuation option. Assembling the longest intervals with the latest stopping point produces a schedule no guideline has ever examined. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Stop when the patient is no longer a candidate for pancreatectomy. This is the only stopping rule all four guidelines share.
text: Standard Evidence D Stop when the patient is no longer a candidate for pancreatectomy. This is the only stopping rule all four guidelines share. Indications Preferred when Every patient, reassessed at each visit rather than once at enrolment. ACG makes it a strong recommendation and adds that it is reasonable to assess the utility of ongoing surveillance in patients over 75, with an individualised approach for those aged 76 to 85 — age limits ACG says in the same paragraph are borrowed from USPSTF colorectal screening and are not supported by evidence. Kyoto 2024 adds a life expectancy under 10 years as a reason to stop. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat it as an age rule. Fitness, not birthday, is the criterion, and an 80-year-old who would accept and survive a distal pancreatectomy is still a surveillance candidate. Evidence & sources Grade D: this is a logical requirement, not a comparative result. No study has randomised stopping against continuing in anyone, and no cost-effectiveness analysis of surveillance in an elderly population exists. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Continue while the patient remains fit — European 2018 and ACG 2018 The European guideline, at GRADE 1B: 'the risk of IPMN progression increases over the time, therefore patients affected by IPMN without indication for surgery should be followed up until they are no longer fit for surgery'. ACG discontinues only on loss of surgical candidacy, with the over-75 assessment above, and explicitly rejects the AGA 5-year rule on the ground that genetic studies put the dwell time to cancer at 15 to 20 years and cancers have appeared in IPMN up to 16 years after diagnosis.
text: Continue while the patient remains fit — European 2018 and ACG 2018 Evidence C The European guideline, at GRADE 1B: 'the risk of IPMN progression increases over the time, therefore patients affected by IPMN without indication for surgery should be followed up until they are no longer fit for surgery'. ACG discontinues only on loss of surgical candidacy, with the over-75 assessment above, and explicitly rejects the AGA 5-year rule on the ground that genetic studies put the dwell time to cancer at 15 to 20 years and cancers have appeared in IPMN up to 16 years after diagnosis. Indications Preferred when The position with the longest follow-up behind it. In 577 branch-duct IPMNs at one US referral centre, 363 were surveilled beyond 5 years for a median of 107 months and 20 of those (5.5%) developed high-grade dysplasia or invasive neoplasm after the 5-year mark, with invasive cancer in 16 (4.4%) and malignant transformation after 10 years in 5 of 121 (4%); the standardised incidence ratio for the 282 patients without worrisome features at 5 years was 18.8 (95% CI 9.7 to 32.8). In 1,404 branch-duct IPMNs in Tokyo, 804 were followed past 5 years for a median of 107 months with a cumulative incidence of 12.0% at 15 years from diagnosis and a standardised incidence ratio beyond 5 years of 5.8 (3.7 to 7.9); among the 737 who would have met the AGA criteria for discontinuation, 23 carcinomas occurred, with a post-5-year standardised incidence ratio of 4.8 (2.9 to 6.8). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The cost is indefinite imaging in a population whose competing risk of death is far larger than their cyst risk. And both standardised incidence ratios are inflated by construction in the same two ways: each counts high-grade dysplasia as an event against a cancer-registry comparator that counts only invasive cancer — the US cohort supplies a sensitivity analysis restricted to invasive disease, giving 15.6 (7.5 to 28.7), and its abstract carries the 18.8 — and each compares a referral cohort known to harbour a pancreatic cyst against a general population of whom 2 to 7% also harbour one, so part of the excess is detection. The Tokyo authors note that their own incidence exceeds what cyst prevalence and population cancer rates would predict. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Stop at 5 years if stable — AGA 2015, and one of Kyoto 2024's two options AGA 2015 recommends discontinuing surveillance if there has been no significant change in cyst characteristics after 5 years (conditional, very low quality), on a reviewed transformation risk of about 0.24% per year computed by assuming that every pancreatic cancer arises in a cyst. Kyoto 2024 offers two options for a small unchanged branch-duct IPMN after 5 years — 'stop surveillance' or 'continue surveillance for possible development of concomitant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma' — and states that surveillance may be discontinued for cysts under 20 mm with no morphological change and no worrisome feature after 5 years, with consideration of patient condition and life expectancy (SIGN 2+, grade C).
text: Stop at 5 years if stable — AGA 2015, and one of Kyoto 2024's two options Evidence C AGA 2015 recommends discontinuing surveillance if there has been no significant change in cyst characteristics after 5 years (conditional, very low quality), on a reviewed transformation risk of about 0.24% per year computed by assuming that every pancreatic cancer arises in a cyst. Kyoto 2024 offers two options for a small unchanged branch-duct IPMN after 5 years — 'stop surveillance' or 'continue surveillance for possible development of concomitant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma' — and states that surveillance may be discontinued for cysts under 20 mm with no morphological change and no worrisome feature after 5 years, with consideration of patient condition and life expectancy (SIGN 2+, grade C). Indications Preferred when Small stable cysts in older patients, where the competing-risk argument dominates: among 1,617 presumed branch-duct IPMNs stable for at least 5 years, all-cause mortality was 4.9% and disease-specific mortality 0.3%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The AGA version was not restricted by size, rests on a population-level estimate with no data comparing cancer rates in stable against changing cysts — the guideline says so — and has been repeatedly criticised. Kyoto's version is explicitly conditional, size-limited to 20 mm, excluded from younger patients and from those with familial or genetic risk, and offered as one of two permissible courses, so a pathway that adopts it cannot claim evidential support for the course it chose; the guideline records that the two options exist because most Japanese physicians accept the low progression risk of a small stable lesion while remaining concerned about concomitant adenocarcinoma. Kyoto's own counterweight is a Japanese series of 732 patients with branch-duct IPMN under 15 mm in which 22 pancreatic carcinomas occurred, cumulative incidence 2.2%, 4.6% and 7.4% at 5, 10 and 15 years, 14 of the 22 being concomitant adenocarcinomas. The best estimate of what happens after an uneventful 5 years in a guideline-adherent cohort is 2.7% (1.9 to 3.7) at 10 years and 6.1% (4.3 to 8.3) at 15, from a centre that surveilled more intensively than Kyoto advises and whose authors say so. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Guideline (AGA 2015) reviewed estimate: transformation risk about 0.24% per year Assumes every pancreatic cancer arises in a cyst; no stable vs changing cyst data

lead: Stop by age and size — the standardised-incidence-ratio argument Not a guideline position, but the best-quantified one. In an international cohort of 3,844 presumed branch-duct IPMNs with no worrisome features or high-risk stigmata at diagnosis, 1,617 (42%) developed none in the first 5 years, and in that subgroup the standardised incidence ratio for pancreatic cancer was 2.29 (95% CI 1.22 to 3.91) overall, 1.12 (0.23 to 3.39, from 3 cancers) in patients aged 75 or older, and 0.95 (0.11 to 3.42, from 2 cancers) in patients 65 or older with stable lesions of 15 mm or less.
text: Stop by age and size — the standardised-incidence-ratio argument Evidence C Not a guideline position, but the best-quantified one. In an international cohort of 3,844 presumed branch-duct IPMNs with no worrisome features or high-risk stigmata at diagnosis, 1,617 (42%) developed none in the first 5 years, and in that subgroup the standardised incidence ratio for pancreatic cancer was 2.29 (95% CI 1.22 to 3.91) overall, 1.12 (0.23 to 3.39, from 3 cancers) in patients aged 75 or older, and 0.95 (0.11 to 3.42, from 2 cancers) in patients 65 or older with stable lesions of 15 mm or less. Indications Preferred when The authors' own proposal: discontinuation could be justified after 5 years of stability in patients over 75 with cysts under 30 mm, and in patients 65 or older with cysts of 15 mm or less. It gives a programme two defensible numbers rather than one blanket rule, and it is the only one of the three cohorts that excluded worrisome features by design, so it is the only one describing the lesion a stopping rule would actually be applied to. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Four limits, each of which the paper states and none of which survives into the recommendation. The intervals are wide because the events are few — two and three cancers — so 'no different from the population' is a failure to exclude a threefold excess, not a demonstration of safety. The standardised incidence ratio falls with age because the comparator population's pancreatic cancer incidence rises steeply with age, which the paper says explicitly, so the rule licenses stopping in exactly the group whose absolute risk is highest. Size is not neutral within the stable group: cysts above 30 mm with no new feature for 5 years had a standardised incidence ratio of 10.29 (4.12 to 21.21). And the group this applies to cannot be identified at diagnosis — 20.2% developed a worrisome feature and 1.8% a high-risk stigma during follow-up, so this is the 42% who stayed stable, known only in retrospect. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: In a fit patient, consider stopping cyst surveillance while remaining alert to a separate pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
text: Reasonable Evidence C In a fit patient, consider stopping cyst surveillance while remaining alert to a separate pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Where surveillance stops but the patient is still fit, consider stopping for the cyst while remaining alert to a concomitant adenocarcinoma elsewhere in the gland. Indications Preferred when This is Kyoto 2024's second option in plain terms, and it has a mechanistic basis. Of 68 pancreatic carcinomas in 1,404 branch-duct IPMNs, 30 were concomitant ductal adenocarcinomas arising elsewhere; cyst size and duct diameter predicted the IPMN-derived cancers but not the concomitant ones, and older age was the only risk factor for a concomitant cancer. In the later 3,179-patient analysis from the same centre, 68 of 138 carcinomas were concomitant, the worrisome-feature count did not predict them, and they were metastatic at diagnosis three times as often as the derived cancers (21% against 7.1%). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Kyoto 2024 puts the yearly incidence of concomitant adenocarcinoma at 0.4 to 1.0%, about 3 to 5 times the age-matched population — but adds that most of these data come from Japan, where the whole resected pancreas is sectioned at 5 mm and clinicians are primed to look for the entity, and that elsewhere the risk in an IPMN patient appears similar to the general population. Do not quote the Japanese figure to a Houston patient as their own risk. Evidence & sources If the concomitant-cancer risk really is background outside Japan, the case for indefinite surveillance of a stable small cyst weakens considerably. This is the single biggest unresolved question behind the stopping debate. One related guideline position also fails to replicate: Fukuoka 2017 and Kyoto 2024 both treat a family history of pancreatic cancer as raising the risk of concomitant adenocarcinoma, and Kyoto halves the post-resection surveillance interval on it, but in the 3,179-patient Tokyo cohort a family history was not associated with carcinoma incidence, overall or by carcinoma type. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Guideline estimate: yearly incidence of concomitant PDAC 0.4–1.0%, about 3–5 times the age-matched population Mostly Japanese data; elsewhere risk appears similar to the general population

lead: Do not call stopping a discharge without telling the patient what is being accepted.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not call stopping a discharge without telling the patient what is being accepted. Why Why Say the numbers: that a cyst of this size, stable for this long, in a person of this age, carries a risk of pancreatic cancer close to that of anyone else their age; that the risk is not zero; and what symptoms should bring them back. Additional cautions Additional cautions A letter saying 'no further follow-up required' in a disease where one referral cohort found 4.4% invasive cancers after year 5 is not an honest account of the decision, and it leaves no route back in. Say also what the number rests on: of the 64 patients in the low-risk international cohort who were eventually resected after 5 years or more, 24 (38.1%) had high-grade dysplasia or invasive cancer, so when these cysts do declare themselves they are often already advanced. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not let surveillance stop by default, through missed appointments or a lapsed recall.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not let surveillance stop by default, through missed appointments or a lapsed recall. Why Why A stop is a decision with a date, an owner and a note. Overdue is not stopped. Additional cautions Additional cautions The commonest way surveillance ends in practice is that nobody books the next scan. That is indistinguishable in the record from a considered decision and is not one. Operational requirement, grade D.

lead: Kyoto 2024 — interval by risk factor Yearly imaging for patients without additional risk factors, and every 6 months for those with a family history of pancreatic cancer or high-grade dysplasia in the resected specimen. Continue as long as the patient remains fit to undergo additional therapeutic intervention. IPMN-specific surveillance may be stopped 5 years after a total pancreatectomy for non-invasive disease. Graded SIGN 2+, recommendation C.
text: Kyoto 2024 — interval by risk factor Evidence C Yearly imaging for patients without additional risk factors, and every 6 months for those with a family history of pancreatic cancer or high-grade dysplasia in the resected specimen. Continue as long as the patient remains fit to undergo additional therapeutic intervention. IPMN-specific surveillance may be stopped 5 years after a total pancreatectomy for non-invasive disease. Graded SIGN 2+, recommendation C. Indications Preferred when The spine of this page, and the only one of the four that stratifies the post-resection interval on something other than the grade of the resected lesion. It is also the only one that quantifies what is being looked for: median cumulative 5-year incidence of clinically significant remnant lesions 10% (range 0 to 21%), of all remnant lesions 19% (8 to 28%) and of invasive remnant lesions 4% (1 to 10%), with the risk continuing to rise beyond 5 years. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid No comparative data support 6 months over 12 in either group; these are consensus intervals built on observational risk factors. One of the two factors also fails to replicate: in a 3,179-patient surveillance cohort a family history of pancreatic cancer was not associated with carcinoma incidence, overall or by type, although it was associated with concomitant adenocarcinoma in the resected series Fukuoka 2017 cites (11.1% against 2.9%, P=0.002). Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Kyoto 2024 quotes median cumulative 5-y remnant incidence: clinically significant 10% (range 0–21%), any 19% (8–28%), invasive 4% (1–10%); risk rises after 5 y No comparative data for 6- vs 12-month intervals; consensus intervals
Resected series cited by Fukuoka 2017: concomitant adenocarcinoma 11.1% with vs 2.9% without family history, P=0.002 Not replicated for carcinoma incidence in a 3,179-patient surveillance cohort

lead: ACG 2018 — interval by grade All surgically resected IPMNs require postoperative surveillance (strong, very low quality). For low- or intermediate-grade dysplasia with no residual cyst, MRI every 24 months appears reasonable; for high-grade dysplasia or invasive cancer, MRI or EUS every 6 months. Resected mucinous cystic neoplasms without cancer require no postoperative surveillance (strong, low quality), as do resected serous cystadenomas and pseudocysts; solid pseudopapillary neoplasms are followed yearly for at least 5 years.
text: ACG 2018 — interval by grade Evidence C All surgically resected IPMNs require postoperative surveillance (strong, very low quality). For low- or intermediate-grade dysplasia with no residual cyst, MRI every 24 months appears reasonable; for high-grade dysplasia or invasive cancer, MRI or EUS every 6 months. Resected mucinous cystic neoplasms without cancer require no postoperative surveillance (strong, low quality), as do resected serous cystadenomas and pseudocysts; solid pseudopapillary neoplasms are followed yearly for at least 5 years. Indications Preferred when Simple to run, and the only one of the four that explicitly releases a resected mucinous cystic neoplasm from follow-up. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid ACG reports recurrence in 17 to 65% of IPMNs resected with cancer and 13 to 31% after high-grade dysplasia, at a median of 19 to 47 months and a range of 4 to 180, which are very wide bands, and 0 to 22% after low- or intermediate-grade dysplasia, for which the 24-month interval has no comparative support. ACG also states that conflicting results exist on the risk after resection of low- or intermediate-grade disease and that there is insufficient evidence to support no surveillance in that group — so its own 24-month interval is a compromise rather than a finding. The strong recommendation releasing a resected mucinous cystic neoplasm rests on a 90-patient series and a 344-case review in which no lesion under 3 cm with a normal CA 19-9 and no concerning features harboured high-grade dysplasia or cancer, which is an absence of events in modest series. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: ACG 2018 quoted ranges: IPMN recurrence 17–65% after cancer, 13–31% after HGD (median 19–47 mo); 0–22% after low/intermediate-grade dysplasia Very wide bands; 24-month interval for low-grade disease has no comparative support

lead: European 2018 — lifelong, intensified for high-grade or main-duct disease Lifelong surveillance following resection of an IPMN as long as the patient is fit and willing to undergo surgery if indicated. IPMN with high-grade dysplasia, or main-duct IPMN, every 6 months for the first 2 years then yearly.
text: European 2018 — lifelong, intensified for high-grade or main-duct disease Evidence C Lifelong surveillance following resection of an IPMN as long as the patient is fit and willing to undergo surgery if indicated. IPMN with high-grade dysplasia, or main-duct IPMN, every 6 months for the first 2 years then yearly. Indications Preferred when The most explicit on the condition that makes post-resection surveillance meaningful at all — that the patient would accept a second operation. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid The most imaging-intensive option over a lifetime, and the recommendation is a consensus position derived by GRADE from observational evidence only. Its own supporting figures: recurrence after resection is possible 5 to 10 years out and similar for branch-duct and main-duct disease at 7 to 8%, with 5.4 to 10% after low-grade dysplasia at a disease-free survival of about 52 months, against above 50% after high-grade dysplasia or an associated invasive carcinoma at a disease-free survival of 29 months. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: European 2018 quotes post-resection recurrence 7–8%, similar branch/main duct; 5.4–10% after LGD (DFS about 52 mo) vs above 50% after HGD/invasive (DFS 29 mo) Consensus by GRADE from observational evidence only

lead: AGA 2015 — no routine surveillance without high-grade dysplasia or cancer AGA 2015 recommends against routine surveillance of pancreatic cysts without high-grade dysplasia or malignancy at surgical resection (conditional, very low quality), and MRI every 2 years after resection of a cyst with invasive cancer or dysplasia.
text: AGA 2015 — no routine surveillance without high-grade dysplasia or cancer Evidence D AGA 2015 recommends against routine surveillance of pancreatic cysts without high-grade dysplasia or malignancy at surgical resection (conditional, very low quality), and MRI every 2 years after resection of a cyst with invasive cancer or dysplasia. Indications Preferred when Stated here because it is the position a referring clinician may have applied, and because the page should say where it sits. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid It conflicts with all three of the other guidelines, which surveil every resected IPMN, and the AGA concedes that no case series report outcomes in the group it proposes to discharge. The two recommendations are also argued in opposite directions in consecutive paragraphs: post-resection imaging after dysplasia is justified on a field defect, and no surveillance after a benign resection on the inference that such patients are unlikely to have one. The best recurrence series gives 65 of 381 patients (17%) recurring at a median of 17 months, with 5- and 10-year disease-free survival of 82% and 78% and recurrence in 28 of 299 non-invasive lesions (9%) — low, but not nothing, and later than the invasive recurrences. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Single series: recurrence 65 of 381 (17%) at a median of 17 mo; 5- and 10-y DFS 82% and 78%; non-invasive lesions 28 of 299 (9%) Non-invasive recurrence low but not nil, and later than invasive recurrence

lead: Base the schedule on the recurrence pattern, which depends on invasion, on the margin and on subtype, not on the fact of having had an operation.
text: Standard Evidence C Base the schedule on the recurrence pattern, which depends on invasion, on the margin and on subtype, not on the fact of having had an operation. Indications Preferred when In 412 resected IPMNs with near-complete follow-up at one centre, 65 of 381 (17%) recurred over a median of 58 months and 5- and 10-year disease-free survival were 82% and 78%. Invasive IPMN recurred in 37 of 82 (45%) against 28 of 299 (9%) for non-invasive disease (P<.001) and much earlier, at a median of 19 against 52 months; IPMN at the resection margin gave 25% recurrence (15 of 59) against 14% (42 of 301) with a negative margin (P=.008). In non-invasive disease, high-grade dysplasia at the margin independently predicted recurrence (hazard ratio 20.9, P=.03) while low- or intermediate-grade dysplasia did not; in invasive disease the tubular subtype was the independent predictor (hazard ratio 2.7 over colloid, P=.02). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Those two hazard ratios come from 10 margin-positive patients and 84 invasive cases respectively and are reported without confidence intervals, so use them for direction and not as effect sizes. Recurrence here means the radiologic appearance of a new IPMN, with growth of lesions knowingly left behind excluded by definition and most recurrences never histologically confirmed, so the distinction between true recurrence, progression of residual disease and a field defect is settled by the definition rather than by evidence. Follow-up intensity also differed by design between the groups — 6-monthly for 3 years after invasive IPMN against yearly then 2- to 3-yearly after non-invasive — so the later median recurrence of benign lesions is partly a detection interval. Only 2 patients (0.5%) developed a metachronous ductal adenocarcinoma, but 19 patients with a concomitant adenocarcinoma were excluded from the recurrence analysis beforehand, so this series cannot be used to estimate the risk of a new cancer elsewhere in the remnant, which is the risk post-resection surveillance is usually justified by. Evidence & sources The authors' own conclusion was that recurrence of non-invasive branch-duct IPMN is infrequent — 1 of 197 (0.5%) recurred as a malignant tumour, which is a single patient — and that surveillance may be avoided in selected cases. Set against that, Fukuoka 2017 cites a series in which the 1-, 5- and 10-year risks of a new IPMN after resection of 130 non-invasive lesions were 4%, 25% and 62%, with further surgery needed in 1.6%, 14% and 18% and invasive IPMN developing in 0%, 7% and 38%, and the wider literature it reviews gives 1 to 20% recurrence and 2 to 7.8% invasive recurrence. Late events are real: in the 412-patient series 4 of the 5 patients reoperated beyond 4 years had an oncocytic lesion, one recurring 11 years after the original resection. This page records the disagreement rather than resolving it. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Single-centre series: recurrence 65/381 (17%) over a median 58 mo; invasive vs non-invasive 45% vs 9% (P<.001); margin positive vs negative 25% vs 14% (P=.008) Recurrence = new IPMN on imaging, mostly unconfirmed; follow-up intensity differed by group

Guideline-cited series of 130 resected non-invasive lesions: new IPMN 4%, 25%, 62% at 1, 5, 10 y; invasive IPMN 0%, 7%, 38% Secondary citation of one series; reviewed literature gives 1 to 20% recurrence

lead: Where a residual branch-duct cyst was knowingly left in the remnant, record exactly where it is and surveil it as a cyst in its own right.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Where a residual branch-duct cyst was knowingly left in the remnant, record exactly where it is and surveil it as a cyst in its own right. Indications Preferred when A multifocal branch-duct IPMN in which a total pancreatectomy was rightly declined — Kyoto 2024 states that multifocality does not raise the risk of high-grade dysplasia or carcinoma and that only the highest-risk lesion should be resected. In the 412-patient series a residual branch-duct IPMN of a median 10 mm was left in the remnant in 33 patients (9%); over a median of 61 months these grew to a median of 13 mm, none developed worrisome features or high-risk stigmata, and none required reoperation. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let the residual cyst disappear from the record between the operation note and the surveillance plan. Kyoto 2024's remnant surveillance applies for as long as the patient is fit for further intervention, which means the plan has to name what is being watched. Evidence & sources Thirty-three patients with no progression is reassuring and is also a small number over a median follow-up of 5 years, in a series whose own authors say they cannot rule out that the retained lesions harboured high-grade dysplasia. It is not a basis for discharging a remnant cyst. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Take a family history of pancreatic cancer after the operation if it was not taken before, because in Kyoto 2024 it halves the remnant surveillance interval.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Take a family history of pancreatic cancer after the operation if it was not taken before, because in Kyoto 2024 it halves the remnant surveillance interval. Indications Preferred when Every patient at the first postoperative visit. Kyoto 2024 names a family history of pancreatic cancer — defined as pancreatic cancer in one or more first-degree relatives, per the CAPS group — and high-grade dysplasia in the initial specimen as the two factors that increase the risk of a remnant lesion, and recommends 6-monthly rather than yearly imaging in either case. Fukuoka 2017 reports the supporting data: 23% recurrence against 7% with a family history (P<0.05), the only independent preoperative predictor (odds ratio 4.2, 95% CI 1.3 to 14.1), and concomitant adenocarcinoma in 11.1% against 2.9% of 324 resected cases. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid There are no comparative data behind the 6-month figure, and the risk factor does not replicate in surveillance: in a 3,179-patient cohort a family history was not associated with pancreatic carcinoma incidence, overall or by carcinoma type. Kyoto also states that a family history raises the incidence of concomitant adenocarcinoma without increasing the risk that the IPMN itself progresses from low-grade dysplasia. A family history may open a hereditary-risk discussion that is wider than this page and belongs with genetics, where germline ATM, BRCA1, BRCA2, MLH1 or CDKN2A mutations define a different population. Evidence & sources Grade D: consensus interval on an observational risk factor that one large cohort could not reproduce. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Guideline-reported: recurrence 23% vs 7% with vs without family history (P<0.05), OR 4.2 (95% CI 1.3–14.1); concomitant adenocarcinoma 11.1% vs 2.9% Did not replicate in a 3,179-patient surveillance cohort; no comparative data for 6-month interval

lead: Do not discharge a patient after resection of a non-invasive IPMN on the AGA rule without saying that the other three guidelines disagree.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not discharge a patient after resection of a non-invasive IPMN on the AGA rule without saying that the other three guidelines disagree. Why Why If the programme adopts the AGA position, write it down as a deliberate departure from Kyoto, ACG and the European guideline, and audit the remnant recurrences it produces. Additional cautions Additional cautions AGA 2015 recommends against routine surveillance of resected cysts without high-grade dysplasia or malignancy; Kyoto 2024, ACG 2018 and the European guideline all surveil every resected IPMN. A patient discharged under one guideline and recalled under another has been managed inconsistently, not flexibly. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not surveil a resected serous cystadenoma or a drained pseudocyst.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not surveil a resected serous cystadenoma or a drained pseudocyst. Why Why ACG states that resected serous cystadenomas and pseudocysts require no follow-up. Close the episode and say so in the letter. Additional cautions Additional cautions Leaving these on a surveillance list is the clearest avoidable waste in the whole pathway: in 2,622 patients the entire international serous cystadenoma series produced three serous cystadenocarcinomas and one disease-related death. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: International series, 2,622 patients: three serous cystadenocarcinomas and one disease-related death

lead: Look at the papilla with a side-viewing duodenoscope, not a forward-viewing gastroscope, and describe the lesion by compartment: ampullary-duodenal, intra-ampullary, or ampullary-ductal.
text: Standard Evidence D Look at the papilla with a side-viewing duodenoscope, not a forward-viewing gastroscope, and describe the lesion by compartment: ampullary-duodenal, intra-ampullary, or ampullary-ductal. Indications Preferred when Every suspected ampullary neoplasm. NCCN specifies a side-viewing endoscope in the workup. PERIPAN asks endoscopists to classify the lesion as ampullary-duodenal (visible change on the duodenal surface) or as sitting inside the ampulla, and to say when it looks like an intra-ampullary papillary tubular neoplasm — an elevated papilla covered by relatively preserved mucosa — because that tells the pathologist what to cut for. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not accept a forward-viewing look as the examination. In familial adenomatous polyposis a short transparent cap on a gastroscope visualised the duodenum and ampulla in 95% of patients, so cap assistance is a workable substitute; an uncapped forward-viewing pass is not. Evidence & sources The compartment predicts the histology, and it inverts the usual intuition: ampullary-duodenal tumours are mostly intestinal subtype, while ampullary-ductal tumours — endoscopically the subtle, dimple-like ulcerations — are mostly pancreatobiliary. The unimpressive lesion is the dangerous one. In Adsay's 249-case series the four anatomic subsets had 3-year survival of 73% (intra-ampullary papillary-tubular-neoplasm-associated, n=61), 69% (periampullary-duodenal, n=12), 41% (ampullary-ductal, n=36) and 54% (ampullary-NOS, n=140, 55% of cases). Read in full the ordering is softer than the numbers suggest: the omnibus log-rank across the four groups at 1 year gave P=0.167, and the authors call the subsets prognostically distinct on pairwise comparison of the Kaplan-Meier curves rather than on a significant overall test. No confidence interval is given for any estimate anywhere in the paper, no multivariable model adjusting for T stage, nodes or invasion size is reported although one is described in the methods, the favourable periampullary-duodenal group has 12 patients of whom 6 were node positive, and invasion size — the variable that drives the ordering — was in part derived by applying an invasive-to-non-invasive ratio read off the slides to the gross size rather than measured. The categories were assigned retrospectively by the same authors who devised the scheme, with no blinded reassignment and no interobserver statistic, so the reproducibility of the gross algorithm the whole classification rests on is untested. Use the compartment to tell the pathologist what to cut for, not to give a prognosis. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Retrospective series, 249 cases: 3-y survival intra-ampullary 73% (n=61), periampullary-duodenal 69% (n=12), ampullary-ductal 41% (n=36), NOS 54% (n=140) Omnibus log-rank P=0.167; no CIs; unblinded retrospective subset assignment

lead: Add EUS and MRI with MRCP before committing to an endoscopic resection, and record intraductal extension as a length, not as a yes or no.
text: Standard Evidence C Add EUS and MRI with MRCP before committing to an endoscopic resection, and record intraductal extension as a length, not as a yes or no. Indications Preferred when Any lesion that might be taken endoscopically. ESGE recommends EUS and abdominal MRCP for staging ampullary tumours (strong recommendation, low quality evidence) and NCCN suggests EUS in all lesions that might be removed endoscopically, to assess intraductal or parenchymal invasion. Against surgical pathology as the reference, EUS in 102 patients gave 80% sensitivity and 93% specificity for any intraductal extension, accuracy 91%, AUROC 0.87 (95% CI 0.76–0.97), and ERCP in 81 patients gave 83% and 93%, accuracy 84%, AUROC 0.88 (0.77–0.99). Overall EUS accuracy for local tissue invasion was 90% (90 of 100). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat EUS as a reliable way to separate an adenoma from a T1 cancer, and read the headline accuracy by stage rather than overall. The 90% figure is carried almost entirely by correctly calling 65 of 66 lesions confined to the ampulla: accuracy was 98% for T1 but 78% for T2, 80% for T3 and 78% for T4, with 7 patients understaged (duodenal wall 4, pancreas 1, other structures 2) and 3 overstaged — so EUS systematically understages in exactly the categories that would change the operation. A separate single-centre retrospective series of 120 biopsy-proven adenomas reported overall T-stage accuracy of 81.7% with 93.9% sensitivity and 45.5% specificity for the adenoma/T1 category and 50.0% sensitivity for T2, but there EUS erred mostly towards overstaging (20 overstaged, 2 understaged), and its nodal accuracy of 75.0% with N1 sensitivity 62.5% rests on only 16 operated adenocarcinomas, 3 of the 8 node-positive patients having been called N0. Either way, a node-negative EUS does not establish N0. Evidence & sources Compared against ERCP rather than surgical pathology, EUS sensitivity for intraductal extension fell to 56% with 97% specificity (accuracy 90%, AUROC 0.77, 95% CI 0.64–0.89), missing 6 of 12 bile duct extensions, so the reference standard changes the answer. Three limits that the full text makes clear. First, the reference standard is partly circular for the lesions that matter most: in endoscopically resected adenomas, absence of intraductal extension was assumed whenever resection was complete with a negative margin and cholangiography was clear, which already incorporates endoscopic judgement and inflates specificity and accuracy. Second, the three comparisons use non-overlapping subsets of the same cohort (90, 102 and 81 patients) selected by whether an ERCP or a resection specimen existed, so EUS and ERCP were not read in the same patients and the claim that they perform similarly is not a paired comparison. Third, sensitivity rests on 9 to 12 patients with intraductal extension, which is why the intervals are wide. Two incidental findings from the same series are worth carrying: 10 of 58 papillectomy specimens (17%) proved non-adenomatous despite an outside biopsy reported as adenoma, and EUS-FNA diagnosed adenocarcinoma in 6 of 7 (86%) but adenoma or advanced adenoma in only 1 of 5 (20%). Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not place a biliary stent before planned surgery as a routine; stent for cholangitis or fever, for severe symptomatic jaundice, or when the operation is being delayed, including for neoadjuvant therapy.
text: Standard Evidence C Do not place a biliary stent before planned surgery as a routine; stent for cholangitis or fever, for severe symptomatic jaundice, or when the operation is being delayed, including for neoadjuvant therapy. Indications Preferred when This is NCCN's stent position for ampullary adenocarcinoma, and the randomised evidence behind it is strong but borrowed: in 202 patients with cancer of the pancreatic head, preoperative biliary drainage raised serious complications within 120 days from 39% to 74% (relative risk for early surgery 0.54, 95% CI 0.41–0.71, P<0.001). ERCP-guided drainage is preferred over the percutaneous route when drainage is needed, stents should be as short as feasible, and a fully covered self-expanding metal stent is preferred when neoadjuvant therapy is planned because it can be exchanged or removed. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Read the limits honestly, because they are larger than the headline. That trial enrolled cancer of the pancreatic head — 92% of the 196 patients had adenocarcinoma, site was carried only as a pancreatic-versus-periampullary covariate and no ampullary subgroup result is reported anywhere. Bilirubin was 40–250 µmol/L. Surgery-related complications alone did not differ (early surgery 35 of 94, 37%, versus drainage 48 of 102, 47%; relative risk 0.79, 95% CI 0.57–1.11, P=0.14), so on the question clinicians actually ask — does operating on a jaundiced patient carry more surgical risk — the trial is null. The entire excess was procedural: drainage-related complications occurred in 47 of 102 (46%) against 2 of 94 (2%), dominated by cholangitis in 27 patients (26%), stent occlusion in 15 (15%) and a need for stent exchange in 31 (30%). Mortality did not differ (any cause 12 of 94, 13%, versus 15 of 102, 15%; relative risk 0.85, 0.42–1.72) and median stay was 14 against 16 days. NCCN also states that a self-expanding metal stent should only be placed once a tissue diagnosis is confirmed — an uncovered metal stent in an undiagnosed papilla is a self-inflicted problem. Evidence & sources Downgraded from B to C on the full-text read, and the reason is not the trial's conduct but what it tested and in whom. The intervention was a 10 Fr plastic endoprosthesis left for 4 to 6 weeks; the authors' own closing recommendation is that drainage during neoadjuvant treatment might be better achieved with metal stents, which concedes that the intervention tested is not the one now used. The design was a noninferiority comparison with a 10 percentage-point margin and one-sided alpha 0.05, and it is universally cited as showing that drainage causes harm. Only 61% of patients went on to resection and 31% had a palliative bypass, and the palliative subgroup showed the largest difference (surgical complications 18 of 33, 55%, versus 5 of 28, 18%, P=0.003) — so the result is partly driven by patients in whom stenting would now be definitive therapy rather than preparation. Events were counted to 120 days from randomisation, which gives the drainage arm a 4 to 6 week period at risk with no equivalent in the early-surgery arm. Separately, a stent across the papilla degrades the endoscopic and EUS assessment that the papillectomy decision depends on, which is a second and ampullary-specific reason to stage first where the clinical situation allows. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Early surgery vs preoperative drainage: serious complications by 120 days 39% vs 74%, RR 0.54 (95% CI 0.41–0.71), P<0.001; surgery-related 37% vs 47%, P=0.14 Pancreatic-head cancer, no ampullary subgroup; 10 Fr plastic stents; excess was drainage-related

lead: Name the histologic primary by epicenter: ampulla, duodenum, distal bile duct or pancreatic head. Shared surgery does not imply shared prognosis.
text: Standard Evidence D Name the histologic primary by epicenter: ampulla, duodenum, distal bile duct or pancreatic head. Shared surgery does not imply shared prognosis. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Name the tumour by its epicentre and stop writing periampullary once the specimen is in hand — ampullary, duodenal, distal bile duct and pancreatic head cancers share an operation and not a prognosis. Indications Preferred when PERIPAN defines ampullary carcinoma as arising from any segment of the ampulla of Vater, distal cholangiocarcinoma as having its epicentre in the common bile duct above the sphincter of Oddi with no or minimal ampullary involvement, and duodenal carcinoma as having its epicentre in the non-ampullary duodenum. It recommends that periampullary be avoided in pathology reports and cancer-registry submissions, and used before resection only when imaging cannot identify the epicentre. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let the shared Whipple collapse the distinction. Pancreatobiliary-predominant ampullary carcinoma — the worst-prognosis tubular ampullary group — still had median survival of 41 months against 15.6 months for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, and 1.97 times the hazard of death (95% CI 1.42–2.72, P<0.001) when matched for size and node status; in Adsay's series the ampullary-ductal subset's 3-year survival was 41% against 11% for 113 pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas. The distinction does not change the operation; it changes what you tell the patient and how you read every adjuvant study. Evidence & sources PERIPAN is explicit that the historical habit of pooling these tumours is why the adjuvant literature cannot be reconciled: inconsistent definitions and high interobserver variability have hindered consistent conclusions, particularly about adjuvant chemotherapy. There is a corollary that cuts the other way and belongs here. Applying the strict epicentre definition reclassified 68 of 317 previously labelled ampullary cases (21%) as pancreatic (33), duodenal (16) or common bile duct (19) carcinomas secondarily involving the ampulla. Removing those cases removes mostly the worst-prognosis tumours, so part of the survival gap between ampullary carcinoma and pancreatic cancer in the modern literature is a definitional effect rather than a biological one. The comparator cohorts in that series were convenience groups from the same archives with no matching for stage, size or treatment, and adjuvant therapy was not recorded at all. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Observational: 3-y survival 41% vs 11%, ampullary-ductal subset vs 113 pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas Comparators were unmatched convenience cohorts; adjuvant therapy not recorded

lead: ERCP or percutaneous cholangiography when cross-sectional imaging and EUS leave the ductal extent unresolved — accepting the added morbidity.
text: Reasonable Evidence C ERCP or percutaneous cholangiography when cross-sectional imaging and EUS leave the ductal extent unresolved — accepting the added morbidity. Indications Preferred when An indeterminate stricture, or a lesion where the length of intraductal growth will decide between papillectomy and resection. ERCP matched surgical pathology as well as EUS did for intraductal extension (83% sensitivity, 93% specificity). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid NCCN notes that ERCP and PTC add diagnostic capability beyond EGD, EUS and CT but carry increased morbidity and even mortality. Do not order one to confirm what EUS and MRCP have already established. Evidence & sources Intraductal ultrasound at the same session performed well in the one series reporting it — sensitivity 87.5%, specificity 92.5% and accuracy 90.2% for carcinoma in 72 patients, with T-stage accuracy 86%, 71% and 86% for T1, T2 and T3 and nodal accuracy 75% — but that paper is cited here from its abstract only; the full text was not obtained, so its selection, blinding and reference standard cannot be checked. ESGE itself only suggests intraductal ultrasound in selected patients, with routine use balanced against training, cost and pancreatitis risk. Note too that the EUS-against-ERCP comparison behind this string is not a paired one: the two tests were compared in different, availability-selected subsets of the same cohort. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Single series (abstract only), 72 pts: IDUS for carcinoma sensitivity 87.5%, specificity 92.5%, accuracy 90.2%; nodal accuracy 75% Abstract only; selection, blinding and reference standard could not be checked

lead: PET/CT when MRI cannot be performed, and MRI for indeterminate liver lesions.
text: Reasonable Evidence D PET/CT when MRI cannot be performed, and MRI for indeterminate liver lesions. Indications Preferred when NCCN's own sequence: MRI for indeterminate liver lesions as clinically indicated, with PET/CT substituted when MRI is not possible, such as in a pacemaker-dependent patient. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Not a staging test in its own right in this disease, and no ampullary-specific performance data support it as one.

lead: Germline testing at the point of diagnosis, not after the operation.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Germline testing at the point of diagnosis, not after the operation. Indications Preferred when NCCN recommends genetic testing for inherited mutations in any patient with confirmed ampullary adenocarcinoma or a positive family history, using comprehensive hereditary-cancer panels, with counselling for anyone positive for ATM, BRCA1, BRCA2, CDKN2A, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PALB2, PMS2, STK11 or TP53, or with a positive family history regardless of mutation status. The supporting ampullary data are much thinner than the recommendation: in a nationwide Dutch series of 90 resected carcinomas diagnosed under age 50, mismatch-repair deficiency was found in 11 of 23 duodenal carcinomas (47.8%) but only 1 of 23 ampullary (4.3%) and 2 of 44 pancreatic (4.5%), and it was that single ampullary patient and those two pancreatic patients in whom deficiency proved attributable to Lynch syndrome. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not quote that series as showing concordance between deficiency and a hereditary cause in ampullary cancer. One of one is not an estimate, no confidence interval appears anywhere in the paper, and the 4.3% ampullary deficiency rate is indistinguishable from pancreatic cancer and lower than the roughly 10% to 15% reported in unselected ampullary series — which would mean selecting by young age performs worse than testing everyone, the opposite of the paper's framing. The cohort is also resection-specimens-only from 23 cooperating laboratories, with 72 of 162 eligible patients (44%) not included because material was not supplied and no comparison of included against excluded patients offered. The case for germline testing at diagnosis rests on NCCN's recommendation and on the family consequences of a positive result, not on this prevalence estimate. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
