lead: Do not stage this tumour on a portal-venous CT of the abdomen alone.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not stage this tumour on a portal-venous CT of the abdomen alone. Why Why Use the pancreatic protocol with chest imaging, and add EUS and MRCP when an endoscopic resection is in question. Additional cautions Additional cautions A single-phase abdominal CT answers neither the depth question nor the intraductal-extension question, and both decide the operation. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not let a self-expanding metal stent be placed across an undiagnosed papilla.
text: Avoid Evidence D Do not let a self-expanding metal stent be placed across an undiagnosed papilla. Why Why NCCN: metal stents only once tissue diagnosis is confirmed; a removable or fully covered stent where the diagnosis or the plan is still open. Additional cautions Additional cautions It prevents subsequent endoscopic resection and alters the specimen, and may be unnecessary if the lesion proves to be a benign adenoma.

lead: An adenoma biopsy does not exclude underlying carcinoma: reported sampling false-negative rate 20–40%.
text: Standard Evidence C An adenoma biopsy does not exclude underlying carcinoma: reported sampling false-negative rate 20–40%. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Treat a biopsy that reads adenoma as the least severe possible diagnosis, not the final one — the reported false-negative rate for invasive carcinoma beneath an ampullary adenoma is 20% to 40%, and the cause is sampling, not interpretation. Indications Preferred when Every patient in whom the management plan rests on the biopsy. NCCN states that endoscopic biopsies of ampullary adenocarcinoma have poor diagnostic accuracy with high false-negative rates of about 20% to 40%, and that final pathology has repeatedly reported carcinoma in lesions initially called adenoma. PERIPAN puts the false-negative rate at 20% to 30% for exactly this distinction and attributes it to sampling bias — the carcinoma within the adenoma not being represented. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not reason from the biopsy to the operation as if the two were the same question. In a 10-year single-institution series, 90 of 252 patients with an ampullary biopsy had a follow-up biopsy or resection specimen; 55 (61.1%) were concordant and 35 (38.9%) discordant, with 8 of the 35 discordances (22.9%, and 8.9% of the 90) a major one — and all 8 were a benign biopsy with a malignant resection, 7 of them attributed to superficial sampling and only 1 to interpretive error. In 44 endoscopic papillectomies done for lesions judged benign, 14 (32%) harboured adenocarcinoma missed on the prior biopsies: invasive adenocarcinoma in 9 (20.5%) and adenoma with intramucosal carcinoma in a further 5 (11.3%), with a further 5 (11.3%) non-adenomatous lesions wrongly called adenoma. Evidence & sources This is the single most consequential error in this disease, and it is not reducible by more biopsies alone. PERIPAN: acquisition of biopsy material from the accurate site is key and more important than the number of biopsies — but it recommends a minimum of three targeted biopsies of viable abnormal tissue, because fewer than three is a sampling choice masquerading as a result. Both supporting series understate the problem rather than overstate it, and in opposite ways. The 8.9% major-discrepancy rate is computed on the 36% of patients who had follow-up pathology, and those are precisely the patients whose biopsy or clinical picture raised concern, so it is a lower bound. The 32% occult-carcinoma rate comes from a cohort in which 35 of the original 79 papillectomies (44.3%) had already been excluded for a malignant biopsy or a suspicious endoscopic appearance — it is the rate after the obviously malignant lesions were removed. The same institutional series reports biopsy sensitivity for malignancy of 60% (12 of 20) and cytology 56% (5 of 9), rising to 89% (8 of 9) combined, but those are 9-to-20-patient estimates with no confidence intervals, cytology was ordered in 88% of non-ampullary periampullary but only 17% of ampullary tumours, and 3 of 5 pathologists knew the malignant cytology result before signing out the biopsy — so the incremental value of adding cytology is not estimable from these data. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: PERIPAN-quoted biopsy false-negative rate 20–30% for carcinoma beneath an ampullary adenoma, attributed to sampling bias NCCN quotes a wider 20–40%; more biopsies alone do not fix sampling

lead: Score the malignancy risk explicitly before choosing between an endoscopic and an open operation, rather than carrying an unstated impression into the decision.
text: Standard Evidence D Score the malignancy risk explicitly before choosing between an endoscopic and an open operation, rather than carrying an unstated impression into the decision. Indications Preferred when Any biopsy-proven adenoma where the choice of operation is live. In 127 non-familial periampullary adenomas taken to pancreatoduodenectomy at 8 institutions, 59 (46.4%) proved malignant on final pathology; age 65 or over (odds ratio 3.2, 95% CI 1.3–7.9), bile duct 9 mm or more (3.3, 1.4–10.1), any preoperative symptom (7.7, 2.1–26.8) and high-grade dysplasia on biopsy (7.5, 2.6–19.8) were independent predictors, weighted into a 0–6 score (age 1, duct 1, symptoms 2, high-grade dysplasia 2). In a separate single-centre retrospective cohort of 91 patients, 24 (26.4%) biopsy-proven adenomas were upgraded after resection — 4 to carcinoma in situ and 20 to adenocarcinoma — with high-grade dysplasia on biopsy (odds ratio 6.66, 95% CI 1.52–29.08) and ductal dilatation over 7 mm (10.96, 2.25–53.42) independent predictors in the paper's Table 4; its abstract reports 6.86 (1.58–29.79) and 11.12 (2.27–54.37), a discrepancy the paper does not explain. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not use the score to justify a Whipple in the low-risk group: in that series the patients at no or low risk had a higher rate of major postoperative complications than the intermediate and high-risk groups, though the three-group comparison was not significant (51.7%, 27.1% and 29.4%, P=0.11) and significance appeared only after the strata were collapsed at a score of 3 and adjusted for comorbidity, obesity, duct size and parenchymal texture (odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 1.01–8.6, P=0.047). The simpler reading of that inversion is physiological rather than prognostic: patients with benign pathology have soft, non-atrophic glands and non-dilated ducts because nothing is obstructing them, and fistula risk follows gland texture and duct size. The score is a shared-decision instrument, and the authors present it as one. Evidence & sources Downgraded from C to D on the full-text read, and the recommendation to score explicitly stands while the score itself should not be quoted to a patient as a calibrated risk. Four reasons. The score was derived and evaluated in the same 127 patients with no split sample, no bootstrap, no c-statistic, no calibration plot and no sensitivity or specificity at any threshold, and the authors state that validation was impossible. Its strata appear three different ways in the same paper: the abstract gives low risk n=26, intermediate 59 and high 26 with malignancy rates of 10.3%, 44.1% and 88.2%, the results text gives 11.5%, 41.7% and 84.6%, and Table 4 gives 3 of 29, 26 of 59 and 30 of 34 — so the calibration cannot be checked from the published data. Every patient in the cohort had a pancreatoduodenectomy, so the score is calibrated on a population already judged to need resection, which is not the population facing the choice. And two of its four components — any preoperative symptom, worth 2 points on a list that includes fatigue, nausea and dark urine, and a bile duct of 9 mm or more — are proxies for obstruction rather than for neoplastic progression; jaundice and biliary stenting were dropped from the model as redundant with symptoms, which concedes the point. Lesion size did not predict malignancy (median 2.9 against 3.5 cm, P=0.3, missing in 27 of 127) and EUS findings are absent from the paper entirely. [REGISTRY] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Retrospective cohort: 59/127 (46.4%) malignant at PD; predictors age ≥65 OR 3.2 (95% CI 1.3–7.9), duct ≥9 mm 3.3, symptoms 7.7, HGD on biopsy 7.5 → 0–6 score Derived and evaluated in the same 127 resected patients; no validation, c-statistic or calibration

lead: For a deep or intra-ampullary lesion that forceps cannot reach, use EUS-guided fine-needle biopsy rather than aspiration or brushings.
text: Standard Evidence D For a deep or intra-ampullary lesion that forceps cannot reach, use EUS-guided fine-needle biopsy rather than aspiration or brushings. Indications Preferred when Hard-to-reach, deep-seated intra-ampullary lesions — typically ampullary-ductal carcinoma or an intra-ampullary papillary tubular neoplasm covered by intact or ulcerated mucosa. PERIPAN recommends EUS-FNB here, and prefers core biopsy over cytology because the distinction between reactive and neoplastic atypia on cytology is extremely challenging and because tissue permits immunohistochemistry and molecular work. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not rely on aspiration or brushings alone. In one 72-patient series transpapillary forceps biopsy by itself detected 68.7% of carcinomas — a false-negative rate of 31.3% — with 100% specificity, and combining it with intraductal ultrasound raised sensitivity to 97% and accuracy to 94.5%; that paper is cited from its abstract only, since the full text was not obtained, so treat the increment as a direction rather than a number. The general point does not depend on it: in a separate series EUS-FNA diagnosed adenocarcinoma in 6 of 7 cases but adenoma or advanced adenoma in only 1 of 5. Evidence & sources EUS-FNA or brushings may be added to FNB to raise yield in difficult cases, but not substituted for it. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: 72-patient series: transpapillary forceps biopsy alone detected 68.7% of carcinomas (specificity 100%); with intraductal ultrasound sensitivity 97%, accuracy 94.5% Cited from abstract only; treat the increment as a direction

lead: Resample, once, with the endoscopic compartment named on the request form — then stop.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Resample, once, with the endoscopic compartment named on the request form — then stop. Indications Preferred when A non-diagnostic or discordant first biopsy where the compartment was not stated. PERIPAN is explicit that precise information on the site of the lesion relative to the duodenum, ampullary channel, bile duct, pancreatic duct and pancreas, and the presence or absence of intracanalicular growth, changes how the specimen is cut: if ampullary-ductal origin is suspected from the dimple-like endoscopic appearance, the pathologist takes deeper sections to look for subtle cancer growth. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not keep resampling in pursuit of a negative result that will not change the plan. If a third negative biopsy would not alter the operation, the patient needs a decision, not another endoscopy — and each ampullary biopsy carries a pancreatitis risk. Evidence & sources In a prospective screening series of 102 patients with familial polyposis the papilla was abnormal in 87 of 97 biopsied there, and among the 80 patients biopsied at both sites the papilla was twice as likely to be adenomatous as the peripapillary area (81% against 41%) — so an ampullary biopsy in polyposis is high-yield and is also why it is now discouraged. The harm figure most often quoted, that 30% of available tests showed an asymptomatic amylase rise after ampullary biopsy in a prospective series of 35 polyposis patients, together with a handful of case reports of acute pancreatitis, reaches this page through a narrative review rather than from the primary studies; that review has no protocol, no second reviewer, no risk-of-bias appraisal and no pooling, so the figure is an unweighted quotation. If a biopsy of the ampulla is unavoidable, taking it from the 9-to-1-o'clock sector, away from the pancreatic orifice, has been suggested. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Report high-risk features and tumour budding on the biopsy, even when T and N stage cannot be assessed.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Report high-risk features and tumour budding on the biopsy, even when T and N stage cannot be assessed. Indications Preferred when Any biopsy or ampullectomy specimen. PERIPAN asks for presence of non-invasive neoplasia versus invasive carcinoma, histological type including poorly cohesive morphology, grade, lymphatic, vascular and perineural invasion, and tumour budding. High budding — three or more budding foci per ×200 field — is reported as an independent predictor of overall survival with a stronger prognostic impact than tumour stage or nodal metastasis. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not over-read a budding score from a biopsy. PERIPAN acknowledges that the invasive front, where budding should be assessed, may not be represented in the biopsy at all. Note also what the claim rests on: the threshold of three or more budding foci per ×200 field has no reproducibility data of its own, the prognostic claim comes largely from the same institutional tradition that produced the ampullary subtype classification, and PERIPAN grades the recommendation low evidence and weak. Budding is reported because it may be the only prognostic variable available in a specimen that cannot be staged, not because it has been validated against T and N stage in independent cohorts. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not perform a papillectomy to obtain a diagnosis when adenoma has not been proven.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not perform a papillectomy to obtain a diagnosis when adenoma has not been proven. Why Why Prove the adenoma first. This is ESGE's first recommendation in ampullary tumours and it is a strong recommendation on low-quality evidence. Additional cautions Additional cautions The cost of ignoring it is measurable, and it is the most important single finding in the European comparison of these two operations. Final histology was neither adenoma nor adenocarcinoma — mostly hyperplastic or chronic inflammatory tissue — in 270 of 1,115 endoscopic papillectomy patients (24.2%) and 25 of 169 transduodenal surgical ampullectomy patients (14.8%), while advanced cancer (T2 or above, or node positive) was found in 122 papillectomy (10.9%) and 62 surgical ampullectomy (36.6%) patients. Roughly a third of the procedures in each arm were therefore performed for the wrong indication: either there was no neoplasm to remove, or the disease was already beyond what a local resection can treat. The authors call the rate of poor indications still high for both operations. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Do not subtype the carcinoma on the biopsy in order to drive definitive treatment when the patient is going to resection.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not subtype the carcinoma on the biopsy in order to drive definitive treatment when the patient is going to resection. Why Why PERIPAN: subtyping and biomarker assessment on biopsy material should be done only if it may influence subsequent treatment — that is, mainly in a patient who may not have surgery. Otherwise subtype and test for mismatch-repair deficiency on the resection specimen. Additional cautions Additional cautions About 40% of ampullary carcinomas show a mixed or hybrid phenotype — 94 of 232 cases by consensus of three of five blinded observers, against pure pancreatobiliary in 74 (32%) and pure intestinal in only 13 (6%) — so the subtype seen in a biopsy may not represent the tumour. The reproducibility study that established this warns explicitly that caution is warranted when applying the classification to biopsies and tissue microarrays, and in its own side experiment two fields from a single tumour shown blind to eight observers were called pancreatobiliary by 6 of 8 and hybrid by 2 of 8 for one field, and intestinal by 4 of 8 and mixed by 4 of 8 for the other. It also selected tumours with an invasive component over 3.0 mm, which removes the small intra-ampullary lesions that a biopsy is most likely to represent. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Mixed/hybrid phenotype in 94 of 232 (about 40%); pure pancreatobiliary 74 (32%), pure intestinal 13 (6%) Only tumours with invasive component >3.0 mm; authors warn against applying it to biopsies

lead: Endoscopic papillectomy by direct snare resection without submucosal injection, aiming at en bloc removal, at a high-volume centre.
text: Standard Evidence C Endoscopic papillectomy by direct snare resection without submucosal injection, aiming at en bloc removal, at a high-volume centre. Indications Preferred when Ampullary adenoma without intraductal extension. ESGE recommends papillectomy in this group (strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence), recommends en bloc resection of adenomas up to 20–30 mm to achieve R0 and reduce recurrence (strong, low quality), and recommends direct snare resection without submucosal injection (strong, moderate quality). NCCN agrees that adenomas without suspicion of adenocarcinoma, including those with high-grade dysplasia, may be safely removed endoscopically, and that this should be done at a high-volume centre. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not attempt a technically infeasible resection. En-bloc intent generally applies up to 20–30 mm; 30–40 mm lesions require individualized expert assessment. ESGE suggests surgery for technical infeasibility, examples including size >4 cm or obstructing diverticulum, and for intraductal extension >20 mm. Evidence & sources Submucosal injection is specifically not recommended: it lifts the mucosa away from the ductal structures the snare needs to engage and makes the anatomy harder, not easier. ESGE grades that recommendation strong on moderate-quality evidence, which the subsequent literature does not quite support — the 2025 European comparison of papillectomy with surgical ampullectomy notes that the evidence remains contradictory and that submucosal injection was still used in 24.2% of its matched endoscopic cases. The more useful warning about en bloc intent is that technical success and histological completeness are different things: in 798 Japanese patients, en bloc resection was achieved in 89.0% and technical success in 94.9%, yet only 58.6% of en bloc resections (416 of 710) were ultimately R0, the rest downgraded by thermal artefact or margin involvement. An en bloc resection is a better starting point for a margin assessment, not a guarantee of one. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: 798 Japanese patients: en bloc 89.0%, technical success 94.9%, but only 58.6% of en bloc resections R0 (416 of 710) R0 lost to thermal artefact or margin involvement; en bloc is not a margin guarantee

lead: Place a prophylactic pancreatic duct stent, and use a wire-guided technique if that is what it takes to get the stent in.
text: Standard Evidence C Place a prophylactic pancreatic duct stent, and use a wire-guided technique if that is what it takes to get the stent in. Indications Preferred when Every papillectomy. ESGE recommends prophylactic pancreatic duct stenting to reduce post-papillectomy pancreatitis (strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence). In the only randomised trial of the stent itself, 19 patients were allocated after en bloc snare ampullectomy; pancreatitis within 24 hours occurred in 3 of 9 analysed unstented patients (33%) and none of 10 stented patients (P=0.02). In practice the stent is placed in the large majority of cases — 93.6% of 798 Japanese papillectomies and 73.6% of one 106-patient Korean cohort, where stenting was associated with less pancreatitis on multivariable analysis (odds ratio 0.205, 95% CI 0.044–0.945, P=0.042). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Give both halves when consenting, because the randomised evidence is weaker than the recommendation it supports. That 19-patient trial was stopped early at a pre-specified interim look triggered when the unstented pancreatitis rate reached 30%, against a planned 25 patients per arm, and it reports three different results from the same data: 33% against 0% as treated (P=0.02), 25% against 0% excluding the patient in whom stent placement failed (P=0.05), and 25% against 9% by intention to treat, counting that patient in the stented arm, where significance is lost (P=0.3). The outcome window was 24 hours, so bleeding, perforation, papillary stenosis and recurrence were not captured at all. In a 45-patient randomised pilot of wire-guided against conventional papillectomy, the wire-guided technique placed a stent in 22 of 22 (100%) against 15 of 23 (65%, P=0.004) but its primary endpoint was negative — pancreatitis 4 of 22 (18%) against 3 of 23 (13%), P=0.960, numerically worse in the arm designed to prevent it. The much-quoted finding inside its conventional arm, pancreatitis in 3 of 8 patients who ended without a stent (37.5%) against 0 of 15 with one (P=0.032), is a post-randomisation comparison between patients who differ precisely by whether bleeding and oedema allowed a stent — that is, by procedural difficulty, which is itself a cause of pancreatitis. The stent probably matters; the route to placing it does not; and neither trial establishes the size of the effect. Evidence & sources Downgraded from B to C: the two randomised trials behind this string comprise 64 patients and 10 pancreatitis events between them, one was stopped early and negative on its own intention-to-treat analysis, and the other missed its primary endpoint, so ESGE's grading of moderate-quality evidence overstates what exists. The recommendation stands because the direction is consistent and the intervention is cheap and reversible. Pooled complication figures for endoscopic ampullectomy in the polyposis literature are haemorrhage 4%–21%, pancreatitis 4%–30% and perforation 2%–3%, quoted there as unweighted ranges; in individual cohorts adverse events occurred in 259 of 798 (32.5%, severe in 3.9%, with one procedure-related death), 37 of 136 (27.2%), 26 of 106 (24.5%) and 7 of 44 (15.9%), and the series reporting the lowest rates are also the ones that measured enzymes only in symptomatic patients. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Wire-guided vs conventional papillectomy: primary endpoint not met, pancreatitis 4/22 (18%) vs 3/23 (13%), P=0.960; stent placed 100% vs 65%, P=0.004 45-patient randomised pilot; pancreatitis numerically worse in the wire-guided arm

lead: Tell the patient before the procedure that about one in five will recur, and that recurrence is late as often as early.
text: Standard Evidence C Tell the patient before the procedure that about one in five will recur, and that recurrence is late as often as early. Indications Preferred when Consent for every papillectomy. In 22 Japanese tertiary centres, 776 patients with confirmed ampullary adenoma or adenocarcinoma had cumulative recurrence of 13% (95% CI 11–16) at 1 year, 20% (17–23) at 3 years and 22% (19–26) at 5 years; R0 resection was achieved in only 416 of 798 (52.1%), with R1 in 176 (22.1%) and an indeterminate Rx margin in 206 (25.8%), and even after R0 cumulative recurrence was 4.9% at 1 year, 11% at 3 years and 13% at 5 years. In a 136-patient single-centre cohort where 124 (91.2%) achieved complete eradication, recurrence occurred in 20 (16.1%) at a mean of 3.2 years, range 0.5 to 9.75 years, a rate of 5.8 per 100 person-years (95% CI 3.6–8.8), and 9 of the 20 recurrences (45%) appeared after the first two years of surveillance. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not present papillectomy as a definitive operation with a short follow-up, and do not quote a single recurrence rate as though the series were measuring the same thing. They are not. The Japanese study counted any histologically confirmed neoplastic tissue, with no requirement for a prior negative surveillance endoscopy, and its median time to recurrence was 6 months (3 months after R1) — so a large fraction of its 18.3% is residual disease. The single-centre study required one negative surveillance endoscopy first and allowed multiple treatment sessions inside its definition of complete eradication, which converts early incomplete resection into a non-event and shifts the curve rightwards. The two 20% figures are not comparable, and the honest statement at consent is that about one in five patients will need further endoscopic treatment of the papilla, early or late. Recurrence rate in the single-centre cohort did not differ by baseline pathology — 5.2 per 100 person-years for low-grade dysplasia, 6.9 for high-grade dysplasia and 7.7 for adenocarcinoma, with overlapping intervals. Evidence & sources Margin status is the strongest predictor and is reported twice in the Japanese paper: against R0, the abstract and discussion give hazard ratios of 2.95 (95% CI 1.85–4.71) for R1 and 2.30 (1.44–3.68) for Rx, while Table 2 gives 2.95 (1.87–4.66) and 2.38 (1.49–3.81) for the same comparisons — a small discrepancy, but it means two models were in play and neither is identified. Rx behaved almost identically to frank R1 by 5 years (34% each), which suggests an indeterminate margin is largely an undetected positive one. In a 106-patient Korean cohort a positive or uncertain margin predicted early recurrence (odds ratio 4.023, 95% CI 1.088–16.387, P=0.048) and piecemeal resection predicted late recurrence (6.610, 1.760–24.820, P=0.005) and non-curative resection (5.424, 1.582–18.600, P=0.007) — estimates drawn from 11 to 13 events against 5 or 6 covariates, with intervals spanning an order of magnitude, and with the early-versus-late split defined by the timing of a first surveillance endoscopy that was itself left to the endoscopist. Two further cautions on the timing claim. The Japanese cohort found the later treatment era 2015–2020 an independent predictor of recurrence (hazard ratio 1.57, 1.09–2.26, P=0.016) with no mechanism beyond more procedures by less experienced operators, which could equally be more intensive surveillance. And in the single-centre cohort recurrence was more frequent after en bloc than piecemeal resection (19.4% against 7.0%) and after an initially complete than an incomplete resection (16.5% against 6.1%) — the signature of detection bias in how residual disease was classified, reported in that paper without comment. Its mean follow-up of 2.8 years is also shorter than its mean time to recurrence of 3.2 years, and the single recurrence at 9.75 years is what drives the suggestion of ten-year surveillance. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: 22-centre cohort, 776 pts: cumulative recurrence 13% (95% CI 11–16) at 1 y, 20% (17–23) at 3 y, 22% (19–26) at 5 y; R0 in only 416 of 798 (52.1%) Counted any neoplastic tissue, no prior negative endoscopy; median recurrence 6 mo (much residual)

lead: If en bloc removal is impossible and benign disease would otherwise require pancreatoduodenectomy: consider piecemeal resection plus residual-tissue ablation, accepting higher recurrence.
text: Reasonable Evidence C If en bloc removal is impossible and benign disease would otherwise require pancreatoduodenectomy: consider piecemeal resection plus residual-tissue ablation, accepting higher recurrence. Full explanation i Full explanation Recommendation: full explanation and evidence × Piecemeal resection with ablation of visible residual tissue, accepting a materially higher recurrence rate, where en bloc is not achievable and the alternative is a pancreatoduodenectomy for a benign lesion. Indications Preferred when A large or awkward adenoma in a patient for whom the operative alternative carries real risk. Most patients with a non-curative initial resection in the 106-patient cohort were still managed endoscopically — endoscopic success was 93.4% against curative resection in 76.4%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not call it equivalent. Piecemeal resection was the independent predictor of both late recurrence (odds ratio 6.610, P=0.005) and non-curative resection (5.424, P=0.007) in one cohort and of recurrence overall in the Japanese national cohort (hazard ratio 1.69, 95% CI 1.07–2.65, P=0.023), and it destroys the margin assessment the next decision depends on. Ablation at the index session is not a rescue either: in the European cohort, 69 of 481 adenoma cases (14.4%) had argon plasma coagulation or radiofrequency ablation during the index papillectomy, and if those are counted as probable R2 resections — which is what visible residual tissue means — the primary success rate of papillectomy alone falls from 80.2% to 65.9% (317 of 481). Retreatment then cascades: of 40 adenoma patients given endoscopic retherapy, 17 (42.5%) were still incomplete at the next follow-up and needed a second session, and 12 of the remaining 15 (80%) needed a third. If the patient's malignancy risk is high, piecemeal papillectomy is the wrong operation rather than a smaller one. Evidence & sources Piecemeal resection occurred in 16 of 106 (15.1%) in one cohort and 16 of 44 (36.4%) in another, and en bloc intent failed to deliver an assessable R0 margin in 41% of en bloc Japanese cases, so this is a common situation and worth planning for rather than discovering. Both the 80.2% and the 65.9% figures appear in the European paper without a single preferred estimate, and the reclassification of ablated cases as R2 is the authors' retrospective assumption — a reasonable one, and still an assumption. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: Japanese national cohort: piecemeal resection independently predicted recurrence, HR 1.69 (95% CI 1.07–2.65), P=0.023; en bloc intent gave no assessable R0 margin in 41% None

lead: Papillectomy with close surveillance for high-grade dysplasia or an early carcinoma found after the fact, rather than automatic conversion to resection.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Papillectomy with close surveillance for high-grade dysplasia or an early carcinoma found after the fact, rather than automatic conversion to resection. Indications Preferred when A margin-negative specimen in a patient whose operative risk is substantial. In a propensity-matched Korean multicentre cohort of 127 papillectomies whose final pathology showed high-grade dysplasia or adenocarcinoma, drawn from 485 papillectomies in a 1,607-patient registry, 5-year overall survival was 89.2% with papillectomy alone (22 matched patients) against 82.3% with subsequent radical surgery (33 patients), P=0.861, over a median follow-up of 43.3 months; unmatched the figures were 91.9% against 82.3%, P=0.443. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Read the recurrence curves, not the survival curves, and note that two endpoints missed significance in the same direction. Matched 5-year recurrence-free survival was 66.1% with papillectomy alone against 86.7% with surgery, P=0.052, and in the adenocarcinoma-only subgroup (30 against 25 patients) it was 61.4% against 82.6%, P=0.066, with 5-year overall survival 83.2% against 85.0% (P=0.652). A 20-point absolute difference that misses significance in 55 patients is not equivalence. Margin status is what makes surveillance defensible, and it is not a small effect: within the papillectomy-alone group, patients with both lateral and deep margins positive had significantly worse overall survival than those with negative margins (P=0.007) or a positive lateral margin alone (P=0.015), and recurrence-free survival was worse for any positive margin. Evidence & sources Downgraded from C to D on the full-text read. T stage is never reported anywhere in the paper — in a cohort where between a third and three-quarters of patients had adenocarcinoma, the absence of any T1a-versus-T1b distinction removes the single variable on which the clinical question turns, since T1b carries a substantially higher nodal metastasis risk. Nodal status is unknown in the papillectomy-alone arm by definition, so the two arms are compared with different information. Immortal time bias is unaddressed and runs against the paper's own conclusion: patients had to survive and remain fit for up to 3 months to enter the surgery arm, while anyone who did not stayed in the papillectomy-alone arm, and no landmark analysis is performed. Matching discarded 72 of 94 papillectomy-alone patients to find 22 matches for 33 surgical patients, inverting the usual ratio, and the groups still differed on the proportion with adenocarcinoma afterwards (63.6% against 75.8%) with no balance diagnostics reported. Allocation was by the treating physician on exactly the variables used for matching, surveillance intensity was left to each of 9 hospitals, and median follow-up of 43.3 months is used to report 5-year survival. The most robust part of that paper is its diagnostic table, which is worth carrying separately: pre-papillectomy forceps biopsy agreed with the papillectomy specimen in 82.1% (300 of 365) of lesions called low-grade dysplasia, 60.3% (35 of 58) called high-grade dysplasia and 91.4% (32 of 35) called adenocarcinoma; of 365 called low-grade, 44 (12.1%) were upgraded after resection, 33 to high-grade dysplasia and 11 to adenocarcinoma. lead: Refer for surgical or expert endoscopic assessment when papillectomy is technically infeasible, including selected lesions >4 cm or intraductal extension >20 mm.
text: Avoid Evidence C Refer for surgical or expert endoscopic assessment when papillectomy is technically infeasible, including selected lesions >4 cm or intraductal extension >20 mm. Why Why ESGE suggests surgical referral on weak, low-quality evidence in these settings. Lesion diameter, intraductal extent and access are distinct considerations; assess 30–40 mm lesions and limited ductal extension individually in an expert centre. Additional cautions Additional cautions The completeness data support the boundary rather than only the opinion, though they are thin: among 58 patients referred for papillectomy, complete resection was achieved in 53 overall (91%) but in only 4 of 5 (80%) with intraductal extension defined by EUS and 4 of 7 (57%) with it defined by ERCP — five and seven patients respectively, so treat the direction as real and the proportions as illustrative. The larger Japanese cohort makes the same point with more patients: where ductal extension was confirmed pathologically, R0 was achieved in only 28 of 137 (20.4%). tied_results: Multicentre cohort: R0 achieved in only 28 of 137 (20.4%) with pathologically confirmed ductal extension

lead: Do not discharge a patient after a papillectomy.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not discharge a patient after a papillectomy. Why Why Enrol every patient in the surveillance schedule at clinical decision 9 before the procedure, and say so at consent. Additional cautions Additional cautions Recurrences occurred out to 9.75 years and nearly half appeared after the first two years in the cohort that looked for them longest, so a two-year follow-up programme is designed to miss them. The caveat that belongs with that figure is that the same cohort required a negative surveillance endoscopy before counting an event, which pushes early residual disease out of the recurrence count and the curve to the right; the ten-year recommendation rests on one patient recurring at 9.75 years. What is not in doubt is that recurrence after a histological R0 is common — 11% at 3 years and 13% at 5 years in 416 R0 patients — so a negative margin is not a discharge criterion. lead: Negative margins, adenoma only — endoscopic surveillance NCCN: patients with ampullary adenoma and negative margins after endoscopic removal should be endoscopically observed.
text: Negative margins, adenoma only — endoscopic surveillance Evidence D NCCN: patients with ampullary adenoma and negative margins after endoscopic removal should be endoscopically observed. Indications Preferred when A complete en bloc resection with clear deep and lateral margins and no invasive component. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Not a discharge. All patients who have had endoscopic removal or surgical ampullectomy need endoscopic surveillance — only pancreatoduodenectomy for adenoma removes the need. lead: Positive margins, adenoma only — endoscopic re-excision NCCN: patients with positive margins after endoscopic removal can be re-excised, or have surgical ampullectomy or pancreatoduodenectomy.
text: Positive margins, adenoma only — endoscopic re-excision Evidence D NCCN: patients with positive margins after endoscopic removal can be re-excised, or have surgical ampullectomy or pancreatoduodenectomy. Indications Preferred when Residual adenoma that is visible and reachable, in a patient who will tolerate repeated procedures. Most non-curative endoscopic resections are salvaged endoscopically. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not re-excise repeatedly in a patient whose malignancy risk score was high to begin with, or where the deep margin rather than the lateral margin is the problem. lead: Invasive adenocarcinoma in the specimen — pancreatoduodenectomy NCCN: where adenocarcinoma is found, pancreatoduodenectomy. Patients who undergo adenoma resection by pancreatoduodenectomy need no surveillance.
text: Invasive adenocarcinoma in the specimen — pancreatoduodenectomy Evidence D NCCN: where adenocarcinoma is found, pancreatoduodenectomy. Patients who undergo adenoma resection by pancreatoduodenectomy need no surveillance. Indications Preferred when An unexpected invasive carcinoma, particularly with a positive deep margin, lymphovascular or perineural invasion or poor differentiation. This is clinical decision 5 from here. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid A papillectomy specimen cannot stage the nodes, and nodal involvement is frequent even in early T stages — so a decision to stop after papillectomy for invasive disease is a decision to accept unknown nodal status. lead: Agree the orientation and the margins with the pathologist before the specimen leaves the room, in writing.
text: Standard Evidence D Agree the orientation and the margins with the pathologist before the specimen leaves the room, in writing. Indications Preferred when Every ampullectomy specimen, endoscopic or surgical. NCCN requires either direct communication between the endoscopist or surgeon and the pathologist, or a clearly documented method on the requisition, marking the deep (radial) margin, the duodenal mucosal margin and any other relevant margin. PERIPAN asks for the size of the invasive carcinoma and the margin status to be reported on ampullectomy specimens, and for the specimen to reach the pathology department fresh and be fixed within about 30 minutes. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not let a non-pathologist open or section the specimen, and do not drop a whole specimen into formalin — PERIPAN says both explicitly. If pathology is unavailable, refrigerate. Evidence & sources An indeterminate margin is not a neutral result. In the 798-patient Japanese cohort an indeterminate Rx margin carried a hazard ratio of 2.38 for recurrence against R0 (95% CI 1.49–3.81; reported as 2.30, 1.44–3.68 in that paper's abstract), close to the 2.95 for a frankly positive margin, and by 5 years cumulative recurrence after Rx and after R1 was the same at 34% — so an unreadable margin behaves like a positive one. Rx accounted for 206 of 798 specimens (25.8%), which makes this the commonest ambiguous result in the whole pathway and one on which ESGE offers no recommendation at all. Orientation failures manufacture indeterminate margins. Note too that margin status in that cohort was assessed locally at 22 centres with no central review and no interobserver data, which is an argument for writing the local method down rather than for discounting the finding. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
tied_results: 798-patient cohort, recurrence vs R0: indeterminate Rx margin HR 2.38 (95% CI 1.49–3.81), R1 HR 2.95; 5-y cumulative recurrence 34% after both Rx and R1 Abstract gives Rx HR 2.30 (1.44–3.68); margins read locally at 22 centres, no central review

lead: Surgical ampullectomy as the intermediate step after a failed endoscopic resection of a benign lesion, at a centre with the expertise — see clinical decision 4.
text: Reasonable Evidence C Surgical ampullectomy as the intermediate step after a failed endoscopic resection of a benign lesion, at a centre with the expertise — see clinical decision 4. Indications Preferred when NCCN places surgical ampullectomy between endoscopic re-excision and pancreatoduodenectomy for positive margins after endoscopic removal, and states that it can be chosen at surgical centres where there is expertise for the technique. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Positive margins after a surgical ampullectomy route the patient on to pancreatoduodenectomy in the same NCCN algorithm, so this is a step that can be spent rather than a destination. Evidence & sources In the European cohort, R0 after transduodenal surgical ampullectomy was 90.5% (57 of 63) against 73.1% (416 of 569) after papillectomy (P=0.001), and for adenoma alone 92.9% (53 of 57) against 80.2% (386 of 481, falling to 65.9% once index-session ablation is counted as a probable R2 resection). Two things qualify the comparison. The surgical arm has 63 patients and 6 cancers, so every surgical subgroup figure rests on single-digit numerators, and the only procedure-related death in the study was in that arm. And advanced cancer was found in 36.6% of the surgical specimens against 10.9% of the endoscopic ones, which says as much about who was selected for surgery as about what surgery achieves. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not record a piecemeal resection as R0.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not record a piecemeal resection as R0. Why Why Call it what it is, and let the surveillance interval and the conversion discussion follow from that. Additional cautions Additional cautions Piecemeal resection independently predicted both late recurrence (odds ratio 6.610, P=0.005) and non-curative resection (5.424, P=0.007), and the margin it leaves cannot be assessed. An R-status assigned to an unassessable margin is the start of an avoidable recurrence. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Transduodenal surgical ampullectomyEXPERTISE NCCN lists surgical ampullectomy for an adenoma with positive margins after endoscopic removal and states it can be chosen at surgical centres where there is expertise for the technique; it does not list it for invasive carcinoma.
text: Transduodenal surgical ampullectomy Evidence D EXPERTISE NCCN lists surgical ampullectomy for an adenoma with positive margins after endoscopic removal and states it can be chosen at surgical centres where there is expertise for the technique; it does not list it for invasive carcinoma. Indications Preferred when A demonstrably benign adenoma that endoscopy cannot clear, in a patient in whom a pancreatoduodenectomy is a disproportionate operation. In the largest comparison — 569 papillectomies against 63 transduodenal ampullectomies drawn from a 1,673-patient European database of 58 centres — R0 was 90.5% against 73.1% (P=0.001), and for adenoma alone 92.9% against 80.2% (P=0.01); recurrence after a histological R0 was 2 of 63 (3.2%) against 82 of 512 (16.0%), P=0.01; severe adverse events were 2 of 63 (3.2%) against 11 of 569 (1.9%), P=0.38. In 62 propensity-matched pairs, R0 was 90.3% against 72.6% (P=0.02), recurrence 3.2% against 8.0% (P=0.07), reinterventions were more frequent after papillectomy, and overall survival was comparable. The burden difference is the one unambiguous finding: median procedure time 227.5 against 30 minutes and median hospital stay 14 against 3 days (both P<0.001). Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Not for invasive carcinoma, and not for an ampullary neuroendocrine tumour. Downgraded to grade D because the comparison that favours this operation is built in a way that favours it. The 62 matched pairs are 98.4% of the eligible surgical patients but only 10.9% of the eligible papillectomy patients, so the surgical arm is its whole population while the endoscopic arm is a 1-in-9 selection chosen to resemble it. Matching omitted intraductal extension, duct dilation and index-session ablation — the variables that most obviously drive both the choice of procedure and the chance of R0 — and intrabiliary extension and duct dilation still differed after matching (21% against 8.1%, P=0.01; 45.2% against 30.6%, P=0.001). Follow-up was 37.5 against 15.5 months after matching (P=0.006) and surveillance was asymmetric, with endoscopic patients routinely re-scoped and biopsied and surgical patients not, so the recurrence comparison is not a like-for-like one and no time-to-event analysis of recurrence is presented. The R0 comparison is between a fragmented endoscopic specimen and an intact surgical one read by local pathologists at 58 centres over 14 years with no central review, which structurally favours surgery. With 63 surgical patients, 6 cancers and 1 against 2 severe adverse events in the matched arms, the safety comparison has no power to detect the morbidity difference that drives the clinical choice. On neuroendocrine tumours, a 14-patient single-institution retrospective series reported R0 in all 8 pancreatoduodenectomy patients against 3 of the 4 transduodenal cases with a reported margin (75%), and nodal involvement in 7 of 8 (88%) after pancreatoduodenectomy against 1 of 6 after transduodenal resection, where nodes were examined in only 1 of the 6, and concluded that the transduodenal approach may provide an inadequate oncological resection and can understage these tumours. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×

lead: Pancreatoduodenectomy for a benign or premalignant lesionEXPERTISE NCCN: if endoscopic removal is not possible, pancreatoduodenectomy can be performed; and patients with positive margins after ampullectomy can go on to pancreatoduodenectomy. Patients who have an adenoma resected by pancreatoduodenectomy do not need surveillance.
text: Pancreatoduodenectomy for a benign or premalignant lesion Evidence C EXPERTISE NCCN: if endoscopic removal is not possible, pancreatoduodenectomy can be performed; and patients with positive margins after ampullectomy can go on to pancreatoduodenectomy. Patients who have an adenoma resected by pancreatoduodenectomy do not need surveillance. Indications Preferred when A high malignancy risk score, repeated failed endoscopic and transduodenal attempts, or Spigelman stage IV polyposis not suitable for endoscopic therapy. In the 127-patient multi-institutional series of non-familial periampullary adenomas taken to pancreatoduodenectomy, 59 (46.4%) proved malignant — so in a selected high-risk group this is often the correct cancer operation performed before the cancer was proven. The authors concede the selection plainly: every patient in that cohort had already been judged to need a Whipple, the true denominator including patients managed endoscopically or by transduodenal resection is unknown, and their own earlier single-centre figure was 29%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not use it as the default for a low-risk adenoma. In that same series the patients at no or low risk of malignancy had more major postoperative complications than the intermediate and high-risk groups, although across the three strata as defined the difference was not significant (51.7%, 27.1% and 29.4%, P=0.11) and reached significance only after the strata were collapsed at a score of 3 and adjusted (odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 1.01–8.6, P=0.047); the published malignancy rates per stratum appear three different ways in the same paper. The quoted morbidity and mortality for pancreatoduodenectomy in ampullary disease are 27%–59% and 2%–10%, and the operation also carries a higher fistula risk here than in non-ampullary disease — clinically relevant fistula in 83 of 310 ampullary resections (26.8%) against 557 of 4,722 non-ampullary (11.8%), odds ratio 2.73 (95% CI 2.09–3.57), on a cross-dataset comparison rather than a within-cohort one. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: Multi-institutional, 127 non-familial adenomas at PD: 59 (46.4%) malignant; major complications 51.7% vs 27.1% vs 29.4%, no/low vs intermediate vs high risk, P=0.11 Selected cohort, all already judged to need a Whipple; true denominator unknown

lead: Pancreas-preserving duodenectomy in familial adenomatous polyposis with uncontrollable benign duodenal disease.
text: Reasonable Evidence D Pancreas-preserving duodenectomy in familial adenomatous polyposis with uncontrollable benign duodenal disease. Indications Preferred when Spigelman stage IV disease without malignancy, where endoscopic therapy can no longer control the duodenum. Pancreatoduodenectomy is the operation when duodenal cancer is present, and an intraoperative frozen section can decide between them when malignancy is in doubt. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Counsel against the morbidity honestly: reported in-hospital morbidity is 49% regardless of indication, with other series at 60%–76%, long-term pancreatitis 16%–21% and exocrine insufficiency 30%–60%, and 30-day mortality from 2% to 29%. Adenomas in the neo-duodenum are eventually found in 50%–78% of patients at a median of 46 to 75 months, so the operation does not end surveillance, and 3 of 47 patients (6.4%) in one series developed adenocarcinoma afterwards at a median of 9.25 years. All of these figures reach this page through a narrative review that reports them as unweighted ranges across series of 6 to 49 patients, with no protocol, no risk-of-bias appraisal and no pooling — use them to frame the conversation, not to quote a number. Evidence & sources There is no long-term evidence that endoscopic therapy reduces cancer risk or prevents this operation. The review that sets this out is blunt about it: across 7 cohort studies published in a decade, totalling 181 polyposis patients, five reported residual or recurrent disease in 78%–100% of non-ampullary and 15%–38% of ampullary disease, one found that stage IV patients downstaged by endoscopic therapy subsequently progressed faster than patients with primary progression, and only one reported duodenal adenocarcinoma after endoscopic therapy at all. Its authors go as far as to suggest it may be time to reconsider the use of endoscopic therapy in these patients. That is why the choice belongs in a multidisciplinary discussion with the patient rather than in an algorithm. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Do not perform a transduodenal ampullectomy for invasive carcinoma in order to avoid a pancreatoduodenectomy.
text: Avoid Evidence C Do not perform a transduodenal ampullectomy for invasive carcinoma in order to avoid a pancreatoduodenectomy. Why Why If the lesion is an invasive adenocarcinoma, the operation is a pancreatoduodenectomy with regional lymphadenectomy — clinical decision 5. Additional cautions Additional cautions It cannot stage the nodes, and nodal status is the dominant prognostic variable: in 313 pathologically re-reviewed ampullary resections, median overall survival was 107.5 months for node-negative against 32 months for node-positive disease (P<0.0001), with 45% node positive on a median of 11 nodes examined. A National Cancer Database analysis of 8,127 resections, cited here from its abstract only because the full text was not obtained, reports lymph node metastasis in 56.7%. NCCN's own summary is that ampullectomy has lower morbidity and mortality but a higher recurrence rate, and the European comparison bears that out at the extreme: of 88 invasive cancers treated endoscopically, R0 was achieved in 30 (34.1%), and endotherapy alone succeeded in 34 of 75 T1a (45.3%) and 5 of 13 T1b cancers (38.5%) — it failed in roughly two-thirds of T1 disease. Evidence & sources Evidence & sources i Evidence & sources Evidence & sources ×
tied_results: NCDB analysis: lymph node metastasis in 56.7% of 8,127 ampullary resections Cited from abstract only; full text not obtained

lead: Pancreatoduodenectomy with standard regional lymphadenectomy, dissecting the SMA margin meticulously and treating margin status as the thing that is actually in your hands.
text: Standard Evidence C Pancreatoduodenectomy with standard regional lymphadenectomy, dissecting the SMA margin meticulously and treating margin status as the thing that is actually in your hands. Indications Preferred when Every resectable invasive ampullary adenocarcinoma. NCCN's goals are an R0 resection with regional nodes, meticulous perivascular dissection as for pancreatic cancer, recognition of the need for venous resection and reconstruction, and intraoperative exclusion of peritoneal, liver and distant nodal disease. Reported 5-year survival after pancreatoduodenectomy for ampullary adenocarcinoma is 32% to 78%, with morbidity 27%–59% and mortality 2%–10%. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not treat the margin as a reporting formality. In 313 ampullary resections, surgical margin positivity correlated with nodal stage (P=0.001). Under the CAP protocol tumour at or within 1 mm of a margin is a positive margin, but NCCN states plainly that this is extrapolated from rectal cancer data and that there is currently a lack of definitive evidence for what constitutes an adequate margin in ampullary resection specimens. NCCN suggests frozen section of the pancreatic neck and bile duct about 5 mm back from the transection to avoid cautery artefact, and further excision to achieve 5 mm of clearance if tumour is within that distance. Evidence & sources Prognostic factors across series are lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, size and stage, ulceration, differentiation, nodal burden and margin status, but the data vary widely. Perineural invasion is the clearest of them in NCCN's own summary: median survival 18.7 against 51.9 months with and without it in 70 patients (P=0.001), and 5-year survival 36.8% against 72.1% in 89 patients (P<0.001). One ampullary-specific operative point from the multi-institutional adjuvant series is worth knowing before consent: ampullary pancreatoduodenectomy carried a higher fistula risk than non-ampullary, with a mean Fistula Risk Score of 4.3 against 3.6 and a soft gland in 73.9% against 52.9% (both P<0.001), and clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula in 83 of 310 (26.8%) against 557 of 4,722 (11.8%), odds ratio 2.73 (95% CI 2.09–3.57) — a comparison made against a separate fistula-study dataset with no matching for era, centre or surgeon, so treat the direction as real and the magnitude as approximate. [EXPERTISE] Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×

lead: Harvest and count the nodes, and report the number involved rather than only node-positive or node-negative.
text: Standard Evidence C Harvest and count the nodes, and report the number involved rather than only node-positive or node-negative. Indications Preferred when Every resection. A National Cancer Database analysis of 8,127 ampullary resections placed the inflection point in the survival hazard at 20 examined nodes and concluded that a minimum of 20 is needed to stratify prognosis and minimise stage migration, with the log-odds nodal classification the most prognostic of the four schemes tested; that paper is cited here from its abstract only, because the full text was not obtained, so the derivation of the threshold cannot be inspected. PERIPAN, finding no ampullary-specific evidence, recommends adhering to the same minimum lymph node yield as for pancreatic cancer — where groups have proposed 11 to 17 as a quality indicator — until better data exist, and recommends revisiting the specimen and submitting more tissue when the count falls short. Contraindications & cautions Caution / avoid Do not read a low count as reassurance, and do not read nodal substaging as a settled gain. In 313 pathologically verified resections the median number of nodes examined was 11, only 150 (48%) had 12 or more, and 45% were node positive overall but 56% among those with 12 or more examined. Substaging by metastatic node number gave median survival of 107.5 months for N0, 40 months for one to two involved nodes and 24.5 months for three or more (P<0.0001), with 5-year survival 62%, 31.5% and 30% and adjusted hazard ratios of 1.6 (95% CI 1.1–2.4) and 1.9 (1.1–3.2), P for trend 0.018 — a modest effect whose lower confidence bounds nearly touch 1. The N1 and N2 5-year estimates are essentially identical, which is the comparison clinicians actually use. AJCC 8th edition uses one to three and four or more as its N1 and N2 boundaries. Evidence & sources Two findings from the full text of that nodal series change how it should be quoted. First, the clean N0-versus-N1 separation does not survive adequate sampling: restricted to the 150 patients with 12 or more nodes examined, median survival was not reached for N0, 74 months for N1 and 29 months for N2 (P=0.02) with 5-year survival 64%, 52% and 38% — the N0 and N1 curves converge, which implies that part of the apparent value of substaging in the whole cohort comes from understaging in the half with fewer than 12 nodes. The authors note the convergence and still recommend the scheme. Second, adjuvant therapy data were not available at all, and node-positive patients are precisely those most likely to have received chemotherapy, so the N1 and N2 hazard ratios are confounded by treatment in an unknown direction. N2 cases were also markedly over-represented at the one institution using a different gross dissection method (26% against 13.5%), so the N1/N2 split is partly a marker of which laboratory handled the specimen. Nodal risk rises steeply with T stage in the series NCCN tabulates — 28.0%, 50.9%, 71.7% and 77.3% for T1 to T4 in one of 450 patients, and 11.3%, 28.4%, 43.8% and 100% in another of 259 — which is also why a papillectomy for invasive disease leaves a real question unanswered. Explanation and evidence i Explanation and evidence Explanation and evidence ×
